ASRS:1791077.n: On initial climb out lost #2 yaw damper followed soon thereafter by a Yellow Pump Lo Press ECAM (Electronic Central Aircraft Monitor). System pressure fluctuated several times from zero to normal, 3000 psi, and finally remained normal throughout approach and landing. Based on prior Yellow system intermittent pressure issues compounded by having Yellow Pump Depressurization Function deferred, elected to return to ZZZ. No [priority handling] declared since system returned to normal pressure. Intermittent hydraulic system failure. Immediately upon takeoff from ZZZ received ECAM for Yellow HYD (Hydraulic) Press Low. Right ECAM showed pressure falling on Yellow system to 0 psi, pressure then began to climb back up and stabilized at 3050 psi. This same sequence happened 3 times in an approximately 2 min window. Due to history with the Yellow HYD system on the previous day ZZZ1-ZZZ leg, we elected to return to ZZZ to have maintenance look at the system.Intermittent failure of the Yellow HYD pump.
ASRS:1791077.s: The crew experienced an intermittent Yellow hydraulic pump failure and yaw damper loss on initial climb, causing pressure to fluctuate between zero and 3000 psi. Due to prior system issues and a deferred maintenance item, they elected to return to ZZZ without declaring an emergency.

ASRS:1791079.n: FL350 we encountered severe turbulence in IMC. Momentary loss of control led to course and altitude deviations about 30 degrees and 500 ft. We likely entered the tops of building convection not seen on radar. Given the scenario it would be tough to identify how we could have avoided the turbulence. A more thorough preflight weather briefing and communication with Dispatch and ATC could have possibly helped.
ASRS:1791079.s: The crew encountered severe turbulence in IMC at FL350, causing momentary loss of control with 30-degree course and 500-foot altitude deviations. The pilot attributed the event to entering unseen convective tops and suggested better preflight weather briefings and communication could have helped.

ASRS:1791092.n: Auto Press 2 failed and cause the cabin pressure to drop which triggered a Dif Press warning. We requested a lower altitude from ATC and were cleared down. We did not have to deviate. Shortly after the decent Auto Press 1 took over and balanced the pressure out.The cause is unknown the aircraft was downed after landing for the same issue.No more broke planes. During FFOD power up, we had a 'auto press 2 fail' status message momentarily but it cleared. I didnt think much of it. Cruising at 33,000 ft. about 40mins away from ZZZ, I felt my ears popping a bit and the cabin rate fluctuating from 0 to -500 fpm (back and forth) and lowering the cabin altitude. We eventually got a diff press warning, I was pilot flying. Cabin pressure was normal. I initially mistakenly called the wrong checklist. The FO (First Officer) request lower, and ATC granted it. By the time we pulled out the Quick Reference Handbook for the emer depress warning, auto press 2 fail status came up and our warning was gone. I guess cpc 2 had failed and auto switched to number 1. We leveled off at 24,000 ft. Masks were never worn and priority handling wasn't requested. I called the FAs (Flight attendants) in the back to see if they noticed anything, they said they didn't. Also, when we put flaps 45 on landing, the rate rapidly dropped to -1,000 fpm and back to 0, which isn't normal. I wrote it up in ZZZ in full detail. We were supposed to keep the plane for a AGS turn. Maintenance deferred auto(cabin) press controller 2. Part of our mel had the crew check the manual controller works. When we did, we had a green advisory message about cabin pressure being greater than 8,000 ft. I was on the phone with the ODP, local Maintenance was there, they were talking to Maintenance Control and Maintenance Operation Director, and we didn't know why that message was there and how to make it go away. We ended up doing a plane swap. We trying all kinds of troubleshooting methods but were not successful.
ASRS:1791092.s: The crew experienced an Auto Press 2 failure at 33,000 ft causing a differential pressure warning, prompting a descent to 24,000 ft where Auto Press 1 took over. Although maintenance deferred the controller, subsequent troubleshooting failed to resolve the issue, resulting in an aircraft swap.

ASRS:1791095.n: The Captain, who is quite experienced, hypothesized that this scenario may have been caused by the movement of fuel while accelerating and climbingIt is not clear whether this scenario is associated with the FCOM1 Ch. 28 NOTE concerning Fuel entering the center tank from the vent system and causing erroneous center tank quantity indications as high as 300 lbs [over takeoff limit].Weight Restricted departure from ZZZ. When Takeoff Performance Data was received, it was noted that prior to Takeoff, fuel quantity must be less than 9652.The Captain briefed that we would taxi out with both engines and APU on, and requested I coordinate with ATC to taxi to a location where we could burn the necessary fuel prior to takeoff.As directed by ATC, we taxied to hold short of Runway XX, and for the next 25 or so minutes burned fuel at this location. Once within approximately 60 lbs of the target 9650, APU was switched off and Captain directed me to advise ATC that we would soon be ready for departure. The Before Takeoff Checklist was completed and fuel verified above MIN FUEL and, at that moment, just 40 lbs above the 9650 maximum fuel for takeoff.We were subsequently cleared for takeoff, and during the acceleration, it was noted that the total FOB was surprisingly increasing by several hundred pounds, and the center tank quantity was increasing. At the moment of rotation, the FOB showed several hundred pounds more than the 9620 we confirmed prior to accepting Takeoff clearance. During initial climb center tank quantity continued to increase up to approximately 200 lbs.If this scenario was related to the FCOM1 NOTE, it would be educational to include this NOTE in the Fuel System CBT Training as a gentle reminder to all.
ASRS:1791095.s: During a weight-restricted departure from ZZZ, the crew burned fuel to meet limits, but total fuel and center tank quantities increased during acceleration and climb. The Captain hypothesized this was caused by fuel movement or vent system issues, resulting in erroneous quantity indications exceeding the takeoff limit.

ASRS:1791110.n: All normal procedures and company checklists accomplished prior to takeoff clearance. Takeoff roll initiated at XA03z on Runway XXL ZZZ. Acceleration and aircraft systems normal through approximately 120 KIAS. At approximately 120 KIAS, EICAS message 'L Hyd Qty' displayed. Captain called the item and stated continue. Normal takeoff continued. Soon after rotation an ever increasing list of EICAS messages began to display. The highest order EICAS message was 'L HYD SYS PRESS' followed by numerous items 'RUDDER RATIO', etc. A quick check of the status page indicated 0 fluid remaining. After takeoff checklist was accomplished. Approach Control was advised we needed to be vectored for a return and that we needed a few minutes to work through the issue. The Captain operated as pilot flying throughout using the autopilot, and took the left comm [radio] while I worked through the multiple non-normal QRH checklists in succession. While working on the completion of non-normal QRH checklists, the Captain notified ATC, and we received vectors for an ILS to RWY XY at ZZZ. Approach and landing checklists were completed, and the aircraft landed without event. Aircraft control on the ground was normal, and aircraft taxied to Gate XX under own power. On takeoff roll around 120 KTS with V1 at 132 KTS EICAS message L Hyd Qty low". Announced 'continue' and elected to continue takeoff believing quantity just needed to be topped off. After liftoff around 400-800 feet master caution "L Hyd press" and associated cautions. Checking status page showed Left Hydraulic quantity 0. Requested runway heading. Completed after takeoff checklist followed by non normal for the loss of Left Hydraulic quantity. Notified ATC and vector for return to ZZZ. Normal landing and taxi back to ramp. After block in, Maintenance found hydraulic fluid covering left outboard wing. discovered left spoiler POV (Positive Overflow Venting) valve had failed resulting in total loss of left hydraulic quantity."
ASRS:1791110.s: The flight crew continued takeoff after a low left hydraulic quantity warning at 120 KIAS, but suffered total system loss shortly after rotation due to a failed spoiler POV valve. They returned to ZZZ for a safe landing, where maintenance confirmed the valve failure caused fluid leakage over the left wing.

ASRS:1791133.n: When arriving at new aircraft, the ground power was connected. The temperature in the back of the plane was stifling - it had to be 95 degrees Fahrenheit in the plane. I told my forward Flight Attendant (FA) and we reported to Captain. Passengers were allowed to board and they immediately began taking off as many clothing layers as possible. FAA and company regulations still require everyone to wear masks, despite CDC warnings that masks should be removed when overheated. As the AFT FA, I am responsible for making announcements in a mask, which is laborious and requires many more breathing pauses than usual. Saying the announcements with a mask, in ridiculous heat is more, exhausting, distracting, and physically concerning. My only focus was being able to breathe and the health of my passengers. I walked to the front of aircraft to get some air, but also to get water for the poor passengers. Thankfully, the plane did cool off in the air, but it was still extremely uncomfortable.Extreme heat conditions on the airplane combined with mandatory mask compliance for passengers and crew caused this event. Crews can be terminated/lose benefits if removing masks on board the aircraft in front of passengers. Until recently, FA's were not required to wear masks while making announcements. Passengers can be fined/lose flight privileges for removing masks. The threat of the FAA fines and penalties under the new federal mask mandate appears to supersede common sense safety practices and concern and care for crews and passengers.Masks, may help prevent viral spread (there is much data to refute those claims), but prevents the passengers and crew to breathe much needed fresh oxygen. The effects of not getting enough oxygen and the potential for hypoxia were ingrained into me during FA training. I am greatly concerned that airlines and the FAA are continuing to put the safety of passengers and crew at risk with mandatory mandates that restrict fresh oxygen, which can cloud judgement and critical thinking abilities. Heat exhaustion and the need for fresh oxygen when wearing masks was acknowledged by the CDC. Of course, the CDC recommended spacing of self 6 feet away, but plane passengers and crew do not have the luxury of a 6 foot distance. Mandatory mask mandates on planes should also come with the ability to tell passengers and crew to remove masks when feeling anxious or stressed or when breathing is compromised. If one feels sick or faint because of heat and a mask, the ability to lower a mask on a plane should be allowed. FAs should be empowered to use their common sense when enforcing masks in extreme heat conditions. The 'appearance of safety' seems to be aviation's new standard of practice rather than 'actual safety' of anyone on board an aircraft. This is a very serious shift in thought for the FAA and airlines. The unintended consequences of these 'appearance of safety' standards are frightening.
ASRS:1791133.s: A Flight Attendant reported extreme heat and breathing difficulties during boarding and pre-flight while wearing a mandatory mask. The reporter attributed the safety concern to the combination of stifling cabin temperatures and FAA mask mandates that prevented crew and passengers from removing masks despite heat exhaustion risks.

ASRS:1791134.n: Upon doing the cabin sweep, I notice [Passenger in] X1 talking on the phone and asked her to turn it off. I only knew she was on the phone because her phone was facing up in her palm and I could see the active phone call with the phone screen. She seemed to act like she was complying, but she was still talking. Her mic for the phone was inside of her mask, so I would never have been able to say she was on the phone had I not seen the phone. I told the forward she was still on the phone.People hide their cell phone microphones in the masks all the time. It is hard to tell when they are actively talking or just singing along to a tune.If it is so hard for me to discern an active phone call is taking place with a passengers face covered, I have to wonder what else people can hide inside a mask that could cause me, fellow passengers, crew or the plane harm. 3D printers can make all kinds of gadgets - including sharp objects - that could hide in a mask, not to mention the possibility of any kind of explosive that could be detonated between the teeth.COVID masks - supposedly are for crew and passenger safety, but these federal masks on airplanes create more safety concerns. I know the masks appear to keep us safe from the dreaded COVID, but the reality is the masks pose a much greater safety risk than COVID. I can't see what people are actually doing (talking on the phone or not). I can't identify a human trafficking victim from any other masked passenger. I can't identify a bad actor hiding in a mask from an innocent one in a mask. I can't smell alcohol, smoke, or even jet fuel when wearing a mask, which is required of me at all times - especially in my jump seat.The ability to do my job as a safety professional on an aircraft is greatly reduced thanks to these mask mandates. I am really surprised that the FAA and airlines care more about the optics of safety than the actual safety on board a plane these days.
ASRS:1791134.s: A flight attendant reported a passenger in seat X1 continued talking on a phone hidden inside a mask during a cabin sweep. The crew member stated that mandatory mask mandates hinder safety monitoring by obscuring visual cues and preventing the detection of potential threats or hazards.

ASRS:1791157.n: After doing a prolonged run up [in] the PA-28 on Runway XX (after having massive avionics upgrades at a shop on the field) we noticed slight elevations in CO (Carbon Monoxide) in the cockpit. 25-40 ppm. My student and I were aware and I said to keep the window open and keep the heat and vents closed (which resolved the issues) and the levels went back down to an acceptable range. After being cleared to depart with a right turn out to the east of the airport the student and I briefed our takeoff and emergency action that would be taken in case of an emergency. A few seconds after rotating I stated feeling symptoms of what I believed to be from the CO. I was going to give the plane to my student so I could open the door for air as he warned me of the sensor reading close to 250 ppm of CO. I got tunnel vision as well and extreme dizziness and headache and told him to open the window, which is in the left side. Fearing we only had seconds before I lost consciousness and that he would be not far behind me I entered into a steep right bank nose lose attitude [received priority] and tried to make it to the intersecting Runway (XX) I was unable to make it to the runway and was able to land on the taxiway. As soon as we stopped I opened the door and then responded to the tower and waited for emergency personnel. A mechanic on the field informed us the next day there was a crack in the exhaust (unsure of the size) in a place I would not have been able to see. I believe my actions were correct both in timing and place of landing.
ASRS:1791157.s: A pilot and student in a PA-28 experienced carbon monoxide poisoning during takeoff due to an undetected exhaust crack. The pilot executed an emergency landing on a taxiway after suffering symptoms and receiving a 250 ppm sensor reading, avoiding a runway landing.

ASRS:1791162.n: I was flying into AWO. The winds favored Runway 29 as they were out of 270 at 10 knots with peak gusts of 21 knots. All aircraft had been landing [Runway] 29 all day. I was making all of my turn calls doing laps in the pattern and noticed that there was an aircraft in the patter behind me. They had no lights on, so I checked my Foreflight running on Sentry to see if they had an ADSB beacon and they did not show up. I made a few calls asking if anyone else was in the pattern and repeatedly made my calls Crosswind, Downwind, Base, and Final all landing Runway 29. I incorrectly assumed that anyone else with common sense would also be landing [Runway] 29 given the strong gusty conditions. On Final approach, out of the corner of my eye, I noticed an aircraft to my left coming in on Runway 34. At AWO there is a hot spot on the final approach where incoming airplanes could converge. We were less than 100 feet off a collision course if evasive action was not taken. The other aircraft made no modifications to their course and I immediately climbed 100 feet to avoid a potential collision. I decided to land long to taxi over and see who was flying the aircraft and under what conditions.The aircraft which had two people inside both wearing headsets. While taxiing past them I called their tail number on the radio and received no response.I believe that whoever was flying the aircraft was intentionally avoiding awareness that they were indeed flying and were doing so in a way that endangered me and others in the area.
ASRS:1791162.s: The pilot reported a near-collision on final approach to Runway 29 at AWO with an aircraft landing on Runway 34 without lights or ADS-B. The pilot climbed 100 feet to avoid the collision, attributing the incident to the other pilot's failure to monitor the radio or acknowledge the runway change.

ASRS:1791182.n: Tower arranged for VFR flight following with ZZZ Departure, transponder code XXXX and a climb to 5,500 feet. I set my altitude alert selector to 5,500 feet. Airborne, I establish contact with ZZZ Departure of my departing altitude and climbing altitude of 5,500 feet. ZZZ cleared me on course to my destination and acknowledge and confirmed my climbing altitude. Shortly thereafter he handed me off to ZZZ1. It was extremely busy and congested, I had to wait several moments before I could establish contact with ATC. My initial contact I stated my departing altitude and climbing to 4,500 feet and not 5,500 feet, ATC did not inform me to notify them of any altitude changes. (realizing my previous transmission with ZZZ Departure I indicated that my cruising altitude would be 5,500 feet which they acknowledged). I stated an incorrect (previously stated to ZZZ Departure climbing to 5,500 feet) altitude that I was climbing to. I immediately tried to correct my climbing altitude with ATC while slowing my climb at approximately 4,800 feet. However, due to radio congestion this took several moments to advise ATC that I was climbing to 5,500 and not 4,500 feet. Due to radio congestion ATC did not receive my correction. ATC was also a little distorted in their communications, later on Controller advised all that could've been possibly due to wearing a COVID mask and [being] shorthanded. ATC informed me of traffic at 5,000 feet on my right side. ATC gave that IFR traffic a turn to the right and shortly thereafter give me a turn to the left. I did not see the traffic visually however I had them on my traffic avoidance system. Once clear of traffic I was given clearance to destinations.
ASRS:1791182.s: The pilot reported a VFR flight following error where they initially told ZZZ1 they were climbing to 4,500 feet instead of the cleared 5,500 feet. Radio congestion and distorted communications prevented the pilot from correcting this mistake before ATC issued traffic avoidance turns for an IFR aircraft at 5,000 feet.

ASRS:1791196.n: I listened to the ATIS and prepared to taxi out for the short flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 in the new to me aircraft. We had come in a few hours earlier and had no adverse radio issues at all. Reviewing the NOTAMs earlier I had filed away that the Tower was on part time status, most likely due to COVID, and would be closing in the afternoon.After startup we called Ground and did not hear a reply. On our arrival they had told us to stay on the Tower frequency, so we tried that one. Still no response and we tried each a few more times.We listened to the ATIS again and noted that it talked about the Tower closing and that it was many hours old. The passenger in the right seat was also a very experienced ATP rated pilot and CFI and he told me 'The Tower is closed'. I remembered that possibility from my NOTAM search earlier in the day and asked him how he knew. He said it was on our Foreflight app and he heard XA30 on the ATIS.That seemed plausible to me, so we reverted to CTAF procedures, announced our taxi on the Tower frequency, and proceeded to Runway XX. I did glance up at the Tower, just in case, and saw no light gun signals but the Tower was soon out of view. Part way to the runway we were intercepted by an airport vehicle and the driver pointed to his radio. I switched our radio to the second nav/com and was able to establish communications with the ATC facility.In retrospect, this was a good example of a display of expectation bias. We fit the facts we were experiencing into the theory we had developed for what was going on and we were mistaken. I knew that when a Tower closes they say so on the ATIS broadcast, but being so old I thought maybe they had just forgotten to do so. We both had XA30 in our minds as the closing time and discussed that it was now XB30, but we missed the fact that on the ATIS and the NOTAM XA30 was the opening time and it was UTC, not local time. The radios worked fine on the way in, they must be working fine now, etc.In reality we were wrong on all accounts and it is a good thing that we were able to establish ATC contact before taking off which would have only complicated things for all.
ASRS:1791196.s: Two pilots in a new aircraft at ZZZ failed to contact ATC due to misinterpreting UTC opening times as local closing times on the ATIS and NOTAMs. An airport vehicle intercepted them during taxi, prompting a radio switch that restored communications before takeoff.

ASRS:1791198.n: Taxi test. Taxied on parking area - turning maneuvers and braking - the wind was light maybe 6 - 8 knots. Took it down the runway 3 times. The last trip down to run-up area could feel wind really pushing me. Decided to return to hangar. Gust caused a steep pitching motion, tried to counter with down to level. But airspeed had dropped and stalled -landing on hard on side of runway. No injury. Had to shut ELT off. One of the pilots called them to tell everything was OK. [Another pilot] told me the wind picked up suddenly and gusting to more than 22 knots also one witness observed it. [A local pilot] that came out wondering if my ELT was transmitting. I told him I had turned it off. Center had called him to investigate it. He called them and told them everything was OK.
ASRS:1791198.s: During a taxi test, a pilot experienced a sudden wind gust exceeding 22 knots that caused a stall and a hard landing on the runway side. The incident resulted in no injuries but triggered the ELT, which the pilot subsequently deactivated after confirming safety with witnesses and ATC.

ASRS:1791228.n: We encountered moderate, approaching severe turbulence at 39,000 feet. There was was a SIGMET for the area to our south for turbulence 32,000 feet to 40,000 feet, I requested 30,000 feet and received clearance to 30,000 feet. We began a descent and the turbulence stopped completely at 38,500 feet. I slowed the descent and requested 36,000 feet. We had no response and continued a slow descent. PANZ then queried if we were still descending to 30,000 feet. I asked again for 36,000 feet and we were cleared to 36,000 feet. At 34,500 feet we began a climb to 36,000 feet. About that time ATC contacted us on VHF and clarified why we were descending so slowly. I responded that I made 2 requests for 36,000 feet and also tried on VHF. There is a VHF dead zone of about 180 miles between 2 remote transmitters and we were unable to make contact at the initial descent.
ASRS:1791228.s: The flight crew encountered turbulence at 39,000 feet and requested a descent to 30,000 feet, later asking to stop at 36,000 feet. Due to an 180-mile VHF dead zone, initial requests were not heard, causing a communication delay with ATC before the crew was cleared to 36,000 feet.

ASRS:1791268.n: I was pilot monitoring on this flight. ATC was giving us vectors for a visual approach to RWY XX at ZZZ. We were at 2,000 feet on a right base between waypoints ZZZZZ and ZZZZZ1 (1,500 feet MSL) when we told Approach we had the airport in sight. We were cleared for the visual and told to contact Tower. I said 'glide slope alive' and the First Officer asked for gear down flaps 15. I looked down to select the Tower frequency (which I didn't have preselected) and told them we were on the visual for RWY XX. We were cleared to land. When I saw we were capturing the localizer I noticed that the glide slope was now full scale deflection (low). The First Officer had selected a lower altitude (1,100 feet) on the MCP without telling me and so we were below the final approach fix altitude of 1,500 feet at ZZZZZ1. I called for a go around and we were vectored back around for a successful landing. The cause was a long flight across the country with last minute vectors to final for a visual approach led to the First Officer thinking we were high nearing the FAF and incorrectly setting an altitude lower than glideslope intercept altitude without verbally advising the Captain.
ASRS:1791268.s: The Pilot Monitoring and First Officer experienced a glide slope deviation during a visual approach to RWY XX at ZZZ. The First Officer incorrectly set a lower MCP altitude without verbal coordination, causing the aircraft to drop below the final approach fix altitude and necessitating a go-around.

ASRS:1791270.n: I, the First Officer, executed the charted Visual Approach. Landing was uneventful and rolled to taxiway Tango before passing controls to the Captain to taxi to gate. As we exited the runway Tower gave taxi instructions to the gate. and to '... stay with me'. I read back the taxi instructions and the Captain repeated them as he commenced taxi from the runway and stated 'flaps up'. I then commenced my after landing flow, raised the flaps, checked speed brakes stowed, autobrakes off, flight directors off, wing lights off, steady and strobe to steady, trimmed to 5 units, check weather radar off, cycled ramp (though not needed) to active in VHF2, and started removing flight pertinent printer strips. By this time we were somewhere near the Bravo, Golf, Sierra taxiway junction. I briefly looked up as Captain stated, 'There's Golf'. I don't remember what I heard exactly that caused me to look up again, some reference to Golf taxiway perhaps. But when I looked up I did not recognize where we were. I saw lighted taxi signs for Sierra, Golf, and Bravo in the distance to the left. I could see blue taxiway edge lights all around but nothing in front of us. The blue taxi edge lights were very disorienting especially without a lit taxi center line. Our taxi and turnoff lights were so dim that they were essentially useless. The moon was providing more light than they were. On my IPAD I could see our own ship, we were on Golf but heading the wrong way. The Captain had turned right instead of left. At that point he turned left in an attempt to get back to Alpha taxiway, I assume. He did make me aware that he was concerned about accidentally crossing on to the runway. Due to the very poor lighting and the sea of blue taxi edge lights, taxiway was difficult to discern from anything else. All you could see was directional taxi signs in the darkness and blue taxi lights scattered about. The Captain turned left until there was a break in the blue lights with the Bravo sign visible just a little further away so it did appear as though we were turning on taxiway Bravo though I could see no yellow line. I told him I didn't see the taxiway, I think we're going in to no man's land, and Captain said, no, we're on Golf, there's the sign for Bravo. I was confused about the blue lights, they didn't seem to be oriented right and the our ship was sort of on Golf but pivoting so I allowed the events to progress thinking maybe I was just disoriented. When we proceeded ahead the ground before us was just dark. Really no discernible features except for blue taxi lights up ahead that seemed to mark the edge of Bravo. I said I think we're off the taxiway. Captain stopped. We exchanged thoughts on the best way to proceed from that point. We called tower to confess. Tower took a look, said we were just near Bravo, or Golf, I can't remember exactly but he was not concerned which taxiway we ended up needing to get to the gate. I thought we might not be on prepared surface but the Captain was sure we were still on the taxiway just facing the wrong direction. So I told him clear to the right, let's turn all the way back around and take Bravo. The Captain turned tight right and proceeded back the way we came. The jet stopped and thinking it was an incline the Captain added power and we rolled back on taxiway center, turned left on Bravo, took Foxtrot then Alpha to the gate, tower then stated, 'Not a problem guys, the snow plows do more damage than you'. No other occurrences from then on. We did discuss the possibility that we may have left the taxiway. The Captain was confident we had not and I was inclined to believe him since I could not see the ground beneath us, we were just avoiding taxi edge lights. I told him I would check and do an external walk around once we shut down. During deplaning maintenance met me before walking out. She asked me if the landing was rough and I said, actually, no, the landing was great... WHY? She showed me a shot on her cell phone of our nose strut and this is your nose gear. It was covered with dirt. I went down to look at it and it was dirty but both tires were still intact at that point and I saw no evidence of anything else on the mains or the engines. The mains were spotless, engines were clean. I came back up, told the Captain the mains were covered in dirt on the tires and on the lowermost part of the strut. I then stepped out of the cockpit while he talked to maintenance. We turned the plane over to maintenance, they said they would check out the gear and clean it off and we left, still not sure we actually left the taxiway. The wind was blowing in excess of 30 knots and dirt was blowing all over. We chalked it up to that.It was dark, really dark on that end of the airport. The taxiways are a conglomeration that looks more like spaghetti. The whole area is labeled HS1, for good reason. They are difficult enough to navigate in daylight, much less at night with no centerline lighting, a plethora of edge lights all outlining various 'islands' on the field, taxiway ID and directional signs for every taxiway that intersects in HS1 and a useless taxi light. That is a lot of scattered lights with no reliable taxi light to help gauge distance. The Captain was disoriented. Golf taxiway is constructed right on the curve at a 45 degree angle. The directional sign at night can make the left turn on Golf easy to miss especially with the opposite direction of Golf being directly in front of you. I, the First Officer was task distracted. I was performing after landing flow and cockpit cleanup. The Captain had told me during this trip that he was once based in [the area] and was very familiar with this airport, not to mention he was a check airman. My guard was down and I was not as diligent as I normally am during the taxi operation. Being tired and expectation bias. It was night, the end of the day in serious winds. The Captain and I were exhausted most of our mental energy on planning the approach and landing given the conditions that night. The approach was not exactly a standard one we do all the time, and we were not landing on the usual runway you get at this airport. A better taxi light would have alleviated much of the confusion. The lights are not adequate. Neither of us was really sure that we ever left the taxiway. Taxiway centerline lights. There are many islands outlined in blue and no green center lights to actually show the trail through the maze of them. Distance judging is difficult in the dark and it was dark for us. Those lights would have helped. I should have stayed more engaged in the taxi phase to back up my Captain. Getting lost is going to happen and there are two of us for a reason. I allowed myself to get disoriented as well. Landed Runway 31 LGA. Cleared at taxiway T. ATC gave us T;B;G;A to gate. Turned right on Taxiway G instead of left. Area was extremely dark, appeared to taxi over some Foreign Object and Debris (FOD) on taxiway G. After arriving at gate was informed one nose tire was flat. The area around taxiway G is confusing, especially at night. The area is not marked well and very dark making it extremely hard to find correct taxiway. Light up the area better. Better taxiway designations. Area should be redesigned.
ASRS:1791270.s: The First Officer and Captain of a jet taxiing at night at LGA turned right instead of left on Taxiway Golf due to poor lighting and disorientation. They likely left the paved surface, resulting in a flat nose tire and dirt on the gear, attributed to inadequate taxiway illumination and crew fatigue.

ASRS:1791286.n: ATIS reported active Runway 28 with winds 300 at 23 kts gusting to 37 kts and potential for low level windshear and light snow. Prior to push, the First Officer briefed performance data departure brief for windshear with engine anti-ice on, Runway 28 with less than 1/8 in. wet snow. Captain directed deice type 1 given a break in the light snow and increased visibility while awaiting push. Aircraft pushed back onto deice pad, type 1 was applied, ground crews confirmed clean aircraft surfaces, and engine starts were completed. Ground Control provided initial taxi instructions 'Taxi Runway 28 via Alpha, cleared cross Runway 33'. After making the left hand turn from Quebec to Alpha taxiway, Ground Control informed us of a wind shift from 300 to 320 degrees, a 27 kts. crosswind for planned Runway 28 departure, and offered Runway 33 instead. We accepted the Runway change given the nearly 40 kts. gust aligned with Runway 33.Captain elected to continue taxiing on Alpha given the concern of additional snow, while the First Officer completed the Runway change in the FMS and briefed the updated departure heading of 330. Approaching the intersection of Alpha and Mike taxiways Ground Control directed 'Taxi M, cross Runway 28'. Remembering the initial taxi instruction of Alpha cross Runway 33, the Captain mistakenly continued straight instead of turning right on M, leading to a Runway incursion on Runway 33. The First Officer was distracted in verifying all Runway change steps had been completed and did not recognize the error until holding short of Runway 28 on Alpha. The First Officer called tower and reported position, at which point crew reoriented, finished the Runway change discussion, and departed Runway 33 without issue. The root cause was misapplication of previous taxi clearance by the Captain, combined with insufficient First Officer backup due to the Runway change tasks. I would suggest adding the intersection of Mike and Alpha taxiways as a potential hot spot worth pre briefing prior to push back. Stopping the aircraft on Alpha to complete all necessary Runway change steps and briefings would have allowed the First Officer to be more proactive with taxi instructions. After receiving Type I deicing we called ground for taxi. Winds were very strong and ATIS advised ILS in use to Runway 28 and Runway 28 for departure. This was briefed and expected. Ground Control cleared us to taxi from the ramp to Runway 28 via Alpha, cleared to cross Runway 33. Halfway down taxiway Alpha, ground gave new winds and offered Rwy 33 for departure. It was a 27 knots crosswind for Runway 28 so we accepted. New taxi instructions were taxi to Runway 33 via M, cleared to cross Runway 28.There was no SID to change or rebrief so I slowed the jet while the First Officer ran the numbers, changed the runway in the FMS and greened up the speeds which were the same. This all occurred before the missed right turn on taxiway Mike. I turned on the turnoff lights and said, clear left, clear to cross, lights are on and rolled across Runway 33. Approaching the end of Alpha, we switched to tower frequency and was asked our position. We said we were about to make the turn onto Lima, short of Runway 33. The error was brought to our attention. We advised we were holding short of Runway 33 at Lima and we were ready for departure. We were cleared for Take-off, with no further dialog regarding the error. Runway 33 was not closed but it was not the active runway and we followed our original taxi instructions.There were several things going on that contributed to the error. De-icing and holdover considerations, wind shear advisories in effect forcing non-standard takeoff procedures and a late runway change with taxi instructions similar to the original. Failure of both pilots following along the 10-9 chart at night with blowing snow.We reviewed the expected taxi route from the ramp to the expected departure Runway (28). There were no Hot Spots to brief and getting there via Alpha is very simple. I think we could benefit from a Hot Spots circle and reference on the 10-9 chart here in SYR. We may have felt a little rushed as we blocked out late and were trying to get airborne before the snow started again.
ASRS:1791286.s: The flight crew experienced a runway incursion on Runway 33 while taxiing to Runway 28 after accepting a late runway change due to high winds. The Captain mistakenly followed the original clearance instead of the new instruction to turn onto Taxiway Mike, compounded by the First Officer's distraction with FMS updates and poor chart monitoring in blowing snow.

ASRS:1791302.n: The flight was cruising at 35,000 ft. (FL350) in Instrument Meteorological Conditions (IMC). The flight attendants had been briefed earlier about turbulence along the route of flight. When the turbulence became constant moderate, the flight attendants were informed via the public address (PA) system to 'take their seats.' The flight was deviating around weather and needed a left deviation and attempted request a deviation from ATC, however, due to frequency congestion this was causing a delay in deviation. The Captain executed the deviation out of safety (emergency authority) and had the First Officer announce the deviation to ATC, not long after the deviation severe turbulence was encountered lasting approximately one minute. The aircraft was out of control with large airspeed, attitude, and altitude deviations. The severe turbulence caused a 500 foot altitude deviation (35,500 ft.) which triggered a TCAS alert. All automation disconnected in the turbulence and the Captain assumed manual flight control. The second aircraft was acquired visually, and the Captain manually maneuvered to regain control, avoid the aircraft, and return to 35,000 ft. Once clear of the turbulence, the auto-throttles and autopilot were re-engaged, and ATC informed about the location and magnitude of the severe turbulence. The First Officer was tasked to check on the status of the flight attendants and passengers. There were no flight attendant or passenger injuries. Both during flight and upon landing, Maintenance Control, Dispatch, and Operations was kept informed of the severe turbulence encounter along with crew and passenger status. A combination of active weather with turbulence across much of the central United States, high workload environment, saturated ATC frequencies.One cannot control the weather, gather as much information as possible about the route and possible threats along the way.
ASRS:1791302.s: The crew encountered severe turbulence while deviating from weather at FL350, causing automation disconnects, a 500-foot altitude deviation, and a TCAS alert. The Captain manually maneuvered to avoid a nearby aircraft and regain control, resulting in no injuries despite high workload and frequency congestion.

ASRS:1791338.n: Upon door closure Flight Attendant Y came up to me and informed me she was having problems with a passenger who is refusing to put his mask on. I told her I would go to the back while she checked the doors for me. I went to handle the passenger and she did closed doors and made the announcement. We both said cabin secure. I noticed the flight deck door was closed and had assumed she had done cabin secure for me seeing as I was tending to this passenger and she had done door closure for me. I continued on with the safety briefing. Approximately one minute into the safety briefing the Captain opened the flight deck door to inform me that no one informed him of cabin secure. Me and Flight Attendant X both became aware that we had assumed the other person had secured the cabin door and quickly re-secured the cabin. We continued on with our briefing.I believe we both made the mistake because of the destructive passenger. I had assumed that while I was tending to this passenger she had took over all of my duties and she assumed that I was going to finish my duties once I got back up into the gallery. I also believe the pilots close the door on their own to keep warm which is why we had gotten confused on the door being close.
ASRS:1791338.s: During pre-flight, the First Officer and Flight Attendant Y failed to verbally confirm cabin secure while managing a disruptive passenger, leading the Captain to open the flight deck door. The crew attributed the error to miscommunication caused by the passenger and confusion over the flight deck door being closed for warmth.

ASRS:1791363.n: My student and I were returning to the home airport from the local practice area after a training flight. Since this was the student's 2nd training flight, I was explaining the correct traffic pattern entry and radio calls to him. I made the initial radio call 10 miles away from the airport and stated location, altitude and intentions. A short time later, a Mooney checked on to the CTAF and announced his location and intentions. I noted to myself that the Mooney was near us, but behind and decided to be vigilant. The wind favored landings on Runway XX that day, which meant that we would have to fly from the practice area to the northwest of the airport to an area southwest of the airport in order to make the 45 degree entry to the right traffic. I was a bit concerned as the student and I were flying in a Cessna 150 which is very slow and was worried about being overtaken by the faster Mooney as we both set up for the traffic pattern entry. I made my next radio call at a location approximately 4-5 miles northwest of the airport and stated that we intended to maneuver for the 45 degree entry to the traffic pattern. I also directed the student to descend to traffic pattern altitude. I continued to visually scan for the Mooney. Since I expected the Mooney to overtake us and since the right of way rules state that overtaking aircraft should pass on the right, I spent most of my time searching on our right. The pilot of the Mooney made a radio call and stated a position and distance from the airport that was very similar to ours. I became even more concerned about the possibility for a collision and made an additional radio call with our revised position and stated that we were in a Cessna 150, in an attempt to inform the Mooney pilot of our speed and the possibility for collision. The pilot of the Mooney made another radio call and stated his position, which was very similar to ours, 5 miles west of the airport. I became very concerned about the situation and began to aggressively scan for them. I didn't feel that it would be appropriate to divert towards the airport, as it would cause me to conflict with the traffic pattern. I also didn't feel that it would be appropriate to divert away from the airport, as I expected the Mooney to pass on the right. A very short time later, the Mooney passed by us on our left and slightly above us. It appeared to me that we were vertically separated by less than 200 feet and laterally separated by less than 200 feet.I realized after the fact, that I had allowed myself to continue into the possibility of a collision because I felt I had the right of way as the slower aircraft and because I did not want to cause my student an undue expense of maneuvering away from the airport. I noted that the other pilot made three radio calls that expressed essentially the same position and distance from the airport, yet I made no attempt to escape the situation. In the future, I will be more aggressive about maneuvering out of or away from potential traffic pattern conflicts.
ASRS:1791363.s: A Cessna 150 instructor and student experienced a near mid-air collision with a Mooney while approaching the traffic pattern. The incident occurred because the instructor relied on right-of-way rules and failed to maneuver despite similar position reports, resulting in less than 200 feet of vertical and lateral separation.

ASRS:1791376.n: In my aircraft (Aircraft X) I was positioned at the approach end but off Runway XX at ZZZ Airport, in preparation for taking Runway XX for my second takeoff of the morning. An aircraft (Aircraft Y) with a male voice pilot called inbound for Runway XY. Shortly, a female voice pilot in a Hawker aircraft (Aircraft Z) called 10 miles out for Runway XX. I radioed and advised I would wait for landing traffic Runway XY. Then, Aircraft Z called her turn to base for Runway XX. Shortly, Aircraft Y radioed he was on a 5 mile approach for Runway XY. I visually saw the incoming Aircraft Z on final approach for Runway XX at the same time she called final for Runway XX. The pilot of Aircraft Y radioed he would change to downwind for Runway XX. Aircraft Z passed visually by me as I was perpendicular to the Runway XX. I watched her land, complete her taxi and turnoff off the runway on XX taxiway, about midfield, when she called clear of Runway XX. I checked to my sides and scanned for Aircraft Y, but did not see that aircraft. I felt that with the passage of time that occurred Aircraft Y was downwind Runway XX and behind my field of vision. I called taking Runway XX with a left turnout to leave the area. I rolled, lifted off, maintained Runway XX heading for 3/4 to 1 mile, then turned left while continuing to climb. Then I heard the pilot of Aircraft Y say an aircraft just crossed under him. I looked back and saw his aircraft above, perpendicular to and ahead of my flight path. I radioed that I had just departed Runway XX having given a prior announcement that I was making a left turnout and that I thought he was much further downwind. He repeated that I crossed underneath him. I said I was sorry, but that I calculated him much further downwind based upon his call of change to downwind [Runway] XX. There was no other comment from either of us.
ASRS:1791376.s: The pilot of Aircraft X departed Runway XX at ZZZ Airport while Aircraft Y was on downwind, resulting in Aircraft X crossing beneath Aircraft Y. The reporter attributed the near-miss to misjudging Aircraft Y's position based on its radio call to change to downwind.

ASRS:1791392.n: I had to repeat control instructions because the pilot didn't understand what I said because I'm wearing a mask while controlling aircraft.Wearing masks while working traffic is not safe. I thought we were for safety first. The positions are socially distanced so requiring us to wear masks in addition is not safe, nor is it necessary for the health of others. This mandate is not following the science and is unsafe for the control of air traffic.
ASRS:1791392.s: An air traffic controller reported that a pilot failed to understand instructions due to the controller wearing a mask. The controller stated that the mask mandate is unsafe for air traffic control operations and unnecessary given social distancing measures.

ASRS:1791396.n: We recently received a mandate to wear masks on position and I have been complying with that, however the masks cause my glasses to fog up. This is a problem with all the FAA issued masks, and the disposable masks. There are no masks that don't cause my glasses to fog up. I have tried the tape tricks and all the bending and positioning tricks that I can think of and my glasses still fog up.Since the FAA has mandated this, it has been a problem.Essentially, the FAA is asking me to void my medical every time I am on position. If I do not wear my glasses, my medical is invalid. Having fogged up glasses is like not wearing them at all, as far as vision goes.Allow us to take our masks off on position. That would fix the problem.
ASRS:1791396.s: An air traffic controller reported that FAA-mandated masks cause their glasses to fog up, rendering vision impaired and effectively voiding their medical certificate while on position. The controller requested permission to remove masks on position to resolve this safety issue.

ASRS:1791460.n: During climb out, upon reaching 7,000 feet, I noticed smoke in the cockpit. At that time, I performed the memory items associated with that issue. I then relayed to Approach that we would be leveling off at 7,000 feet and requested direct 'ZZZZZ' [intersection] for the RNAV XX back in ZZZ. We also relayed that we were experiencing smoke in the cockpit. After coordination with ZZZ1 Approach, ZZZ OPS and the ZZZ Airport OPS we returned to the field without incident. We were met by the applicable trucks and rescue staff at our pre-planned point. We then did an emergency evacuation, per the checklist. I believe there was an electrical issue in the Captain's circuit breakers.
ASRS:1791460.s: During climb out at 7,000 feet, the pilot encountered cockpit smoke, suspected an electrical issue in the Captain's circuit breakers, and returned to the field. The crew performed an emergency evacuation upon landing, where they were met by rescue staff without incident.

ASRS:1791483.n: IAS Disagree followed shortly by a ALT Disagree, autopilot disconnect. Complied with IAS Disagree Quick Reference Handbook. Informed ATC would not accept a descend via clearance or airspeed closing restrictions. Let them know we would slow and configure early to determine safety. At some point before doing the normal descent checklist the Engine Electronic Controls (EECs) went into ALT. We discovered this during annunciation test because there was no Master Caution, only ENG light during test and then looking at overhead (this system is archaic). The IAS and ALT Disagrees were intermittent even with EECs in ALT continuously. Landing uneventful. Informed Maintenance Manager, [local] Maintenance and submitted a report. Captain standby, ground speed and ATC ground speeds were close while First Officer's Airspeed and Alt appeared inaccurate. First Officer ran QRH - good job. Captain flew and communicated with ATC.
ASRS:1791483.s: The crew experienced intermittent IAS and ALT disagrees causing an autopilot disconnect and EECs switching to ALT mode during descent. The First Officer executed the QRH while the Captain flew the aircraft to an uneventful landing after informing ATC of the inability to accept speed restrictions.

ASRS:1791485.n: On final at the final approach fix for Runway XXR at 170 knots we configured aircraft with gear and final flaps of 25. We received and EICAS message of TE Flap Disagree", the flap indicator was between 20 and 25. We evaluated the situation and discussed how the go around would be executed, then informed ATC and performed a go around without flap retraction not exceeding 137 KTS. We successfully ran the QRH and were vectored back to [Runway] XXC to an uneventful landing with a reference speed of 127 KTS and taxied to the gate. We notified ATC knowing we would be in a non-normal landing configuration. Emergency vehicles were not requested but present for the landing." On Runway XXR at the final approach fix at 170 KTS we configured aircraft with gear and final flaps 25. We received an EICAS message of TE FLAP DISAGREE" the flap indicator read between 20 and 25 degrees. We evaluated the situation, discussed how the go around would be performed not exceeding 137 KTS. While being vectored back to land we ran QRH successfully and were vectored back to [Runway] XXC to an uneventful landing with a reference speed of 127 KTS and taxied to park. We did notify ATC knowing that we would be in an abnormal flap configuration. Emergency vehicles were not requested but present."
ASRS:1791485.s: Pilots on final approach for Runway XXR at 170 knots received a TE Flap Disagree EICAS message with flaps between 20 and 25 degrees. They executed a go-around at 137 knots, completed the QRH, and landed uneventfully on Runway XXC in the abnormal configuration with emergency vehicles present.

ASRS:1791495.n: Crew sent ACARS and called on Satcom with high temp on #10 brake. Maintenance Control conferenced in on Satcom. Temp cooled after lowering gear. Duty Officer also talked to crew. Crew decided to [advise ATC] to have trucks standing by in case of [brake] overheat or fire. Jet landed no event.
ASRS:1791495.s: The crew reported a high temperature on brake #10, which cooled after lowering the gear. They advised ATC to have trucks standing by for potential fire, and the jet landed with no event.

ASRS:1791496.n: Notice the flight did a missed approach. Sent [Name] on ATC desk a teams message asking if he was aware of any issue since no ACARS was sent. Name checked and found out they [advised ATC] due to a flap issue and requested Runway XX.Maintenance issue with flap caused this issue.This was a mechanical issue with Aircraft X.
ASRS:1791496.s: The flight crew executed a missed approach on Aircraft X due to a mechanical flap issue. They advised ATC of the problem and requested Runway XX, with no ACARS message initially sent.

ASRS:1791555.n: I am a private pilot, multi-engine student. I was working with my instructor on a variety of things that morning in the practice area. We came back to the airport and proceeded to perform some touch and go landings on Runway XX, left traffic. We performed two touch and go landings, then a full stop landing. We taxied back and performed two more touch and go landings before the tower asked us to switch to right traffic (five landings in total). On downwind, the nose gear light didn't come on immediately. The hydraulic lever would kick back telling us it was pressurized and I had visual confirmation that the front gear was down.We performed three more touch and go landings to do our best to confirm that the gear was down and locked. I recall the nose gear light would flicker from time to time. We performed the checklist items accordingly but could not get the nose light to stay on when extending the gear. Every time the hydraulic gear lever would return to neutral and the gear was visible in the mirror. My instructor requested to the tower that we switch to the non active Runway (XY) so that he could land and get out to see what was going on with the gear. With the instructor flying, he chose to feather the left engine after the gear was lowered. No flaps were used. Upon landing, he shutdown the right engine. The plane initially acted normal but started to veer to the right as we continued down the runway. I could feel that he had very little directional control. He also has no brakes on the right seat position so he yelled 'left brake!, left brake!' I pushed the left brake as hard as I could and the plane turned left enough to stay on the runway, however shortly thereafter the nose gear collapsed. We skidded to a stop, shut everything down and exited the plane. The right engine hadn't stopped in time so the prop was damaged from contacting the runway. The left engine was feathered so there didn't appear to be any damage to it. The plane was removed from the non active runway and brought back to the hangar. I have no idea what we could have done differently as we had hydraulic pressure and visual confirmation that the gear was down (bad switch?). The previous touch and go landings were fine with no adverse steering issues. Perhaps the nose gear wasn't getting a lot of contact during the touch and goes but I still had directional control prior to him landing. Feathering the left engine obviously saved that from damage. The intent was to only gently land and inspect prior to taxing back to the hangar, but due to other circumstances the plane veered right, was corrected with left brake and the nose gear still ended up collapsing.
ASRS:1791555.s: A private pilot and instructor in a multi-engine aircraft experienced a nose gear collapse during a full-stop landing on a non-active runway after the nose gear indicator light failed. The aircraft veered right due to limited directional control, requiring left brake application, which resulted in the gear collapsing and right propeller damage despite visual confirmation of gear extension.

ASRS:1791565.n: During a routine training session of multi-engine student instruction on DATE, we experienced nose gear indication problems which terminated with a collapsed nose gear and right engine/propeller damage.Numerous maneuvers had been performed involving several landing gear extension retraction cycles, and 5 takeoffs and landings, all normal until last 3 patterns during which nose gear initially showed locked then unsafe. Several touch and go landings(3) were performed during which we attempted to lightly touch nose wheel to move into locked position and get the safe indication. Some of those attempts were firm enough to confirm gear was actually down and locked. Landing gear hydraulic lever had returned to center and gear was visible in mirror every time. Checklist items for a single light out, handle returning to neutral, gear warning horn active was followed and in addition three touchdown taps indicated to me gear was extended. Discussed with student all actions and elected to land on Runway XY instead of active [Runway] XX so we could land, roll out gently, stop, and shut down so I could visually inspect the gear. After we were cleared to land on Runway XY I feathered left engine on base, continued approach, conducted gump's and final checks. As main gear contacted runaway I pulled mixture on number two engine and although initial touchdown was normal, aircraft began a slight yaw to the right along with some unusual noise like rubbing or scuffing. Felt similar to right main tire going flat quickly followed by greatly increasing yaw, much worse than a flat tire. We applied left full rudder pedal but yaw was increasing dramatically aircraft was nearly 30 degrees to centerline and about to leave runway. As there are no wheel brakes on my side of aircraft so I loudly instructed student 'left break, left break, left brake, left brake 'which he did, straightening out aircraft parallel to centerline approximately 6 ft. from edge of runway. Shortly after this nose gear collapsed and remaining 1 to 200 ft. of runway was done on the nose of the aircraft and the main gear. Once stopped, we shut off master, generators, avionics, fuel and vacated aircraft. Myers aviation removed airplane and put in our hanger. Upon inspection and disassembly it was discovered that nose wheel was turned past the stops to the right, tire scuff marks, and hydraulic actuator bent 90deg in fully extended position most likely due to excessive side load. Upper drag link assembly tubing cracked, separated, other parts bent or damaged and all located except one turn limit stop pin.
ASRS:1791565.s: During a multi-engine training session, the instructor and student experienced a nose gear collapse and right engine damage after repeated gear cycles and touch-and-go landings. Post-incident inspection revealed the nose wheel was turned past stops, causing excessive side loads that bent the hydraulic actuator and cracked the drag link assembly.

ASRS:1791572.n: While training a student pilot in ground reference maneuvers and lazy eights, we suffered a complete loss of power. engine restart procedures were executed and were unsuccessful. Our area of operation is in a humid coastal area. We are well versed in the use of carb heat and many times it is on for most of the flight. It was on continually this day. The area that we use for this training has many good hay meadows and pastures to complete a forced landing. Our landing was very good and we were able to land our Piper j3 with no damage or injuries whatsoever. We used less than 1/2 of the field to execute the forced landing.After the landing and securing the aircraft it was noticed that we had several areas below the carburetor where fuel was continually dripping out of the airbox in substantial amounts. We assumed the carb float was stuck and flooded the engine out.After disassembly of the Stromberg carburetor in the shop we found a good amount of small gray beads and flakes in the float bowl that could be easily crushed into a powder. one of these beads was lodged in the carburetor main fuel jet cutting off the fuel flow to the carburetor venturi. In maintenance during the [previous] annual the carburetor fuel bowl plug was removed and the fuel that was captured was visually inspected for contaminates. There were none. during an inspection of the disassembled carburetor after the forced landing it was found that this drain is not the lowest point in the fuel bowl and the only way to really be sure that all of these contaminates are out is to disassemble the carburetor. We also checked the carb fuel screen and it was clean. The gascolator had a small amount of what appeared to be rust and aluminum flakes in it but not enough to cause any issue. We purchased a lead test kit and tested the gray particles from the float bowl. They were found to be lead. We have been running nothing but locally sourced 100LL fuel for the past year. This event seemed to be a big enough deal that it was worth sharing to possibly prevent others from suffering a forced landing due to a similar issue.
ASRS:1791572.s: A student and instructor in a Piper J3 experienced a complete power loss during training due to lead particles clogging the carburetor jet. They executed a successful forced landing with no injuries, later discovering the contamination originated from the fuel system despite prior inspections.

ASRS:1791578.n: End of Course Check for Private [license]. We were on left base while a Yak aircraft was right base. Yak was cleared number 2 cleared to land. We started turn to final early just to create spacing from the YAK. At that time the Yak also started his turn to final. We had visual on him until about 1/2 mile final when we lifted our high wing. After that he was above us. I told the student to conduct a Go Around and sidestep to the left since the traffic was on top of us. The tower asked the Yak once he landed if he ever saw us. He responded with no he was cleared to land.
ASRS:1791578.s: A student pilot conducting a Private license check on left base executed a go-around after a Yak aircraft on right base climbed above them during the final approach. The Yak pilot, who was cleared to land, reported never seeing the student's aircraft.

ASRS:1791579.n: I was inbound to ZZZ from the southeast at 1,500 feet MSL, making entry for a left-hand downwind for Runway XX. Listening on CTAF, there was a Helicopter flying the practice ILS [Runway] XY into ZZZ, about 5 miles out. There were two aircraft ready to go on Runway XX, a Cirrus Aircraft X and an experimental Aircraft Z. The Helicopter continued to make position reports, e.g. 'ZZZ Traffic, Navy helicopter on 4 mile final, ILS [Runway] XY'The Cirrus started to roll on Runway XX, while the Helicopter was now on about a 0.5 mile final for runway XY. As I overflew the field, I watched as the Helicopter and the Cirrus were on a collision path headed towards the intersection of runways at ZZZ. While the Cirrus was on the roll, he inquired on CTAF if the Helicopter had the Cirrus in sight. The Helicopter said it did and being a helicopter, was able to immediately with a swift pitch up maneuver, reduce airspeed and come to a hover before the runway intersection, thus preventing a collision. The Cirrus continued to take off and fly the upwind leg up and out of the airport. I believe the issue stemmed from the Helicopter making radio calls including IFR terms while the pilot in the Cirrus may have been a VFR only pilot. The inclusion of 'ILS' may have caused confusion with the Cirrus pilot, making them feel that the helicopter was farther away than reality.
ASRS:1791579.s: A pilot inbound to ZZZ observed a Navy helicopter on a practice ILS approach and a Cirrus taking off on intersecting runways. The helicopter avoided a collision by hovering before the intersection, likely caused by the Cirrus pilot misinterpreting the helicopter's ILS radio calls as indicating greater distance.

ASRS:1791581.n: While returning to 7F3 on a student training flight I was informed on the CTAF that there were numerous powered parachutes(PPC) in the vicinity of the airport. One pilot stated that 2 PPC were at 1,500 ft. on downwind to Runway 18, the runway in use. Another pilot had to abort his landing because of 2 PPC over the runway as he was approaching the runway on a simulated engine out pattern. There were approximately 12 PPC's in the air and I could see that they were interfering with approaches, upwind legs and on downwind. After maneuvering to avoid them I changed the pattern to a non standard right pattern and still encountered them on that side of the airport at different altitudes. They do not have radios, and being slow are hard to see, especially the light of a low, soon to be setting sun.This is a very unsafe airport , especially for training, when these PPC's are operating. 7F3 is a high student pilot training facility and this needs to be addressed ASAP.
ASRS:1791581.s: A student pilot training at 7F3 encountered approximately 12 radio-equipped powered parachutes interfering with approaches and downwind legs at various altitudes. The pilot aborted a simulated engine-out landing and switched to a non-standard right pattern to avoid the slow, hard-to-see aircraft, deeming the airport unsafe for training.

ASRS:1791583.n: I received the relief briefing from the previous controller and was briefed that an aircraft wanted to do multiple practice approaches at a satellite airport. The aircraft was on the climb out instructions when I instructed him to turn right heading 180 for vector for an ILS. The aircraft replied to that instruction and began to fly that heading. A minute or so later I noticed that the aircraft was veering to the right of the assigned heading. I instructed them to turn 10 degrees right. He didn't reply and I gave him the instructions again. He did not reply this time either. This is when I first became aware of this aircraft being NORDO (No Radio). I began to reach out multiple times to the aircraft and after a little time I heard him reply that he went back to the tower. I then questioned him as to why would he return to the tower frequency and gave him another instruction.The aircraft again did not respond. I also asked him to ident if he could hear me transmitting and that failed. Now I was becoming worried as I was aware this aircraft was level at 2,000 ft. and there is a Minimum Vectoring Altitude (MVA) south of him 5 to 6 miles that is 3,000 ft. I reached out to Tower to ask them if they could try to reach out to the aircraft. I also had another aircraft in the vicinity that I inquired if he could hear me and if that aircraft could transmit for me and try to contact the aircraft. Both of those attempts failed as well. I was now getting nervous as he was headed towards the two antennas with the MVA's at 3,000 ft. I then reached out to him on guard frequency and stated that if he heard me to climb immediately to 3,000 ft. I also alerted the Supervisor what was going on. Now I was seeing the aircraft entering the MVA area of 3,000 ft. and I transmitted in the blind a MVA alert and for them to climb immediately. There was still no contact with this aircraft. Now another aircraft was also trying to reach the NORDO aircraft as they heard the concern in my voice. After some time the pilot called me and said he was ready for the vector onto the ILS. Thats when the other aircraft transmitted the climb information and they began to climb. The aircraft then called me and stated he is having a serious problem with his radios and wanted to return to their departure airport. I then gave him vectors to return where the aircraft landed safely.I have no recommendations. This was an event that as a controller I did everything I could think of to get in contact with the aircraft but he was truly NORDO. In conclusion it was a equipment issue that caused the incident.
ASRS:1791583.s: An air traffic controller lost radio contact with a pilot climbing at 2,000 feet, causing the aircraft to enter a 3,000-foot Minimum Vectoring Altitude area. The pilot eventually reported a radio equipment failure, received climb instructions via another aircraft, and returned safely to the departure airport.

ASRS:1791615.n: During cruise, a flight attendant advised us via the interphone that a cabin fire was occurring, without going into detail. We prepared for the possibility of diverting to the nearest suitable airport, but after conferring with the cabin crew, the Captain determined that the fire was the result of a cell phone with an overheated battery being tossed into the aisle and burning a small area on the carpet. The smoldering carpet was extinguished, and the phone battery was cooled and placed in the thermal containment bag. We continued to ZZZ1 without further incident.
ASRS:1791615.s: During cruise, the flight crew responded to a cabin fire report caused by an overheated cell phone battery burning the carpet. The smoldering carpet was extinguished, the battery was cooled and contained, and the flight continued to ZZZ1 without further incident.

ASRS:1791629.n: During climb out from ZZZ, passing FL330 we noticed the Master Caution light flickering. We discovered it was the Low Pressure light for Hydraulic System A Engine Driven (ENG 1) pump. After leveling at FL370 the ENG 1 low pressure light then came on steady. We executed the checklist and turned the pump off. We then referenced the Hydraulic quantity and noticed the A system quantity was at 20% and B system was at about 88%. The quantity in system A then continued to decrease, reaching 0% within a few minutes. The System A ELEC 2 low pressure light was not illuminated at this point. We decided to divert to ZZZ1 and advised ATC. We reviewed the Loss of System A checklist and planned our diversion to ZZZ1. On downwind for Runway XX in ZZZ1 we lowered the gear early as planned. After the gear came down we got the low pressure light for the System A ELEC 2 pump. We completed the checklist for Loss of System A and continued our approach. After landing we discovered the Alternate Nosewheel steering was not working. We stopped the aircraft on the runway. We checked the hydraulic quantities and noticed the system B quantity was now at 47%. We were subsequently towed to the gate.
ASRS:1791629.s: During climb from ZZZ, the crew experienced a total loss of Hydraulic System A pressure, prompting a diversion to ZZZ1. Following landing, alternate nosewheel steering failed and System B quantity dropped to 47%, requiring the aircraft to be towed to the gate.

ASRS:1791669.n: During ZZZZZX arrival into ZZZ descended to 12,000 at ZZZZZ. Prematurely started descending to ZZZZZ1 (11,000) before reaching ZZZZZ2. ATC deleted speeds, was a little preoccupied checking speed, making sure I did not have a speed deviation. First flight in almost three months.I need better situational awareness. ZZZZZX Arrival, After we leveled off at 12,000 feet at ZZZZZ, the FO set next altitude of 11,000 feet for ZZZZZ1 with confirmation. Approach Control notified us of a new ATIS. During our level off at 12,000 feet I copied the new ATIS. I looked up at the PFD and noticed we had vacated 12,000 feet prior to ZZZZZ2, and shortly after crossed ZZZZZ2.[Suggest a] digital ATIS.
ASRS:1791669.s: During the ZZZZZX arrival, the First Officer prematurely descended to 11,000 feet before reaching ZZZZZ2 while the Captain was distracted by ATC speed deletions and a new ATIS. The pilot attributed the altitude deviation to poor situational awareness on their first flight in three months.

ASRS:1791689.n: First leg was a block turn back in ZZZ. Fluid leaking under right main gear. Maintenance performed the following corrective action: REMOVED AND REPLACED RH GEAR TRIM CYLINDER RELIEF VALVE. I asked the maintainer whether he needed to bleed the brakes since he cracked the closed system. He told me to cycle the brakes and if they felt good we were good to go. Legs 2 was the subsequent takeoff. After takeoff, gear handle would not move. QRH procedure offered no resolution. Declared priority handling. Conferenced maintenance and Operations Control in the air. Uneventful landing ZZZ Runway XX. The following was the maintenance corrective action: CONFIRMED FAULT, GEAR HANDLE WILL NOT RETRACT IN ANY CONFIG. T/S SYSTEM AND FOUND MLG HYDRAULIC INTERLOCK CYLINDER NOT EXTENDING WITH SYSTEM 3 PRESSURE, WHICH MECHANICALLY INHIBITED TRAVEL OF GEAR HANDLE. DUE TO TRIM CYLINDER RELIEF VALVE RECENT CHANGE, SUSPECT RESIDUAL AIR IN SYSTEM. BLED TRIM CYL RELIEF VALVE, NO AIR. BLED HYD FUSE, FOUND A SIGNIFICANT AMOUNT OF AIR-ENTRAINED FLUID. BLED INTERLOCK CYLINDER. NO FLUID CAME OUT AT FIRST, FOLLOWED BY A SIGNIFICANT AMOUNT OF AIR ENTRAINED FLUID. AFTER BLEEDING, SYSTEM WORKS NORMALLY, INTERLOCK EXTENDS AND RETRACTS AS NORMAL, REF [type aircraft] AMM 32-31-05-2 AND AMM 32-37-03-2. JACKED ACFT AND SWUNG GEAR TO VERIFY A POSITIVE FIX. GEAR SWINGS NORMALLY WITH CORRECT INDICATION MULTIPLE CYCLES. ACFT OK FOR SERVICE. Is it reasonable to draw a connection between leg 1 and leg 2 as to cause and effect for the gear handle stuck in the down position? After extensive research, I wasn't able to find a definitive answer as to a correlation. However, during my research, I discovered that it is maintenance procedure to bleed the hydraulic system after relief valve replacement. Interestingly enough, I even asked the mechanic about this. He response was to me was to set and release the brakes a few times, and then he asked me if they 'felt okay'. When I replied that 'They seemed normal' he said 'You're good to go'. Obviously, I wasn't good to go. I should also mention that after the job was declared complete, I went down to observe the new valve. There was hydraulic fluid everywhere including a 3 foot diameter puddle under the valve. As the Captain, when I ask specific questions about a maintenance procedure, it is unacceptable to be given incorrect information by maintenance or be lied to by maintenance. Why wasn't the procedure completed correctly? Why isn't there a check and balance system in place to verify mechanics are completing maintenance actions? I demand an answer to these questions as well as why there was so much air in the hydraulic system which inhibited gear handle movement. Crew contacted me via radio, shortly after takeoff. Captain advised that they were unable to raise the gear and will be returning to ZZZ. Captain advised gear was down and locked but said he will [advise ATC] as a precaution. Earlier, flight did a block turn back due to a hydraulic leak at the gear. Maintenance repaired the leak by replacing a valve. Not sure, at this time, if that played a part with the gear not retracting. Flight landed safely and Manager was notified.
ASRS:1791689.s: Following a block turn for a hydraulic leak, maintenance replaced a gear valve but failed to bleed the system, leaving air that inhibited gear retraction on the next leg. The crew declared priority handling, landed safely, and maintenance later confirmed the fault was caused by air-entrained fluid from the incomplete bleed procedure.

ASRS:1791692.n: Descending on the STAR arrival around 11,000 ft. the FO (First Officer) deployed spoilers to slow and as the handle was moved we received a EICAS message for Hyd system pressure 'L', hyd quantity, spoilers, rudder ratio etc. We selected hydraulic synopsis and noted left quantity '0' and pressure was low. As the fluid depleted the PTU engaged and L hyd pressure came up to 2800-3000 psi. We asked for an extended downwind for Runway XX and referenced the QRH HYD SYSTEM PRESSURE (L ONLY). We leveled at 6,000 ft. heading southwest. Slowed to 210 kts. and the FO continued flying as I accomplished the required items. After checking landing distance we decided to request Runway XY in case of steering issues or fluid leakage to not shut down Runway XX. We [advised ATC] asking for men and equipment standing by even though pressure was adequate. In the event any other systems were compromised. We configured to Flaps 1 normal. Continued to configure and slow and lowered the landing gear on an extended 15 mile final so we would have time to deal with any other issues that may arise. I took the controls as pilot flying and briefed the FO on various options we had in case of missed approach or control issues on the ground. FO did a tremendous job monitoring and capturing errors as they arose like finalizing checklists and call outs. We landed normal and stopped on Runway XY, cleared the runway at XX and stopped for crash rescue inspection of left wing area. We were informed fluid was leaking aft of number 1 L engine and shut down the L engine. We started the APU and shutdown R engine. We were informed brake temps were less than 150 and no smoke or fumes present. I referenced the various checklists regarding fluid loss and was told the leak had slowed. We coordinated with ZZZ operations, maintenance and ground control when fire rescue requested a clean up for hydraulic fluid on taxiway. Then maintenance tugged us back to the ramp at Gate XX. Failure of hydraulic component during descent while deploying speed brakes/flight spoilers. But I missed the fact at first that the loss of pressure on checklist has various systems and at first I referenced the pressure loss of L and C and then realized it was just the L quantity and pressure we were dealing with. I was the Pilot Flying, on descent through 11,000 ft. I deployed the flight spoilers. Shortly after, we had a master caution 'L HYD SYS PRESS' along with associated messages and lights on the hyd system panel on the overhead panel. The CA (Captain) checked the status page, when I looked at the status page L hyd quantity was at or near 0, and the pressure was normal (near 3000). There appeared to be a hydraulic leak with the PTU operable. I continued flying, we asked for vectors for an extended approach. The CA ran the checklist and [advised ATC]. We ran the HYD SYSTEM PRESSURE left only found on QRH 13.1.5. The checklist refers to a situation where the PTU is inoperable or complete loss of hydraulic fluid.
