We considered either one of these situations conceivable, so we opted for extended vectors and early configuration in case we needed alternate extension on either the flaps or the landing gear. We also elected to land on Runway XY so we wouldn't shut down Runway XX in case nose wheel steering was unavailable. The CA took the aircraft for the approach and landing. We configured and landed using flaps 20 per the checklist and cleared the runway uneventfully. Upon clearing, the fire trucks met us and informed us that we were leaking hydraulic fluid out of our left side. We turned on the APU and shut down both engines and the leak stopped. Maintenance towed us to our gate uneventfully.[Cause was a] Failed O Ring on left hydraulic system equipment.
ASRS:1791692.s: The crew experienced a left hydraulic system leak and pressure loss while deploying spoilers during descent at 11,000 ft. They executed an extended approach, landed safely on Runway XY, and were towed to the gate after maintenance identified a failed O-ring as the cause.

ASRS:1791706.n: Upon takeoff from Runway XX we received a Master Warning prior to V1 'R 14TH STAGE DUCT and the Captain initiated a rejected takeoff. We turned off the runway and allowed brakes to cool. The Captain completed the QRH for BRAKE TEMP OVHT. We contacted our Dispatcher, MOD, ZZZ Ops, the regional controller for company, and Maintenance Controller to discuss safest plan of action. The tires were inspected by fire department for any damage and abnormal heat signatures. We taxied back to gate after running checklist and communicating 2 in and 2 out. We returned to gate without issue. Unexpected failure of 14th stage duct very close to V1 causing a high speed rejected takeoff. I don't have any. It was an unexpected failure/warning message." Was taking off of Runway XX initiated the takeoff procedure just prior to the one red Master Warning occurred decided to reject takeoff. Once rejected takeoff was initiated V1 was passed. Since rejected takeoff procedure had already been initiated decided to continue with the abort. Pulled off the side of the runway onto taxiway. Break temperature monitoring system was indicating hot had ops truck rolled for suspected tire damage. Fire trucks did a brake temperature analysis said everything was in normal tolerance. Waited for breaks to cool down taxi back to the gate and deplaned.Before push back we were having fuel calculation issues since extra fuel was added to the center tank. Got on the phone with our MOD in order to resolve the issue was provided guidance in order to ensure safe flight. We then followed those guidelines. Throughout entire procedure a Pax (Passenger) Door Unsafe Caution message kept popping up due to an MEL and a faulty sensor. It was briefed that if we received this message on the takeoff roll we would continue the flight. So upon receiving the red Master Warning having to overcome the startle and surprise was difficult. It took a while to process that this was not the Pax Door Unsafe Caution message.A quicker initiation of the abort procedure would have saved us from exceeding V1. Since it was so incredibly close to V1 when the event occurred it requires more attention and that critical phase in order to ensure that abort is commenced.
ASRS:1791706.s: The crew rejected takeoff on Runway XX after a "R 14TH STAGE DUCT" Master Warning appeared just before V1, resulting in a high-speed abort that exceeded V1. The aircraft returned to the gate after brake cooling and tire inspections, with the reporter citing the unexpected failure and delayed abort initiation as key factors.

ASRS:1791749.n: I am writing about two events that occurred at ZZZ. I do not believe either event was a violation of FAA policies but I wanted to be sure I reported both of them to protect myself.On [Date] I was preparing for a 45-degree entry into the left traffic pattern for Runway XX in ZZZ. I made my second CTAF call 4 miles from the airport and announced my intention to enter the pattern 'on the 45, left traffic for [Runway] XX.'A few minutes later, a pilot flying a Diamond announced he was 'turning left crosswind for [Runway] XX.' He asked whether I was in the left downwind or still 'on the 45.' I replied that I was still on the 45 but would be turning left downwind momentarily. He then announced that he was 'turning left downwind for [Runway] XX.' Just to be safe, I announced that I would perform a 360 degree turn for spacing. The other pilot flew the downwind leg, then I entered. No issues.A few days later I received a call from an FAA POI asking about a 'near miss' that had been anonymously reported, probably from someone on the ground. She kept coming back to my 360-degree turn. I explained the situation and referred her to ATCLive, a web site that archives radio calls.I also expressed my confusion over why this was a concern. I had been trained that using spacing maneuvers is the conservative and correct approach at uncontrolled fields if the pilot is in ANY DOUBT about the safety of entering.The second event occurred 15-20 minutes later. This did not come up in my conversation with the FAA POI. It only occurred to me later that this may have been the near miss she was inquiring about. Here's a summary:I was on a one-mile final for Runway XX at the same airport on the same morning, about 20 minutes after the entry I described above. I was flying patterns that morning to maintain proficiency. I looked to my left as I flew the final approach and saw a glider landing on the 'Glider XX' runway to my left.He was descending from above me and he was slightly ahead of my aircraft. It is very difficult for me to measure feet in this situation so I cannot be certain of the distance. But it did not feel like a near miss in any way. No evasive action was taken by either one of us. We were both flying straight in to our respective runways and lined up on our center lines.Let me be clear about something -- while I do not believe this was a 'near miss;' I don't believe two aircraft landing on parallel runways, with one aircraft being a glider, is a safe practice and I normally would have extended my downwind and/or base to create more room. However, I never heard the glider pilot's CTAF calls -- if indeed there were any. Also, the glider was above me so I couldn't see him until he descended in front of me and to my left. Some conclusions:I have flown in and out of ZZZ for five years. For an uncontrolled field, it is one of the most dangerous airports I have ever flown, and that includes ZZZ2 inside ZZZ3 Class Bravo. Traffic on any given day is packed with student pilots, private pilots, traveling pilots coming to ZZZ and -- worse yet -- gliders on a parallel runway to the active non-glider, powered runway. It's a mess. Making matters worse, there are five airports in a narrow corridor between the mountains and ZZZ1 Class B airspace -- four of which are uncontrolled. And to finish this night mare off, a very active parachute operation at ZZZ4.It's a disaster waiting to happen.
ASRS:1791749.s: The pilot reported two events at uncontrolled airport ZZZ: a spacing 360-degree turn during a 45-degree entry to avoid a Diamond aircraft, and a close encounter with a glider on a parallel runway during final approach. The pilot attributed the risks to high traffic density, lack of glider radio calls, and the airport's complex environment.

ASRS:1791758.n: I am a student pilot that was performing my initial solo cross country. I had safely completed the initial leg, and was returning to ZZZ. On final, in the flare, I experienced an unanticipated crosswind gust, which resulted in the airplane dropping suddenly and causing a hard landing on the left main gear. I applied full power to go around and re-attempt the landing. I noticed that the airplane was yawing more than usual and recognized the airplane was operating in an abnormal condition. Shortly thereafter, I heard a radio call that a landing gear was visible on the runway at which point I realized that I had lost my left main gear. I continued to fly the traffic pattern under radio guidance from a CFI who was on the ground while I burned fuel and prepared for an emergency landing. On final, under instruction from the CFI, I cut all fuel and powered down the aircraft, while continuing to fly the airplane to a landing. I landed on the right main gear and the aircraft settled to the ground ultimately skidding on in its belly as it made contact with the runway surface. Due to the lack of directional control from only having the right main gear, the aircraft skidded left off the runway and came to rest in the grass left of the runway surface. I was able to exit the aircraft safely with no physical injuries. Following the event, I was interviewed by an Aviation Safety Inspector from the CITY Flight Standards Office and discussed the details shared above in its entirety.
ASRS:1791758.s: A student pilot performing a solo cross-country return to ZZZ experienced a hard landing on the left main gear due to a crosswind gust, causing the gear to detach. The pilot subsequently executed an emergency belly landing off the runway under CFI guidance, exiting safely with no injuries.

ASRS:1791765.n: Night landing on Runway XX bounced and as recovering from second bounce received call from TWR (Tower) to exit left onto Taxiway XX. Stopped plane on RWY (Runway) and called TWR for directions to [Taxiway] XX. Told to proceed down RWY. Next call from TWR was to exit left on [Taxiways] XY2, XY and hold short [Taxiway] XX. Turned off at [Taxiway] XY2 and started down [Taxiway] XY looking for sign for [Taxiway] XX. Saw sign for [Taxiways] XX/XY. Before coming to complete stop, noticed plane approaching from left on Taxiway XX. Accelerated to get out of way and inadvertently crossed Runway XX. Too late saw runway hold lines. TWR called and requested telephone call for possible runway incursion.Factors:1. kept speed up because other planes in pattern, resulting in bounce.2. landing longer than planned.3. received taxi instruction from TWR while in active landing phase.3. loss of situational awareness of position on runway, called TWR for direction.4. should have asked for more specific information from TWR.5. Should have reviewed airport diagram in more detail for names and positions of taxiwaysin cause of landing long.6. In hindsight, should have stopped as soon as turned from [Taxiway] XY2 to XY and asked TWRfor further instructions when didn't see edge of Taxiway XX.Corrective Actions:1. Review Airport diagram2. Review Airport signage from Wings/FAA programs3. Fly with instructor and work on taxiing.
ASRS:1791765.s: The pilot bounced during a night landing on Runway XX, received conflicting taxi instructions while on the active runway, and inadvertently crossed Runway XX while accelerating to avoid another aircraft. The incident was caused by landing long, loss of situational awareness, and receiving taxi clearances during the landing phase.

ASRS:1791774.n: This was a cross country flight with a commercial student. After being vectored, we were cleared to land on the right parallel runway at ZZZ. Another aircraft at the airport was cleared to land on the left runway. They apparently heard the right runway as they got uncomfortably close. They corrected to the left runway, but not before passing directly underneath us, with the difference in altitude showing only 200 ft. on my EFB (Electronic Flight Bag). Fortunately we were high, so we held our altitude until the other aircraft was able to turn away and landed without incident.
ASRS:1791774.s: A commercial student pilot and instructor on approach to ZZZ experienced a 200-foot vertical separation when another aircraft, mistakenly cleared for the right runway, passed directly underneath them. The other crew corrected to the left runway after the near-miss, and both aircraft landed without incident.

ASRS:1791775.n: I was acting as the instructor for a student pilot training flight. Myself and my student were in the traffic pattern for multiple touch and go's. There were several airplanes in the pattern, and as one aircraft was on the upwind, we had just turned final. About 400 feet following a standard 3 degree VASI (Visual Approach Slope Indicator), I noticed a truck moving from the ramp area toward our landing runway. I kept an eye on the truck and continued to work with my student. We made all standard radio calls on the CTAF, and all other traffic in the pattern were making consistent radio calls.As we continued our descent to land, the truck crossed the runway hold short line and entered the active runway. At this point, we were roughly 100 feet on short final. I instructed my student to go-around, as he was the pilot flying. My student made a timely go-around to avoid the truck that had entered the runway. I recognized the truck as being a hangar tenant for a private hangar located across the airport. The private hangars are not owned or rented by the airport's operator, and crossing the runway is one of two ways to access the hangars. The other access point does not involving crossing runways. The truck never made a call to cross via a handheld radio, and I don't believe the occupant of the truck was using any sort of radio to actively monitor the airport traffic before crossing the runway.
ASRS:1791775.s: An instructor and student pilot in a training aircraft executed a timely go-around at 100 feet on short final to avoid a truck entering the active runway. The incident occurred because the hangar tenant crossed without radio communication or monitoring airport traffic.

ASRS:1791780.n: Owner contacted me to evaluate the aircraft for future flight. The aircraft was looked over, fueled, new battery. After run up, I intended to high speed taxi aircraft on the runway to evaluate engine power. Upon the last taxi the aircraft lifted into the air unintentionally. The engine ran rough upon which I made a teardrop pattern and landed the aircraft, touching down on the grass median between the runway and taxi way. I got onto the runway, taxied to the end and back to the ramp. There was no damage to the airport property or the aircraft. The aircraft was taxied back to the ramp and tied down.
ASRS:1791780.s: A pilot evaluating an aircraft unintentionally lifted off during a high-speed taxi run-up. The engine ran rough, prompting a teardrop pattern and a grass median landing with no damage to the aircraft or airport property.

ASRS:1791783.n: At approximately XA:37 on [Date], pilot was flying 18-19 nautical miles northwest of ZZZ at 4,000 feet MSL and 2,300 RPM, performing an oil and gas production patrol. Pilot noted the engine began running rough. The pilot performed appropriate procedures, ensuring tanks were selected on both, mixture was rich, throttle full, and scanning magnetos and master. The pilot was able to hold altitude with the power maxed out at 2100-2200 RPM. The pilot squawked 7700 and made a call on Guard. Pilot received a call back on Guard from a nearby helicopter who relayed to ZZZ1 Approach. Pilot turned toward nearest airport, ZZZ2 and pitched for Vx, following a pipeline right-of-way in to the airport. Pilot repeated intentions to land in ZZZ2 on Guard and CTAF. Pilot then called company CEO (Name) to alert of the problem. Approximately 10 nautical miles west of ZZZ2, left the right-of-way course and followed Interstate for approximately 20 miles until it intersected a final approach for Runway XX at ZZZ2. Over the time this incident occurred, aircraft gained 700 feet of altitude, which was carried until landing was assured. Aircraft was taxied clear of the runway to the FBO and parked.
ASRS:1791783.s: During an oil and gas patrol at 4,000 feet, the pilot experienced rough engine running and declared an emergency. The pilot diverted to ZZZ2, following a pipeline and interstate to land safely after gaining 700 feet of altitude.

ASRS:1791793.n: During Phase 2/3/D inspection of a Cessna 441 aircraft, the flight control cables were being inspected. It is required to check the cables every Phase D (24 months). During the inspection, it was found that the RH elevator cable was severely frayed in the aft cabin, under the pulley right as the cable rotates upward to go into the tail section. After removal, it was found that the cable only had two remaining stands [strands]. It is estimated that approximately 60% of the cable was frayed. The frayed area of the cable sits directly under the pulley when the elevator is in the down/resting position. The cable has been replaced and no other locations of frayed cable were detected. This was clearly in a critical fatigue area. We just wanted to relay this find in regard to the severity of the cable condition.
ASRS:1791793.s: During a Phase 2/3/D inspection of a Cessna 441, mechanics found the right elevator cable severely frayed with only two strands remaining under a pulley in the aft cabin. The cable was replaced after being identified as a critical fatigue failure, with no other frayed cables detected.

ASRS:1791799.n: The staffing has been really poor. We have taken a few hits because of people being out with coronavirus or close contact. I just wanna say on Day X that I worked a X AM to Y PM shift and that was the beginning of my week. It was tough to get caught up from the fatigue of that for a shift in the very first part of my week. Also, I have worked X weeks in a row with only a single day off.I took a handoff Aircraft X IFR from ZZZ [Center] (X SECTOR) at 4,000 destined ZZZ [Airport]. Airspace configuration was north based on ZZZ1 [Airport] international traffic. This required me to vector Aircraft X around the ZZZ1 [Airport] Final Box. I did so. Because of the staffing we were told or encouraged to not work VFR overflights or VFR practice approaches that day. I don't know if that word was past two adjacent facilities, But I was trying to eliminate as much of the VFR traffic as I could by terminating them whenever they checked on from other facilities or by denying services.ZZZ [Center] (Y SECTOR) handed off Aircraft Y, VFR at 4,500, but the pilot never checked in. I had to call ZZZ [Center] (Y SECTOR) and ask for communications. I had no intention of working Aircraft Y. I wanted to be able to communicate with the pilot to terminate Flight Following in order to concentrate on other tasks. I had the Flight Data controller remove Aircraft Y from the NAS.While I'm doing this, a couple of things happened at or about the same time. Aircraft Z checked on the frequency and was in the ZZZ1 [Airport] Final Box under the Class Bravo Airspace. Aircraft Z requested clearance into the Class Bravo airspace and to navigate VFR to a hospital that I hadn't heard of and was not mapped. I was trying to determine where exactly the hospital was. At or about that same time I had an aircraft (Aircraft A) check on my frequency (the wrong frequency), wanting clearance into the Class Charlie airspace at ZZZ2 [Airport] for closed traffic. Aircraft A should have made the request on ZZZ1 [TRACON] frequency XYZ.Y. I looked over to my left and the ZZZ1 [TRACON] Controller looked and sounded busy so I decided to accommodate Aircraft A and then point out Aircraft A to the ZZZ1 [TRACON] Controller. I issued all of the instructions for Aircraft A. I also accomplished all of the coordination for the Aircraft Z with the Final Controller. When I finally get Aircraft Y on frequency I told him I was too busy to accommodate VFR flight following, told him squawk VFR and radar service terminated. At some point I drop the track on the wrong aircraft. I drop the track on Aircraft X IFR to ZZZ [Airport].I'm shocked that I did not realize that I dropped the track on the wrong flight, but for whatever reason I did not. I'm pretty sure I was pretty tired by this point. My previous session in the day ran almost 2 hours, during which I took an absolute pounding. I am further shocked that at no time in the session did I realize and correct my mistake.Later in the session I took the hand off on Aircraft B from ZZZ1 [TRACON] Y Sector. Aircraft B was requesting 6,000. Departure 3 & 4 were being worked by one controller, who was probably the busiest controller in the room. I decided to give Aircraft B, 4,000 as a final altitude.Aircraft B was now IFR at 4,000 southwest bound and on a converging course with Aircraft X. I don't remember the destination for Aircraft B. Aircraft X is tracking pretty much direct ZZZ [Airport] I don't remember if I had given them direct or not. I noticed Aircraft B was converging with limited target at 4,000, which was Aircraft X. I called the traffic to Aircraft X. Seeing the conflict I decided to climb Aircraft B to 5,000. I don't recall if Aircraft B ever called the traffic in sight, but I know, after watching the replay that I never had more than 500 feet separation between the two flights.Still not realizing my mistake, Aircraft X calls ZZZ [Airport] in sight. I ask who he is and where he came from. Not one of my better moments. At some point, I began to remember Aircraft X and I start the track on the flight, make the appropriate entries in the scratch pad, coordinate with the ZZZ1 [TRACON] Y Sector Controller for landing ZZZ [Airport], inbounded the flight to the Tower, and cleared Aircraft X for the visual approach to ZZZ [Airport].I know this recommendation will be laughed out of the office, however it would be terrific if the terminal world had a version of EDST [En-route Decision Support Tool] along with a monitor/terminal to view and amend flight data at your position. This technological implementation is frankly overdue and it is a genuine travesty that we don't have it.
ASRS:1791799.s: An air traffic controller, fatigued by poor staffing and long shifts, accidentally dropped the radar track of an IFR aircraft while managing multiple VFR requests. This error caused a loss of separation with a converging aircraft, requiring the controller to manually re-establish the track and clear the flight for a visual approach.

ASRS:1791803.n: Metroplex! They built a new departure and arrival procedure that doesn't allow for flyby procedure. Aircraft X on the new JOHKR [SID] procedure was told they are laterally separated. Aircraft Y on the new RNDRZ STAR. The problem is Aircraft X did a fly by which is completely allowed. There was a loss of three miles because if the aircraft does the flyby you don't have enough mileage. You need to either move the JOHKR or RNDRZ one mile because there is not enough space to allow for the flyby. Also you need new people overseeing these issues. The people overseeing this are super offended if anything is brought up. Minor tweeks need to be done! We have other issues that are being turned down because of this.
ASRS:1791803.s: A pilot reported a three-mile separation loss between Aircraft X on the JOHKR SID and Aircraft Y on the RNDRZ STAR due to an unpermitted flyby maneuver. The reporter attributed the issue to flawed Metroplex procedure design and unresponsive oversight personnel.

ASRS:1791816.n: Aircraft X checked in from 40 miles north of the airport requesting opposite direction arrival Runway 14. I coordinated with Medford Tower and they denied it due to an aircraft with a controlled departure time even though the departure would not have been a factor. I told Aircraft X unable and they requested the RNAV 32 Approach via SAMIE so I cleared them for the approach via SAMIE at or above 10,000 feet. As Aircraft X was following the course a VFR tag popped up near the approach path about 11 miles south of the airport (they appeared to depart from an uncontrolled airport that is directly in the approach path) so I issued traffic multiple times and gave Aircraft X an altitude restriction for traffic but when Aircraft X got closer to the unidentified target the target climbed and turned at the Aircraft X resulting in a TCAS RA at which point the Aircraft X climbed and eventually requested an altitude to maintain and wanted lower for a Visual Approach. Due to terrain I was unable to descend them low enough and had to issue vectors around for the ILS 14 Approach which the aircraft conducted and landed safely. I then had another arrival requesting the RNAV 32 Approach and the unidentified target was still a factor.The RNAV 32 Approach flies directly over an uncontrolled airport that is frequently used by VFR aircraft and also follows a very busy VFR area over a highway that aircraft not on flight following use for navigation. This approach is inherently dangerous due to the number of aircraft that fly along it's path without communication with Approach Control and because it flies through a valley between mountainous terrain giving ATC few options to avoid conflict with aircraft that can't be seen by our radar until reaching above 4,000 feet. I recommend that Medford airport should be allowed to advertise Runway 14 arrivals with Runway 32 departures. Whoever decided that we can't advertise that needs to come have a look at the arrival/departure procedures available at Medford and give an actual answer as to why? Runway 32 arrivals are much more dangerous to aircraft than Runway 14 due to mountainous terrain, and Runway 14 departures are far more dangerous when also arriving Runway 14 because the departure procedure for Runway 14 turns aircraft around directly in the face of aircraft arriving runway 14 creating an opposite direction conflict with FAR less control and restriction than we would have with a 14 arrival and 32 departure. Opposite Direction Operations requires a 10 mile cutoff where the opposite direction conflict created by a Runway14 arrival with a Runway 14 departure does not allow us to turn aircraft until a much higher altitude resulting in risky behavior. Runway 32 even has a departure procedure that provides safe divergence from opposite direction arrivals called the EAGLE 6 Departure. Until someone actually comes to the facility and understands the dangers of not being able to advertise Runway 14 arrivals with Runway 32 departures there will be many more close close calls that could have been safely prevented. It is an easy fix with amazing benefits for controllers, pilots, and preventing air carrier delays.
ASRS:1791816.s: An Air Traffic Controller reported that Aircraft X experienced a TCAS RA while on the RNAV 32 Approach due to an unidentified VFR aircraft climbing and turning toward it. The controller vectored the aircraft for a safe ILS 14 landing and attributed the conflict to the approach's path over an uncontrolled airport and mountainous terrain.

ASRS:1791820.n: It was a typical busy day with many requests both inbound and outbound. Aircraft X called Ground Control on Taxiway Lima between the parallel runways requesting taxi to the northwest ramp. I issued 'taxi via Lima, Kilo, cross Runway 21 and hold short Runway 26 right at Kilo.' As the pilot read back the taxi route he appeared to hesitate and start a slight right turn onto Runway 21. I asked the pilot if he was familiar with taxiing between the parallel runways to which he replied 'no.' I then issued plain language instructions 'continue straight ahead and taxi kilo is the last right turn. As you make the turn the hold bars come up really quick so as you turn, slow to a stop. The pilot acknowledged my instructions. As the pilot turned on Taxiway Kilo he passed the hold short bars. I immediately reached out to Aircraft X and told him to stop. At that time another aircraft was calling Ground Control with a request. Aircraft X stopped prior to the runway edge line. I then made Local Control - North aware and advised the Controller to send around the traffic that was on about a 1-1/2 mile final. I had issued the hold short instruction but in his confused taxiing I missed the hold short readback as I was attempting to stop the aircraft from turning on to Runway 21. The airport recently painted a yellow taxi line that leads off of Taxiway Lima and onto to Runway 21. I've seen several pilots get confused while taxiing and follow that yellow line inadvertently. The airport also painted some enhanced taxi lines and runway markings on the ground. I believe the yellow line leading off Taxiway Lima is and will continue to confuse pilots. I think additional signage in the midfield clearly showing taxi routes would help the pilots who continue to 'get lost' while taxiing in these hotspots.
ASRS:1791820.s: An Air Traffic Controller issued taxi instructions to Aircraft X between parallel runways, but the pilot hesitated and nearly entered Runway 21 due to confusion from a new yellow taxi line. The controller intervened with plain language instructions, stopping the aircraft before the runway edge and diverting an approaching aircraft on final approach.

ASRS:1791837.n: I was Pilot Flying. Just after liftoff, the nose trim ran high speed nose up on its own. I waited a quick moment and told the Captain that I was not doing that trim command, and then pushed forward on the yoke to stop the runaway. After retracting the flaps, I relaxed forward pressure and the trim continued nose up runaway at slow speed. I pressed the electric time nose down on the yoke, and the up trim stopped its uncommanded nose up runaway. Then we ran the Stabilizer Runaway Checklist and returned back to ZZZ uneventfully. During takeoff from ZZZ, at approximately 300 ft. AGL, the aircraft trim began running continuously, high-speed, in the 'Nose-Up' direction. The F/O (First Officer) stopped the trim by pushing forward on the yoke. This action stopped the trim movement. At 1,200 ft. AGL, after retracting the flaps, the trim began running again, continuously 'Nose-Up' in the slow-speed mode. This time the F/O used the Electrical Trim switch in the opposite direction and this action stopped the movement. We ran the Runaway Stabilizer Checklist and returned to ZZZ for an uneventful approach and landing.
ASRS:1791837.s: The Pilot Flying experienced an uncommanded high-speed nose-up stabilizer trim runaway at 300 ft AGL during takeoff from ZZZ, which resumed in slow-speed mode at 1,200 ft AGL after flap retraction. The crew stopped the runaway using forward yoke pressure and the electrical trim switch, then returned to ZZZ for an uneventful landing after completing the checklist.

ASRS:1791857.n: Cargo Air Carrier Ground Personnel shipment was found with un-declared Dangerous Goods while being inspected by a [company] Manager. The shipment was not accepted, but was refused prior to tender. We found 12 small boxes of UN3481, Lithium Ion Batteries. As per the item, it appears to be AirPods (2nd Generation) for Iphones. Models A2032, A2031, and A1938.
ASRS:1791857.s: Ground personnel discovered undeclared UN3481 lithium-ion batteries in a cargo shipment during a manager's inspection prior to tender. The shipment containing 12 boxes of iPhone AirPods was refused and not accepted for transport.

ASRS:1791858.n: The flight was a 737-900 with carpet. The freight/DG was 2022 pounds. We only had 3 bags listed for the flight. Per the new policy, we are suppose to secure the DG with 9 bags of ballast or 450 pounds of mail. There is no real way to secure this amount of DG while following the new policy. We were instructed to load the freight per company policy and followed it. We were instructed to load 14 feet long of Dangerous Good, Weight 2022 pounds;3 Bags listed for flight and load planner approved 450 pounds of Weight Balancers.
ASRS:1791858.s: Load planners and crew on a 737-900 freight flight reported an inability to secure 2,022 pounds of dangerous goods per new policy requiring 9 ballast bags or 450 pounds of mail. Despite the conflict, the team loaded the cargo and approved weight balancers following company instructions.

ASRS:1791902.n: I was handed a [Dangerous Good Form] that included UN3077. In the ERG the narrative states under Fire or Explosion: Containers may explode when heated, and under Health: Inhalation of material may be harmful and Fire may product irritating, corrosive and/or toxic gases. I refused the items.I'm quite concerned that this type of HAZMAT was attempted to be carried on our aircraft.I tried to get further information on the goods. None were available locally at the time. I refused to carry the items.
ASRS:1791902.s: A crew member refused to load UN3077 dangerous goods after reviewing the Emergency Response Guide, which warned of explosion and toxic gas risks. The reporter declined the shipment because no further information on the hazardous material was available locally.

ASRS:1791906.n: We momentarily exceeded the max altitude of 13,000 feet at ZZZZZ [Intersection]. Upon realizing this, we quickly returned to 13,000 feet as per the departure.The Captain was hand flying the departure, which was new to both of us. In hindsight, because we were both unfamiliar with the departure, it should have been on autopilot for reduced workload. He had also been off for several months, and I had just returned from a week of vacation.We could have verbalized the new departure as at least a minor risk factor and made an initial decision to engage the autopilot sooner after takeoff.
ASRS:1791906.s: The crew momentarily exceeded the 13,000-foot limit at ZZZZZ during a hand-flown departure unfamiliar to both pilots. The Captain, returning after months off, and the First Officer, returning from vacation, attributed the error to high workload and a failure to engage the autopilot sooner.

ASRS:1791907.n: Cockpit filled with 'smoke' after turning on packs following de-ice. [The apparent] cause was De-icing fluid must have gotten into the bleed air system. We got some from the APU supplied bleed air. I had hoped that the engine bleed air system was not affected, but it was actually worse. We de-iced during heavy snow and I halted the process when it was apparent that the intensity of the snowfall was such that the entire Type I/Type IV process wasn't sufficient to stay ahead of the snowfall. Turning on the packs with APU bleed air we experienced 'smoke' in the flight deck but none in the cabin. Packs off stopped the problem. We waited 30 mins until the snow lessened and completed de-icing. Hoping that the problem has corrected itself I put the packs on using engine bleed after waiting 3 minutes. However, the 'smoke' returned even heavier. FA's (Flight Attendants) reported a slight smell. We returned to the gate and the aircraft went out of service. Never saw this in XX years of flying.
ASRS:1791907.s: The pilot reported smoke in the flight deck after turning on packs with APU and engine bleed air following de-icing in heavy snow. Suspecting de-icing fluid entered the bleed air system, the crew returned to the gate, and the aircraft went out of service.

ASRS:1791908.n: Approximately 5 minutes at gate, after gate return, while discussing Weight and Balance issue with ramp supervisor, #1 FA (Flight Attendant) said #2 FA reported electrical burning smell that had since dissipated. We called for Maintenance. Maintenance techs arrived quickly within 5 minutes and said no odor/smell noticed by them.Asked for FA 2 to come to flight deck and explain the odor. She again said it was a burning smell and it was still there though not as strong. She said she could 'taste' it. At that point I told gate agents we would deplane the aircraft. I advised FA's and made an announcement for Passengers to deplane. I asked 2 to fill out a form and called the Dispatcher who said he would look for another plane.Passengers off aircraft, went to back and discussed issue with FAs. #4 now said he also could 'taste something metallic'. I advised FAs to leave the aircraft also while we talked to Maintenance. I inquired if anyone wanted or needed medical attention to which the answer was 'no' by all. I then completed and submitted the smoke/odor form with information gained while discussing the situation with FAs in the jet bridge. They now said there had also been a musty smell. Logbook entry made and discussed with techs. All fume/odor event SOPs completed.A new aircraft was assigned for the flight. While waiting for the cleaners in the jet bridge with the FAs both 2&4 said they had tightness in their foreheads and 4 said his taste was still a little metallic. I asked them to call for FA supervisor while I also asked the gate agents to do the same so we could evaluate everyone's fitness for duty.I called the Duty Chief, and explained the situation. I then discussed the situation with [name], FA supervisor via gate telephone who said another supervisor was on her way to the aircraft. FA supervisor, came to the aircraft immediately and talked to the FAs who said they were physically ok. We then all discussed the issue together and all FAs said they were fit for duty and felt better.We arrived in ZZZ1 after an uneventful flight and the First Officer and myself waited for the FAs to make sure they were still feeling OK. Everyone said they were fine.Possible cause perhaps a tailwind on engine shutdown
ASRS:1791908.s: The flight crew and cabin crew reported an electrical burning and metallic odor at the gate, leading to passenger deplaning and aircraft replacement. Although maintenance found no odor, the crew experienced temporary symptoms, and the pilot suspected a tailwind during engine shutdown as the possible cause.

ASRS:1791911.n: I was the PF (Pilot Flying) on Aircraft X from ZZZ2-ZZZ1. I flew the RNAV RNP [Runway] XX approach with rain and wind in the vicinity. I attempted to configure early but a strong tailwind made it challenging. I encountered a wind gust which caused me to counter increasing airspeed by pitching up and slightly reduce power to maintain airspeed and continue configuring. This resulted in a position higher than anticipated. The PM (Pilot Monitoring) noticed this also and we articulated that. About that time, ATC directed a go-around. We executed the missed approach and climbed to 3,000 [feet] on vectors for another approach.Noting the conditions, I configured early for the second RNAV RNP XX approach. Rain and wind were still predominant throughout the approach but fewer gust excursions and we remained stable throughout the approach all the way to minimums. At minimums, we both had the approach lights and runway environment in sight and I continued the approach. As I turned final aligning with Runway XX, I lost sight of the runway environment due to the weather. The PM called go around and I initiated go around procedures. We climbed to 3,000 feet on vectors as directed by ATC. We communicated with one another and ensured we were both in the green, we had ample fuel, and agreed to attempt a third approach. On the third RNAV RNP XX approach, I configured early again and remained stable throughout the approach. The wind was still a factor though and required careful monitoring and aircraft correction to maintain a stable approach. Fully configured and in the vicinity of arriving at minimums, ATC advised a wind shift on the field of 330 degrees at 26 knots of wind. ATC asked for our intentions. Due to airline limitations on Maximum Tailwind Component for Landing, the PM told ATC we could not land and we would go-around. ZZZ1 Tower handed us off to ZZZ Departure and they advised us that they 'turned the airfield around' and they would give us vectors for the ILS RWY XY approach and we would be 'number 1' to the field. Again, the Captain and I communicated that we were both in the green, we noted that we had ample fuel, and we prepared for an ILS approach to Runway XY.After intercepting the localizer for the ILS to Runway XY, I configured fully and continued down the glideslope from the final approach fix. It was raining outside and was windy but we remained stable. Shortly prior to 1,000 feet AGL, it grew increasingly difficult to maintain a stable approach. I told the PM that I didn't feel comfortable, the weather was worsening, and it was likely that we would not be stable at 1,000 feet. We agreed and elected to go-around. Just as I began the go around procedure, we encountered a Wind Shear Warning and I proceeded with the Wind Shear escape maneuver. We exited the conditions quickly and transitioned to ATC's directives. We quickly agreed to divert to ZZZ3 and the PM informed ATC of our intention to divert. We climbed to 3,000 feet and flew vectors to ZZZ3.We flew the ILS RWY XYC approach and landed safely at ZZZ3 and taxied to the gate. We shut down the aircraft with approximately 7.4k pounds of fuel remaining. During the deplaning process, the Captain coordinated with the Maintenance and Dispatch and agreed to continue on to ZZZ1 as the weather cleared the area. We added fuel departing with 11.8k pounds of fuel. The Captain flew as the PF and I was the PM for the return flight to ZZZ1. The Captain maintained appropriate communication throughout the event. He communicated with the passengers explaining as best as possible what occurred and what we were doing to ensure their safety while doing our best to land at our intended destination. He kept the flight attendants apprised of the situation after each approach and we discussed each approach, verified we were both in the green, and maintained situational awareness at all times. Flew RNAV RNP [Runway] XX approach. FO (First Officer) was PF (Pilot Flying) and was configuring the aircraft early. He was at gear down, flaps 15, and we encountered a wind gust that drove the airspeed indication almost to redline. The FO raised nose slightly and reduced power to slow the airspeed in order to continue configuring the aircraft. As this occurred, aircraft got a little high. As PM, I noticed this and was in process of informing FO when ATC said that we looked a little high and to just go around. We executed the missed approach as directed by ATC and climbed on a heading to 3,000 ft. to vector for another approach.On the second RNAV RNP XX, FO configured the aircraft early and shot approach to minimums. At minimums, approach lights and runway lights were visible, but as we turned to final approach, visibility was lost. I called go-around, and FO initiated go-around. We climbed on a heading to 3,000 feet. We communicated with each other that we were both in the green, had plenty of fuel, and prepared for another approach.On the third RNAV RNP XX, the FO had fully configured the aircraft, when ATC advised that the wind had shifted out of the north at 330 degrees and we had 26 knots of wind at our tail. ATC asked our intentions, I told them that we could not land with those winds and that we were going around. At that point, ATC handed us off to departure, and departure immediately advised us that they had turned the airport around and could give us an immediate left downwind to be number 1, shooting ILS Runway XY. FO and I communicated with each other that we were both in the green, had plenty of fuel, and prepared for an approach using the new runway.On attempt to Runway XY, we intercepted localizer and G/S. We had continual high winds indicating to me that the aircraft would not be able to remain stable throughout approach and landing. As PIC, I called for a go-around. FO communicated to me his agreement, and I immediately notified Tower of our intention to divert to ZZZ3. FO initiated the miss. As he did, we encountered a brief Wind Shear Warning. FO finished cleaning aircraft up and we diverted to ZZZ3 without incident.We were vectored to ZZZ3 and landed on Runway XYC and taxied to the gate with 7.4 pounds of fuel. I called Dispatch and she said we had plenty of fuel to get to ZZZ1 but as a precaution due to the frontal weather passage, she added more fuel and brought us up to 11.8 pounds. After the front passage, I flew the aircraft as PF uneventfully to ZZZ1. During all of the approaches and the divert I kept the flight attendants up to date and communicated with the passengers at all times. We exercised good situational awareness and followed SOPs during the entire flight.
ASRS:1791911.s: The First Officer flew Aircraft X from ZZZ2 to ZZZ1, executing multiple go-arounds on RNAV RNP and ILS approaches due to wind gusts, lost visibility, and a 26-knot tailwind exceeding limits. A wind shear warning during the final go-around prompted a diversion to ZZZ3, where the crew landed safely before returning to ZZZ1 after refueling.

ASRS:1791916.n: Green laser event, continued to landing. Still had symptoms the next day but flew one leg as pilot monitoring, ZZZ to ZZZ1. Still having pressure symptoms in left eye.
ASRS:1791916.s: A pilot experienced a green laser event during landing and continued to fly one leg as pilot monitoring from ZZZ to ZZZ1 the next day. The pilot reported ongoing pressure symptoms in the left eye.

ASRS:1791930.n: During brief, maintenance write up for 'Cargo Door' caution had been reported with no prior pressurization issues and MEL issued. This was an additional threat to monitor for. Upon departure, we received a 'cargo door' caution message, and noted the pressurization was indicating decreasing cabin pressure. The QRH procedure was called for and ran. Due to fluctuating pressurization indications, it was decided to divert to ZZZ1 for further investigation into the issue.In my opinion, this event was caused in part due to lack of recent currency as both pilots had been on COVID leave. More important though was lack of threat and error management which led to rushing the QRH procedure. This was a time threat and there was ample opportunity to slow down and evaluate the condition. During the departure phase, there was some task saturation with multiple contacts with ATC and normal checklists procedures.In the future, I need to be more aware of my fellow crew member's task saturation condition level and be pro-active to verbalize when we need to make time and slow things down to avoid rushing through abnormal procedures. Knowing the history of the maintenance issue, we should have completed the departure phase of the flight, requested to level off at 10,000 feet to reduce the workload, and run the QRH at that time. Then, evaluate the condition and determine the best course of action. During the departure briefing I mentioned to the First Officer that we needed to have the Cargo Door checked by ground personnel prior to departure per deferral and failed to do so.I have had this same deferral several times before and was overconfident with the knowledge that nothing has happened since the initial write up. I have been out on COVID leave since December. This was my 1st flight back online. I did not sleep well the night before, I ate something that did not agree well with me for a late lunch the previous day. I was borderline wanting to call in fatigued but thought how bad it would look after 30 hours at the hotel.Don't eat tainted food. Get better rest. Have some sort of reminder to make sure the deferral requirements are met before departure.
ASRS:1791930.s: The crew diverted during departure due to a cargo door caution and pressurization loss, citing rushed QRH execution caused by task saturation, lack of currency, and fatigue. The pilot attributed the error to failing to verify ground checks for the deferred item and rushing the procedure instead of leveling off to reduce workload.

ASRS:1791982.n: On Aircraft X to ZZZ at around XA:00 local time in our descent we received an EGPWS 'Terrain terrain, pull up pull up'. From 3,500 ft. on downwind CA (Captain) [Name] asked me to bug 2,500 ft. on the altitude knob. As we were descending I had mentioned to him that it looked like there may be rising terrain ahead of us. Continuing down to 2,500 ft. shortly after we were given the EGPWS audio to pull up. CA [Name] then clicked auto pilot off, added power and pitched up clearing any terrain that lie below us. The rest of the approach proceeded with no other complications. We had debriefed after engine shutdown at the gate. Looking forward I feel that my actions in this case would be to maybe be more assertive with my thoughts on the possible rising terrain in front of us and suggest to wait to descend until a base turn.
ASRS:1791982.s: During descent to ZZZ, the First Officer and Captain received an EGPWS terrain warning at 3,500 ft after descending to a 2,500 ft bug. The Captain disengaged the autopilot and pitched up to clear terrain, with the First Officer later noting they should have been more assertive about rising terrain before descending.

ASRS:1792041.n: Upon completing the flight in ZZZ Tech Ops requested me to look at aircraft exterior problem. I met him and he showed the forward drain mast had failed and was detached from fuselage but still attached by the drain tube. A visual inspection showed that the trailing 75% of the fairing attach point had been fatigued and failed for some time. There was a fresh break in the forward 25% of the fairing attach point. All components looked intact, but dangling by the drain tube. I did the walk around in ZZZ1, and with total certainty the fairing was in place and attached. It did not appear that a ground object or bird had caused the damage. I believe it just structurally failed during the flight. Tech Ops said they had entered the discrepancy.
ASRS:1792041.s: The pilot inspected the aircraft after landing and found the forward drain mast fairing had structurally failed during flight, leaving it dangling by the drain tube. Fatigue cracks were observed at the attach points, and the pilot ruled out ground or bird strike as the cause.

ASRS:1792059.n: Taking off [Runway] XXL, we had a flight control malfunction. As I was advancing the thrust levers, we immediately began to drift to the right and it felt like the left rudder was jammed. When I tried applying the left rudder, the left brake would actuate. We quickly realized this and rejected the takeoff before reaching even 10 knots as I could not correct to get back on center line. We taxied off and went back to the gate without further incident. Upon arrival at the gate, Maintenance came to inspect the aircraft. Maintenance thought the rudders were operating fine when they inspected the plane and could not tell the left side felt jammed/locked up. Because of this, they wanted us to do a HIGH SPEED taxi. Because nose wheel steering was normal, I said I would be willing to taxi the aircraft but not at a high speed. Before even leaving the ramp area, it was evident to all parties the left rudder pedal was still activating the brake and felt jammed/stiff.The most concerning thing about this incident is we experienced the flight control malfunction only on the takeoff roll and the fact that Maintenance did not know what normal operation of the rudder pedals felt like. They were ready to sign-off on the plane after the proposed high-speed taxi. It felt undermining to me as a flight crew member that Maintenance did not believe our issue/write-up. More concerning is the fact Maintenance could not tell the rudder pedals were functioning improperly at the gate even though the FO (First Officer) and I could easily feel the left side was not operating correctly. NOTE: Aircraft X had A SIMILAR ISSUE before during takeoff in ZZZ1. I had the same trouble with a rejected takeoff due to a pulsating brake and veering to the right, which ended in a high-speed reject. REFER TO [Report], DATE. This was the first time I had a brake/rudder issue in Aircraft X.
ASRS:1792059.s: Flight crew rejected takeoff on Runway XXL due to a left rudder malfunction that actuated the left brake and caused right drift. Maintenance failed to detect the issue at the gate, despite the crew's report and a similar prior incident on the same aircraft type.

ASRS:1792080.n: During preparation for our flight, all pre-flight items and activities were normal. There were no discrepancies were noted. We departed ZZZ for ZZZ1. Once in cruise, the Captain and I noticed the oil quantity decreasing. We consulted the QRH for low oil quantity. As the quantity continued to decrease, the Captain called dispatch and maintenance for any guidance or assistance they could give. The tech told the Captain to follow the QRH. The Captain and I began discussing engine shutdown and diversion scenarios. The oil level eventually fell to zero. Over a period of time, the oil pressure also began to fall slowly and we now were consulting the low oil pressure and engine shutdown procedures in the QRH. In the descent to ZZZ airport , the oil pressure dropped to where the QRH directs engine shutdown. We followed the engine shutdown checklist and [advised the TRACON]. We were vectored for a Visual approach to runway XX. When we transferred to ZZZ1 tower, we were cleared to land. A few miles from landing, ZZZ1 tower advised us that ZZZ2 tower reported possible missing cowlings from our engine. The Captain informed me that he was going to stop on the runway to find out if there was aircraft damage before proceeding to the gate. The landing and rollout were normal and we stopped the aircraft on the runway. After an inspection of the aircraft, the fire commander gave us the all clear to proceed to our gate with rescue personnel following. At the gate and after the jet bridge was brought to the aircraft, we were met by two mechanics. We briefed them on the situation and they went outside to investigate. Once they opened the cowls, I went down to find out if they had any idea what happened. I could see that the inner cowl was covered with oil on the inside, but there was no evidence of oil on the outside of the nacelle and only a little had dripped on the ground. I was told by one of the mechanics that they found an 'oil plug' in the bottom of the inside cowl when they opened the engine cowls. I returned to the cockpit to brief the Captain with the information I acquired on the ramp.
ASRS:1792080.s: Pilots on a ZZZ to ZZZ1 flight experienced decreasing oil quantity and pressure, leading to an engine shutdown during descent. Mechanics later found a missing oil plug inside the engine cowl, which caused the leak and required a runway stop for inspection before taxiing to the gate.

ASRS:1792083.n: Cleared for takeoff on Runway XXR at ZZZ. XX passengers. Aircraft GW about 125,000 lbs. Aircraft accelerated normally using auto-throttles. At about 80 knots, the Right Bleed Trip Off light illuminated. I immediately began the rejected take off procedure. The airspeed may have gotten as high as 90 knots before spoilers and brakes began to decelerate. The aircraft slowed to taxi speed, we turned off at the first taxiway, and returned to the gate. No secondary indications or warning lights. No indication of hot brakes.Recency may have been a minor factor. I had only flown once in the last 30 days. Maybe I could have begun the rejected take off even sooner if I had flown more recently and more often. Still, I think my reaction was pretty good. I believe my decision to abort was a good one.Recency could have been an issue. As soon as I saw the light, I checked the airspeed at 80 and decided to abort. Maybe if I had been flying more regularly, I could have caught the light and reacted even sooner. At any rate, the aircraft GW was 125,000, the deceleration was controlled, and another aircraft was immediately available. Cleared for takeoff. Everything normal and as I said the 80 knots call we got an amber light. Captain asked what have we got, I responded with amber bleed trip light. He elected to reject at approximately 85-95 knots. Cleared runway at A taxiway .Technically speaking, we were just above 80 knots and should have continued but the Captain elected to reject the takeoff. We both discussed it at the gate and both agree that a lack of recent consistent flying may have caused 'quick trigger.'We could have done another quick reject/departure brief holding short to emphasize what reject procedures are.
ASRS:1792083.s: The Captain rejected takeoff at 85–95 knots on Runway XXR after a Right Bleed Trip Off light illuminated at 80 knots. The crew attributed the early abort to a lack of recent flying experience, noting they technically should have continued the takeoff.

ASRS:1792085.n: We setup pre-flight like normal for Runway XX. No takeoff data for Runway YY. After push off the gate we were assigned Runway YY for departure. Before starting we got the data from ACARS for Runway YY. We took our time and entered it in the box. Then briefed the engine out for Runway YY. Since not flying much in the last year I tried to be helpful by entering data on the performance page since I was PF. I took extra caution to confirm the flap setting going to flaps 2 for Runway YY from flaps 1 for Runway XX which was setup in pre-flight and briefed. After starting engines we did flight controls prior to moving since it was a short taxi. Then we completed the before takeoff checklist to the line. Upon reaching Runway YY we were running the before takeoff checklist below the line when I saw we still had Runway XX selected. After noticing that the tower cleared us for takeoff. The First officer changed the runway and we finished the checklist. After taking the runway when I selected flex there was a pause then an ECAM for thrust not being in the detent. I looked down trying to adjust thinking it was set and only just slightly out of the detent. Upon realizing something wasn't right by not getting set power went TOGA as FO also called TOGA and continued as per training and AOM.Not flying much during the pandemic. Even taking our time when things got out of sequence trapping one error not realizing there was more to do. I have been through the training on this exact scenario and thought how could this happen. Well it was incredibly humbling getting lead down the path and once you realize it it's already happened. We literally caught the error during the before takeoff checklist and thinking since we trapped the error during the checklist and completed it that we were ready.Flying more. Any interrupt in the checklist EVEN if you literally trap the error during the checklist start over. Once you trap one error stop and take a minute to regroup then rerun the checklist. Don't think since you fixed it while running the checklist you are done. We entered Runway XX into the FMS since we had no takeoff data information about Runway YY. Upon push back, ATC suggested Runway YY was preferred for the winds. I sent a request for data through ACARS. As a crew we entered the new data into the performance page and reviewed the engine out departure for Runway YY. The Captain decided to start both engines and preform the before takeoff checklist to the line prior to taxi so that I would not be task saturated on the short taxi out. As we proceeded to taxi and complete the checklist below the line, the Captain saw that the correct runway was not in the FMS. I corrected the runway and we continued to finish the checklist. When cleared for takeoff the Captain set the thrust levers in the flex detent, we received an ECAM stating the thrust was not in the detent. The Captain, as well as I thought that possibly the levers were not properly placed in the detent. When I realized something was not quite right I called for TOGA and the Captain immediately pushed the thrust to TOGA.After being off for almost a year myself and the Captain not flying much on reserve as well as taking leaves was a large factor. Though we caught one error with the checklist we did not follow through and catch the other. I have had this very scenario in my first simulator about 2 years ago and still fell down the path. We should have restarted the checklist from the top once we saw that there was any incorrect information in the FMS.Follow our training! Try to stay current as best as possible. We worked as a crew and had a good outcome, it would've been an even better one had we just redone the checklist.
ASRS:1792085.s: The crew entered incorrect runway data into the FMS after a runway change, causing a thrust detent ECAM warning during takeoff. They applied TOGA thrust and continued the departure safely, attributing the error to low recent flight time and failing to restart the checklist after correcting the initial FMS input.

ASRS:1792162.n: I was working on my Aircraft X on [Date], when I started my work the day was windy above 40 knots so my screen inspection was postponed. I was then helping my partner on the service check inspection assigned to him. Later on in the night around the wind slowed down. I had already picked up my job packings (seals) and a tire pressure gauge. When I started to set up to do my job card my partner went to stores to get me a torque wrench. I completed the TGB (Transfer Gear Box) inspection screens for both Engine 1 and Engine 2. Two coworkers [Name] and [Name1] preformed both 1 and 2 engine run. I preformed leak check inspections on both engines, I found no leaks. I heard that the aircraft I was working on had an oil leak. I don't know if the oil leak had anything to do with the work I preformed on the engines. I don't believe I properly documented the inspection for Engine 1 scavenge screen. This is my first time doing this job, I believe my work was preformed good, although my paper work was not documented properly, at the time it seamed that I needed to preform both engine inspections. Assigned chip detector card for #2 Engine. Later that night AMT (Aviation Maintenance Technician) came to me for leak check of both engines. I question as to why are we leak checking both engines when only #2 Engine was assigned. AMT inform me he also did the #1 Engine. He leaked check both engines and I informed him of documenting #1 Engine's work. Work card changed to work card and does not indicate on the card left or right engine, making it confusing for the AMT. I did not follow up with the AMT to verified #1 Engine's chip detector was done.On paperwork specifically state which engine requires the work to be accomplished.
ASRS:1792162.s: A mechanic performing a first-time TGB inspection on Aircraft X failed to properly document the Engine 1 scavenge screen check due to confusing work cards that did not specify the engine side. This documentation error occurred alongside an unrelated reported oil leak, prompting a recommendation to clearly state which engine requires work on paperwork.

ASRS:1792168.n: Requested 131,000 lbs of fuel at departure. Speaking with fueler, Name 1, and myself all agreed to put 40,000 lbs of fuel in the #3 fuel tank. I was in the flight deck while #3 fuel tank was being fueled. Once the fueler was done fueling the #3 fuel tank Name 1 verified the fuel added by verifying the fuel sticks #6 and #7 in fuel tank #3. We then entered the fuel stick numbers into the fuel stick calculator where we determined the total fuel added to tank #3. We got approximately 36,600 lbs of fuel. We then went to the maintenance office and consulted with our lead. We had determined that the fueler had shorted us on the fuel load for fuel tank #3. We then called to have an additional 3,000 lbs of fuel added to fuel tank #3. Once the additional fuel was added to fuel tank #3 we verified this on stick #6 multiple times by both Name 1 and myself. Stick #7 had already been checked and was indicating full. We verified stick #6 and it too indicated the correct calculated fuel for fuel tank #3. We used the fuel calculator to verify again that we had the correct fuel in tank #3 with 40,000/lbs. Once this was all done we discussed with the flight crew the error that occurred with the first fuel load and the addition 3,000 lbs added to fuel tank #3 to give us a total of 40,000 lbs of fuel for fuel tank #3. They were content with this and after deicing the aircraft we pushed them off the gate. Once the aircraft departed, I gave the log sheet to my lead Name 2 to enter into workbench. He had entered it as was written. During the last fuel upload to tank #3 I made a correction to the log page indicating the new stick indications for sticks 6 and 7 giving us a total fuel load in tank # 3 of 40,000 lbs. I forgot to correct this new total fuel on the log sheet. However, the stick indications showed that the correct fuel was in tank #3. The engine flameout I feel needs to be investigate further to determine if there was something that we could have done to prevent this. During transit of Aircraft X through ZZZ it had a fuel MEL for #3 tank that requires us to fuel by stick. The two AMT's (Aircraft Maintenance Technicians) assigned to it were Name 3 and Name 1. I asked them to transfer the fuel out of #3 tank so that they were able to fuel #3 tank using the fuelers receipt and then verify that the fuel is correct with the sticks. After they had fueled the aircraft they brought the fuel slips and their tank readings into the lead office. At that time they calculated what they put onboard and showed me the stick readings they had, after putting the information into the stick calculator we found that #3 tank was at 36,491 lbs, so at that time I asked them to add more fuel bringing the #3 fuel tank to 40,000 lbs to match the #1 tank. We then called for the fueler to return to aircraft to bring the #3 tank to the correct level. After that the only information I have is what the times for fuel completion and off aircraft. After the airplane left I was asked to enter the log pages for the aircraft which I did. After I had checked into the log page that I entered for Name 3 I had missed entering the lbs added which was actually incorrect but wasn't changed on the log page only the sticks were changed and initialed. The log page stated that the total uplift to #3 engine was 36,491 which I missed when entering. If you calculate per the corrected stick and inch the total is actually 39,904 lbs, these figures are per the fuel calculator supplied by Company. Need to be more careful entering log pages and double check for accurate imputing.
ASRS:1792168.s: Maintenance technicians and a fueler under-fueled Tank #3 on Aircraft X during pre-departure, requiring an additional 3,000 lbs to reach the target 40,000 lbs. Although physical stick checks confirmed the correct load, the log sheet was incorrectly entered with the initial lower figure, and the reporter noted a subsequent engine flameout requiring investigation.

ASRS:1792183.n: To do my job as Captain I must inspect and declare my Hazmat to my Dispatcher. Before my flight I filled out a Hazmat form given to me by my company to declare Hazmat. On this form I am obligated to declare how many boxes, contents, how much of each Hazmat, hazard class, their location in the airplane and various other Hazmat information. Nowhere on my company given form is there a space for the packing group of each Hazmat. When I called in to my Dispatcher on the phone to let them know all the information I had written on the form the Dispatcher told me that I was released for flight. Upon landing at my destination I was ramp checked by an FAA Hazmat inspector. She informed me that it was odd that my packing groups were not declared. I told her the truth that I did not tell my Dispatcher the packing group information on the Hazmat and that I only told the Dispatcher what was on my form. She asked me how the Dispatcher could get this information and I told her that I regularly mail in each individual Hazmat slip that contains all the Hazmat information for each individual box including packing groups. It is company policy to mail these slips and forms in and I follow our policies. After this encounter I went to my company FOM and found nothing pertaining to declaring packing groups on our FOM page describing how to fill out our Hazmat forms.
ASRS:1792183.s: The Captain declared Hazmat to the Dispatcher using a company form lacking a packing group field and received flight release. An FAA inspector later noted the missing packing groups, which the Captain attributed to the form's design and company policy requiring separate mailed slips.

ASRS:1792193.n: After trimming for level flight and while adjusting the prop for cruise, the airplane suddenly started shaking violently at a regular and high frequency. Thinking that something had gone wrong with the prop, I reduced throttle to try to reduce the severity of the shaking, but this had no apparent effect. Engine oil pressure and temperature were both well within the green range. We had just departed a nearby airport, so turned around to land. I noticed that keeping the nose of the airplane up required significant back pressure. Adjusting the trim appeared to have no effect. Enroute to the airport the shaking suddenly stopped. We continued to land without incident. After stopping the airplane on the ground we inspected the trim tab and found that it was stuck in nose-down position. Looking underneath the elevator, we found that the trim-tab control rod was not connected where it usually met the horizontal stabilizer. The end of the trim-tab control rod towards the stabilizer appeared to have been bent and broken. It appeared that at some point the rod broke and jammed. After replacing and reattaching the trim control rod the airplane is operating normally and has been returned to service. Speculation is that at some point the bolt connecting the rod had either partially failed or come loose, causing uneven stress on the control rod, eventually resulting in failure due to metal fatigue. The elevator trim cable had recently been replaced but it is not clear if the control rod had been touched as part of that work. Inspection of this connection point can be done simply and quickly during pre-flight and may benefit from increased awareness as a possible or likely point of failure.
ASRS:1792193.s: The pilot experienced violent shaking and trim failure shortly after departure due to a broken elevator trim control rod. The aircraft landed safely after the shaking ceased, and post-flight inspection revealed the rod had detached from the horizontal stabilizer, likely due to metal fatigue from a loose bolt.

ASRS:1792204.n: I inadvertently flew into R-5017B following along I70 Northeast of Las Cruces Int'l Airport (LRU) due to poor chart verbiage. I am requesting an update be made to the VFR charts here in this area to be more clear about R-5017B. Currently, on the chart it reads 'R-5017B EXCLUDES THE AIRSPACE AT AND BELOW 1500 ft. AGL'. I fly all across the United States testing ground based communications for leakage on certain frequencies for FAA and FCC compliance. I fly these grids at 1500 AGL and when I checked my Las Cruces grid (as I always check the airspace I'll be flying in) I noticed that the grid was partially inside of R-5107B yet noticed the text on the chart and was surprised (to what my interpretation was) that I was going to be able to hit the grid over the town of White Sands seeing as I fly my grids at and below 1500 AGL. I was not on flight following as all my grids in this are were in uncontrolled airspace and I was more free to switch between the different CTAF's I would be able to monitor traffic and report positions on. It wasn't until I called up center to get flight following from my on site station to ABQ that I was told to copy a number for pilot deviation. I have sent pictures of the VFR chart to many very seasoned pilots along with a few CFI's today after my incident without telling them what happened, each of their interpretations of the text on the VFR charting was identical to mine. I hope that my experience today helps to hopefully change the chart to make it more clear, that there is only a very small specific area for the excluded airspace and to prevent further pilot deviation in this area.
ASRS:1792204.s: A pilot conducting ground-based communications testing inadvertently entered R-5017B northeast of Las Cruces while flying at 1500 feet AGL due to ambiguous chart verbiage regarding airspace exclusions. The pilot received a deviation notice from Air Traffic Control and requested a chart update to clarify the restricted area and prevent future incidents.

ASRS:1792218.n: I was on short, short final for Runway XX at ZZZ with a touch-and-go clearance. At an altitude of approximately 400 ft. AGL and about 0.4 SM from the runway threshold, ZZZ Tower cleared a Cirrus for takeoff. As the Cirrus began entering the runway, I rejected the landing and began to apply full power before the tower instructed me to go around and side-step to the right. I acknowledged the go-around, and requested a north departure, which was granted to follow the Cirrus that had just taken off. I'm unsure whether ATC inattention, loss of awareness of spacing, or simply the desire to get that traffic out caused this unsafe clearance to be issued. I would expect that controllers be aware of traffic on final and not issue conflicting releases of departing traffic.
ASRS:1792218.s: A pilot on short final for Runway XX at ZZZ rejected a landing at 400 ft AGL after Tower cleared a Cirrus for takeoff. The pilot attributed the unsafe clearance to potential ATC inattention or loss of spacing awareness regarding the arriving aircraft.

ASRS:1792222.n: I was in level cruise at 11,000 [ft.] in clear VMC flying on an IFR flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1, following the filed airway on autopilot. I was on with ZZZ2 approach, the normal facility that handles this patch of airspace, and had received proper IFR advisories regarding other aircraft. My aircraft has an advanced glass panel with ADS-B In traffic information which I monitor as part of my scan - particularly when using the autopilot to reduce physical workload. Suddenly, I saw a traffic alert pop up on my avionics and it showed an aircraft at the same altitude, or within about 100 feet, very close to my location and approaching from behind with approximately a 30 knot overtake. The speed and the 000000 identifier confirmed that it was not an ADS-B 'ghost' and I became alarmed. I asked approach if they saw said airplane and I looked over my right shoulder, out the rear window to see a low wing, single engine airplane that I estimated was about the size of a BE36 or PA46 bearing down on me at high speed and a similar altitude. ZZZ2 said they had just seen the ADS-B target pop up and didn't know who it was and weren't talking to them. The aircraft was so close and approaching so fast that I immediately disconnected the autopilot and put my airplane into a rapid descent to avoid. The aircraft passed very close, but I was luckily below it by that time. ZZZ2 switched me to ZZZ3 Center and I also reported the same issue. The facilities had the aircraft on radar and ADS-B, but could not identify who they were. I found the target on a flight tracker app and was able to get the ICAO 24 Bit code, which identified the aircraft as a T34C (Ironically, a modified military trainer version of the aircraft I was flying). Not only was I affected, but other IFR and VFR aircraft had to contend with this unsafe behavior as well. The aircraft flew along it's merry way at primarily an IFR altitude, not talking to literally anyone. This was unsafe and improper. I have no idea if the folks flying that airplane saw me, but I sure knew I didn't want to find out and had to take immediate emergency action to avoid. There is simply no reason for military trainers to be off frequency, even VFR, for any reason. There is even less reason for them to violate regs and fly IFR altitudes while not flying under IFR.
ASRS:1792222.s: A pilot in a T34C at 11,000 feet on an IFR cruise encountered an unidentified T34C flying at the same altitude without radio contact. The pilot executed an emergency descent to avoid a collision after the uncommunicative aircraft approached rapidly from behind.

ASRS:1792232.n: Local training flight from ZZZ. PIC (Pilot-in-Command) was a highly experienced glider pilot receiving a dual flight from this reporter (CFI-Gliders) to demonstrate proficiency for becoming a 'mentor pilot' for this glider club. This was his second flight of this evolution and he had requested to do a simulated rope break. The flight was briefed with the tow pilot before takeoff and also between both pilots in the glider. The takeoff was an aero-tow behind the club tow aircraft and was uneventful. At 300-350 ft. AGL the release was actuated and the glider made an uneventful turn toward the runway end with ample altitude and airspeed. In the course of the approach the pilot-flying extended the air brakes and failed to retract them at an appropriate time to allow adequate remaining altitude for a normal landing on the runway. The pilot-not flying immediately told the pilot-flying to close the air brakes and such action by the pilot-flying was delayed until the pilot-not flying immediately closed the air brakes to avoid collision with the embankment at a lower level. The aircraft struck the end of the runway at a slope embankment about 2 feet below the grass runway surface elevation and came to rest upright and on the grass runway landing surface. Inspection revealed a wrinkle about 6' x 12' on the left lower fuselage just forward of the main landing gear door (single wheel landing gear). No other damage was immediately apparent and both occupants were uninjured and the glider was towed back to the tie down area and disassembled. Later inspection revealed a small wrinkle, about 1/4' height, on the upper surface of each wing about 18' outboard of the wing root.The pilot-flying is commercial rated in gliders and the pilot-not flying was commercial, CFI rated in gliders.Cause: Failure of pilot-flying to maintain adequate altitude on final approach caused by mismanagement of air brakes. Failure of pilot-not flying to recognize and intervene sooner with closing the air brakes when the pilot-flying failed to do so.
ASRS:1792232.s: During a local glider training flight, the pilot-in-command failed to retract air brakes on final approach, causing the aircraft to strike a runway embankment. The CFI intervened late to close the brakes, resulting in minor fuselage and wing damage but no injuries.

ASRS:1792233.n: After completing a run-up, my student and I taxied to the Runway XX hold short line and advised ZZZ Tower, '(Aircraft X), [Taxiway] XX, [Runway] XX, ready for departure'. We received a takeoff clearance from ZZZ Tower and entered Runway XX, after confirming the Runway XX final approach was clear. Upon lining up with the runway center line, my student applied full power, as part of the takeoff procedure. After checking the engine instruments and airspeed indicator conditions, I looked up and observed an airplane flying not more than 300 ft. above our right wing. This airplane (Aircraft Y) then proceeded to overfly us and land not more than 1,000 feet of my airplane on Runway XX, which was occupied by us at that time. I immediately aborted the takeoff and exited the runway at XX1, then advised the tower that we were aborting.ZZZ Tower cancelled our takeoff clearance and questioned Aircraft Y, asking why they executed an unauthorized short approach, which led to loss of separation between our two aircraft and furthermore led to a runway incursion that could have been detrimental.ZZZ Tower did what they could to assist with the situation and made it clear to Aircraft Y that their actions were unacceptable and reckless.
ASRS:1792233.s: A student pilot and instructor aborted a takeoff on Runway XX after Aircraft Y flew within 300 feet of their right wing and landed 1,000 feet ahead while the runway was occupied. The incident, caused by Aircraft Y's unauthorized short approach, resulted in a loss of separation and a runway incursion.

ASRS:1792243.n: This morning while airborne, passenger and I noted heater to be working quite a bit better than usual. Cabin was comfortably warm. The heater had been on for about 30 minutes, normal smells associated with combustion heater were present.
