At the 30-45 minute point both the passenger and I both went to clean eyeglasses at the same time. No abnormal smells were present, just a light smoke. We immediately turned heater to fan only position, opened a window to clear smoke, and returned to the field. Upon contacting Tower, we advised smoke in the cockpit and asked for priority landing. Tower gave instructions for straight in approach and asked if we were [requesting priority]. We replied in the afirmative. Upon landing smoke was minimal, and we continued to the ramp. We were met by the fire department. After looking with heat detection equipment it was determined the plane was not a threat. Maintenance on the field was contacted and we are pending mechanical inspection. No injuries, or related illness as of several hours later.
ASRS:1792243.s: The pilot and passenger experienced light smoke from the combustion heater during flight, prompting an immediate return for a priority landing. Fire department inspection found no threat, and the aircraft awaits maintenance with no injuries reported.

ASRS:1792268.n: 8 miles south of FNL we contacted the FNL Tower to request a touch and go then a departure to the east after the touch and go. The Tower requested that we contact them for a right downwind for Runway 15 when 4 miles south of the airfield. At the 4 mile mark we were unable to contact the Tower due to the fact the frequency was so busy that each time we tried to contact them we were stepped on. We were midfield right downwind by the time we were able to talk to the Tower. They were very upset yet there was nothing we could have done. We were cleared for the touch and go on Runway 15 then an east departure after that.The Tower requested we let them know when we were 4 miles east of the airport on our departure leg. At the 4 mile mark we contacted the Tower to let the Controller know. At the exact same time there was a helicopter that flew over us at less than 300 feet. We told the Tower we had the traffic insight. We had the helicopter in sight yet the Tower did not inform us about this traffic.FNL is a remote Tower and ATC (Tower) has limited visibility around the airport. My experience with this remote Tower is they do not have the same situational awareness that a full manned Tower would have. Congested airspace at FNL. Verbal traffic overwhelmed controller and was unable to get word in edgewise. Our comms were being stepped on constantly. Flying with a CFI we were unable to announce our 4 mile location until actually in a 3 mile downwind for Runway 15. Controller was verbally upset, but was still able to sequence us for arrival to complete a touch and go and make an east departure.
ASRS:1792268.s: A pilot and CFI in a training aircraft experienced communication congestion at FNL Tower, delaying their downwind call until midfield. During the subsequent east departure, a helicopter passed within 300 feet without prior ATC traffic advisories due to the controller's limited situational awareness and overwhelmed frequency.

ASRS:1792271.n: Received clearance to land on [Runway] 28R at MYF. Informed that another aircraft was landing on the parallel 28L runway. Was lined up for 28R. Watched the 28L traffic turn base and final on the ADSB display. Their base to final turn put them very close to my position. ADSB display was indicating yellow for close traffic. I looked outside the aircraft to visually identify the 28L aircraft but it was slightly above and behind me being blocked by the wing. During my quick scan for the aircraft, I inadvertently drifted closer to the 28L extended centerline. I raised the wing and identified the parallel aircraft. I was within several hundred feet of that aircraft. Immediately dove and turned to the right to get away from the aircraft and re-align with the 28R centerline. Rest of approach and landing were normal.
ASRS:1792271.s: The pilot, while lined up for Runway 28R at MYF, drifted toward the parallel 28L centerline due to a blocked visual scan of close traffic. The pilot corrected by diving and turning right to avoid a near-miss within several hundred feet, then completed a normal landing.

ASRS:1792279.n: Began taxi to Runway XX for north departure to ZZZ1. EMS flight with patient on board. Applied power and after plane taxied approx 10-15 feet an uncommanded right wheel hard stop occurred which caused a sharp 90 degree turn. The nose wheel hit a snow bank and the right wing hit a fence post. Reverse power was applied to move plane back onto taxiway. No injuries. Pilot determined that [the] plane was not airworthy and shut down. Company was contacted. Pilot/airport observers/med crew all concurred that it appeared the right brake was stuck or something impeded the movement of the right tire. There was no FOD, ice, or snow on the ramp - dry clear pavement. Wind was 020 at 7 with no gust factor. Unlimited ceilings and unlimited visibility. OAT 45F. Company contacted FAA and pilot was sent for a DOT post accident [incident] screen. Pilot removed from line duty until results of DOT screen are obtained. Event occurred at approximately XA:00 on date. A mechanic was dispatched but then company informed pilot to move plane back off taxiway as no mechanic would be coming that night after all. Pilot reviewed event in detail and determined that nothing was non-standard as far as flows/checklists/standard procedures regarding start and taxi.
ASRS:1792279.s: During an EMS taxi for departure, an uncommanded right brake stop caused a sharp turn, striking a snow bank and fence post. The pilot grounded the aircraft, citing a stuck brake or tire impediment, with no injuries reported and the pilot removed from duty pending a DOT screen.

ASRS:1792281.n: Busy airport traffic pattern on [my] lesson solo. Multiple aircraft in traffic pattern of several different types. I was instructed to make left base for Runway 30L. I started to turn base without being cleared to land. Two aircraft, including myself and another aircraft which was on a very extended downwind south of the delta nearly 5 miles south of where I was turning 'base', were instructed to make a right turn to re-enter the downwind to give landing space to an air carrier. I had never heard this command but interpreted it to mean to make a 360 back into the traffic pattern. Aircraft Y in front of me was given the instruction first and immediately started their turn to the right. When I was given the instruction, I waited to try to ask Gateway Tower what they meant, but the frequency was too busy. I decided to start the turn to the right to make a 360 to re-enter the downwind. Unfortunately, my slow thinking led to me making a turn at the same time that the aircraft in front of me was already almost finished with their turn. This resulted in a near head-on collision. The other aircraft fortunately realized this, pulled up and turned to their right promptly. I saw the aircraft fly over me and assumed it was an aircraft coming south from the gap with an odd pattern entry. Although a bit flustered, I was able to land the airplane and thought of it as a bad coincidence. The flight instructor on-board the other aircraft in the incident, approached me after my flight and asked to discuss once I returned. We discussed the incident and my flight instructor who was not on-board my solo flight, was also notified and joined us in the debrief.
ASRS:1792281.s: A student pilot on a solo lesson at a busy airport initiated a right turn to re-enter downwind without a specific clearance, causing a near head-on collision with another aircraft ahead. The other pilot avoided impact by pulling up and turning right, and the incident was later debriefed with both flight instructors.

ASRS:1792290.n: I was flying solo in an experimental aircraft and just as I was touching the ground on landing experience a wind gust from the right side. I ran out of right rudder and the plane tipped onto the the left wing tip starting a ground loop at approximately 15 mph ground speed. The tail spun around, a prop-strike occurred, then a tail-strike. I climbed out of the aircraft after shutting everything off and was uninjured. The airplane sustained some damage to the empennage and a propeller. No property damage or harm to any person occurred.
ASRS:1792290.s: A solo pilot flying an experimental aircraft experienced a right wind gust during landing, causing a loss of right rudder control. The aircraft ground-looped at 15 mph, resulting in a propeller strike and tail damage, but the pilot remained uninjured.

ASRS:1792293.n: Accidental cutoff of aircraft in traffic patternI had recently gone flying as I hadn't been up much lately, and maintained closed traffic at the airport to re-familiarize myself with the aircraft and work on my landings. Since this airport is the main airport for a flight school, multiple aircraft were joining and leaving the pattern, necessitating Tower to have aircraft extend on departure and downwind legs of the pattern. As I was in a left downwind for Runway XX, Tower instructed all aircraft remaining in the pattern to extend upwind 3 miles after takeoff, and I made note of this as I was planning to do a couple more loops in the pattern. About 30 seconds later, Tower asked if I had the traffic (a PA28) on short final for Runway XX in sight. I did, and Tower cleared me for the option. I performed a touch and go and began climbing on the departure leg.As I was finishing the climb and extending the departure leg, I noted a call from Tower to the PA28 asking for their position, with the PA28 reporting they were in the crosswind leg. Tower then called me to tell me to extend upwind 3 miles and do right traffic for Runway XX. I estimated as having already done about 1.5 miles due to Tower's notification about doing so earlier, and the delay from Tower informing me again was due to the influx of traffic into the airspace. I continued on for about another minute and then began my right crosswind turn. While on the crosswind leg, Tower called the PA28 to inform them that they would be number 4 in the pattern and following traffic on the left downwind. The PA28 reported that they had been cut off on crosswind and would follow the traffic in front of them. Tower called and asked for my position, which I reported as right crosswind, and Tower asked the PA28 if they observed a Skyhawk in front of them. The PA28 responded with an affirmative and Tower informed them to follow me. Several seconds later, I turned onto the downwind leg and was able to observe the PA28 about 3/4ths of a mile behind me and finishing a turn from crosswind onto downwind. Nothing else of note happened after and I chose to make this my last loop in the traffic pattern, and performed a full stop landing a few minutes later.At the time, I knew that I had missed whether or not the PA28 would be right or left traffic. I had heard their report to Tower of being on crosswind as I started my departure leg and felt that they would not be any conflict no matter which pattern they were in. While I do recognize that it is the pilot's responsibility to maintain separation in the Class Delta and that Tower's workload had increased with the amount of aircraft in the airspace, I did not receive any calls notifying me of traffic (earlier in the flight Tower had informed me of traffic ahead of me on upwind and I did not turn crosswind until I was able to verify that they had finished their crosswind turn and passed me on downwind). Since I had cut off the PA28, I figured the only possibility was that I had turned into my crosswind turn too early. However, I was confused about this as the PA28 had reported being on crosswind at least a full minute before I had even started my crosswind turn, and I could not figure out as to how they would then end up behind me.I did end up pulling both my flight data and the PA28's flight data from FlightAware.com and the ATC audio from LiveATC.com to try and piece together what happened, and it seems several factors played a role in this. For starters, I had missed the call to the PA28 informing them that they would be right traffic. This was something I knew I had missed during the flight, and listening to the audio showed that they were told this after I had been cleared to land initially on Runway XX, meaning that I was likely focused on my touch and go instead of calls to other aircraft. I recognize that I need to work on still listening fully to Tower on this phase of flight if I will be rejoining the pattern, as it is importantto have a mental picture of where other aircraft are within the airspace.I also likely did start my crosswind turn early, as the data from FlightAware seems to pinpoint my turn as having started no further than 2.5 miles upwind. This is likely due to me misjudging my timing and distance in the aircraft after takeoff and is something I will need to also work on.With those in mind, the data from the PA28 also shows that it played a major factor in this event. After takeoff, the PA28 extended about 4.5 miles upwind while also drifting left of the runway. As such, their position report to Tower of being in the crosswind was likely when they just started their turn and the amount of time spent in the crosswind would be lengthened due to their drift left. The longer upwind extension would also explain how they ended up behind me once I turned onto the downwind leg. I am unsure if Tower recognized that the PA28 had drifted left and extended so far out, but I am assuming that they did not as no call was made informing me of their position or the potential for conflict.Overall, my own misjudgments of my timing and distance, mistake in missing calls for other aircraft to have an idea of what is going on big picture (as I would have been able to recognize that I would essentially be following an aircraft in the right traffic pattern), and the PA28's over extension and drift on the departure leg contributed to this event.
ASRS:1792293.s: The pilot of a Skyhawk accidentally cut off a PA28 on the crosswind leg while rejoining the traffic pattern at a Class Delta airport. The reporter attributes the incident to their own early turn and missed ATC calls, combined with the PA28's excessive upwind extension and left drift.

ASRS:1792322.n: I departed from ZZZZ1 flying to ZZZZ. Approximately 25 DME west of ZZZZ at XA:18pm local time, I was in a shallow descent passing through 4,200 feet, when I experienced a power loss on the right engine. At the time of power loss, both engines had been operating on the outboard tanks (normal procedure) for approximately 1.7 hrs. I noticed a loss of fuel pressure on the right engine. Assuming the outboard tanks were low on fuel, I immediately selected the inboard tanks on both fuel selectors which contained approximately 30 gallons remaining per side. Emergency electric fuel pumps were also switched on. Passing through 3700 feet within the first minute, airspeed immediately and rapidly decreased from 170kts to 120kts. Emergency procedures were implemented, all throttle quadrant levers pushed forward. The right engine was identified as the issue and verified as producing partial power, R/H engine 20' MP/2000 RPM, L/H engine 40' MP/2600 RPM. I started to secure the right engine, important to note, when pulling back the throttle and prop levers, airspeed rapidly dropped even more. Blue line (VYSE), 106kts was extremely difficult to maintain. By pushing the throttle and prop lever back in the forward position the airplane appeared more responsive. The aircraft was not responding as it normally does during one engine operation. The right engine appeared to be making some power and the propeller low pitch configuration still produced a low airspeed result. At XA:25pm the aircraft passed through 2,000 feet. Blue line airspeed was unattainable regardless of propeller pitch. Maintaining altitude proved impossible. Engine failure was reported to ZZZZ Tower. The nearest airport was searched for, however, ZZZZ2 depiction was not listed. The decision to land off-field was made at XA:30pm. I passed through 1,300 feet and prepared to land on a nearby road. At 500 feet trucks and power lines were noticed. The decision to turn north and land in an empty field was made. Passing through 300 feet it appeared the field was made, the ground looked hard packed between the plant rows. The decision to drop gear and flaps to increase drag and in hopes of rolling out was made. Fuel was shut off and the electrical master switch was shut off. The aircraft was flown to the ground. After landing the aircraft, I exited the aircraft with my crewmember. There were no injuries. I called the authorities to report the accident [incident].
ASRS:1792322.s: The pilot reported a right engine power loss at 4,200 feet due to fuel pressure issues while descending to ZZZZ. Unable to maintain blue line airspeed or altitude, the pilot executed an off-field landing in an empty field with no injuries.

ASRS:1792327.n: Private pilot student working toward a commercial certificate, practicing a simulated engine out within 1 mile of the runway from 2,200 AGL. The student was guiding the aircraft toward the runway. We had passed the threshold and were still high. I (the instructor) was directing coordinated S turns in order to not overshoot the available runway. We were using Runway X with winds approximately 330 at 7kts. On the last turn back toward the runway we were just west of the runway and I then noticed that airspeed was getting too low, we attempted to still land the plane, at this point only about 20ft above ground. We continued the descent and were touching down on the runway but not aligned with the runway. The student initiated a bank to realign the aircraft with the runway and the left wing apparently scraped the runway without any indication on the flight controls. I took the controls and leveled the wings, controlling the aircraft through a bounce. We departed the runway at an angle into the grass median between the runway and taxiway A. We continued the ground roll in the grass, crossing taxiway G before coming to a stop. Upon shutting down and inspecting the aircraft we found the scrape on the left wingtip and corner of the left aileron.
ASRS:1792327.s: A flight instructor and student practicing a simulated engine-out landing from 2,200 feet AGL lost airspeed and touched down misaligned. The student's corrective bank caused the left wingtip to scrape the runway, leading to a bounce and an off-runway excursion into the grass median.

ASRS:1792330.n: Prior to the near-miss event, we made several CTAF calls with our intentions of entering the straight-in left downwind for Runway 32 from the north. An aircraft on the runway then announced their intentions to depart 32 to the north towards the Needles VOR. At this point, it is assumed he was going to make a straight-out departure to the north and climb since he did not specify. Instead, this aircraft initiated a left crosswind departure towards the west while we were entering the left downwind at approximately 1,700 MSL, while the aircraft was at around 1,400-1,500 MSL and crossed under us. My guess is that the other aircraft 'saw and avoided' and stopped his climb at approximately 1,500 MSL while we were at approximately 1,700 MSL. While the aircraft was on the left crosswind climb, I identified traffic and applied throttle, and climbed only approximately 100 feet or so to evade since I spotted the traffic sooner. No calls were exchanged after the near-miss event. In retrospect, I should asked the departing traffic for clarification on his departing direction and entered the pattern at a much higher altitude.
ASRS:1792330.s: The pilot reported a near-miss while entering the left downwind for Runway 32 at 1,700 MSL as a departing aircraft climbed on a left crosswind at 1,400–1,500 MSL. The pilot attributed the event to the departing aircraft's unannounced turn and evaded by climbing 100 feet after spotting the traffic.

ASRS:1792349.n: Moderate turbulence below 14,000 feet. Heavy winds as well. 290/19 G29 on the ground. Cleared Visual Approach 34L. Approach was normal, but Captain very busy dealing with speed fluctuations and turbulence. I was double checking the winds with Tower. Watching terrain as well. Adjusted REF speeds for gusts and prevailing winds. Captain called for flaps 30, I inadvertently moved flap handle to 25 and did not know it. Everything was good until short final, we got Too Low Flaps" aural alert. We executed go-around immediately. Need to look down and see if correct flap detention is selected." On flight to RNO we received a Too Low Flaps warning from the GPWS around 500 feet AGL on an approach to Runway 34L. We had continuous moderate turbulence below 13,000 feet MSL on our approach and that was distracting. We were on a high right base leg because of the terrain. We were cleared for the visual on the right base leg. Also, on base we were gear down flaps 15, and near flaps 15 approach speed. I called for flaps 30 and the Before Landing checklist well above 1,000 feet AGL, because I wanted the extra drag. I did not notice the flaps were at position 25 during the Before Landing checklist. Our REF speed was plus 9 and then increased to plus 15 with the new Tower winds. At about 500 feet AGL we received the Too Low Flaps warning and I did a go-round. We were vectored for another approach to Runway 34L and did a normal landing.I felt task loaded on the approach. I was concerned about the turbulence, terrain, and changing surface winds. I let these additive condition distract me while doing the Before Landing Check List. I should have bought myself more time by asking for a longer down wind on the approach.
ASRS:1792349.s: The crew experienced moderate turbulence and heavy winds during a visual approach to Runway 34L at RNO. Task saturation led to an inadvertent flap setting of 25 instead of 30, triggering a "Too Low Flaps" warning at 500 feet AGL and requiring a go-around before a successful second landing.

ASRS:1792355.n: Visual to 27 at SAN using RNAV Z. Ceiling was BKN015. Crew briefed visual procedures at altitude but was informed that ATIS had changed late in the descent, crew adjusted minimums to account for the updated ceiling. Earlier I had queried the Captain if he preferred flaps 40 for SAN and he said he wanted flaps 30. Vref was 141 knots, wind component added 6 knots for a VTARGET of 147 knots. Captain configured early and we were stable at 1,000 feet AGL with a slightly high VVI (Vertical Velocity Indicator) due to SAN Runway 27 3.5 degree approach and the high weight and subsequent high approach speed. We were visual at that point, I think we broke out at 1,000-1,200 feet. Every time I crosschecked the speed and VVI, the Captain was stable, with the knowledge that the 3.5 degree approach and speed (as mentioned in the Safety Alert) would result in VVI rates over 1,000 feet. I was crosschecking radar altitudes and glideslope guidance more than I usually do, but this is my personal habit for SAN. As I did the normal 'in and out' visual crosscheck, nothing seemed amiss. Directly over or slightly after the parking deck on short final, the Captain slightly adjusted his visual aim point as is common technique at SAN. My eyes were outside at this point. We both heard a 'sink rate...'. I don't know what the second phrase was, as the Captain acknowledged the first sink rate forcefully and almost instantly. I quickly looked inside and I think I saw 'pull up' on the bottom of the PFD for what seemed like an instant. I can't be certain, however, and it can't be understated how fast it went away if indeed it was there. I looked back up and we were two red and two white on the PAPI, slightly fast, and Captain was in what looked like a good position to land. We made a safe landing and applied moderate braking and exited the runway. In the postflight, the Captain and I disagreed about what the second term was at the aural system annunciated. He thinks he heard 'sink rate, sink rate.' I actually don't know what the second term the aural system annunciated was, as I didn't hear it clearly due to the Captain's acknowledgment of it. I do think I saw a very fleeting 'pull up' on the PFD, but I can't be perfectly certain, and Captain is adamant that we didn't get the GPWS warning, only the sink rate caution. I want to be clear that I understand the limitation with regard to the warning annunciator. In hindsight, I can see now that a go-around could have been a prudent decision even though the aircraft appeared to be a safe and normal position for short final at SAN. I want to highlight this issue for a few reasons. It bears repeating that phase of flight, temporal distortion, and flight deck confusion can all conspire to create a situation where two trained and alert crew members can see different things. The other thing I want to highlight is how heavy -800's, going into SAN, can potentially be affected by a flaps 30 approach. I don't know why we don't have recommended flap settings for certain situations. We've all been flying light aircraft for almost a year now and perhaps it would help to remind crews about heavy aircraft with higher approach airspeeds and subsequently higher VVIs in higher altitude environments or steeper approaches like SAN. On approach to SAN when transitioning outside, we briefly received a sink rate call. At the gate, the First Officer was unsure if it was just a sink rate call or sink rate pull up. I adjusted sink rate and landed normally.
ASRS:1792355.s: During a heavy aircraft visual approach to Runway 27 at SAN, the crew received a sink rate warning and possibly a fleeting pull-up alert due to high vertical velocity from a steep approach and high speed. The Captain acknowledged the warning, adjusted the aim point, and executed a safe landing, though the crew later disagreed on the specific aural annunciation.

ASRS:1792371.n: After pushback in ZZZ, Dispatch notified us via ACARS that ZZZ Operations had contacted her and that 'you did not sign her [Dangerous Goods Form]'. However, only the Pilot's copy of the [Dangerous Goods Form] was provided to us by the A Flight Attendant. Prior to pushback, and at the same time the [Dangerous Goods Form] was delivered, we had an intoxicated Passenger removed from the aircraft. Once we reached our cruise altitude, we took pictures of the signed Pilot's copy of the [Dangerous Goods Form] and amended Release and emailed them to the Operations Center and the Dispatcher via the Company provided EFB.First of all, any time HAZMAT/COMAT is transported onboard, a face to face briefing with the Captain should be required. This will build a shared mental model and will allow the Captain the opportunity to efficiently and effectively bring Dispatch into the loop in accordance with the FOM. Personally, any time we carry HAZMAT/COMAT, I will review the FOM as this is not something I do every day, so I can back up the Captain more effectively. Finally, discussing actions to take if unruly Passengers pop up among the whole Crew can help prevent distractions when they do pop up After pushback, ACARS notification from our Dispatcher stated QUOTE 'You did not sign her NOTAC' ie, describing the Ops Agents copy of the NOTAC. Apparently the Ops Agent only handed the 'Pilots Copy' of the NOTAC to the A Flight Attendant, and not directly handing it to the Captain. No 'Ops Copy' was ever provided. Just when this occurred, a Passenger was being removed for behavior of what an intoxicated passenger would exhibit. Once at cruise, photographs were taken of the 'Pilots Copy' of the NOTAC, and of an amended Release stating in the remarks section. Note: 'Raft on flight, refer to NOTAC' -- with our Dispatchers initials and the time of the amendment, and this was emailed to our Dispatcher and Chief Pilot in the Operations Center. Confirmation was received on ACARS that Dispatch was in receipt of our email, sent via Company email on the Captains EFB.
ASRS:1792371.s: After pushback, the crew received an ACARS notification that the Operations Agent failed to provide the required Dangerous Goods Form copy to the Captain, an issue compounded by the simultaneous removal of an intoxicated passenger. The crew resolved the documentation gap at cruise altitude by emailing photos of the signed form and an amended release to Dispatch.

ASRS:1792375.n: This is a General Safety concern. No faults were committed by myself or the Captain. HOU ATC is constantly running 1 frequency to work Tower and Ground Control. This is causing an unsafe level of radio congestion. We could not get a push call in without blocking other aircraft or being blocked ourselves. Finally, once pushed, we had difficulty obtaining a taxi clearance. We finally were told to taxi and hold short of 13L. As we were holding short, we noted several aircraft attempting to push, taxi to and from runways, and obtain landing clearances. We noticed one corporate aircraft that could not obtain a landing clearance until short final, despite multiple attempts on their part, with no answer from Tower.HOU is a complex airport with multiple crossing runways, multiple taxi routes utilized, while also crossing runways. HOU ATC has been utilizing a single Controller for Ground and Tower Ops for most of the last 12 months, since the start of the slow down in air traffic. While this may have worked in the early days of this pandemic, it has turned into its own form of danger as air traffic has steadily increased, especially with the onset of Spring Break travel.I believe I am not alone in my concern that this could cause a serious incident at HOU, as there is no way a single Controller can safely manage traffic on the ground and in the air. I have been to far less complex, and less busy airports that utilize designated Ground and Tower Controllers. Please see to it, that this is not allowed to continue any longer. It poses a danger to our aircraft and our customers.
ASRS:1792375.s: Pilots reported unsafe radio congestion at Houston (HOU) caused by a single controller managing both Tower and Ground frequencies. This staffing arrangement delayed pushback and taxi clearances while preventing a corporate aircraft from receiving landing instructions until short final.

ASRS:1792382.n: While on a vector to a visual to Runway 35R at AUS we were awaiting a turn to the east for left base entry to the runway. At 3000', and in a turn to 090 degrees we [got a] TA on TCAS less than one mile off our right or south course at the same altitude of 3000' and an urgent call from ATC to the traffic 'Whoever is off San Marcos;' to turn immediately to the south. We are convinced it was the traffic that suddenly appeared, and if we didn't make the immediate turn at 30 degrees of bank to 090 degrees would have resulted in a Resolution Advisory, RA, a near miss or very abrupt maneuver to avoid collision. We feel the extended downwind vector down towards San Marcos due to heavy traffic at AUS with one runway open, resulted in us being close to VFR traffic near San Marcos.
ASRS:1792382.s: The crew received a TCAS Traffic Advisory at 3000 feet while vectoring for Runway 35R at AUS, prompting an immediate turn to avoid VFR traffic near San Marcos. The pilot attributed the close call to extended downwind vectors caused by heavy traffic and a single open runway.

ASRS:1792383.n: During climb out of SMF, everything was normal with some occasional light chop. We had asked the Flight Attendants to remain seated due to crossing the Sierra Mountains. We were climbing at approximately .76 Mach. Upon leveling at FL 370, we experienced moderate bordering on severe mountain wave. Our airspeed began decreasing rapidly and the F/O (First Officer) disconnected the autopilot, applied full thrust, and began a shallow descent to regain airspeed. The airspeed decayed to about .70 - .71. It was about a 30 knot decrease. I may be a little off on the Mach numbers. We descended about 500' and the airspeed began increasing. I reported the encounter to ATC and we began climbing back to FL 370. The wave climbed us to FL 375, and at that time we requested a descent to FL 350. The Controller cleared us to descend to FL 350. We did not encounter any additional mountain wave and nothing more than a little light chop. We checked with the Flight Attendants to make sure everyone was alright, and the remainder of the flight was uneventful. I would like to add that the F/O did an excellent job of recognizing and reacting to the situation. We had just leveled off at our cruise altitude of FL 370. (Filed for FL 390 but we were too heavy at that time.) During climb we had anticipated and encounter some light turbulence. Nothing more significant was encountered. WSI (Weather Service International) and Jeppesen weather showed areas of turbulence covering about the first 45 minutes of our flight. Our clearance was on the SCTWN 3 RNAV Departure. We were level at FL 370 when suddenly our airspeed had dropped from M.76 (250 KIAS) to 220 KIAS this was approximately 10-15 above the yellow maneuvering bar on the airspeed indicator and the green vector bar was indicating that the slowing was continuing and at a significant rate. I disconnected the autopilot and autothrottle and pitched down to keep airspeed. I also increased thrust to max and I was able to recover airspeed about 500' low at FL 365. In my attempt to climb back to FL 370 we started climbing at a significant rate and stopped the climb at approximately FL 376. The Captain reported to ATC that we were in MVA (mountain wave activity) and that we were unable to hold altitude. I continued to hand fly until I was sure we were passed the MVA and re-engaged the autopilot. The rest of the flight was uneventful.
ASRS:1792383.s: The flight crew encountered severe mountain wave turbulence at FL 370 after departing SMF, causing rapid airspeed decay. The First Officer manually descended 500 feet to recover airspeed, and the aircraft was subsequently cleared to FL 350 to avoid further wave activity.

ASRS:1792387.n: Departed ZZZ without Dispatch release remark of 'HAZMAT on flight - refer to [Dangerous Goods Form]'. When I discovered the error I notified Dispatch via ACARS.
ASRS:1792387.s: The pilot departed ZZZ without a Dispatch release remark regarding HAZMAT on the flight. Upon discovering the error, the pilot notified Dispatch via ACARS.

ASRS:1792414.n: The FA called the flight deck and reported an electrical burning smell and I had the check the overhead bins and electrical outlets under the seats. No obvious reason for smell. I called Dispatch and Maintenance Control and we continued to destination. We followed the QRH and FM.
ASRS:1792414.s: The flight attendant reported an electrical burning smell, prompting the pilot to inspect overhead bins and seat outlets with no obvious cause found. The crew contacted Dispatch and Maintenance Control, followed the QRH and FM, and continued to the destination.

ASRS:1792417.n: This was me and the First Officer's first flight together. He hadn't had a landing for approximately a month and hadn't been flying a lot recently. It was a beautiful day in ZZZ and we were cleared for the visual to XXL at about 7,000 MSL. We were established on the localizer as a backup and had the runway in sight holding around 210 knots. Approach control handed us off to tower and I checked in. We were cleared to land and told that there would be fighters departing out of ZZZ1, but they would stay below us. The First Officer started too slow and I extended flaps to 2. I started searching for the fighters and saw 2 of them takeoff. I keep my eyes on them to make sure we were clear. First Officer called for the gear and I extended it. I noticed we were still at flaps 2 and we were too fast for flaps 3. We were inside the FAF by this point and it was going to be close for a stabilized approach. The first officer had previously selected the approach mode and we were on course about 300 feet high on the glide path and fast so not correcting. I noticed the power on the engine instruments was not at idle which was strange because we had the approach selected in managed speed and the speed tape showed the target speed well below our current speed. I pointed the power setting out to the first officer and it was also confusing to him why the power was still up. We got to flaps 3 around 1,000 AGL and were still high on the glide path. We leveled off a little to get the flaps to full and then started to correct to glidepath. When we got to 500 feet we were still a good 200 feet high and 15-20 knots above our target speed. The First Officer asked me if I wanted him to go around. There was no traffic and the runway is 2 miles long so I said to continue. We ended up touching down at target speed well within the touchdown zone and cleared the runway. After getting to the gate and shutting down the engines we debriefed the approach. The First Officer said that all along he thought he was setting himself up nicely for the approach and thought it would work. I agreed and then I took myself out of the SA loop when I started searching for the fighters and didn't pay close enough attention to our energy status. When I finally did get back into it I wasn't forceful enough to help. When I pointed out the engines not being at idle I assumed he would disconnect the auto thrust and put the throttles at idle. When he didn't I should have told him too and that alone would have probably made us stable as there was still some time. At any rate I didn't and we were clearly unstable and we both knew it. The only correct option was to execute a go-around. Fuel was not an issue as we ended up landing with 6,500 pounds. I told him that I should have told him to go-around but he should have just executed a go-around without asking. That is the procedure. You don't need permission from the other pilot and permission not to go-around is still wrong anyway. We agreed that the biggest factor that got us going down this path in the first place was his recency of experience and that in order to fix that he should in the immediate future at least, slow down and configure earlier then he thinks he needs to. Going back to our departure briefing I should have taken the first leg anyway since I knew he hadn't flown in a while. This way he could have eased back into it.
ASRS:1792417.s: The Captain and First Officer flew an unstable visual approach to XXL due to the First Officer's lack of recent experience and the Captain's distraction monitoring departing fighters. Despite being high and fast, they continued the landing instead of executing a go-around, later agreeing the Captain should have taken the first leg and the First Officer should have initiated a go-around without asking.

ASRS:1792421.n: I flew the 737 Max aircraft for the first time and noticed an aircraft characteristic that I do not like. The altitude alerting system gives a loud buzz in the headset 900 ft. prior to level off MCP altitude. This buzz drowned out ATC communications twice during climbout due the timing of ATC communications. I was unable to determine what ATC was saying.
ASRS:1792421.s: A pilot flying a 737 Max for the first time reported that the altitude alerting system buzzed 900 feet before level-off, drowning out ATC communications twice during climbout. This prevented the pilot from hearing ATC instructions due to the timing of the alert.

ASRS:1792438.n: I was working Aircraft X and was helping close the front cargo pit when hot scalding coffee came pouring down the front lavatory drain. I have lost count how many times this has happened while I was working a flight in the last few years. I notified the Captain what happen and he said he didn't know the lavatory sink drained right to the outside of the plane. He asked the Flight Attendant and she said she had a 'brain fart' and she was sorry? I'm so glad she was sorry and my face wasn't burned by this careless act!
ASRS:1792438.s: A mechanic working Aircraft X was scalded by hot coffee poured down the front lavatory drain while closing the cargo pit. The reporter attributes the incident to a flight attendant's careless act, noting the captain was unaware the sink drained directly to the aircraft exterior.

ASRS:1792462.n: The above MEL required flying with no FMS, and navigation only by VOR.We tried for over an hour to get proper routing that would allow us to fly to ZZZ via acceptable routing that would allow for proper navigation via VOR/victor airways. Center would not allow acceptable routing. This made our release unreliable for time and fuel calculations. It also meant we did not have redundancy in our navigation. On multiple occasions ATC tried to re-route us and fly RNAV routing. A number of VOR's would not identify automatically and we needed to listen to the Morse code to identify each station. The autopilot would not track the victor airways properly. The autopilot would drift left and right of course. We resorted to using HDG mode and our [electronic tablets] for navigation.We do very little training flying a jet at 36,000 ft. flying solely on VOR navigation. The implications of not having an FMS, are not made very clear in the MEL. For example, no fuel planning, no vertical navigation, what VOR beacons are acceptable for high altitude operations, what does ATC actually go by (understand) versus what the MEL states.Resorted to using HDG mode, radar vectors, and our iPads to guide the aircraft. This report is primarily being done for pre-emptive measures for any deviations and to have the company not use antiquated technology for primary navigation.It should be company policy to not conduct revenue flights without two forms of navigation or without an FMS. It is hard to believe that there were no other available aircraft for use for our flight. ATC needs to be made more aware of when an aircraft is non-RNAV capable as we needed to tell each controller the situation.
ASRS:1792462.s: The crew flew a jet at 36,000 ft without an FMS, relying on VOR navigation per MEL, but encountered ATC routing conflicts, autopilot tracking failures, and unreliable VOR identification. They resorted to HDG mode, radar vectors, and electronic tablets, concluding that revenue flights should not operate without an FMS or redundant navigation.

ASRS:1792468.n: Upon taxiing to [Runway] XXL, a loud banging and grinding sound with vibration and shimmy would happen intermittently on taxi with no real reason. Once crossed XXR we asked ATC if we could pull off and called Maintenance, they agreed best course of action was to gate return. Taxied back in slowly still hearing and feeling strange sounds and vibrations intermittently. Once parked a quick inspection by Maintenance revealed that while everything looked normal when still, once the aircraft was moved (they rocked it) the entire nose gear assembly wobbled and was loose. We were delayed swapped planes and continued [the] day as normal.The aircraft was received like this. It had already flown more than likely like this. There needs to be better discipline on reporting foreign sounds. Also, push crews sound like they are fighting a war when they hook up and disconnect. Maybe there is a correlation there.
ASRS:1792468.s: The flight crew experienced intermittent loud banging, grinding, and nose gear shimmy while taxiing to Runway XXL, prompting a gate return. Maintenance confirmed a loose nose gear assembly, causing a delay and aircraft swap, while the crew noted potential links to prior unreported sounds and aggressive pushback operations.

ASRS:1792473.n: The flight operated from ZZZ to GRK following the the ZZZZZ departure to ZZZZZ1 Intersection and then direct to the airport. This route brings flights from the east to the airport just south of multiple restricted areas. At approximately 12-15 miles east of the GRK at 4,000 feet, We accepted a visual approach clearance for Runway 15. We noted the restricted areas to the north of the field and made a 'dogleg' downwind to base for the runway with a course correction to avoid restricted areas to the northeast, followed by a turn just inside the published ILS Runway 15 FAF for a normal landing. Upon touching down Supervisor wished to speak to our crew and or management to inquire about procedures into the airport.Based on my discussion with the ATC manager on duty at Gray Approach, there have been multiple occasions where other aircraft have penetrated restricted airspace and have had near miss collisions with military UAV's that took evasive action. In some cases the the restricted airspace is within 3 miles of the 15 runway east downwind. Per the traffic manager, controllers EXPECT crews to fly a traditional box pattern while executing visual approaches on left downwind legs to 15 at a rather close distance, or enter a midfield crosswind entry to a right downwind. There are no specific instructions from ATC at the time of a visual clearance to fly a specific pattern. I recommend additional coordination between company management, union, and Gray ATC to develop set of procedures and or additional guidance/recommendations for our flights that can incorporated into 10-7 station pages.
ASRS:1792473.s: The flight crew accepted a visual approach to Runway 15 at GRK and executed a dogleg to avoid restricted areas, prompting a supervisor inquiry. ATC reported that other aircraft have penetrated restricted airspace near military UAVs due to a lack of specific visual approach pattern instructions.

ASRS:1792503.n: Today I was contacted by my Chief Pilot and notified that there had been an IOR (Internal Occurrence Report) written about a flight I flew about a week ago. According to the IOR, 'DG/HM (Dangerous Goods/HazMat) COMAT (Company Materials) loaded on aircraft form received in ZZZ1 with no PIC (Pilot-in-Command) signature or flight information'. Prior to departure I (PIC) was not notified of any DG/HM onboard the aircraft. I am positive that I did not receive a DG/HM PNF (Pilot Notification Form). I am sure that I would have remembered seeing it since it is typically not common to receive them and they are designed to stand out with their chevron red border and bright yellow pilot instructions. In addition, whenever I receive these forms I keep my copy in my flight bag for quite some time and I don't have one for this flight. I am assuming the cause of this error was that the DG/HM was loaded onto the aircraft and then for some reason someone forgot to notify or provide me with the PNF. I feel that in the past the DG/HM procedures we use have worked well. The PNF stands out and requires us to send a spec command through ACARS which serves as confirmation of receiving the form. It also helps that typically the CLR will have comments that there is DG/HM on board. I guess if I had any suggestion it would be that whoever loads the COMAT should then come directly to the flight deck with the form so that there is no middle man, or no time to get distracted or forget about it. The Captain and I performed a routine revenue flight. The ramp personnel loaded some COMAT [Company Materials] cargo without our knowing and we did not receive the proper paperwork for it. No negative outcomes from the flight or the cargo. Forgetting to bring paperwork to flight crew and making them aware of any COMAT cargo that we needed to sign for. Just remembering to bring the proper paperwork to the crew so we know about it.
ASRS:1792503.s: The Pilot-in-Command reported that ramp personnel loaded Company Materials cargo without providing the required Dangerous Goods notification form or obtaining the PIC's signature. The Captain attributed this error to a failure in communication where the paperwork was not delivered to the flight deck, though no negative outcomes occurred.

ASRS:1792508.n: We were being vectored to final for the visual to Runway XXR in ZZZ. Descending out of 9,000 feet in the right downwind of the ZZZZZ arrival we were then given a vector 'Turn right heading 030, descend and maintain 7,000 feet.' It was clear that the Controller was very busy and was working approach for three parallel landing runways with many inbound flights that morning. Our next instructions were, 'Turn right heading 090.' Shortly after the turn to the east we were assigned, 'Turn right heading 150 to join the [Runway] XXR LOC.' This last instruction was given a minute too late. It was already apparent that we were going to fly through the final approach course with parallel traffic joining up for [Runway] XXL. The Captain had been saying prior to this, 'Controller needs to gives us the turn... Controller needs to turn us already... we are going to fly through final.' Sure enough the turn was way too late and the aircraft automation was too slow to make the tight turn. The Captain immediately informed ATC that the vector was issued too late and that we would be flying through the final approach course and correcting west bound to rejoin. I disengaged the autopilot as the automation was not reacting fast enough to recapture the final approach course. ATC then issued us a 190 heading to rejoin the localizer and a traffic advisory to the aircraft that was flying the parallel, saying we were at their 3 o'clock same altitude and correcting west to rejoin [Runway] XXR LOC. Just seconds after the heading to rejoin was issued (We were already in the turn at this time) a TCAS Traffic Advisory went off due to the proximity of the aircraft on the [Runway] XXL parallel visual. Nothing further happened from this event. We were able to rejoin the [Runway] XXR LOC maintain 7000 feet until descent for landing was necessary and we completed a stabilized approach to landing.The cause of this event was due to task saturation for the Air Traffic Controller. Controller was working one approach frequency with dozens of aircraft needing vectors to final for the triple parallel visuals landing south at ZZZ. The automation lag didn't help when trying to join the LOC with the last second instructions however that was mostly mitigated by disconnecting the autopilot and hand flying a more abrupt turn to re-intercept and avoid further deviation.As a pilot (and never having been in to see a behind the scenes look at an ATC approach facility) I cannot tell you exactly what was going on or any, if at all, distractions may have existed behind the microphone at ZZZ Approach that morning. However, I can tell you based on my perception that the controller was talking non-stop with zero breaks between Controller and aircraft transmission and that Controller may have been overloaded during this event.
ASRS:1792508.s: Pilots reported that a task-saturated controller issued late vectors during the ZZZ arrival, causing the aircraft to cross the parallel final approach course and trigger a TCAS advisory. The crew manually disengaged the autopilot to execute an abrupt turn, rejoin the localizer, and complete a stabilized landing.

ASRS:1792528.n: Flying from ZZZ-BUR we were in cruise assigned by ATC to start a descent from FL220 to FL180. Upon passing through FL215 ATC asked us to stop our descent at FL210, we complied and stopped at 210. Upon reaching 210 we received a TCAS TA. The FO and myself immediately looked at the TCAS screen and started to visually look for the traffic. He was getting closer to our six mile ring and he was still climbing, we saw him on our TCAS inside of our six mile ring and now at our same altitude. It was at this time the we received an RA. The FO immediately disconnected the autopilot and started to comply with the RA. At this time ATC told us to climb to FL230 I told him we were complying with an RA event and we could be unable to climb to 230. The RA initially gave us a command to descend at 3200 FPM and then the rate of descent was increased by the RA to 4500 FPM which was complied with. We leveled the aircraft off after the RA was complete at FL190. We asked ATC if he had any further instructions for us, he said to level at 190 and he would be back momentarily. He proceeded to give the other aircraft that caused the RA a phone number to contact center. The pilot sounded like he was possibly in distress in a potentially hypoxic situation from the tone and behavior of his radio calls and struggle to follow any ATC instructions at the time. We continued to descend into Burbank and now on SoCal Approach were given a heading of 150 and 5k feet which took us right over a mountain that gave us a terrain warning momentarily as we leveled at 5k feet. We cross this terrain at 5,000 often on a vector from ATC we happened to cross right over the very peak of this terrain and with the descent rate down we suspect that the rate of closure was too much for the GPWS. Upon landing in Burbank on the ILS Z 8 we received on more TCAS TA/RA as we crossed over ZZZ1 traffic in the pattern below caused our TCAS to give us a 'Monitor vertical speed' we complied and landed at Burbank without further incident.All events that took place were as a result of other aircraft and ATC vectors. We as a crew exercised all appropriate training to comply with all events. While operating ZZZ-BUR level at FL 220, LA center on 132.5, issued a descend and maintain from FL220 to FL190. Passing through FL21.5 ATC amended clearance with a limit of FL210. We leveled off at 210 without any deviation but noticed an aircraft rapidly approaching our guarded zone on TCAS. Momentarily after we noticed this, a traffic advisory was made by the TCAS system and followed by and immediate command for 'monitor vertical speed'. The vertical speed initially commanded was 3700 fpm. The target aircraft did not level off at their assigned altitude. After the autopilot was immediately disengaged and the descent was initiated to the commanded rate, the TCAS prompted 'increase vertical speed' commanding roughly a 4500 FPM decent rate. LA center was notified and after the aural clear of conflict was heard and agreed on the aircraft was level at FL190 and ATC issued a new clearance. With no further issues the flight continued through Joshua approach and then onto SoCal approach. With SoCal approach upon completion of the JANNY5 arrival into BUR SoCal assigned a vector of hdg 190 and descend to 5,000 ft. Level at 5,000 feet we crossed over a mountain peak that was at 3,734 feet. This caused a terrain warning and a subsequent ' terrain terrain pull up'. The aircraft climbed roughly 100 ft since the conditions were VFR and clear. After the terrain clearance was accomplished, SoCal assigned a heading of 110 and 3000 till established and cleared for the ILS-z Runway 8 into BUR. Upon passing over ZZZ1 we received another traffic advisory and that was followed with a RA. The RA did not state any vertical speed as the target aircraft had already passed behind us. The flight landed at BUR on Runway 8 with no adverse issues or events after that point.Continue to follow SOPs and be a vigilante and proactive flight crew and practice good CRM techniques.
ASRS:1792528.s: The flight crew experienced multiple TCAS RAs and a terrain warning during descent from FL220 to Burbank due to conflicting ATC vectors and other aircraft. They complied with all RA commands and terrain alerts, leveling at FL190 and climbing briefly over a mountain peak before landing safely.

ASRS:1792533.n: On a vector to final, about 20 NM south of CLT, I observed the flight mode change from HDG to LNAV, then about 10 seconds later the flight director commanded a turn in the wrong direction. We were expecting all left turns to final, so when I saw the airplane starting to bank to the right, I immediately pressed the TCS button and leveled the wings.The first time that I saw this happen recently, I dismissed it as a fluke. But this has now happened to me 3 times at the same airport on different approaches. I would estimate this is happening on about 15% of all approaches to this airport now. It starts with a vector to the intermediate approach course, arming the LNAV mode, and shortly after switching modes the computer steers the airplane across the approach course, over-corrects back in the opposite direction, and then chases the CDI to a normal alignment.This error in navigation, even though semi-random in frequency, is of such concern that I have been briefing the risk of TCAS activations and NTZ [No Transgression Zone] incursions that could be caused by this computer glitch. At this airport, it is fair to assume that there is always traffic on the simultaneous parallel course. Today, I briefed this possibility with the pilot flying while at cruise, and his reaction when it happened, although not as fast as mine, was understandable. He thought the turn was at first a subtle deviation in the direction of the final course.
ASRS:1792533.s: A pilot reported that on three separate approaches to CLT, the flight director commanded an incorrect right turn after switching from HDG to LNAV. The pilot immediately disengaged the mode to level the wings, citing concerns that this recurring navigation glitch could cause TCAS activations or No Transgression Zone incursions.

ASRS:1792566.n: I had been furloughed and haven't worked the last 5 months. I got my first reserve trip as no 4. I worked my first leg, we were full to the capacity. It was hectic. When I was boarding my next leg, I realized I had not done exit row briefing on my first leg. I did everything I was supposed to, and absolutely have the knowledge of procedure, but having been out of work for 5 months, and working full flight with lots of bags, I think it slipped my mind. I regret forgetting exit row briefing. Had never happened and will never happen again.
ASRS:1792566.s: A cabin crew member on their first reserve trip after a five-month furlough forgot to conduct the exit row briefing on a full first leg. The reporter attributes the omission to the hectic conditions and time away from work, stating it was an unintentional error that will not be repeated.

ASRS:1792587.n: I was traveling from ZZZ to ZZZ1. I experienced radio and GPS problems when trying to activate the runway lights at ZZZ1 around XA:00 local. After 3 attempts to activate the runway lights, I contacted Tucson Approach to see if there were any other ideas to help get the runway lights on. They called the airport to see if Customs was there. As no one was there, I was reaching my personal fuel reserve of 1 hour. The radio I have installed is GNS 430W. I had also had intermittent GPS signal, which resulted in no ADSB. Tucson Approach offered ZZZ2 as an alternate, but the airport was closed for the night. I felt it was much safer to go to TUS, as it has a host of FBO's and services available 24/7. I estimate that my radio at that time had about a 5 mile range. I lost contact with Approach several times, but I was able to hear the transponder code.As I got closer, Approach advised me that I was to enter a Right Downwind for Runway 11L at 4,000 ft. or above, and that I was cleared to land. They also told me to expect light gun signals from the Tower. I was able to acknowledge that transmission and was handed off to Tower. Tower also had a hard time hearing me, describing it as broken and scratchy. I was receiving Tower just fine, as I was close enough to the airport. I landed on 11L without incident and was given progressive taxi to FBO. Once I arrived and shut down, I asked if they had Maintenance available, which they did not. I parked there overnight until I was able to get an Avionics Tech to look at the airplane the next day. The Technician noticed that the 430W was not seated completely due do the design of the radio stack. He was able to quickly solve the problem. We did radio checks with TUS Ground and listened to the ATIS both over the cabin speaker and headsets. This particular aircraft is new to me, and I had not noticed the issue before as I normally operate out of an uncontrolled field. Now I incorporate a visual inspection of the GNS 430W, the audio panel, and the transponder as part of my preflight inspection, specifically looking to make sure they are seated properly, not loose, and functioning as they should. I took for granted that they had been installed correctly from the previous aircraft owner. I trust Maintenance shops to do work and repairs correctly, but it is now a trust but verify as I am the one responsible for the operation of the aircraft and systems.
ASRS:1792587.s: The pilot experienced radio and GPS failures while approaching ZZZ1 due to a GNS 430W unit not being fully seated in the stack. After diverting to TUS and landing safely, a technician confirmed the loose installation caused the communication loss, prompting the pilot to add a visual inspection of avionics seating to preflight checks.

ASRS:1792595.n: I was instructing student in Aircraft X. We were on right downwind Runway 16 at BDN at 4,500 MSL.Aircraft Y pilot made a position call with him being 'on a 3 mile 45 for right downwind 16.' Shortly after that radio call was heard, my student observed the plane being adjacent 50 feet (+/-20 feet) to me at an angle, forcing me to do an evasive dive.I made a radio call after I made the evasive maneuver, that I will slow down and he can turn downwind.
ASRS:1792595.s: An instructor and student in Aircraft X on right downwind at BDN at 4,500 MSL executed an evasive dive after Aircraft Y appeared adjacent at 50 feet. The near-miss occurred shortly after Aircraft Y reported being on a 3-mile 45-degree intercept for right downwind.

ASRS:1792623.n: At around XA:00L time, my instructor and I were practicing engine out procedures per [the training] course. When we tried to complete the checklist for an engine air restart, the propeller failed to unfeather. Upon retrying the checklist, the engine would still not start. We then tried to troubleshoot the engine and nothing would make the propeller unfeather. My instructor made the decision to proceed back [to] the airport and request priority handling. We requested priority with ZZZ Tower requesting to land immediately. My instructor then took over controls, flew us back and landed safely. While he taxied us back, I completed the after landing checklist and we shut down on ZZZ's North ramp. On a training flight in a PA-44-180 with (L)/IO-360-B1G6 engines installed I (MEI) was the PIC the student was acting PIC. At 6,000 ft MSL in the practice area north of ZZZ, I intentionally failed the left engine by bringing the left mixture to cut-off. The student performed his memory items and then checklist items for Engine Failure in flight checklist. He then performed the Troubleshoot checklist and then Engine Feathering and Securing checklist. We maneuvered with the left engine feathered for a few minutes, performing normal level turns using normal banking maneuvers. I then told the student to use the Air Start Procedure to restart the engine in flight. The student performed the checklist and upon completion of the checklist the left engine remained in the feathered position. We completed the Engine Feathering and Securing checklist again and after a few minutes attempted the Air Start Procedure again. After completing the Air Start Procedure a second time the left engine remained in the feathered position. We completed the Engine Feathering and Securing checklist again. The student continued to fly the airplane towards the nearest suitable airport ZZZ. I [requested priority handling] with ZZZ Tower about 10NM to the north. We were cleared straight in for Runway XXR, I handled the checklist and radios while the student flew us towards Runway XXR. At about 5nm from ZZZ I took the flight controls from the student and made a normal straight in approach and landing on XXR. I was able to taxi us to the maintenance facility where we parked and shut down. Maintenance is currently inspecting the aircraft to determine a cause. One thing I could have done differently was to call maintenance on the radio in-flight and explain to them what happened and what we see/hear and they could possibly troubleshoot the problem for us from the ground before advising ATC.
ASRS:1792623.s: During a PA-44-180 training flight, a student and instructor attempted an in-flight engine air restart at 6,000 ft, but the left propeller failed to unfeather despite repeated checklist attempts. The instructor took control, requested priority handling from ZZZ Tower, and landed safely for maintenance inspection.

ASRS:1792632.n: The purpose of this report is to give awareness of the possibility of strong wake vortex and turbulence encounter over large distances at high altitude. This is especially applicable to light and very light jets. In VFR conditions, wake turbulence was encountered from a heavy B777 at a distance of about 25 miles at an altitude of about 30,000 ft. in a BE400XP of about 14,000 lbs. at the time of the encounter. The BE400XP was within 1,000 ft. of the altitude of the heavy B777 25 miles ahead and we were climbing to a higher cruise altitude above the B777. The encounter resulted in temporary turbulence between moderate and severe and the aircraft tried to roll beyond 45-50 degrees twice with uncommanded input from an initial attitude of a wings level climb of about 1,000 fpm. No autopilot was yet engaged. The aircraft was being flown by hand (the autopilot about to be engage as we just entered RVSM airspace) and the upset recovery was immediate but required very large roll corrections to keep the aircraft upright. At the time of the encounter, the heavy B777 was ahead and to the left at about 25 miles and winds were a quartering tailwind of about 78 kts. Given the distance of separation and the amount of wind movement at that altitude, the wake vortex encounter was not expected and a complete surprise. There was no visible contrail from the B777. We thought the vortex would have dissipated well ahead of our point of encounter. Instead, it appears the vortex was strong enough to still be very significant at that distance and was blown across our route with the prevailing winds. The entire event lasted about 5-10 seconds. ATC was then notified and concurred it was most likely the wake of the heavy aircraft 25 miles ahead. Initially, both aircraft had been on a similar flight route. They also initially had closer separation and both paths had crossed at an earlier point in flight with the BE400XP below the heavy B777 flight path with no issue. At the stage of closer separation and route intersection ATC had given us an advisory of the aircraft. I am the FO (First Officer) and I was the pilot flying from the left seat. The CA (Captain) was the pilot monitoring and both of us discussed the possibility of wake vortex encounter with closer separation. We both visually identified the aircraft when in sight distance, and we were careful to avoid known problem areas relative to the B777 where wake vortex would be an issue. As the flight progressed, we moved to a relative position in trail of the heavy B777 with the distance between us and them continually increasing. Eventually we were well beyond any close separation where a wake vortex encounter is normally thought to occur. However, at about 25 miles of separation and within 1,000 ft. of the altitude of the heavy B777, we encountered strong wake vortex as we climbed to a higher altitude. No significant naturally occurring turbulence had been forecast (a large high pressure system was over this area) and none was encountered prior to or after the wake turbulence event. In addition, no other traffic was within 50 miles, this and the B777 distance were re-verified after the vortex encounter.In retrospect, I am not sure there is anything different either the flight crew or ATC could have done to avoid the wake vortex encounter. However, if I had a choice in policy design, I would recommend that all flight crews hand fly the aircraft to cruise altitude even in RVSM airspace. I realize an autopilot is an FAA requirement for operating in RVSM. In addition, many flight departments and large carriers require the autopilot to be engaged more or less right after takeoff. This policy can unintentionally degrade stick and rudder skills as a pilot needs to have a feel and understanding of actual aircraft performance. This is critical at high altitude as aircraft control is more sensitive. An autopilot is not a substitute for actual stick and rudder skills even at high altitude. (Autopilots canfail.) Upset recovery has happened in the real world at high altitude. This is an example of a well-trained, competent, and alert flight crew encountering an unusual attitude event in circumstances one would not expect the event to occur. I also question whether an autopilot would have impeded the recovery time as the 'startle effect' could be more pronounced. In addition, I think that being in RVSM airspace can give a false sense of safety as heavy aircraft are routinely on route in very close proximity to light aircraft. I see this as not only an awareness issue for flight crews but system stakeholders in general (ATC, FAA policy teams, flight departments, etc).
ASRS:1792632.s: The First Officer hand-flew a BE400XP climbing near 30,000 ft. when encountering severe wake turbulence from a B777 25 miles ahead. Prevailing winds carried the vortex, causing uncommanded rolls up to 50 degrees that required immediate manual recovery.

ASRS:1792640.n: I was working Sector X combined with Sector Y when I gave Aircraft X a descent clearance to FL300. I saw that Aircraft Y was potential traffic and though I had time to get back to monitoring the separation. I got caught up with other duties. The Controller at Sector Z mentioned that I may want to watch the Aircraft X and Aircraft Y. When I looked back I increased the descent rate on Aircraft X through FL310 and turned Aircraft Y 20 degrees left. I forgot the Aircraft X turned slightly west at ZZZ VOR. I should have given the Aircraft X a crossing restriction at ZZZ1 [VOR] and anticipated the turn to ZZZ [Airport] after ZZZ1 [VOR]. We are working very short in our area and having to keep sectors combined due to COVID-19 eliminating half our crew including our Supervisor. We now must run CIC and control and train.Get controllers vaccine shots so we can work together again and be back on a regular schedule so we can get used to busy sessions again.
ASRS:1792640.s: An air traffic controller in combined Sectors X and Y issued a descent clearance to Aircraft X to FL300 but lost separation awareness due to high workload and staffing shortages. The controller corrected the situation by increasing Aircraft X's descent rate and turning Aircraft Y left after realizing Aircraft X had turned west at ZZZ VOR without a crossing restriction.

ASRS:1792647.n: I witnessed the Supervisor, who was working Local Control, Ground Contol and the Operations Desk combined have what I would call a near mid air. He had Aircraft X in the right pattern for the runway. Aircraft Y ready for IFR departure at the same runway. What I witnessed was Aircraft Y turning to avoid Aircraft X on the upwind. I heard the Supervisor tell Aircraft X if able turn your crosswind now (he wasn't even at the departure end of the runway, maybe 4,500 ft. down the runway) He then told Aircraft Y [that] Aircraft X was turning crosswind. Aircraft Y then corrected back and continued straight out. The Supervisor told Aircraft Y to start his 315 heading and contact departure. Aircraft Y did not turn until 2 1/2 miles upwind which at that point I had Aircraft Z on the upwind off an adjacent runway.I listened to the tapes because I initially thought Aircraft Y was departing a different runway however after reviewing the tapes he was cleared for takeoff on the same runway as Aircraft X. Aircraft X must have just touched down for his touch and go when he cleared Aircraft Y for takeoff. There was obviously no runway separation which is 6,000 ft. or turned to avoid when Aircraft Y started his takeoff roll. I also heard on the tapes what sounded like Aircraft Y stating he was deviating to avoid. And then later state 'I'm correcting back'. I tried to see the replay but wasn't able to log into the system. The reason I'm reporting this a few days later is because I wanted to review the tapes and was trying to get into the replay system to see if additional separation was lost with Aircraft Z and Aircraft Y after my days off.
ASRS:1792647.s: A supervisor controlling Local, Ground, and Operations cleared Aircraft Y for takeoff on the same runway as Aircraft X, causing Aircraft Y to deviate to avoid a near mid-air collision. The incident resulted from a lack of required 6,000 ft separation, as Aircraft X was still on the runway during Aircraft Y's takeoff roll.

ASRS:1792656.n: When I was assigned a Tower position I inquired as to working a different position as it was my 6th day working and my last round of the day. I was told no. When I got to the tower it appeared to me that Local Control and Ground Control had been on position for the same amount of time. I went to relieve Ground Control and the Supervisor told me 'no your not going to ground' when I inquired about the the time on position he told me that Local Control had been on position over 2 hours. I again asked if I could work Ground Control. The Supervisor did not answer and ordered me to go to Local Control.Another controller in the tower said the Local Controller had requested to go from a previous position to Local when he was relieved without a break. When I first assumed the position the Supervisor asked me if I wanted him to write some of the call signs on the strips. I declined since it did was not busy at the time. This session turned into a heavy arrival push with some departures and multiple crossings. There were numerous data tags constantly overlapping as well as approximately one half separation between several arrivals making it difficult not only to write down the aircraft call signs on the half strips used for this position but also to ensure the preceding arrival was off the runway prior to the succeeding aircraft crossing the landing threshold.The Supervisor stood at the Cab Coordinator position (which was not staffed) actively listening the entire time I was on position. The only coordination performed by the Supervisor was to tell me I could issue a 110 heading out of 1,500 feet which at the time was completely unnecessary as well as a distraction. Aircraft X had been cleared to land and hold short of taxiway whiskey for crossing traffic. I had an Aircraft Z that was going to do a missed approach with a 030 heading behind Aircraft X. Aircraft Y had previously called ready for departure I cleared Aircraft Y for departure then realizing it was not going to work when I did my 3 part scan I complete prior to every departure. I immediately went back to Aircraft Y and cancelled takeoff clearance and instructed them to hold short. The aircraft did not acknowledge, and even if a readback was accomplished and complied with, crossing the hold short line was inevitable. I chose to transmit to Aircraft X to get off the runway to prevent a possible departure creating a more dangerous situation. I have not had the opportunity to listen to the tape but I am almost positive Aircraft X exited the runway at an intersection. Aircraft Y was still northbound entering the runway when Aircraft X exited the runway. Aircraft Y was on the runway on an easterly heading and asked to verify if cleared for departure. I advised negative and instructed to hold in position to alleviate any further confusion on Aircraft Y part. After a short time went by I then cleared Aircraft Y for departure. At that point the Supervisor asked me if there was anything he needed to be looking into.I advised since he wasn't aware of what happened 'I didn't know' and then told him what is written above. I think it would be a good idea if a new Supervisor who may not be fully aware of the ins and outs of the facility during extreme pushes to have a Cab Coordinator opened. Also for whatever the reason, the Supervisor is unable to keep abreast of what is happening while actively listening with a headset standing 3 feet from the busiest position, then opening a Cab Coordinator would have been a good call. Perhaps a Cab Coordinator would have caught the situation not going to work prior to my clearing the aircraft for departure to begin with and would have definitely helped with the numerous crossings.
ASRS:1792656.s: An Air Traffic Controller working Local Control during a heavy arrival push nearly caused a runway incursion after clearing a departure that conflicted with a landing aircraft. The Controller attributed the near-miss to Supervisor inattention and the lack of a staffed Cab Coordinator to assist with complex traffic coordination.

ASRS:1792798.n: Aircraft X, ZZZ-ZZZ1, on decent into ZZZ1 at about 7,000 feet the gear warning audio went off 'landing gear-landing gear-landing gear' in a very loud tone in both headset and speaker. A quick troubleshooting of the system showed #2 radar altimeter 0 feet to -5 feet and #1 normal for 7,000 feet (hidden) no CAS message or other evidence of a fault. Left us with no direction for check list. We tried selecting the gear override switch but that was of no help silencing the audio. In my 35 years at this airline I have experienced many in flight emergencies including 5 engine failures however never in all those experiences has it been so hard to concentrate on dealing with the problem with the continued very loud 'landing gear-landing gear' over and over with no way to turn it off. It was also very evident to the forward flight attendant and most likely front half of the aircraft passengers. When we have a fire we get multiple warnings but we can silence the audio warning wile we work the problem. The other part that bothers me from a safety standpoint is we have two radar altimeter systems #1 and #2 if both are in agreement that's one thing but in this case only one was faulty. We should not get to this level of alarm during a disagreement or miss-comparison. I propose that we find a solution or fix so in the future crews can have an option in some way to silence this type of warning after they have acknowledged the problem. In our case we lowered the gear to silence the warning, this might not always be the best course of action.
ASRS:1792798.s: The flight crew of Aircraft XZZZ-ZZZ1 experienced a loud, unsilenceable landing gear warning during descent at 7,000 feet caused by a faulty #2 radar altimeter reading zero feet. Unable to silence the audio via override or checklist, the crew lowered the landing gear to stop the alarm, noting the warning was excessive for a single sensor disagreement.

ASRS:1792814.n: At FL210 master warning fuselage doors illuminated. Ran appropriate checklists, and talked to the flight attendants. It was deemed that the aft passenger door was not properly seated. We advised ATC and decided to divert to the nearest suitable airport (ZZZ). Safe outcome of flight.We eventually got on call maintenance to the aircraft, without having a definitive answer, it was decided the most likely issue was that the door may have never been closed and latched properly. The aft passenger door was opened and closed in ZZZ1.After maintenance ops check good, and getting refueled we continued to ZZZ2.I do feel as though our crew handled the situation well. I think some take aways are that while we were closest to ZZZ, there was a thought in the back of my head thinking that turning back to ZZZ1, or continuing to ZZZ3 were also good options, however the checklists drove us to nearest suitable which was ZZZ.
