In the future I would probably make the same decision, but it has given me thought. I also wonder if it would be good procedure to have the flight attendants just push on the door handle prior to departure to have one more check on the door security. One of our flight attendants had this exact same experience on this airplane approximately 1 week prior so there seems to be a systemic issue to address here.
ASRS:1792814.s: The flight crew diverted to ZZZ at FL210 after a master warning indicated the aft passenger door was not properly seated. Maintenance later suspected the door was never latched correctly, noting a similar incident on this aircraft one week prior.

ASRS:1792816.n: This flight was significantly delayed coming from ZZZ1-ZZZ. While awaiting the arrival of the aircraft I called my Dispatcher to double check latest conditions in ZZZ1. She informed me that Runway XX was up to a 5-5-5 braking action and that several arrivals were coming in with no issues. We quick turned in ZZZ we were the crew taking over the flight in ZZZ. Turbulent flight into ZZZ1, uneventful until landing rollout. Weather had been Freezing rain and freezing drizzle all day in ZZZ1. During landing rollout at approximately 30 kts. Tower told us to exit at Taxiway XX and contact Ground. We began to slide straight ahead on the runway I released the brakes and let the aircraft roll down the runway, we advised tower unable we will take exit XY. All taxiways were apparently closed except Taxiway XX or down to the end of the runway. We were instructed to continue down to the end of runway and exit onto Taxiway XZ. Upon reaching the end and beginning to slow about 5-10 kts ground speed the aircraft slid more significantly this time. We were able to regain traction after stopping briefly. We luckily did not slide off the runway nor taxiway. We reported braking action poor to ZZZ1 Tower which they immediately relayed to their Operations vehicles. I don't know the last time the runway was treated prior to our arrival, but it appeared to be about an inch of slushy icy accumulation. OAT was -1C. The walkways and ramps used to deplane passengers were treated with ice melt but extremely slick and dangerous, we had several passengers lose their footing while exiting the aircraft and on the ramp.I was hesitant based on my gut feeling for accepting the flight. I have experienced 5 winters in ZZZ1 in my 5 years at (Airline), each time freezing rain or drizzle is involved has been this exact experience. I understand that we want the operation to get our guests to their destination but I feel no one should have been operating into ZZZ1 today. The National Weather Service had issued an ice storm warning which was definitely evident on our near runway excursion. Next time I will trust my gut and refuse the flight in the interest of Safety. These ice storms are very dangerous and risky to operate in, I hope we can definitely avoid this in the future.
ASRS:1792816.s: The flight crew experienced a near runway excursion during landing rollout at ZZZ1 due to poor braking action from freezing rain and slushy ice accumulation. Although they regained traction and exited safely, the incident resulted in passengers slipping on treated but slick ramps, prompting the pilot to question the decision to operate into the ice storm.

ASRS:1792823.n: Taxiing to Z10 in the Z concourse at ZZZ we entered the ramp area without checking in with Ramp Control due to our confusion with ground clearances instructions. We were waiting on Y Taxiway to taxi to our gate and instructed by Ground Control to 'follow an aircraft ahead into West (the ramp area leading to our gate).' Usually these instructions are followed by 'contact Ramp Control.' However today we did not get those instructions. We followed preceding aircraft into West. I stopped on the north taxi lane without pulling into our gate and instructed my FO to check in with Ramp Control to make sure were cleared in. They in turn informed us that we needed to get clearance to enter the ramp and 'that Company A has been entering the ramp without clearance all week.' Hopefully this report will stop a clearly recurring problem. Maybe our confusion with ground controls clearance isn't only unique to us. We operate at many airports with Ramp Control and I can attest that there are standard instructions that we as pilots look for as cues such as being told to 'contact ramp control' before entering ramp. Compounding my confusion is the non-standard operations at airports because of COVID where air traffic is down, and Ramp Control has been frequently out of service. I thought I did the right thing by stopping to query my instructions. I admit I'm still getting used to the Z concourse procedures at ZZZ having operated at ZZZ even before all the construction. I should have queried earlier right at the boundary of the ramp and relayed the instructions I was following. Also, we observed another Company A aircraft read back the wrong instructions going into the West Ramp Control. They were told to taxi Y to West. The pilots read back 'taxi to the gate.' Which is incorrect because they were told to taxi to the ramp area not straight to the gate. Not sure if they were able to follow the instructions correctly. I'm more aware and learned from this experience and will be more vigilant going into ZZZ in the future.
ASRS:1792823.s: Pilots taxiing to Z10 at ZZZ entered the ramp area without Ramp Control clearance due to ambiguous Ground Control instructions and confusion over standard procedures. The crew stopped to verify clearance, noting a recurring issue where other operators also entered without authorization or misread taxi instructions.

ASRS:1792825.n: My Captain and I were ferrying an aircraft from ZZZ-ZZZ1. We were taking off Runway XX and after takeoff our lavatory smoke detector alarm started beeping. After direction from the Captain we [advised ATC] and made the decision to return to ZZZ. We requested direct ZZZ to hold and set up for our return. As we were entering the hold the alarm had stopped, we decided to still return to ZZZ as it was the safest decision and we could not verify that there was no fire. As we were holding we set the aircraft up to return, calling Company and following procedures for our return. After we finished setting ourselves up and getting ready we ran the checklists that we needed to, we requested vectors for to return to ZZZ and requested an ILS. We returned to ZZZ without any further issue and had fire trucks meet us on the runway to verify that there was no fire. After we verified there was no fire we taxied back to the ramp and shut down the aircraft. Lavatory fires or indications are handled by flight attendants, we did not have any on board so we treated this like a regular fire and returned to field in a safe and efficient manner.The Captain's workload was extremely busy, my recommendation/lesson learned is to help the Captain out sooner in any way possible including helping by offering to take flight controls and lessen the Captains workload. Another recommendation is having a procedure for pilots in the event of [lavatory] fire for pilots when no flight attendants are on board.
ASRS:1792825.s: Two pilots ferrying an aircraft from ZZZ-ZZZ1 returned to ZZZ after a lavatory smoke alarm activated during takeoff. They landed safely with fire trucks verifying no fire, noting the need for specific pilot procedures when flight attendants are absent.

ASRS:1792895.n: Helicopter piloted by Pilot X and Pilot Y 3 miles NW of ZZZ at XA:20 received priority handling due to a Number 2 Engine Electrical Control Unit failure in flight. Pilot X advised ATC and landed to a closed (NOTAMed out) taxiway. The aircraft landed safely but was unable to be moved to an alternate location due to the failure.
ASRS:1792895.s: Pilots X and Y landed a helicopter safely on a closed taxiway 3 miles NW of ZZZ at XA:20 after a Number 2 Engine Electrical Control Unit failure. The aircraft could not be moved to an alternate location due to the failure.

ASRS:1792896.n: We were cleared for takeoff and started our taxi onto Runway XX. Once lined up, we held our brakes did our 2000 RPM engine run to check engine instruments one last time before starting the takeoff roll. All engine instruments were in the normal operating ranges. I am the flight instructor and as the student released the brakes and went full power, I started to lower the mixture to simulate an abnormality on takeoff. While the mixture was being changed, I noticed a rattling, so immediately went back to full mixture and stopped the training simulation. I reached for the throttles and that is when the right gear gave in and we dropped on the right side of the aircraft. Throttles were full idle and mixtures were then cut off. We notified ZZZ Tower of our situation and afterwards completed a full shutdown of the aircraft while waiting for personnel to arrive.
ASRS:1792896.s: A flight instructor and student experienced a right main gear collapse during a simulated engine abnormality on takeoff. The instructor attributed the failure to the gear giving way while reaching for the throttles, resulting in the aircraft dropping to the right side and requiring a full shutdown.

ASRS:1792900.n: In the VFR sectional chart issued Feb 25, 2021, the Danville VOR (DNV) has the wrong frequency listed. It should be 111.0. It is listed here as 110.0, which is the frequency for a nearby VOR CMI. I noticed while flight planning my student solo cross country flight.It seems plausible a NAVAID could be mistakenly tuned to the nearby one and be a safety factor. Hope it's fixed in the next issue.
ASRS:1792900.s: A pilot identified an incorrect frequency for the Danville VOR (DNV) listed as 110.0 instead of 111.0 on the February 25, 2021, VFR sectional chart while flight planning a student solo cross-country. The error could cause a pilot to mistakenly tune the nearby CMI VOR, posing a safety risk.

ASRS:1792913.n: My student and I were conducting a routine multi engine training flight. As part of this flight we had decided we would be doing a full engine shutdown, feather and in air restart. We shutdown and feathered the engine at 4,000 feet. About 1-2 minutes elapsed before we briefed and began to run through the engine restart procedure. When we engaged the start, we only got a half rotation from the propeller. We tried a couple different restart variations, priming, different throttle and mixture positions, but we still had the issue of not getting enough power to turn the engine over enough times to unfeather it. After 3-4 start attempts, all of the electrical components in the cockpit became inoperative. Avionics, intercom, transponder and transponder were all inoperative. After all the avionics and intercom shut off, we began to troubleshoot the issue. We recycled the avionics master, minimized electrical load and squawked 7600 in the event the transponder was still transmitting. I knew we needed to start back towards the airport regardless of whether we got the electrical system back up, because the likelihood of us getting the engine restarted with a clear electrical issue was slim to none, seeing as getting an engine out of feather takes a significant amount electrical power. Our next course of action was to get in touch with ATC. We did not have cell service at 4,000 ft., (altitude at which the shutdown occurred) so we started a slow descending left turn (into the good engine) in hopes of getting service. I was not going to let us go below 3,000 [ft.]. At around 3,500 ft. I got enough cell service to call ZZZ Approach, using the Bluetooth on my headset and phone to talk with them. I told ZZZ Approach we had experienced an electrical failure and that we were also single engine. At this time I also [received priority]. Approach was able to give us a heading to fly to intercept final and during that time while we proceeded towards the airport, we ran through our engine securing checklist and single engine approach and landing checklist, we briefed the landing and determined I would fly the final approach and landing. With the checklist and briefing done, all that was left was to fly the approach. We got our landing clearance over the phone, got the gear down and established a final approach speed of 125 MPH. The landing on Runway XX was uneventful, with the aircraft touching down in the first 3rd of the runway. ARFF (Airport Rescue and Fire Fighting) units were on alert and followed us down the runway to where we exited at Taxiway XX. As we were coming to a stop on [Taxiway] XX all our avionics turned back on, so we were able to contact Ground to get our taxi clearance back to the [FBO]. An air guard fire personnel did a quick check of the aircraft, asked if we were ok and then we were able to taxi back to our flight school ramp without incident.
ASRS:1792913.s: During a multi-engine training flight, an instructor and student experienced an electrical failure after failed attempts to restart a feathered engine at 4,000 feet. They contacted ATC via cell phone, received priority, and executed a single-engine landing with ARFF support before avionics restored on the taxiway.

ASRS:1792922.n: About one hour from landing, we started to smell a faint burning scent from the packs. It was very faint, but noticeable. It smelled like glycol or plastic burning. It remained constant until we initiated a descent from FL390-FL370. The smell became more pronounced. For lack of another checklist or procedure, we ran the smoke fire and fumes QRH. The smell was only in the cockpit and not the cabin. Since we could not determine the source. We deemed it appropriate to take the safest course of action to expedite getting the aircraft on the ground with no undue delay. We [advised ATC] and asked for CFR (Crash Fire Rescue) to meet us to check for anything out of the ordinary upon landing. We initiated a high speed descent and approach, and performed a safe landing. CFR met the aircraft and checked it over and we taxied to the gate.
ASRS:1792922.s: Pilots detected a faint burning smell in the cockpit during cruise, which intensified during descent from FL390 to FL370. They executed a high-speed descent and safe landing with Crash Fire Rescue standing by, as the source remained undetermined.

ASRS:1792936.n: Prior to pushing, the outgoing Flight Attendant told me the air bag at [Seat] XXE was out. After some clarification she meant the life vest at [Seat] XXE was falling out. This distraction had us focusing on adding the MEL to the Release. We we're subsequently given the HAZMAT Dangerous Goods Form just prior to push and failed to verify that there was no remark on the Release regarding the HAZMAT.
ASRS:1792936.s: The pilot and outgoing flight attendant discussed a life vest issue at Seat XXE before pushback, causing a distraction that led to adding an MEL to the Release. Consequently, the crew failed to verify the Release for HAZMAT remarks after receiving the Dangerous Goods Form just prior to push.

ASRS:1792943.n: While conducting a Captain OE (Operating Experience) I was doing the exterior pre-flight and noticed a large area of oil under the left engine on the ground. When looking closer I could see a large area of old oil dripping from under the cowling and could see active drips on the pavement. I consulted with my OE student and he entered a log item in the ACARS while I called OPS on the VHF radio to have Maintenance come out to inspect the engine. I then went back to the ramp level to speak with the technicians. When the two maintenance technicians got to the plane, they told me the oil was from an over service of the engine. They then inquired with the mechanic that did the ETOPS service check and he said he did not add any oil to the engine. They then told me it was from the scupper and that it was normal leakage. I was not sure that this was true and asked if they would open the cowling to have a look. One mechanic opened the cowling and he just lifted it slightly but did not investigate beyond a cursory look and told me he would sign it off as it was fine and nothing to worry about. We accepted the aircraft and flew to ZZZ. As we progressed, I noted we were losing approximately one quart of oil per hour. During our five-hour flight our quantity in the left engine dropped from 21 to 16. We made another log entry for our arrive at ZZZ. After parking I went to the ramp level and noticed the oil was already pooling beneath the engine less than 15 minutes after arrival. I checked the maintenance action on the flight after our write up and saw ZZZ Maintenance found a broken seal on the left IDG (Integrated Drive Generator). This is very concerning as the ZZZ1 Maintenance team placed us in a position where could have lost the IDG, engine and or created a fire hazard during a 180-minute ETOPS flight.
ASRS:1792943.s: The Captain observed active oil leakage from the left engine during pre-flight, which maintenance initially dismissed as normal scupper leakage without a thorough inspection. Post-flight inspection at ZZZ revealed a broken left IDG seal, causing significant oil loss during the ETOPS flight and creating a potential fire hazard.

ASRS:1792944.n: Shortly after takeoff, we noticed a fuel imbalance of about 1,200 pounds with the right tank showing a lower quantity. As we were monitoring the fuel gauges, Flight Attendant called to advise a passenger noticed fluid coming out of the right wing after takeoff. Captain was able to balance the fuel.After established in cruise for about 10 min, started to notice another fuel imbalance in progress. Captain ran FUEL LEAK QRH and noted time and fuel quantities. Got to a fuel imbalance of 650 pounds within 20 min.At this point Captain and I concurred that it looked like we had a fuel leak. Advised ATC of the situation and requested to divert to ZZZ1. Continued and finished QRH checklist. Performed an engine shutdown followed by a single engine landing.
ASRS:1792944.s: The flight crew detected a fuel leak from the right wing shortly after takeoff, causing significant imbalance. They diverted to ZZZ1, shut down the affected engine, and completed a single-engine landing.

ASRS:1792975.n: Upon holding short of the runway in ZZZ, we experienced a burning odor in the cockpit during the pneumatic ice protection test. We contacted Maintenance and began troubleshooting. Both packs were individually giving us a burning odor. The flight attendant had called us to let us know that he smelled it too. We then returned to the gate. Once at the gate, we submitted 2 write-ups, one for the burning odor and one for a flickering Multi-Function Flight Displays screen that was progressively getting worse. I was informed later that this plane had the same issue the month prior. After our write up, maintenance could not reproduce the problem and signed the aircraft off. I later learned, from my flight attendant who was now with the new crew on the same plane, upon engine startup, they immediately began to smell burning fumes. This was following the sign-off from maintenance. Flight crew shut down packs and taxi back to the gate.Captain recommended replacing all duct work and packs as burning odor/fumes seems to be a common issue, or find out what is causing so many similar problems.
ASRS:1792975.s: Flight crew and a flight attendant detected a burning odor during a pneumatic ice protection test while holding short in ZZZ, prompting a return to the gate. Maintenance could not reproduce the issue and signed the aircraft off, but the next crew smelled fumes immediately upon startup, forcing another return to the gate.

ASRS:1792976.n: While on descent into ZZZ on the ZZZZZ arrival we experienced a BLD 1 LEAK Master Warning with associated EICAS and red inscription messages. The FO (First Officer) proceeded to run the QRH, while I asked for immediate vectors to ZZZ along with a descent to exit IMC and icing conditions. ATC granted the descent, as well as direct ZZZ. The bleed leak warning was still occurring while the FO waited the requisite 3 minutes as per the QRH. This prompted me to [receive priority] as the eventual end of the QRH procedure is to secure the engine should the leak not extinguish. As we descended out of icing conditions, the BLD LEAK message extinguished, prompting no further action from the QRH. At this time I notified the FA (Flight Attendant) with a TEST briefing as to the nature of our [situation], that the immediate threat had passed and we would be landing normally. I also made a PA to the passengers to inform them that they may see ARFF (Airport Rescue and Fire Fighting) vehicles around the aircraft on landing. We continued to a normal landing on XXL in ZZZ and taxied to the gate with no further assistance required.Master Warning bell with associated EICAS and red inscription messages.Unknown problem in bleed system caused a BLD 1 LEAK Master Warning. Aircraft had been written up 3 days prior for same issue with associated maintenance entry clearing the write up.QRH ran, ATC advised to clear icing conditions, proceeded to normal landing in ZZZ.Possibly more in-depth look at bleed system whenever a leak detection warning occurs beyond ops check good. On the ZZZZZ arrival into ZZZ we descended into a cloud layer and encountered icing conditions. Within 30 seconds of the anti-ice system being turned on we received a 'Bleed 1 Leak' EICAS message. As Pilot Monitoring, I ran the respective QRH associated with that message. Still being in icing conditions we decided it would be best if we advised ATC to gain priority and also since we did not know how thick the icing cloud layer was. Upon waiting the 3 minutes as stated by the QRH we exited the icing conditions and within 30 seconds the bleed leak message and inscription went away thus ending the QRH procedure. We continued to ZZZ, landed and taxied to the gate normally.
ASRS:1792976.s: During descent into ZZZ in icing conditions, the crew received a BLD 1 LEAK warning and executed the QRH while requesting priority and a descent to exit the ice. The warning extinguished after leaving the icing layer, allowing for a normal landing with no further action required.

ASRS:1792987.n: In cruise we got a ECAM alert of hydraulic blue sys low press followed by blue hydraulic low quantity. Followed ECAM checklist and contacted Dispatch to discuss option. Determined it best to continue to ZZZ. We advised ATC and landed on Runway XX.It was an unforeseen event that was handled according to company passengers and policies. During cruise, the ECAM notified us of a HYD B RSVR LO LVL failure with associated B SYS LO PR. Followed ECAM procedure and secured B SYS Hydraulics. Notified Dispatch, evaluated situation, advised ATC and landed safely in ZZZ.The decision to continue to ZZZ was a good one, giving the crew and myself plenty of time to assess and not rush. First Officer (Pilot Flying) did a good job staying on task while I handled the problem with Dispatch and the Flight Attendant crew. He also did a nice job flying.Failure of an electrical HYD pump cannot be planned for. Good crew coordination makes the response to the problem easier to handle.
ASRS:1792987.s: During cruise, the flight crew received ECAM alerts for blue hydraulic system low pressure and quantity, followed by a blue reservoir low level failure. They secured the blue system, coordinated with Dispatch and ATC, and landed safely at ZZZ, attributing the successful outcome to effective crew coordination.

ASRS:1793040.n: Flying over the hills under ZZZ Class Bravo Airspace in IMC and Terrain Awareness (EPGWS) activated with a 'Terrain Terrain Pull Up' aural command. I clicked the TOGA (Takeoff/Go-Around) button and began a climb and briefly entered visual conditions with some terrain in sight. We advised ZZZ [TRACON] of our climb. ZZZ [TRACON] was perplexed as he stated that the Minimum Vectoring Altitude in our sector was 3,200 [feet] MSL. We were instructed to maintain 3,500 [feet] MSL and the flight continued without incident.Event due to possible sensitive Terrain Awareness Warning System/EGPWS. The crew treated the event as a terrain threat an acted accordingly.
ASRS:1793040.s: The flight crew flying in IMC over hills in ZZZ Class Bravo airspace received a Terrain Awareness Warning System alert and executed a climb to 3,500 feet MSL. The controller noted the Minimum Vectoring Altitude was 3,200 feet, suggesting the event was caused by a sensitive system warning.

ASRS:1793055.n: Cleaners in ZZZ are not following policy for waiting for all passengers to leave aircraft before they board to clean, and not following crew instructions to remain off the aircraft. Cleaners must wait for all passengers to deplane prior to boarding the aircraft.Cleaners in ZZZ are aggressively pushing their way into the forward galley to remove trash from the carts during the deplaning process. This impedes the flow of deplaning passengers and obstructs the ability of flight attendants to manage the flow of passengers and maintain door and safety compliance. Cleaners are insisting that flight attendants leave the galley area so they can work, they say operations has told them to move the crew to accomplish the cleaning task. Allowing cleaners to pull carts and trash while flight attendants and passengers are deplaning creates safety hazards (bumps, trips, and impacts from trash removal) and does not allow for safe social distancing as per company policy. Cleaners also leave bags on the floor posing a trip hazard for crew and passengers deplaning, as I was deplaning a cleaner had left a gray cleaning tote below a jump-seat and I tripped over it falling into the bulkhead.
ASRS:1793055.s: Cleaners in ZZZ boarded the aircraft before all passengers deplaned, obstructing flight attendants and creating trip hazards with trash carts and bags. The reporter tripped over a cleaning tote left on the floor, citing that cleaners ignored crew instructions and company safety policies.

ASRS:1793073.n: I was in a Super Cub flying toward an uncontrolled airport. The pattern was very busy including some fast-moving aircraft so I veered off east of the airport planning to wait until the pattern cleared so that I could land my slow flying plane. I was just at 4NM from the airport.An instructional flight with a CFI and a student made a radio call that they were 'on the 45 to the left downwind for 23'. Shortly thereafter they passed underneath me from a blind spot behind me and to the right, east.The instructor was upset feeling that I was 'in the downwind' for 23 without making radio calls. At the time of the near miss, I was a few hundred feet inside the 4 NM airport area. From a visual perspective, I did not think that I was anywhere near the pattern, except for jets which I would have expected to be higher than my 2,300 feet.I was barely inside the 4 NM airport area and had not made any radio calls, intending to maneuver well east of the field to wait on traffic to quiet down.One contributing factor of the near miss was me not making a radio call that I was at the edge of the airport 4NM area. A contributing cause was a light aircraft at pattern altitude over 4 NM from the airport considering themselves to be in the pattern.I did contact the pilot of the other aircraft to 'debrief' the situation and I plan to discuss with the leadership of the flight school.
ASRS:1793073.s: A Super Cub pilot and a CFI with a student experienced a near miss near an uncontrolled airport while the Super Cub waited east of the pattern at 2,300 feet. The reporter attributed the incident to their failure to make radio calls and the other aircraft's assumption they were in the pattern while over 4 NM away.

ASRS:1793083.n: On descent for landing ZZZ engine lost all power. I immediately told ZZZ tower that I had a priority situation and was experiencing engine failure. I rocked the wings, turned fuel back and forth, put throttle in out, mixture also, along with checking mags etc. Engine finally came back to some power and then all power returned. Continued on for a successful landing at ZZZ. Upon parking aircraft at the hanger had fuel topped off, it took 24 gallons to top. I had 12 gallons remaining. Checked airplane out with mechanic and found broken mixture control cable as the cause. Cable was completely severed at the carburetor.
ASRS:1793083.s: During descent for landing, the pilot experienced a total engine power loss due to a severed mixture control cable. After restoring power through troubleshooting, the pilot landed safely, and a mechanic later confirmed the broken cable as the cause.

ASRS:1793086.n: Got to location failed to research the airspace. Was relying on the manufacture's Geo fencing to guide me with airspace. Violation was discovered by company UAS coordinator. Violation was discussed and corrective action for further use is understood. We discussed and now understand the difference between Geo fencing and the NAS. I going further, will look up airspace before flights. I will not fly in controlled airspace without proper authorization.
ASRS:1793086.s: A pilot failed to research airspace before a UAS flight, relying solely on manufacturer geo-fencing, which resulted in an airspace violation discovered by the company coordinator. The pilot acknowledged the error, understood the difference between geo-fencing and the NAS, and committed to checking airspace and obtaining authorization before future flights.

ASRS:1793087.n: The first 3,000 feet of Runway 14 has excessive dips and divots that are bottoming out our landing gear struts during landing rollout and during takeoff. On landing Runway 14, after touchdown with the thrust reversers deployed, we felt the main landing gear struts fully compress and the aircraft nearly bounce. The nose strut also bottomed out and we were pushed into our seats hard. This occurred around 80-100 knots and the dips continued down the runway fully compressing our struts each time. On departure from Runway 14, the same thing happened. We are concerned that without an immediate repair to the runway, that these dips and divots will grow and potentially cause harm to the aircraft landing gear and structure which would cause a landing or takeoff accident. It's that bad.
ASRS:1793087.s: Pilots reported that excessive dips and divots in the first 3,000 feet of Runway 14 caused landing gear struts to bottom out during takeoff and landing rollouts at 80–100 knots. They warned that without immediate repairs, this runway condition could damage the aircraft structure and cause an accident.

ASRS:1793096.n: Aircraft X was on an LDA Approach. I had not cleared them for the approach because I was trying to descend the aircraft for the Visual Approach. Just leaving 9,000 feet, the aircraft took a hard left turn. I keyed up and turned them to a 010 heading to which they stated they were having autopilot problems. The aircraft started descending below 8000 feet. I issued a Low Altitude alert. Shortly after, the aircraft took another hard left turn. I did not reissue a low altitude alert but restated altitude and heading with immediately. Because of this, I broke the aircraft following him off the approach and re-sequenced him. Aircraft X landed without further incident.I'm not sure what else to do in this situation. Pilots need to learn to fly without their autopilot. Everyone is way too reliant on technology and need to get back to the basics. While transitioning from the RNAV arrival to the LDA Approach, my autopilot malfunctioned and caused the airplane to deviate from the approach. I was below the cloud bases and in VMC. I attempted to fly the airplane without the autopilot and regain the appropriate heading and altitude, while troubleshooting the autopilot issue. I was given a vector and an altitude by the approach controller and I did not maintain that altitude during the trouble shooting efforts. I went below 8,000 feet which is below the minimum vectoring altitude in that area.My fixation on troubleshooting the autopilot and not devoting full attention to flying the airplane caused this issue. The fact that I was in VMC further added to my lack of focus, as I was clearly able to see and avoid any terrain in the area. Focusing solely on the task of flying the airplane would have prevented this issue from occurring.
ASRS:1793096.s: An Air Traffic Controller and pilot of Aircraft X experienced an autopilot malfunction during an LDA approach transition, causing the aircraft to deviate and descend below 8,000 feet. The pilot attributed the incident to fixation on troubleshooting the autopilot while in VMC, resulting in a missed altitude clearance and re-sequencing before a safe landing.

ASRS:1793100.n: Aircraft X was on vector to RWY XX off the downwind. Ceiling was marginal, but I was confident I would get the airport in sight, at least by 070. I vectored Aircraft X in front of Aircraft Y on the straight-in. This situation happened less than 10 minutes prior to another report I just filed with a pilot deviation so I was already frazzled from that. I turned Aircraft X heading 090, they did not respond, immediately re-keyed 'Aircraft X, heading 080.' The pilot read back correctly. They were level 080. My vector had the aircraft practically straddling the 080/070 MVA line. My PTL (Projected Track Line) showed a left turn, I descended Aircraft X to 070. Almost immediately, the aircraft showed a right turn. I immediately corrected Aircraft X to a 070, realized I had given the descent and tried to stop at 080. The aircraft went to 075 in a 080 MVA. At this point, Aircraft Y is going to run them over, so I turn Aircraft X south at 080. I didn't have time to exchange traffic and he would pass about 2nm West. As Aircraft Y was approaching ZZZZZ, I cleared the aircraft for the approach even though they were not yet tail to tail because I knew the aircraft wouldn't descend quite yet. When I saw the aircraft side by side, I climbed Aircraft to 090 because 7nm south, Restricted Area XXXX was active to 090. Upon review, Aircraft X showed 081 and I was informed I had a LoSS [Loss of Separation Standards] in addition to three separate pilot deviations.I guess I should have waited a second longer to climb Aircraft X, that would have prevented the LoSS, however, delaying any more could have put him in an unsafe situation with the Restricted Area where they are shooting artillery. I truly showed the aircraft side by side and waited as long as I could to climb to ensure I would clear Aircraft X, I thought I was legal. Choose the lesser of the evils. I truly thought I had crossing/diverging. I wish I wouldn't have descended the Aircraft X to 070 either, but he read back the turn, I saw the turn start with the PTL and pushed him down because I needed to with Aircraft Y coming fast behind, and already being extended from Aircraft Z I had to break off in the earlier situation. The fact I have two back-to-back pilot deviations, one go-around from it, and when I go on break and have to spend my break doing a report, to then be told I had a LoSS, rather than even giving me even a few seconds to get my bearings is why management in this facility is worthless. Back to back, high stress situations, and we would rather tell you that you [are no good] at your job rather than good job, or are you doing okay even. I'm not mad at them calling the LoSS, I take responsibility for observing my scope wrong since. I'm upset that rather than even attempting to care about their employees, they immediately try to make them feel worse.
ASRS:1793100.s: An air traffic controller vectored Aircraft X and Aircraft Y during approach, resulting in a Loss of Separation Standards and three pilot deviations. The controller attributed the incident to misinterpreting the radar scope under high stress while managing conflicting traffic and an active restricted area.

ASRS:1793101.n: My D-side had reminded me about a pending confliction that I needed to resolve which I had put off. I was a little annoyed with myself and as such my resolution was perhaps a bit more aggressive than needed. Headings were issued to both aircraft and it worked out fine. I had intended to have Aircraft X on course before he neared the adjacent sector boundary but I didn't check on it quite soon enough. I remember thinking that it would work out fine but I was apparently slightly off in my estimation and the aircraft got within 2.5 miles of the adjacent sector boundary - without actually crossing the boundary - without a pointout, which my D-side also failed to notice.I never did notice the event, Management informed me later as they'd coincidentally been monitoring the sector.I had perhaps gotten a little complacent from the routine and experience. I'll be extra sure to follow up on any headings issued so as to ensure the aircraft involved perform as expected, and to be more vigilant in protecting my airspace boundaries.
ASRS:1793101.s: An air traffic controller issued aggressive headings to resolve a conflict, causing Aircraft X to approach within 2.5 miles of a sector boundary without a pointout. The controller attributed the oversight to complacency and admitted to failing to verify the aircraft's position before it neared the boundary.

ASRS:1793125.n: Good VFR day, cleared departure out of ZZZ to TEHRU, then direct MTJ. Just prior to TEHRU we informed the DEN Center controller that we would be requesting the ILS [Runway] 17 and was expecting to be vectored to the localizer. Instead, we were given 'direct DIRDY, Cross DIRDY at or above 13,000 feet, cleared for the ILS 17.'Loaded that into the MCDU, which inserted the procedure turn depicted to the north, after BRUUK. As the track from GEJYU to BRUUK is 78 degrees off the localizer course we figured this was the only 'legal' way to fly it, based on our clearance, so wasn't surprised. (Coming from the west side of the localizer there is a DME arc with a lead-in radial depicted to account for that steep angle, but not from the east. Again, we assumed the procedure turn was the only legal way to turn onto the localizer.)Although the crossing altitude for GEJYU is 10,800 feet the initial procedure turn altitude is 12,500 feet so we crossed GEJYU somewhere above 13,000 feet on our descent to 12,500 feet. Unfortunately, when we visually picked up the airport this made us too high to ask for a visual approach so we decided to just fly the procedure turn, as planned.After becoming established in the procedure turn outbound, the Controller asked us what we were doing and said most flights just join the localizer and go directly toward the runway. After some back-and-forth about this, while we were in the turn back toward BRUUK, he said 'low altitude alert, climb and maintain 13,000 [feet]' (we were still at 12,500 [feet], and VFR). We climbed to 13,000 feet, called the runway in sight, and were cleared for the visual approach.Long story short(er), there was obvious confusion on our part regarding how this approach was supposed to be flown, as well as, I believe, based on our conversation, the Controller's. After landing we looked over the chart for 5-10 minutes, looking at all the various notes, etc., before finally noticing the 'NoPT' note depicted under the 9,000 feet MEA listed for the leg from GEJYU to BRUUK.I saw the altitude and NoPT but when looking at the routing in the FMS and the procedure turn altitude assumed it wasn't intended for flying the full approach. I also don't understand why we would expect to intercept a localizer from a 78-degree angle when, I believe, while being vectored to an intercept, the intercept heading given by ATC is required to be within 30 degrees of the localizer course. If we had flown the depicted track from GEJYU to BRUUK as apparently expected on this approach, I believe the airplane would have overshot the turn onto the localizer by at least 1-2 miles. As for the low altitude warning the airplane was flying the published procedure turn on altitude which would lead one to believe you were in protected airspace?
ASRS:1793125.s: The flight crew and Denver Center controller experienced confusion during an ILS 17 approach at ZZZ due to a missed "NoPT" chart note. The crew unnecessarily flew a procedure turn, triggering a low altitude alert, before climbing to 13,000 feet and completing a visual approach.

ASRS:1793127.n: I was Pilot Flying. On approach to Runway XXR at ZZZ, after calling for the landing gear down and flaps 15, we noticed that we had three green and three red landing gear indications. The overhead panel showed three green indications. We were able to complete the QRH and Landing Checklist and determined that the landing gear was down and locked. We continued the approach with the intention of landing. At approximately 500 feet AGL, we received the oral warning 'TOO LOW GEAR.'I was no longer sure that the landing gear was down and locked. I called for the go-around and executed the go-around procedure. We decided to leave the landing gear down and cleaned the flaps up to 5 degrees. The Captain was working the radios and informed ATC of the go-around. ATC gave us a heading and cleared us to 2,000 feet. They asked for the reason of the go-around. The Captain informed them that we were having landing gear indication problems. The Captain then decided to request priority handling.We completed the QRH and were able to get three green indications without red indications. The Captain informed ATC we had solved the problem and could continue for another approach and landing. ATC assigned us Runway XXL. We set up the FMC, re-briefed the approach, completed all of the appropriate checklists, flew the approach, and landed uneventfully on Runway XXL. We taxied to the gate, shut down the engines and completed the Shut Down Checklist. While at the gate we had realized that due to workload, we had forgotten to inform the flight attendants of the priority handling situation.To prevent this from happening again, we need to slow down, and complete all briefings to the Flight Attendants and Passenger cabin prior to landing. Just because we were able to solve the landing gear problem and workload was heavy, does not alleviate the duty to inform the Cabin Crew.
ASRS:1793127.s: The Pilot Flying executed a go-around at 500 feet AGL due to conflicting landing gear indications and a "TOO LOW GEAR" warning. After resolving the indication issue, the crew landed safely but failed to brief the cabin crew about the priority handling due to high workload.

ASRS:1793137.n: Near midair collision with a personal 'drone' remotely piloted aerial vehicle, roughly 18' square in size. Occurred on the SCBBY2 arrival, TAKOE TSN for RWY 26R, at 6,000 feet MSL, 3.5nm East of KALEA Intersection. FO (First Officer) was pilot flying and picked up tally off the nose inside .5 nm, low-hi, rapidly moving from right to left. Jumpseater also gained visual situational awareness at the left cockpit window #2. Both FO and Jumpseater estimate the drone passed less than 50 feet in elevation from the left wing and certainly within the lateral wingspan distance of the aircraft, which confirmed the visual ID of a drone vs. a bird. Captain was pilot monitoring and did not see the drone but reported location, altitude, time, and general description to SoCal Approach moments after the incident with the information FO passed to him. We continued the approach to land without incident.
ASRS:1793137.s: During the SCBBY2 arrival to RWY 26R at 6,000 feet MSL, the First Officer and jumpseater observed a drone pass within 50 feet vertically and laterally of the left wing. The Captain reported the incident to SoCal Approach, and the crew continued the approach and landed without further incident.

ASRS:1793152.n: This was the first leg of a 3-day trip and my 2nd trip in several months. I had not flown in several months due to COVID scheduling (but I have remained current with a PC simulator). I was having difficulty in clearly hearing ATC and through the interphone in flight. I was the pilot flying at the time of the event. My First Officer has been enduring a highly antagonistic situation in the home life, which may have found its way to the flight deck, creating an unanticipated stressor. My First Officer was distressed over these interactions, resulting in a secondary distraction.On approach, my First Officer (the pilot not flying) believed we were issued a clearance down to 2,400 feet and read back the misunderstood altitude of 2,400 feet. I did not catch the altitude clearance. Descending below 3,400 feet, ATC advised us of a low Altitude Alert and informed us that we were meant to be at 3,400 feet. We apologized and explained it was a misheard clearance. ATC asked us to climb back up to 3,400 feet and advised us we were still cleared for the approach. We complied and continued without incident.We discussed as a crew the intention to submit a report that evening. Being a bit rusty on operating in the physical environment and with the remainder of a 3-day to focus on (including a line check), I inadvertently forgot to write the report. After our first 2 legs, I was scheduled to split from my First Officer to fly with a line check pilot (per my request prior to the trip) out of an abundance of caution, due to being out of the physical environment for so long. It may be because we were no longer operating together that my First Officer and I forgot to submit our reports in a timely fashion (without having each other as a reminder).My job as a Captain is to ensure the aircraft is flown in a safe manner and that we comply with ATC instructions. The responsibility comes down to me to maintain total situational awareness in all phases of flight. I became inadvertently disconnected from the communications loop as pilot flying. This resulted in a breakdown of a good multi-crew concept, as well as an unsafe situation and unintentional deviation from ATC instruction. I must remain more diligent and vigilant as a crew member in all aspects of flight, regardless of assigned duty in order to maintain safe and compliant operation.It is also imperative that I participate in SMS in a timely manner, consistent with company standards. To be an effective team leader, it is also my duty to ensure my crew members take part in SMS. This can only enhance safety for our colleagues and industry as a whole. It was never my intention to neglect to submit a report, but unfortunately it was mistakenly forgotten. I should make reminders for myself to stay on task with necessary reports. In the future I may find it helpful to set reminders in my phone whenever issues like this arise. On approach to land, as the First Officer and PM for the leg, I responded to ATC's instruction to descend to 2,400 feet. My Captain did verify with me the altitude to descend too, since Captain had not heard it clearly. I advised that the assigned altitude was 2,400 feet. It wasn't until we were descending below 3,400 feet that ATC checked in and advised that we were to level off at 3,400 feet. We did proceed to climb back to 3,400 feet and continued the approach to land.The altitude of 2,400 feet was above the FAF altitude and ATC did not correct me when I replied to ATC with the confirmation to descend to 2,400 feet. It was then that, with the 2,400 foot altitude assignment being a bit lower than expected, even though ATC had not corrected me when I responded with a 2,400 foot altitude assignment, I should have verified the altitude assignment.In the future, as a First Officer and soon to be Captain, I will be more vigilant with all procedures and in the interest of safety and full compliance, verify that all direction and communications are clear, concise and without question. If this is ever in doubt, I will take full responsibility and take all steps necessary to ensure a safe and compliant flight.
ASRS:1793152.s: The Captain and First Officer descended below 3,400 feet on approach after mishearing an ATC clearance for 2,400 feet, causing a low altitude alert. The crew climbed back to 3,400 feet and landed safely, attributing the error to communication difficulties, personal stress, and the Captain's recent lack of flight time.

ASRS:1793183.n: Shortly after takeoff we received a bird strike in our Number 1 Engine that caused considerable damage. Based on the engine vibration as well as the unusual noises coming from the aircraft, we determined it was necessary to immediately return for landing at ZZZ. I received priority with air traffic control and the First Officer continued flying the aircraft. There were no ECAM actions or QRH follow ups. Although there were high vibration indications as well as some initial fluctuations with N1, N2 and EGT (Exhaust Gas Temperature), the engine parameters remained in the realm of normal. Therefore, the First Officer and myself did not see any reason for shutting the engine down in flight. We landed safely, let the airport personnel do a quick inspection of the aircraft on the taxiway and then returned to the gate.It all went fairly well. There was a startle factor with this event. But, in general we followed everything we learned in training. However, I may have delegated the re-configuring of the aircraft to the First Officer a bit too soon. He did that on his own. It was all done correctly. But, I don't remember doing the normal acceleration altitude call outs. I did all the standard communication procedures to ATC, cabin crew, passengers and Dispatch. Then, rejoined the First Officer for the approach preparation. The First Officer handled flying the aircraft as well as his communication with ATC perfectly.There is nothing that I can suggest that would prevent this from happening again. We always have to contend with the hazards associated with migratory waterfowl. Always consider that as a threat during that time of the year as well as keep a vigilant lookout. During takeoff approximately 700-800 feet we struck birds. We returned to ZZZ.Do not allow birds near airports.
ASRS:1793183.s: The flight crew experienced a bird strike in Engine 1 at 700–800 feet after takeoff, causing high vibration and noise but no parameter exceedances. They returned to ZZZ for a safe landing without shutting down the engine, attributing the event to migratory waterfowl hazards.

ASRS:1793195.n: On departure lost Number 2 Pitch Trim, Autothrottle, 1 and 2 Autopilots and FO (First Officer) Flight Director. Number 1 Pitch Trim already deferred. Also, MEL that restricted us from RVSM airspace. Performed ECAM/ QRH procedures and could not reset Pitch Trim or Autothrottles. No autopilots were recovered and only manual trim available. [Received priority from ATC] as a precautionary measure. Returned to departure airport ZZZ. No further problems noted. Uneventful landing.Cause - System malfunction of Pitch Trim and Autopilots.Suggestion - Will await Maintenance final action/correction. On departure at acceleration altitude we had Pitch Trim 2 fault. Pitch Trim 1 was already deferred. The ATS (Autothrottle System) lever also tripped off and I had FD2 flag on my pad. After the aircraft was cleaned up and the after takeoff checklist completed. I selected my FD switch to get FD1 on my PFD (Primary Flight Display). We accomplished the ECAM. Neither Pitch Trim 2 or ATS off reset. We ran the pitch fault QRH. It was no help. We elected to [advise ATC] and land in ZZZ.Cause - Pitch Trim 2 fault with Pitch Trim 1 deferred already.
ASRS:1793195.s: The crew experienced a Pitch Trim 2 fault, Autothrottle trip, and Autopilot loss on departure with Pitch Trim 1 already deferred. They returned to ZZZ for an uneventful landing after failing to reset systems via ECAM and QRH procedures.

ASRS:1793199.n: While cruising at FL380, ATC advised us of traffic approaching us at 10 miles, opposite direction, FL370. My First Officer visually verified the traffic, but we did not relay this to ATC. Within 40 seconds from being notified we initially received a (TA) Traffic Advisory then immediately followed by an (RA) Resolution Advisory. My FO (First Officer) immediately disengaged the autopilot and flew the RA commands. As PM (Pilot Monitoring) I backed up my FO due to the high altitude deviation and climb. I immediately then advised ATC of our situation and actions. We initially climbed 700-800 feet before the RA commands stopped. Once stabilized and safe, we descended back to our cruise altitude of FL380. At one point the RA indicated the Learjet was within 200 feet of our aircraft. There was no communication from the [Learjet] or ATC concerning their deviation from assigned altitude.From what we can determine, the Learjet vacated its assigned altitude of [Flight Level] 370 and continued to climb. At no point did we hear any communications from them or ATC speaking to them. They could have been with another controller/Center frequency. Clearly, we were RVSM airspace.[Suggest] the Learjet not vacating its assigned altitude and ATC advising the Lear of [their] deviation would correct this situation. There was no acknowledgment or explanation to us for the deviation or error. In cruise at FL380, ATC advised us of traffic at 1o'clock and 10 miles. I was able to gain sight of the called Learjet shortly. Within 40 seconds we had a Traffic Advisory (TA) followed by a Resolution Advisory (RA). I disengaged the autopilot and flew the RA commands to climb. The Captain as Pilot Monitoring advised ATC we were climbing for an RA. I maintained sight of the traffic and saw him pass just beneath our right wing and during the maneuver as little as 200 feet below us. Once stabilized with the traffic no longer a factor I descended down to our assigned altitude and reengaged the autopilot. At no point did we hear any communication to the Learjet from ATC regarding us as they were supposed to be at FL370.Better communication via ATC needed to both us and the Learjet if they saw any altitude deviations from the Learjet. Did not hear other than the initial traffic call was given and only to us.
ASRS:1793199.s: Pilots cruising at FL380 executed a TCAS RA climb after a Learjet at FL370 deviated upward, passing within 200 feet. The reporter attributed the near-miss to the Learjet's unannounced altitude change and a lack of ATC communication regarding the deviation.

ASRS:1793216.n: We were on a dual IFR time building cross-country flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1. After receiving take-off clearance on Runway XXR. On the ground roll, the engine indicated were all green, after rotation, during the climb at 100 ft., there was a significant drop in RPM for 2 seconds then the engine went back to normal. I looked down to check for the carb heat was off, mixture full rich, fuel selector on the left tank, the fuel pump was on, verified everything. Then, the engine RPM dropped again. So, I decided to land with the remaining runway, power to idle, glide down to the runway. I [advised ATC], landed safely with the remaining runway, and taxied back to the ramp. After post-flight inspection, we squawked the airplane.
ASRS:1793216.s: During a dual IFR cross-country climb at 100 feet, the pilot experienced two significant RPM drops despite verifying fuel and mixture settings. The pilot executed a safe landing on the remaining runway with power at idle and subsequently grounded the aircraft for inspection.

ASRS:1793225.n: The FO (First Officer) was flying and we were on the visual approach to RWY (Runway) 22 and we got a Caution Obstacle message. We started a turn and visually kept clear of the obstacle. We continued the visual approach and were stable. We descended to 2,000 [feet] MSL before turning on final and a tower off the right side of the aircraft caused us to get the alert. In hindsight we should have maintained 3,100 feet until passing BRIDL. Transferring from Approach to Tower and upon passing Lexington VOR (HYK) we were asked to descend to 3,000 [feet]. Flying towards the departure end of [Runway] 22 we were asked if we had a visual of the airport. The Captain was non flying and answered yes. Then the Tower said that we were cleared for visual [Runway] 22 and a helicopter on the north end of the field was operating. That put us on a 45 downwind and once on the downwind, I then put 2,000 [feet] on the altitude selector. As per procedure 1,000 [feet] AGL is the lowest we can put in the selector. I then gradually decreased my descent from 3,000 and called for flaps setting three at speed 160 [knots] then gear down to be configured by the Runway 22 touchdown zone point. My descent was shallow and we did have the ILS 22 in the MCDU as reference. Turning within the outer-marker BRIDL we got an obstacle call. I was referencing an obstacle as referenced on the approach plate at 1,997 [feet] marked with an arrow at 1,997 [feet]. We were at 2,500 feet still descending as I looked to the right. I was about to call obstacle and perform the go-around procedure as per SOP but the call quickly ended. The call as per SOP is the trigger call 'Obstacle, Pull Up.' The call ended and we continued the standard turn. We were configured flaps five on the base leg and the continued on final. We descended once we captured the glide slope. We put 3,100 [feet] which was the missed approach procedure. The startling part of the flight was the obstacle call which we then started to look for something else, since we already had the tower obstacle in sight and we both confirmed the sighting.I think that in the future it's best to enter the traffic pattern and just follow the approach itself.
ASRS:1793225.s: The First Officer flying a visual approach to Runway 22 received a Caution Obstacle alert at 2,500 feet caused by a tower on the right. The crew visually cleared the obstacle and continued the approach, concluding that maintaining 3,100 feet until passing BRIDL would have prevented the alert.

ASRS:1793247.n: We had a charter flight to ASE. The passengers wanted to go to Aspen but the weather and winds prohibited us from going there. We filed a flight plan to RIL and proceeded. I was the flying pilot. About 30 minutes away we saw the weather in ASE had improved so that we could get in and out. We called ATC and let them know we wanted to make the change. We changed the destination in the FMS and started the new routing to ASE. At one point we had trouble loading the approach into the FMS and I allowed myself to get involved in fixing the FMS. We were given a descent to 13,000, but 12,000 got set in the altitude selector. We were in visual conditions and were looking for the field. passing 12,600 we were told by ATC that we needed to climb to 13,000 as the MSA in our area was 13,000. I began a climb back up When ATC call back and said climb now low altitude alert. While climbing We immediately called the field in sight and were given a clearance for a visual approach. The approach was stable and we landed without incident. As we were taxing in we were given a phone number to contact for a possible deviation. I called the Tower and gave them my name certificate number and contact phone number for their paperwork. I believe that being the flying pilot and allowing myself to get involved in an FMS issue distracted me from catching the wrong altitude being set in the altitude selector. Following company procedures of flying the aircraft while letting the non-flying pilot program the FMS would have allowed me to recognize the altitude error and correct it. We were filled into RIL airport but passengers wanted to get into ASE. The weather cleared out of Aspen so we changed flight plan to arrive into ASE. We were cleared to ASE airport and getting set up for the LOC DME E. While being vectored for the visual approach and watching the weather in the area, we descended below MSA close to JARGU by 300 feet. ATC informed us. We were in VMC conditions and saw airport but descended before calling airport in sight and before being cleared for the visual approach. We should have followed altitudes on the LOC DME E. We rushed ourselves because it was getting late and we wanted to get in and back out of Aspen before sunset. Resolved by getting back to altitude and calling airport in sight and cleared for the visual.
ASRS:1793247.s: The flying pilot descended 300 feet below the 13,000-foot MSA near JARGU while distracted by FMS programming and rushing to land before sunset. ATC alerted the crew to the low altitude, prompting an immediate climb and a subsequent safe visual approach to Aspen.

ASRS:1793251.n: After completing maneuvers in the practice area, we went to shoot the RNAV Runway XX into ZZZ. This approach was done under the hood with the left engine throttle closed for a simulated engine out approach. This approach was done successfully with a few touch and goes done afterwards. After completing the touch and goes we contacted approach, and went back to the Practice Area. After the engines warmed up to ideal operating temperature, due to the warmer weather we decided we were going to shut down the right engine entirely and feather the engine. Pulling the mixture to idle cutoff, and prop lever to feather, we did just that. After 1-2 minutes we tried to restart the engine. After running the checklist the engine prop turned over a few times but did nothing more. As the prop was turning over the electrical system stopped working and we had no avionics, nor could my instructor and I hear each other in our headsets. We tried to start the engine several more times, but the prop wouldn't turn over, as the battery wasn't charging and what we assumed at the time, the electrical system had failed. We then squawked 7600, ran the engine failure checklist, and my instructor contacted Tower over his phone, for clearance back into the airport, and from there we squawked 7700. On the final approach my instructor and I could talk to each other once again, but after running the descent before landing checklist and turning on the left fuel pump, my instructor and I no longer could hear each other as the electrical system seemed to be overloaded. After landing, around 5-7 minutes our avionics came back on, and we could then talk to the controllers and was able to taxi back to the parking area of the flight school. During the incident the weather was clear, winds were calm, and pressure was roughly 30.35 inches.
ASRS:1793251.s: Pilots conducting a simulated engine-out RNAV approach shut down the right engine, causing a total electrical failure that disabled avionics and headsets. They declared an emergency, landed safely, and regained electrical power five to seven minutes after touchdown.

ASRS:1793267.n: Taxiing back to the hangar at ZZZ after a training flight with a student. As we turned onto Taxiway H, I saw Pilot Y attempting to start his recently purchased BE23. It was parked at the tie downs and facing the X Hangars. I taxied past him and commenced to make a U Turn back to our hangar. As I was taxiing slowly in front of hangar X-E, I saw and heard the BE23 start up and rev up to very high RPM. I thought that was out of the ordinary. I then saw the plane start to come directly at us while picking up speed. Seeing Pilot Y's face, I could tell that he was not in control of his aircraft. I quickly increased throttle and was able to get out of his way as he impacted hangar X-E. I re-positioned my plane and shut down. We were not impacted by the BE23. I exited the plane and walked over to check on Pilot Y. He was uninjured and walked out of the aircraft.
ASRS:1793267.s: The reporter, taxiing a training aircraft at ZZZ, observed Pilot Y lose control of a BE23 during startup, causing it to accelerate into Hangar X-E. The reporter evaded the collision by increasing throttle; Pilot Y exited the damaged aircraft uninjured.

ASRS:1793295.n: A FAA HazMat inspection was performed as we parked. It was revealed to us by the Inspector that our HazMat ERG book was out of date on our company EFBs. The Inspector told us that it is available for download every four years. We had the 2016 version, the 2020 was available. As soon as I went inside and connected to WiFi, I downloaded the latest ERG and contacted company dispatch.
ASRS:1793295.s: During a post-parking FAA HazMat inspection, an inspector discovered the crew's Electronic Flight Bags contained an outdated 2016 Emergency Response Guidebook instead of the available 2020 version. The pilot immediately downloaded the current guide via WiFi and notified company dispatch.

ASRS:1793296.n: The Deviation event occurred over or around the HLMET intersection on the LDA Runway 35 approach into Salt Lake City International. ATC instructions were to proceed direct to HLMET, Cross HLMET at 11,000, cleared for the approach. Somewhere just seconds before or after crossing HLMET I descended to an altitude of approximately 9,600 MSL. The altitude on approach after crossing HLMET is 10,000 MSL until crossing the nest fix PEDLE. However after becoming distracted (which I will explain later), I noticed my altitude got down to that approximately 9,600 MSL for which I knew was not right, and immediately began corrective action while simultaneously ATC queried my altitude and I made mention of correcting. I saw I was just passed HLMET and quickly climbed back up to the crossing altitude of 10,000 MSL. Shortly later the controller mentioned the possible pilot deviation may have led to a loss of separation, although no TA/RA's were issued by either aircraft. Here is where I want to bring to attention the possible safety issue as related to the situation and what resulted in me becoming distracted and task saturated. Starting at an ATC controller back before TRACON, which was Salt Lake Center and while on the QWENN 5 RNAV Arrival off the MLF VORTAC transition, I was left extremely high by the center controller, for which I was expecting to receive the 'Expect' crossing restriction at FRNZY intersection at 15,000 MSL on the chart. I could hear multiple aircraft in front of me getting the FRNZY at 15,000 MSL restriction, but also complaining of being left very high and possibly not being able to make it. As I started to see the FMS computer show a required 3,500 FPM decent to make that restriction, I thought I better ask the controller for a descent, however the frequency was congested and it took many more minutes until finally the controller just issued me to now cross FRNZY at 16,000 MSL and 250 KTS. I replied that I would do by best, but it would be tight to make. Mind you that this new altitude required my attention to reprogram the altitude into the FMS as I anticipated and setup for 15,000, and still it showed a required 3,800+FPM decent to make it. I immediately initiated the decent for which I used the VNAV mode in the FMS/autopilot to make the crossing, which also required idle power and the activation of the aircraft's speed brake system to induce drag to not over-speed in the decent. During the decent on the arrival there was also light to bordering on moderate rime icing in IMC and snow showers. When the engines are at idle power they do not produce enough bleed air to keep the Anti-Ice/De-Ice systems operating, for which I got warning that they were not being kept hot enough, so I was trying to introduce small amounts of power to try and get more bleed air flowing to those systems, all the while trying not to over-speed and setup for the instrument approach. Being single-pilot this induced a very high work load, which caused me to become task saturated and behind on preparing for the approach. After finally passing FRNZY at the 16,000 MSL altitude and still in icing conditions and IMC I was simultaneously passed to TRACON approach control which issued me the direct HLMET, cross at 11,000 MSL, cleared approach restriction. I continued the decent down out of 16,000 MSL to 11,000 MSL still using VNAV on the autopilot (more on that later). I noticed I was still nearing around idle power and adding what I could but was still having trouble keeping the speed under control and still behind on setting up the approach. Somewhere around 12,000 MSL I got an indication that the speed brake panels went down, even though I didn't select it. Wondering what happened I looked out the pilot side window at the wing and noticed they were in fact still up, just no longer indicating it in the cockpit. This distracted me, as I knew I needed them extended to maintain my speed and help to try and keep power up and bleed air flowing. It took mybrain a few moments to try and figure out what was going on as there is no abnormal procedure for that in the checklist. I decided to recycle the speed brake switch, for which they then operated normally (retracted and extended), and then gave all normal indications. Throughout that situation is when the altitude deviation occurred, as after I was confident there was not a problem with the speed brakes and they just needed a reset, I accidentally went through the 11,000 MSL attitude down to the approximately 9,600 MSL altitude. Upon speaking with Maintenance later on the ground they feel that the system was activated for so long throughout the decent continuously, they work trapping hydraulic pressure to hold it up, that logically that pressure must have bleed down some, causing them to blow in-trial/down just enough to give an indication in the cockpit that they were sent fully down, and that this was not a malfunction or cause for investigation for repair, especially since they functioned normally after the reset. The indication only looks for full up or full down deflection, so if they blew down a little due to reduction in trapped pressure, it made sense to them. Again they continued to function and indicated correctly the rest of the flight. Back to the VNAV function I used on the autopilot to meet the crossing restriction, as that is the recommended function to meet crossing restrictions, and the function I always use to reduce pilot workload. Somewhere during the sequence of the approximate 3,800-4;000FPM required descent the VNAV system apparently kicked off and defaulted back to just a raw pitch autopilot decent, in which with everything else going on I failed to notice. I can only attribute this to it not liking or taking issue with that rapid of a required decent, and thus defaulted out of it. With 1500+ hours in type, I cannot recall ever descending so rapidly, to were I would have seen or noticed its inability to function through that rapid of a decent. Had VNAV stayed activated, it would have saved the deviation from happening as the approach was loaded with all crossing restriction altitudes and it would have followed them, for which I was also expecting it to do. Although this 'event' happened in Tracon airspace, I feel the safety issue started back in Salt Lake Centers airspace by being left very high on the arrival. ATC needs to be cognizant especially when icing conditions are possible/present some or most aircraft cannot descend that rapidly and keep critical anti-ice/de-ice systems operating properly with idle power descent. Additionally, giving instruction to meet a crossing restriction that requires 3,500+FPM descents is unsafe and not conducive to being able to setup and properly execute a stabilized approach, and leads pilots to get behind. After giving this event thought I am recommending to our flight department to not use the VNAV function of the FMS/autopilot for required descents over 3,000 FPM, but rather use vertical speed mode and monitor carefully. In addition, we will no longer accept any crossing restrictions from ATC that would require over 3,000 FPM, and rather state unable and require a re-sequence back on the arrival via a course reversal to help lose altitude and keep from the pilot getting behind the aircraft and task saturated. Us pilot use the term 'slam dunk' when ATC tries to do this, where they keep you very high and then plop you right on the arrival/approach. This condition does present safety issues due to the above mentioned items.
ASRS:1793296.s: A single-pilot aircraft deviated below 11,000 MSL to 9,600 MSL on the LDA Runway 35 approach into Salt Lake City due to task saturation from managing rapid descents, icing, and a speed brake indication anomaly. The pilot attributed the deviation to VNAV disengagement and high workload caused by ATC issuing crossing restrictions requiring excessive descent rates.

ASRS:1793301.n: Runway XX at ZZZ is through a valley, runway is not always visible when turning final. I was given an extended downwind by maybe 3 miles because of a small aircraft. I missed the turn from base and continued and turned north of the final. Tower asked me where I was as I was off course. I said I did not have visual on the airport. He gave me instructions for reposition, I was slow to follow course correction as I was low, slow climbing stopped the turn. I then asked for [Runway] YY which had better visibility, but I couldn't find that either from where I was.Weather was clear and unrestricted visibility, but area was covered in snow. (not runways or roads). From not making [Runway] YY I got a visual on [Runway] XX which was main landing runway due to winds (3,200 feet, vs 4,400 for [Runway] YY) asked for that. This caused backup of other traffic and then one aircraft in pattern didn't comply with controller's request for heading information. Controller started yelling at him for non-compliance (after yelling at me several times). Unpleasant situation, stressful, tried to remain calm. He gave an instruction on a heading which I was slow to comply in part because there was an aircraft above me in the direction of the turn. I mentioned it to the Controller and he said it was 1,000 feet above me. After I acquired a visual on [Runway] XX and the Controller positioned me and cleared me to land, I landed without incident.I hadn't flown since November due to winter and the pandemic. I was planning on going to ZZZ1 for the day, but decided against it due to lack of recency and stayed local and went to a local airport just to do some VFR practice approaches. All was OK until I turned base to [Runway] XX.I have MS flight simulator 2020 and recreated and solved the issue. Extended center line on Foreflight I think will solve the problem, I'll go back to ZZZ tomorrow and shoot some low visual approaches to see if there is an altitude and distance in which I can see the airport, runway or the valley better with the Foreflight extended center line which I believe will solve the problem for me.Main factor probably was lack of recency due to winter and pandemic. Normally I try to get up every couple weeks at least, but haven't done so since the pandemic and winter.
ASRS:1793301.s: A pilot with limited recency became disoriented while approaching Runway XX at ZZZ due to valley terrain obscuring visual references. After multiple course corrections and delays caused by traffic and controller stress, the pilot eventually acquired visual contact and landed safely.

ASRS:1793302.n: The sector had been very busy. I had earlier dealt with the breakup of an ALTRAV (Altitude Reservation Flight Plan) where almost all of the original information was incorrect and the breakup required coordination with multiple sectors. I had a Radar Assist trainee training on position next to me with approximately 15 hours of training time on that position in the last two months during the flight breakup, and he had left to go assist another sector with the same flight breakup. While the training team was gone, I took the handoff from the adjacent Center sector on Aircraft X. He was level at 6,000 feet and needed a beacon code change.I lost radar contact with him around the boundary, which is not uncommon in that area. He did not check on, but radio coverage is not normally an issue in that area. I don't remember what I was doing, but I was talking to aircraft and looking at the south area of my scope for a while. When I realized Aircraft X had not checked on I tried him on multiple transmitter sites. I then dealt with some other aircraft requests before returning to Aircraft X. At this point, Aircraft X position was identified by ADS-B. The data block was still in coast track because he had never gotten the beacon code change. I had another aircraft near him at 12,000 feet and asked him to relay. I was off line coordinating during the relay. When I returned to the frequency, I dealt with aircraft checking on and their requests before asking the 2nd aircraft if he had gotten a response on the relay. He did not. I called the adjacent sector and asked them if Aircraft X had returned to them or if they had issued any lost communication procedures. The sector said they would reattempt the aircraft and call back. They called and said they were able to get Aircraft X via relay and that he would be coming to me. Aircraft X checked on, and I issued the new beacon code. The data block paired and I radar identified the aircraft and issued an altimeter. As this was happening, the Assist training team returned to my sector.I had an IR (instrument training route) for Aircraft Y that I was blocking for with an exit time of XA44Z, but I had not written down that the aircraft would be exiting at a point which is is my airspace. There is currently a radar outage at one of the radar sites and we are unable to see aircraft southeast of Approach's airspace below 7,500 feet. For the past week, when I have had aircraft come out of an IR route, I instruct them to maintain a VFR climb to 9,000 feet and issue their clearance once I can radar identify the aircraft. When I did that procedure with Aircraft Y, the pilot stated she was in IFR conditions and could not maintain a VFR climb. I was trying to get my Assist to coordinate a block altitude with another sector so I could issue a non-radar clearance, but I was also asking the Assist side trainer if there was a correct way to do this. I had no idea what the correct procedure was.The trainer was not paying attention to the scope and thought it was a hypothetical question, while the trainee had no idea who or what I was talking about. I was very focused on getting Aircraft Y her clearance because she was non radar in IFR conditions with icing in the area. At some point I noticed that Aircraft X was flashing an MSAW (Minimum Safe Altitude Warning) alert. I pulled up the IFR altitude chart, saw that Aircraft X was still at 6,000 feet and entering a block of 6400 feet and issued a climb. I issued 'Aircraft X climb and maintain 7,000 for a low altitude alert' but did not actually issue the low altitude alert. Aircraft X climbed quickly, but I believe they did violate the 6,400 foot block.We should have written procedures for non-radar IR exits. If there is one, I am unaware of it and should receive more training in that area. Since the radar site outage is a daily occurrence right now, and the IR routes are very frequent in this sector I feel like I should know exactly what to do instead of coming up with something that could be completely incorrect and continuing that procedure until it didn't work. I believe my focus on that event is what led me to miss the altitude until the MSAW alert went off. I have had specialized training in MSAW alerts and the issuance of a low altitude alert, but this is my first time ever actually seeing it and I failed to issue it.
ASRS:1793302.s: An air traffic controller lost radar contact with Aircraft X at 6,000 feet due to a beacon code issue and a radar outage, later issuing a climb after an MSAW alert indicated a potential violation of a 6,400-foot block.
