The controller attributed the missed alert to distraction while managing a non-radar Instrument Route exit for Aircraft Y in IFR conditions without established procedures.

ASRS:1793310.n: I was training a Controller on the sector. He gave a descent to an aircraft from 4,000 feet down to 3,000 feet. When the pilot read it back multiple aircraft keyed up at the same time. One of them was the correct pilot, another was another aircraft checking in, and the third was a C17 that thought the transmission was for him to descend to 2,000 feet. The Controller gave the instruction very clearly, and the descent was to a different aircraft to a different altitude. When the pilot called later he said that he always gets a decent to 2,000 feet there so he thought that's what the call was. When [the C17] descended to 2,000 feet that dropped him into a 2,000 foot (Minimum Vectoring Altitude). The altitude was recognized but not before penetrating a 2,500 foot MVA. A climb was issued and the pilot said he could maintain his own terrain and obstruction clearance. But that was after the MVA was already violated. It was obvious when the altitude read back was happening that more than one aircraft were keying up, it wasn't obvious that 3 were. Let alone an aircraft with a very different call sign descending to a very different altitude. This was a pretty clear case of expectation bias. The pilot was made aware of the situation. He said it was a very clear VFR day so he saw all the terrain just fine, and he just thought that is where aircraft got their descent to 2,000 feet.
ASRS:1793310.s: A C17 pilot descended to 2,000 feet due to expectation bias after misinterpreting a descent clearance intended for another aircraft during simultaneous radio transmissions. This action caused the aircraft to penetrate a 2,500-foot Minimum Vectoring Altitude before the controller issued a climb instruction.

ASRS:1793313.n: Aircraft X was holding at 4,000 feet at the missed approach fix (and also initial approach fix) for several instrument approaches at. They had already executed the Missed Approach Procedure once because of weather below minimums. The pilot advised me that they wanted to try again. Since they were already established in a holding pattern published for the ILS approach, I cleared them for the ILS approach and issued the altimeter.The procedure is clear that the only route of flight allowable from holding is via the 10 DME arc to a straight-in course on the localizer. That is what I expected them to fly. I quickly redirected my attention to a sequence of three other aircraft I was trying to shoot a gap with, through a band of weather. At the same time, I had another arrival that was opposite direction, outbound from the same gap. When I was able to finally scan back to Aircraft X I noticed that they were not on the 10 DME arc, and had strayed into a 4,000 foot Minimum IFR Altitude at 3,000 feet. My first thought was that they decided to shoot a different approach, but when queried, the pilot responded that they still planned the ILS. However, their current position did not correlate to any possible point on the Approach.When questioned further, the pilot said that they were direct to a fix to intercept the localizer. They had received neither a direct clearance nor a descent clearance. Without any more questioning, I informed them that the Minimum Vectoring Altitude (technically minimum IFR altitude) in that area is 4,000 feet, and issued a 'cancel approach clearance' and 'climb immediately, maintain 4,000 feet.' The MSAW (Minimum Safe Altitude Warning) did not activate. Because there was no audible alarm, and the fact that I knew 3.000 feet was still a safe altitude, I chose to not use the 'low altitude alert' portion of the phraseology. Later, after discussion with, and as recommended by the Operations Manager, I issued a warning to the pilot.Because this occurrence was a pilot deviation, there is not much from the ATC perspective that would have changed the outcome. Undoubtedly, the pilots' workload was high, due to the missed approach and bad weather. The design of the approach is also somewhat complicated because there are variations including the arc, published holding, and an outbound course on the localizer (which they apparently wanted to fly), but they don't all connect logically. However, the pilots should've queried if unsure.
ASRS:1793313.s: Air Traffic Controller and pilots of Aircraft X were involved during an ILS approach attempt after a missed approach. The pilots deviated from the published holding procedure by flying direct to a fix without clearance, descending below the 4,000-foot Minimum IFR Altitude to 3,000 feet, prompting the controller to cancel the approach and order an immediate climb.

ASRS:1793315.n: ASE Approach has a very bad habit of violating Sector 06's airspace, especially on busy days. Today was a very heavy traffic day, there were continuous EGE departures and arrivals every 5 miles. ASE approach busted our airspace with Aircraft X at 140, called me the D side up for a too late point out. When I wouldn't immediately say point out approved (they only gave a call sign, no CID, and there were data blocks everywhere making it impossible to see) they became belligerent saying he was already in my airspace I needed to approve their point out now! I told them I would not until I made sure it was not going to put aircraft in danger (and it potentially was), they were super angry about that and hung up. This is only one of a LONG list of incidents like this with ASE approach. This is a consistent and habitual issue that must be resolved before someone gets hurt! Between the local time of XA52z-XA59z, ASE approach was observed to have violated our airspace with no attempt at a point out 4 different times with Aircraft Y, Aircraft Z, Aircraft A, and Aircraft B. That is just the 6 minutes of me watching them with an eagle eye. They have caused many close calls with EGE departures and all of us in Area 1 are tired of it.Recurrent training for ASE approach on airspace boundaries and point out procedures. Anything at all to stop this terrible habit from continuing.
ASRS:1793315.s: ASE Approach controllers repeatedly violated Sector 06 airspace with multiple aircraft, including Aircraft X, Y, Z, A, and B, during heavy EGE traffic. The reporter attributes these habitual boundary breaches and failed point-out procedures to a lack of training, creating potential safety risks.

ASRS:1793331.n: Aircraft X was inbound to land Runway XXL. When I issued a turn northbound the pilot questioned the heading. The session is muffled during replay due to the requirement of wearing mask. This creates an undue safety issue when each transmission is time dependent. Since all of our positions are separated by more than 6 feet that mask [should] not be required when working position unless it is an associated hand-off.
ASRS:1793331.s: An air traffic controller reported that a pilot questioned a northbound turn clearance while Aircraft X was inbound to land Runway XXL. The controller attributed muffled transmissions during the replay to mandatory mask usage, which they stated creates a safety issue for time-dependent communications.

ASRS:1793353.n: Fuel leak discovered prior to pushback. Maintenance says 'no big deal happens all the time.' So we ran an engine to see if the leak would seal and shut down and ran 70.20 QRH. Maintenance tells me leak is gone no drips. I opened my window and visually checked the engine and saw fuel leaking at an alarming rate from the bottom of the number one engine. FO (First Officer) and I went outside and measured the rate of drips and we recorded 175 drips per minute. Asked Maintenance why they told us the engine was not leaking, and they denied seeing any leak. We would have taken off with a major fuel leak had we not checked ourselves. Maintenance in ZZZ was pushing us to depart because they needed the gate. ZZZ Maintenance's overriding concern was obviously not for the safety of the passengers and crew. 8 fire crew surrounded the aircraft after the leak was discovered and they said they would not authorize another engine start yet Maintenance asked us to try again to start even though fuel was pouring out of the engine. Just prior to engine start ground crew reported fuel leaking from Number 1 Engine. We performed QRC Fuel Leak. It failed. Logbook entry accomplished. Asked to do engine run. Got permission, coordinated with all, did 5 minute engine run. Shut down engine. Ground personnel said there were no leaks. Captain looked outside window and steady stream of fuel was leaking from engine.Captain and I went down to look at leak and count drops per minute. 175 drops per minute at that point which progressed later to a steady stream of fuel coming out. Fire Department responded with 2 engines. During the ensuing hours, MX (Maintenance) kept trying to get us to do another engine run. Fire Department said due to the amount of fuel leaking they would not allow it at the gate. We absolutely agreed. MX kept coming up to us with documents telling us this was OK, and if we would just do this engine run, all would be well.In spite of this, MX wanted to run a procedure for a 60 or 100 drops per minute engine leak. We were originally at 175 drops per minute and progressed to a steady stream. Clearly this procedure did not apply. Both Captain and I were very uncomfortable with all of this. Jumping back to the leak first being discovered and the need to do an engine run, MX attempted to get us to hurry up with the engine run because a 777 needed the gate. This was mentioned several times, to the point where the Captain became so uncomfortable he had to tell them to slow down, follow procedure, and focus on what we were doing. As the engine run resulted in an even worse problem, Captain refused the aircraft and we left the scene. Operations refused to cancel the flight for a considerable period of time. This delay was so bad, the Captain and I eventually left the airport for a hotel. Scheduling talked to the Captain and informed him we would be flying into our day off, a new part would be flown in, jet fixed, and we were scheduled for an MX ferry flight on the [Date1]. We got to aircraft only to discover no part had been flown in. Nothing had been fixed. MX had done several engine runs and said there was no leak. This was, in my career of flying jets for Company since [Year], and having done many thousands of walkarounds, by far the worst leak I have ever seen. Something in the jet broke. We were told it would be fixed. Nothing was fixed. At this point, we had lost confidence in anything local maintenance was telling us because they were still trying to use a checklist, which they showed us, with very minor 60-100 drops per minute leaks. The part you see in the attached photo was not replaced. Nothing was replaced. We refused the jet again. Numerous attempts were made to get us to do a high powered engine run, which we are 1) not trained 2) there was heavy rain and standing water, making for slick surfaces, so we would not have done it under those conditions anyway. Captain refused jet, and due to the pressure put on us from local maintenance, we left airfield. Scheduling put us on a deadhead flight home the following day. Scheduling sent crew out on [Date2], DH to ZZZ & MX ferry jet Aircraft X back to ZZZ1, even after no repair was made to this part.
ASRS:1793353.s: The flight crew discovered a severe fuel leak from Engine 1 prior to pushback, contradicting maintenance claims that the leak was minor or nonexistent. Despite fire department warnings and a leak rate of 175 drips per minute, maintenance pressured the crew to perform engine runs to free a gate, leading the crew to refuse the aircraft and leave the airport.

ASRS:1793411.n: As pilot monitoring, I was handling the radios. Center cleared us for the 'RNDRZ 1 arrival Runway 26L' which I read back. We had set up for that arrival and runway, validated it, and briefed it thoroughly to include the issues with turning early if cleared for the visual which presented a terrain problem. Upon selection of the Runway 26L runway and the RNDRZ 1 arrival in the box, the aircraft automatically selected the Runway 26L transition which we understood we were cleared for. The Captain and I both verified with the other that we were cleared for the transition and we agreed that what the box presented to us was what we were cleared for. At the waypoint BERBN the jet turned onto the Runway 26L transition as planned. We received a radio call to turn back to a 130 heading and then given subsequent vectors to final and landed without incident. We were told by ATC that we should not have turned onto the transition. Looking back over the arrival and approach plates again and again, I still think we did what we were cleared for. If receiving the clearance for the 'RNDRZ 1 Runway 26L' doesn't mean clearance for the Runway 26L transition I'm not sure what does. Such verbiage at other airports indicates clearance onto the transition. The arrival plate is confusing however because at BERBN it directs the reader to 2 different things at once. It directs the reader to the Runway 26L transition found on the approach plate and also the possibility of continuing on the present heading to expect vectors to final. Even with that, to be cleared for the arrival and runway has always meant cleared for that runway's transition. Furthermore, the transition does not connect with the approach to Runway 26L giving greater weight to the fact that one need not be cleared for an approach to be cleared for the transition. I believe the Captain and I did exactly what we were cleared to do and that our understanding of that clearance corresponds to our experience and training.Causal factors were incorrect chart depiction and the aircraft navigational system automatically linking the Runway 26L transition when that arrival and runway are selected.Chart needs to be revised to make clear when the transition is to be used and when not. The aircraft navigation system needs to be updated to reflect how ATC wants the approach flown.
ASRS:1793411.s: The pilot monitoring and Captain flew a jet on the RNDRZ 1 arrival to Runway 26L, automatically selecting the runway transition at waypoint BERBN. ATC vectored them back, citing an incorrect chart depiction and navigation system auto-linking as causes for the deviation.

ASRS:1793412.n: FO (First Officer) and I both believed with confidence that ATC had instructed us to turn right to a heading upon reaching CLUSO. Neither of us had any doubt about the matter. When we turned at CLUSO, however, ORD TRACON advised us that we were supposed to turn at KAYTO instead. This came as a surprise to both of us. That was the first instance we had any doubt about what our clearance had been. At that point, second-guessing ourselves, the FO and I began to wonder whether we had read back 'KAYTO' or 'CLUSO' when first given the heading clearance. Both waypoints sound similar when pronounced, and this similarity may have contributed to this new doubt. So, we were not sure if the error was ours or ATC's. In any case, ATC informed us that there was 'no problem' with the turn and then gave us further vectors. There was no traffic conflict.In retrospect, the only thing that may have played a role in any confusion that may have occurred with either ATC or with us is that 'KAYTO' and 'CLUSO' can sound similar, causing the wrong term to be ensconced in memory.Consider not having waypoints in close proximity to each other that may sound similar when pronounced.
ASRS:1793412.s: The crew turned right at CLUSO instead of KAYTO due to confusion over similar-sounding waypoint names in the ATC clearance. ATC confirmed no traffic conflict occurred and issued further vectors, though the crew remained unsure if the error originated with them or ATC.

ASRS:1793420.n: We pushed off the gate and taxied out to spot XX to switch to ground. Upon reaching the spot, we contacted ground a minimum of 6 times and sat for more than 5 minutes before finally getting a response. We had planned for runway XXL but were given XY which was unusual for a northbound departure out of ZZZ. We were told to taxi 1, 2 and to give way to company traffic which was passing right to left on [Taxiway] 1. Once the traffic had passed, we made the left turn onto 1 and I announced to the Captain that I was going heads down to change the runways. I changed the runway on the route page and it did not uplink so I glanced at the iPad for a quick check of the numbers. During that quick look, movement caught my eye out of the rear right window and I turned to see another aircraft quickly approaching the Captain's blind spot on either [Taxiway] 3 or 4. I alerted the Captain of the traffic and he aggressively applied the brakes and stopped the aircraft prior to the intersection. The other aircraft taxied past without noticeably altering its speed and we continued taxing once clear. I am confident that both aircraft would have experienced a fuselage to fuselage collision had we not noticed the traffic at the precise moment that we did. Ground controllers were busy and weather was in the area. I don't know where the other aircraft came from but we were never given any reference to the traffic or hold short instructions. Additional staff working the ground frequency for that particularly busy bank in ZZZ. Also, make crews aware that when two taxiways intersect at less than a 90 degree angle on the right side, there is a significant blind spot for the captain which makes checking for traffic very difficult. We were cleared to taxi to runway XX from spot XX via [Taxiways] 1 and 2. The airport had just reopened after being closed for weather. Controllers were swamped trying to give clearances and deal with multiple aircraft. We were not advised of approaching aircraft nor were we issued hold short instructions. Another aircraft was approaching the [taxiways] 1 and 2 intersection on [Taxiway] 2 while we were approaching on [Taxiway] 1. They were coming from our right rear at a 45 very fast. My FO (First Officer) saw him first as he broke into his field of vision he alerted me. I applied mildly aggressive braking to stop while the other aircraft showed no signs of slowing down. If I had not been alerted or even alerted 2 seconds later there would have been a collision in the intersection. It was a dangerous near miss that even after the fact neither ground nor the other aircraft seemed aware of. I contacted ground and told them it was near miss.Airports are starting to get busy again but I feel controllers and pilots are not as current as we were. Someone should have caught this before it happened.Ground is going to have to step up their game if airlines are adding flights to ZZZ. You can't be giving clearances on ground frequency when you are already overloaded. That's crazy.
ASRS:1793420.s: Pilots reported a near-miss collision at ZZZ airport while taxiing to runway XY after a weather closure. The First Officer spotted an approaching aircraft in a blind spot, prompting an emergency stop because ground controllers, overwhelmed by traffic, failed to issue hold short instructions or traffic advisories.

ASRS:1793425.n: Departed ZZZ after an unexpected runway change from Runway X to Runway YL due to high winds. After takeoff I was the PM and the FO was the PF. We were assigned Runway YL ZZZZZ. ZZZZZ1 departure. There was a fair amount of turbulence due to the strong westerly winds flowing over the mountains. On the departure you are supposed to cross the fix ZZZZZ2 below 10,000 feet MSL. We were climbing in VNAV Path and the FO was hand flying. We ended up going thru 10,000 to approximately 10,400 feet MSL due to VNAV not commanding the FD to level off. As the FO who was the PF was returning to 10,000 feet MSL the Controller told us to level off at 10,000 feet MSL, which we were already doing. It was clear and VMC at this time. There were no targets on TCAS and nothing was said about any loss of separation. I immediately rechecked the box to ensure the departure was there and the rest of the altitude constraints were correct, which they were. The flight continued to ZZZ2 uneventful and nothing else was said by the Controller.Last minute runway change was a contributing factor as we more thoroughly briefed the Runway X departure at the gate. The moderate turbulence on departure affected aircraft controllability and instrument scan. The fact that we departed from a field elevation of XXXX feet MSL and 10,000 feet MSL came a lot quicker than normal (flying from home base). The fact had I recently transitioned to the aircraft and have only flown less than 50 hrs since October 2020 and often go 2-4 weeks without flying. Another contributing factor is my lack of HUD experience and the division of duties when looking thru the HUD but not having any navigational information presented on the HUD. Long sit time in ZZZ Departure airport.Take more time to rebrief a departure after runway change. Emphasize the high field elevation and how much quicker we will be at 10,000 feet MSL than what we are typically used to flying out of ZZZ1. Use the HUD for the takeoff but develop a better scan with the navigational display to enhance situational awareness on a departure procedure. Consider the use of a higher level of automation to reduce workload in turbulent conditions.
ASRS:1793425.s: The crew departed ZZZ on Runway YL after a last-minute change, exceeding the 10,000-foot constraint to 10,400 feet due to VNAV not commanding a level-off. Contributing factors included the runway change, high field elevation, turbulence, and the pilot's recent transition to the aircraft.

ASRS:1793441.n: Upon the execution of normal gear extension, flight crew observed the nose gear indication displayed on the aircraft systems page, the nose gear was not down and locked. PIC communicated to the ZZZ Tower that the nose gear indication was not down and locked. PIC asked for a low approach and for the Tower to visually check if the nose gear appeared to be down. Tower Controller confirmed the gear was not down. Flight crew executed QRH procedure associated with gear up/unsafe condition multiple times noting the hand gear pump would not move and there was no hydraulics CAS message. Flight crew then requested an additional low approach and ZZZ Tower indicated that the nose gear still appeared to be retracted, but that the nose gear doors were open. PIC executed missed approach and departed traffic pattern to complete speed turns in attempt to lower the nose gear. Procedure proved to be unsuccessful. Another low approach was conducted and ZZZ Tower said the nose gear still appeared to be up, with the gear doors open. PIC requested priority handling, then gave passengers onboard an additional briefing. Flight crew briefed the landing procedure multiple times and then entered an approximately 15 mile final for Runway XXL at ZZZ. Flight crew fully configured aircraft for landing (with the exception of three gear indicators in down and locked state) at 10 mile final and briefed landing procedure again. PIC landed disabled aircraft on Runway XXL at ZZZ in accordance with procedure for nose-gear unsafe state. Flight crew and passengers evacuated aircraft after it came to a stop on Runway XXL ZZZ. While ground personnel and local responders worked to remove the aircraft from the runway, a police officer came into the FBO with an (estimated 9-10' long) chrome socket/ratchet extender in his hand, and informed the flight crew that he had removed that item from the retracted nose gear. Police officer stated he removed the tool from the location where the aircraft tow pin/head is supposed to be installed for towing and that it was almost as wide as the nose gear door opening on the aircraft.I suggest an additional line item be added to the aircraft's certified Pre-Flight Inspection Checklist and Before Start Checklist that includes wording/verbiage to identify and confirm that a certified tow head, tow pin, or otherwise foreign or unapproved object is not in the nose strut of the aircraft. I also suggest the identification of a clear nose strut tow-pin location be added to the PIC's final before flight walk-around. I suggest additional training and oversight of FBO line personnel that includes a mandate of using certified, tagged and visually identifiable, approved tow pins for the aircraft they are moving and the importance of removing them immediately after ground movement/towing is completed. Upon initial extension of the landing gear, the nose gear did not extend. The flight crew performed QRH procedure. QRH procedure was unsuccessful in extending the nose gear. The flight crew executed a landing on Runway XXL at ZZZ.
ASRS:1793441.s: The flight crew landed a disabled aircraft on Runway XXL at ZZZ after the nose gear failed to extend due to a chrome socket extender left in the nose strut by a police officer. Following unsuccessful QRH procedures and visual confirmation of the retracted gear, the crew executed a safe landing and evacuated all passengers.

ASRS:1793451.n: I operated Aircraft X from ZZZ1 to ZZZ. The weather was low, approximately 600 OVC at ZZZ and rain. I believe we had an alternate of ZZZ2. We planned to shoot the ILS to Runway 7 at ZZZ. I was the pilot flying. We operated the flight to ZZZ normally and got set up for the ILS to Runway 7. I was established on the approach and fully configured at approximately 1,000 feet when I noticed that both the localizer and glide slope were flagged. I was looking at the PFD (Primary Flight Display) and slightly startled by the lack of information. I then glanced to the First Officer's side and noticed his PFD looked normal. I never felt any erratic pitch attitudes but according to FOQA (Flight Operations Quality Assurance), we reached 12 degrees pitch down and up to 2700 FPM descent below 1,000 feet. I remember hearing the aural 'glide slope glide slope' The FO (First Officer) then questioned, 'should we go-around?' I responded yes and initiated a go around. We climbed up to 3,000 feet and requested radar vectors back around for the same approach. I then transferred the controls to the First Officer because his navigation equipment was operating normally. We continued on the approach. At approximately 600 feet I called runway in sight, and he responded landing. We drifted to the right of the approach course, due to the First Officer not reacting to the left crosswind. We were also a bit high on the glide slope. I told him to correct, and asked him if he was able to correct the flight path, he responded correcting. We ended up landing hard and fast. I taxied off normally. I forgot to write up the discrepancy that the airplane lost localizer and glide slope. I believe the cause of this event was due to the gradual failure of the glide slope and my reaction to that. It took us approximately 38 seconds from when the failure occurred until the missed approach was executed. I don't think it would hurt to see this event repeated in a simulator so that I can see it again and understand how I could have reacted better. I was Pilot Monitoring for an approach into ZZZ1. We were conducting the ILS to runway 7 at ZZZ1, and had just passed the final approach fix when the Captain's glideslope malfunctioned and presented a red 'GS' flag. My instruments appeared to continue to provide accurate glideslope indications, and the autopilot remained engaged, coupled to the Captain's side, and continued to fly the aircraft. I don't recall noticing which vertical mode took over in the absence of the GS. I suggested to the Captain that a go-around be made, she waited several seconds to see if the glideslope indications would return, then disconnected the autopilot to execute the go-around. The Captain applied TOGA (Takeoff/Go-around) power. Upon applying go-around power, the pitch attitude further decreased, and the vertical rate of descent correspondingly increased, causing a GPWS sink-rate warning. Visual ground contact was made briefly before the descent was arrested. We continued the climb straight out and contacted Approach for missed approach instructions. This event began with the malfunction of the Captain's side glideslope. This led to a breakdown in situational awareness and crew communication as the aircraft continued to descend in the absence of the glideslope until a go-around maneuver was executed. I believe additional training may be required, both on go-around procedures as well as on equipment malfunctions during approach.
ASRS:1793451.s: Two separate ILS approaches to Runway 7 involved glideslope failures causing unexpected descents and go-arounds. The first resulted in a hard landing after control transfer, while the second triggered a GPWS warning due to delayed autopilot disconnection and pitch loss.

ASRS:1793455.n: We were cruising at FL390 and we called the back for a break. I was the second pilot to exit the flight deck and while in the main cabin I noticed the pitch of the aircraft. I then made a brief break and called to return to the flight deck. Once the flight deck door opened and the A came out I noticed the thrust levers advancing to max power and the airspeed indicator slowly approaching the amber band. I then immediately called for a lower altitude as I took my seat and once I was in my seat I looked at my First Officer and said we need lower now. My First Officer then dialed a lower altitude on the FMC and selected descent via V/S (Vertical Speed). I then gathered all info on what we were experiencing and thought either we had an unreliable airspeed or runaway stabilizer. As I looked back at our altitude, I realized we weren't descending and our airspeed was slowly approaching amber pole. At that time I disconnected A/T (Autothrottle), A/P (Autopilot) and started a slow descent and requested my First Officer to call in our descent to ATC. ATC then notified us that we needed to stop descent at FL370 due to lower aircraft. My training kicked in and I figured if this went back we would need around 10,000 feet to recover so I then requested a vector off course. We then were given 10 degrees left and I leveled off at FL370 continued to hand fly and one by one acquired A/P, HDG, VNAV. Our Airspeed gained approximately 30kts and we were stable at FL370 on a heading. ATC asked why the need to descend and I replied we encountered mountain wave and could not hold altitude. ATC then replied that we were the first to complain of mountain wave. Seconds later an aircraft at FL470 notified of +/- 1000 gain/loss and another airliner requesting lower due to mountain wave. We were then given direct to a waypoint on our flight plan and landed at destination without further incident. Be more vigilant while single pilot operations.
ASRS:1793455.s: The Captain and First Officer encountered severe mountain wave turbulence at FL390, causing uncommanded thrust increases and altitude loss. They manually descended to FL370, vectored off course, and landed safely after ATC confirmed similar reports from other aircraft.

ASRS:1793482.n: While boarding the ramp manager arrived to the flight deck with a NOTOC regarding 20 KG of dry ice being loaded onto the aircraft. The Ramp Manager informed the Captain that it was freight containing pharmaceuticals, not a UN3373. She also told the Captain that [this] was not an expedite item. Moments later the Dispatcher sent an ACARS to tell the Captain to verify that the package was an expedite item. The Ramp Manager again confirmed that it was NOT an expedite item. The Captain called the Dispatcher and they discussed that the package was not a expedite medical supply item or an expedite UN3373 and was therefore limited to 2.5KG per package. Because the package was 20 KG the Captain asked that it not be loaded. After swapping aircraft due to an unrelated Maintenance issue, the Captain went to look at the package and noted that it had a handwritten label saying it was the X Company Vaccine. The Captain noted that because it was not an expedite item it was not labeled normally, i.e., it did not state 'Contains dangerous goods...' and did not have the dry ice placard. It also had a marking indicating that it contained no dangerous goods. When speaking with the Dispatcher again the Dispatcher told the Captain that we were indeed authorized to carry it citing the national state of emergency due to the pandemic. Captain read the FOM chapter pointing out that it was not an expedite medical supply item and not an expedite UN3373 and should therefore be limited to 2.5 kg of dry ice, but the Dispatcher assured the Captain that we could take it. The Captain confirmed that the package would not be able to fly on any other flight that day. After conferring with Dispatch, and the manager who brought up the NOTOC who confirmed the contents the package was loaded on to the aircraft. There were no further issues.Flight crew and Dispatch worked together to determine if the item was safe for transport.Speaking with Dispatch and the Ramp Manager, it became clear that each party agreed that the 20 kg of dry ice would normally exceed the limit for an individual package that is not an expedite medical supply item or expedite UN3373, it was, however, also agreed that this vaccine shipment was somehow excepted from that normal requirement. The cause would seem to be some confusion as to whether or not freight which is not an expedite item that contained medical supplies, specifically the Vaccine, were allowed. Perhaps a lack of guidelines specific to the transport of the vaccine was a possible cause (if such an exemption from policy exists). The Captain determined after speaking with the individual parties that it would be safe to transport.Better guidance, including up to date flow charts, to help navigate this issue. It is not entirely clear whether a medical supply needs to be an expedite item in order to be exempt from the individual limitations of 2.5 kg. Although both the Captain and the Dispatcher initially thought that it does need to be an expedite item to contain more than 2.5 KG, the chapter in the FOM does not expressly say either way. The exception to the limit of 2.5KG appears to be listed under the expedite item section on the maximum limits page of the FOM, but it then states, 'Dry Ice weight may exceed the 2.5 kg (5.5 lbs) limitation, if contained within the UN3373 expedite item or medical shipment.' The use of the word 'or' may indicate that a medical supply need not be an expedite item even though it is located under the expedite item section. This could use clarification. If a medical shipment can exceed 2.5 KG without being an expedite item, then it should be listed as a separate exception. Similarly, if the medical shipment MUST be an expedite item that should also be clearly stated. If there is some exception due to the pandemic for the COVID vaccine that should be conveyed. The current flow chart contained on our system could stand to be updated. Specially, it lists all limits in pounds, but the NOTOC is in KG, which in itself renders the tool useless. Also, the flow chart ask the question 'is dry ice in an expedite item?' This is a yes or no question, but the flow chart only has an option for 'YES.'
ASRS:1793482.s: The Captain, Dispatcher, and Ramp Manager debated loading 20 kg of dry ice for a vaccine shipment that exceeded the standard 2.5 kg limit for non-expedite items. After clarifying that pandemic exemptions likely applied despite ambiguous FOM wording, the crew agreed the package was safe and loaded it.

ASRS:1793493.n: On climb out at SFO, on initial contact with departure control ATC advised us that the preceding aircraft reported a drone near OAK at approximately 4,000 ft. After flap retraction I deemed it prudent to maintain a best rate of climb till out of 4,000 ft. At around 3,600 ft. the FO (First Officer) verbalized he had visual contact with the drone pointing to the 11 o'clock position. Shortly after, I then established visual contact. The drone passed just to our left and under us. I would estimate we came to approximately 500 ft. of it. ATC was notified and flight proceeded to destination without further incident.I'm assuming the drone was not being operated under any legal clearance. Furthermore the drone had no transponder making our TCAS useless in this case. I am pleased with my decision to maintain a good rate of climb until clear of drone.Unfortunately drone sightings around busy airports are becoming more rampant. And like bird strikes, very little is known exactly what type of damage can occur to a jet airliner if a collision occurs. It is my hope that the FAA and law enforcement will do whatever is necessary to protect the airspace that is crucial for safety of flight.
ASRS:1793493.s: During climb out from SFO, the flight crew visually observed an unlit drone without a transponder at approximately 3,600 ft, passing 500 ft to the left and below. The pilot maintained a best rate of climb to clear the 4,000 ft threat altitude, and the flight proceeded to destination without incident.

ASRS:1793504.n: Somewhere after Burns Flat (BFV) at 38,000 ft. and until ZUN VOR, we had encountered first an ATC Fault EICAS message. Oddly then on both transponders. First Officer was the Pilot Flying. So, we discussed and went into the QRH and complied. I had then though to ask ABQ ARTCC if they were able to see us on their radar scope. The controller had replied yes. So when I remarked of our issue, he knew right away that jamming was taking place. Now I didn't clarify if this was any kind of military exercise and if this was normal. He acted as though it was. Shortly after this, we started slowly seeing other EICAS messages. I can't remember the exact order though. I believe the next was EGPWS TERR or so. Then L GPS appeared not too far after this. Maybe R GPS as well, maybe. Eventually we saw UNABLE RNP. So we definitely knew GPS jamming was making sense. The RNP ANP scales on the Pilot Flying Display bottom was like RNP 2.00 ANP 2.93 in amber color. It was clear our GPS was in an inertial mode. I did select radio updating eventually per the QRH's procedural instructions. Center never seem too concerned as nothing else was said. The weather was quite good and while concerned, I had a good idea as we made our way towards ZZZ1, the start of the RNAV star, the GPS navigation would probably return to a normal state and it did. There wasn't any flight safety breaches or traffics conflicts as this event happened entered at cruise. Although, I did forget to make a maintenance log entry required by mandatory reports. I may have been more fatigued than I was aware. Sleep was fragmented in chunks of multiple 2 to 3 or so hrs. on this day. Intentional GPS jamming I suppose. I've never encountered this in my entire career here. Wondering if the military does these exercises, but I would expect we'd be notified via a NOTAM and on our [flight plan] if it was known. I suppose if we knew we could of had a different routing? I don't believe compromised safety as in this case was an issue. It never degraded to a more severe off course deviation and didn't cause traffic conflicts. Don't get me wrong we were concerned and a bit miffed. I will file a security report and read more on the subject of GPS jamming interference's.
ASRS:1793504.s: The flight crew encountered GPS jamming during cruise between Burns Flat and ZUN VOR, triggering ATC Fault, EGPWS, and UNABLE RNP EICAS messages. The controller confirmed radar contact, and navigation returned to normal without safety breaches, though the pilot suspects intentional military interference.

ASRS:1793511.n: We were taking off behind an EMB-170 on 26L. ATL will routinely clear you for takeoff before the aircraft in front of you has rotated and that was the case for this takeoff as well. After we rotated and selected the landing gear to the up position, I noticed some left and right wing rocking which usually indicates wake turbulence. We were climbing out at V2+10 and suddenly we had airspeed fluctuations and received a WINDSHEAR Warning message. Following the windshear escape procedure, I followed the command bars and selected full thrust due to the low airspeed and close proximity to the ground. I believe we received the warning below 600 ft AGL. As I was following the command bars, I noticed the right engine Aircraft X was flashing red. Shortly thereafter, the warning ceased and I pulled the engines back to the flex carats and requested the autopilot be activated to alleviate workload. I monitored the engine for the rest of the flight and it all seemed normal. Once out of sterile, I informed the Dispatcher and Maintenance Control via ACARS of the event and called them arriving at the destination. While on the phone with Maintenance Control after the flight, I checked the engine exceedance log in the maintenance computer menu and it showed that the engine encountered a level 3 event for 6.9 seconds and that the peak temperature was 927degC. The Maintenance Control technician checked the GE engine manual and informed me that while it wasn't outside of limitations, to write it up and they would have local maintenance come and sign it off. The weather in ATL was not gusty and no wind shear was reported in the area.I believe ATL is clearing aircraft too close to other aircraft. Wake turbulence encounters are a threat. Despite being of a similar size, the Aircraft in front of us put off enough wake to rock the aircraft and cause airspeed deviations strong enough to activate the windshear warning system. Encountering wake turbulence in ATL is a common occurrence though it doesn't typically cause windshear warnings to go off.I think there should be either more separation or perhaps a study into whether ATL Tower is following proper spacing procedure. I feel that if we encountered the wake of a larger aircraft, the airspeed deviations could have been more severe and there is not much margin for error when you're climbing at V2+10.
ASRS:1793511.s: The pilot reported a windshear warning and engine exceedance during takeoff behind an EMB-170 at ATL, attributing the event to wake turbulence caused by insufficient separation. The aircraft executed an escape procedure, resulting in a Level 3 engine event that required maintenance inspection despite remaining within limits.

ASRS:1793523.n: Trip began as Flight ABCD, 2-day ZZZ, daytime flying. On the XXth [Date], crew brought in plane with flap issue. Took over one hour to resolve. Just prior to engine start, ground crew said fuel was leaking from Number 1 engine. Followed QRC, ended up doing engine run. Ground crew stated no leaks after engine run. Captain looked out window to see fuel streaming from number one engine. This was never resolved. We refused to fly aircraft. Were told by scheduling a new part was being flown in and we would Maintenance ferry jet home on the XXth [Date], our scheduled day off.On XXth [Date], discovered, at jet, no part had arrived but we were told to ferry jet to ZZZ1 and it would be fixed. After consultation with numerous agencies and several hours, we again refused jet. Nothing had been fixed. Worst engine leak I've ever seen. The directives Maintenance was following were for leaks in the range of 60 to 100 drops per minute of fuel. This became a steady stream the day prior. We refused to fly jet as nothing had been done.Took some time to get hotel, had to self-help. Arrived to hotel. Scheduled to deadhead home on XYth [Date]. Due to mix-up, transportation went to wrong hotel. We missed XA00 flight home. Rescheduled for XD:50 pm flight home. I had a ZZZ turn today, XZth [Date], with a XA50 report. This was illegal crew rest so the crew desk did a mini-pack of my schedule, combined the now 4-day trip with 4 duty periods into a 5 day trip and 5 duty periods with near absolute minimum rest.I spent some time checking on the legality of what was done, with company. It turns out, this extremely onerous now 5 day pairing with very limited rest opportunity was legal. Legal doesn't mean smart or does it mean a pilot really has adequate rest.I gave every effort in an attempt to get adequate rest, but the pressure, once finally in bed, and reflection on the maintenance issues, the mental fatigue caused by the ever-changing schedule, flying into now two days off, and then paired with a trip packing with minimal rest caused sleep to be very difficult. Two-hour time difference, though seemingly minor, comes into play as I'd become acclimatized.I finally realized, as I was about to go to parking lot, I was not safe to fly nor could I certify FFD. I called fatigued.
ASRS:1793523.s: The flight crew refused to operate the aircraft due to an unresolved, severe fuel leak from Engine 1 that exceeded maintenance limits. Subsequent scheduling errors and minimal rest caused extreme fatigue, leading the pilot to report unfit for duty before the next flight.

ASRS:1793592.n: Hazmat can improperly built (loaded) Class 4.3 which requires separation from Class 8. Both of these class shipments were present and did not have required separation. These items were actually right next to each other. All of the Hazmat items were secured under a net. (First Officer) FO noticed lack of required separation and brought to attention of ramp agent. Ramp agent arranged items correctly and re-secured the net. Improper Hazmat can buildup (loaded).
ASRS:1793592.s: The First Officer discovered improperly loaded Class 4.3 and Class 8 hazmat items lacking required separation on the ramp. A ramp agent corrected the placement and re-secured the cargo net to ensure compliance.

ASRS:1793604.n: Descending into ZZZ, we received an RA from a VFR traffic crossing our path below us at approximately 5,500 ft. MSL. We were descending to initially 3,000 ft. MSL to setup for landing on Runway XX (VMC conditions prevailed and the ATIS advertised a visual to Runway XX), but then were told to maintain 6,000 ft. MSL by Center for VFR traffic she was not talking to in our path. Hearing and seeing this scenario develop we shallowed our descent rate to level at 6,000 ft. MSL in an attempt to mitigate a predictive RA scenario. Once level and seeing the traffic was continuing in our direction, we also attempted a turn to avoid the traffic prior to the RA, however the frequency was congested and the turn was too late. Once we received permission to turn and initiated it, we ended up receiving the RA. We complied with the RA, disengaged the autopilot, and also climbed to approximately 6,500 ft. MSL to avoid the traffic showing at one point 400 ft. below us and advised Center of the RA. We were given permission to climb and, once clear of the conflict, to proceed to ZZZ without further issue.The event occurred due to a few factors coming together. The main issue is that the VFR aircraft was maneuvering without talking to ATC so as to avoid traffic. It was also a beautiful day, so there was a lot of GA aircraft the Controller was working with causing the frequency to become very congested. Secondly, the Controller should have issued us a vector or higher altitude to maintain to avoid the traffic as we never had or called aircraft in sight. We could have tried to turn earlier, but the congestion on the frequency prevented this from happening as well.I feel that this issue could have been prevented had the Controller issued us a higher level off altitude, or given us a vector once it was determined that the VFR target could become an issue. I feel that we tried our best to avoid this scenario by shallowing our descent and even requesting a turn. It just came down to the VFR traffic had an unpredictable flight path, the frequency was very congested, and once we received our clearance to turn it was too late.
ASRS:1793604.s: The crew descending into ZZZ received a Resolution Advisory from uncontrolled VFR traffic at 5,500 ft MSL while holding 6,000 ft MSL. The reporter attributed the event to the VFR aircraft's unpredictable path, congested frequency delaying a turn clearance, and the controller failing to issue a vector or higher altitude.

ASRS:1793703.n: We departed ZZZ on a Part 91 leg to ZZZ1. Reaching our initial assigned altitude from approach we were given a climb to 17,000 and that's when we lost EDC2 without making any changes to anything. We were caught totally by surprise. As a result there were several alarms and aural warnings sounding that could not be silenced. That's also when we realized that we could no longer communicate through the intercom and the First Officer had zero radio communication. We communicated through hand signals and loud talking. I was the Pilot Monitoring on this leg but I took controls at this point since I was the only one with radio communication. I pressed the autopilot disconnect button to ensure everything was disengaged and never made an attempt to reactivate it. I leveled at 14,000 and asked for a heading to troubleshoot and run the appropriate checklist. I announced that we had a failure of EDC2 and asked my First Officer to run the checklist. I couldn't hear any part of the checklist but he announced that the last step was to land as soon as practical. I [requested priority handling] and asked for vectors back to ZZZ. I received a heading and a descent and [the] First Officer competed the appropriate checklists for descent and approach. On final approach during our before landing checklist we realized the gear did not indicate down. We aborted the landing and tried to see if the Tower controller could confirm if the gear was down or not. We made the first pass and he thought it was down but asked us to make one more pass with all the lights off in the Tower so they could try to get a better look. Again he said it looked like they were down. I considered calling for the emergency gear extension procedures but I felt a sense of urgency to get on the ground. There were several alarms sounding and we were still struggling to communicate. I was attempting to troubleshoot mentally but hand flying the airplane was my priority. At this point I realized I was getting overloaded and we still had no idea what had caused the failure in the first place. I was worried things could continue to get worse at any moment and I decided to land because so believed it was the safest thing to do. Just before touch down I recognized the gear was not down and I gently applied pressure on the power levers backwards against the flight idle stops to fully committed to the landing. At this point I knew a go around was dangerous. We touched down smoothly on centerline skidded down the runway. We finally came to a gentle halt just slightly off the runway in the grass. We ran the shutdown procedures and evacuated through the door where we were greeted by fire rescue. After walking away without even a scratch I discovered things were starting to come back to me that I couldn't seem to remember during flight. Details about the systems that I've learned in training that I could not dig out of my head while we were in flight. I've learned a lot about myself and how I react when the workload gets high and I know I can handle any future emergency better than this one. That being said, my First Officer and I were the only ones involved and we walked away completely unscathed.
ASRS:1793703.s: A Part 91 pilot and First Officer experienced an EDC2 failure at 17,000 feet, causing communication loss and alarms. They landed gear-up after visual confirmation failed, skidded off the runway into grass, and evacuated unscathed.

ASRS:1793705.n: My student and I were flying a C172 on the RNAV XY at ZZZ, planning to circle-to-land on Runway XX. We made radio calls on CTAF for 10 miles, 5 miles, 3 miles, and when starting to circle. We only heard calls from a plane on short final. During the circling procedure, before we were established on downwind, my iPad with ADS-B In (via Sentry) alerted that there was traffic 10 o'clock, less than a mile. Both my student and I observed the other aircraft, a C152, pass less than 200 feet above us and less than 500 feet horizontally away. I made another call on CTAF and the C152 finally made a radio call that they were performing a teardrop maneuver to the downwind. My student and I proceeded to do a touch-and-go and fly the missed approach procedure on the RNAV XY. We did not hear any more radio calls from the other plane.
ASRS:1793705.s: A C172 pilot and student flying an RNAV XY approach at ZZZ experienced a near-midair collision with a C152 during a circling maneuver. The C152 passed within 200 feet vertically and 500 feet horizontally after failing to communicate its teardrop maneuver until alerted by the C172's ADS-B In system.

ASRS:1793727.n: After landing at MLB I turned off of Runway 9L at Taxiway Mike and was instructed to taxi Mike to the ramp. Due to it being dark and taxiway markings in poor condition. I got confused and accidentally taxied onto Taxiway Kilo. This was despite using a taxiway diagram and being very familiar with the airfield. I realized my mistake when I realized that Mike shouldn't have taxiway lights and turned off of Kilo as soon as possible. Luckily, due to the airport being empty at night, there were no aircraft on the taxiway at that point and I believe this reduced any immediate risk from the mistake, which I attempted to correct as soon as it was safe to do so. ATC did not mention my error to me. This means that either ATC did not notice my mistake or they did not think it was significant enough to mention. I was lucky that there wasn't an aircraft on the taxiway which could have resulted in a major situation. I believe it was a combination of fatigue (hour long night flight at the end of a day) and the dark conditions made it difficult to notice the proper taxiway markings. I believe having aircraft taxi on an unlit taxiway at night is risky as it could be easy to miss on a dark night especially next to a lit taxiway which would draw a pilot's visual attention. Additionally, due to it being my home airport I may have subconsciously paid less attention to the airport diagram than I would have at another airport. Going forward I will pay extra close attention to the airport diagram especially at night when I may have to taxi to an unlit portion of the airfield. This combined with verbally briefing the taxi route out loud could prevent an incident like this from happening again. It is easy to get distracted at night, especially if tired at the end of a flight, and make mistakes like this. So definitely, always use a diagram, double check the route and signs, airports should make sure markings are in good condition. More importantly than just using a diagram is actively reading it and understanding it no matter how familiar with the airport you are.
ASRS:1793727.s: The pilot taxied onto unlit Taxiway Kilo instead of Mike at MLB after landing at night due to poor markings, fatigue, and over-familiarity. No collision occurred as the taxiway was empty, and ATC did not report the error.

ASRS:1793734.n: Upon the commencement of takeoff roll on Runway XX at ZZZ the left rear door jettisoned from the aircraft. The door departing the aircraft was audible. Pilot noticed [the] rear door was missing. Pilot immediately aborted the takeoff and exited the runway returning to the run-up area and shut down / secured the aircraft. Pilot contacted the FBO operator to report the incident. Pilot and aircraft were approached by owner. Door was retrieved from adjacent taxiway. No damage to the aircraft was evident other than the door being jettisoned. The door itself had scuffs on the plexiglass window and sheared off at the hinges but did not appear otherwise damaged. The exterior of the aircraft appeared undamaged. Further, no damage was evident to the airport environment. No injuries to persons occurred. Pilot recalls completing all preflight checklist items prior to start, taxi, run-up and takeoff. PFD (Primary Flight Display) Annunciator indicated all doors and latches were secure. Pilot also performed a visual check indicating doors were secure. Taxi and run-up were performed without incident. Pilot believes that the latch / sensor may have been faulty causing door to jettison during the beginning of takeoff roll.
ASRS:1793734.s: During takeoff roll on Runway XX, the left rear door jettisoned despite the PFD indicating all doors were secure. The pilot aborted the takeoff, and the door was retrieved with no aircraft damage or injuries, likely caused by a faulty latch or sensor.

ASRS:1793739.n: Upon landing at night from ILS Runway 16, we were given right turn onto H1 from Tower. We saw the H1 Taxiway sign on the right and turned inadvertently onto Runway 11/29. Recommend this intersection be labeled a Hot Spot as it's difficult to see at night.
ASRS:1793739.s: Pilots landing at night on Runway 16 inadvertently turned onto Runway 11/29 instead of Taxiway H1 after receiving a right turn clearance from Tower. The reporter attributes the error to poor visibility of the taxiway sign at night and recommends labeling the intersection a Hot Spot.

ASRS:1793758.n: On vectors from Houston Approach for the ILS 14 at GLS. Cleared to intercept the localizer from current heading maintain 2,000 feet. Tracking the localizer inbound at 2,000 feet was given a handoff to Tower. I wasn't cleared for the approach so I asked if I was cleared ILS. Was given clearance and switched to GLS Tower.The glideslope needle went active and I lowered the gear to follow the glide slope down. 400 feet later the glide slope needle flagged out and came in and out. I initiated a climb and realized I was outside of the final approach fix. This was a false glideslope.I climbed back to 1,800 feet and approached the FAF. The real glideslope came in and I completed the approach.I reported the issue via telephone to the Tower after landing.The late clearance from Center for the approach [was a contributing factor]. I didn't brief myself clearly enough on the minimum altitudes until the FAF. I had a big headwind so my internal timer felt right to be descending but the reduced ground speed I was still outside of the FAF.My reaction to realizing the issue was fast. I stopped my descent and started a climb quickly upon seeing the glideslope problems. I then identified the problem and what happened. Resumed the approach when everything was correct.
ASRS:1793758.s: The pilot, while on vectors for the ILS 14 at GLS, descended on a false glideslope after receiving a late approach clearance and misjudging position due to headwinds. Upon realizing the glideslope flagged and they were outside the final approach fix, the pilot climbed to 1,800 feet, re-intercepted the valid signal, and completed the approach safely.

ASRS:1793772.n: Had a ground loop on landing rollout resulting in runway excursion. No one was injured and there was no substantial damage to the aircraft. The winds were light and variable.
ASRS:1793772.s: The pilot experienced a ground loop during landing rollout, causing a runway excursion. With light and variable winds, the incident resulted in no injuries and no substantial damage to the aircraft.

ASRS:1793787.n: While enroute (cruise), an aircraft (C182 tail dragger) suddenly passed over and overtook us in our Piper Warrior at a distance that was close enough to almost cover the wind screen. The student and I were discussing where we would land in the case of an emergency at the time of the incident. We had ADS-B In via ForeFlight and did not see any aircraft around (electronically) just prior to the incident. Weather conditions were clear and we were scanning outside for traffic (visually). Evasive action was not taken as the aircraft passed over us at a slight angle and was to our left side by the time we were able to react. The aircraft then turned to the left (south). We were monitoring 122.9 (ZZZ uses 122.8 which is what I should have been monitoring at that time). My fault in the incident was that I should have been monitoring and announcing on 122.8 instead of 122.9. I do not believe that the Cessna saw us or even realized that we were sharing the same real estate. In the future, I will be more attentive to local frequencies and stay at a higher altitude in that area.
ASRS:1793787.s: A Piper Warrior pilot and student experienced a near mid-air collision with a Cessna 182 during cruise when the Cessna overtook them closely. The pilot attributed the incident to monitoring the wrong frequency (122.9 instead of 122.8) and failing to detect the traffic visually or via ADS-B In.

ASRS:1793788.n: I was climbing out from Runway XX during a 'Go Around' turning from left crosswind to a left downwind at 800 ft. I heard another aircraft reporting entering a left downwind to the same runway. Right after entering downwind I broadcast in the blind looking for a position of aircraft and he told me I had just passed below his belly at about 200 ft. away from his aircraft. I apologized and told him I never saw him until after his call and he was about 1/2 mile off my left wing.A safer practice would have been if I sidestepped to the right during the initial phase of the go around and climbed to 1,000 ft. AGL before turning left into the crosswind. This action would have put me farther away from the airport and would give me a greater view of the area I was turning into.
ASRS:1793788.s: During a go-around climb at 800 ft, the pilot passed below another aircraft on left downwind at a 200 ft vertical separation. The pilot attributed the near miss to not seeing the other aircraft until after its call and suggested climbing to 1,000 ft before turning left as a safer practice.

ASRS:1793790.n: I was flying VFR with one passenger from ZZZ to ZZZ1 for a touch and go and back to ZZZ. In order to avoid the Class B airspace, I planned to do the FLY VFR shoreline route below class B shelf at 2,000 ft. In my cross country flight, I always like to take flight following. I did the same this time starting from Approach followed by ZZZ3 Center. I entered the shoreline [route] after clearing the class D of ZZZ3. I informed the ZZZ3 Center that I will be staying at 2,000 ft. along the shoreline route. When crossing over the [landmark], I was informed of traffic at my 2 o clock. I couldn't see the traffic so I reported by saying 'looking for traffic'. At the same time, I turned a little to the left knowing that the traffic is to my 2 o clock. After about 20 seconds I saw the traffic crossing to my right and felt like it was about 200 ft. in horizontal distance flying at the same altitude. I continued to my planned route to ZZZ2 , performed the touch and go and returned back to ZZZ1 using the VFR shoreline route again at 2,000 ft.
ASRS:1793790.s: A VFR pilot flying at 2,000 ft on a shoreline route reported a traffic conflict with an aircraft at the same altitude and approximately 200 ft horizontal distance. The pilot executed a left turn to avoid the traffic after receiving a warning from ZZZ3 Center and continued the flight safely.

ASRS:1793793.n: While on approach to landing in ZZZ, a gust of wind caused me to abort that landing. I was able to get enough altitude to take the gondola through the tops of trees just ahead of me. Once through the trees, I immediately saw power lines at eye level approximately 20 feet ahead of me. I immediately shut off the propane tank and turned off the burner, attempting to minimize any probable excessive explosion. After hearing the power line break, but not having an explosion and discovering that we were still aloft, I quickly assessed the state of passengers and equipment. Finding absolutely no damage, I turned on the propane tank and relit the burner. My ground team contacted me by radio and I informed them that we are okay and planning to land at the next available opportunity. I flew on and had a safe landing approximately 1/4 mile away. There was no aircraft damage and there were no injuries.
ASRS:1793793.s: The pilot aborted a landing in ZZZ due to wind gusts, then flew a hot air balloon through trees and severed a power line at eye level. After shutting off the burner to prevent explosion, the pilot confirmed no damage or injuries and completed a safe landing nearby.

ASRS:1793827.n: Aircraft X, cleared Visual Approach off a downwind turn behind a Heavy. Aircraft X was pointed away and behind Heavy when cleared to follow the traffic and issued caution wake turbulence. The pilot turned to follow the Heavy at his discretion towards the traffic and the field to a dog leg at about 5.5 miles in trail of the Heavy. Aircraft X joined final approach behind the traffic and I, the Final Radar Controller, observed what looked like a quick radar track anomaly. Quickly followed was an observed turn and quick descent and climb by Aircraft X back towards the field. The pilot promptly advised of a 'complete upset' and that he was back on the turn towards the traffic and on the Visual Approach with out a chance for me to issue any instructions.Later to find out this verbiage meant the aircraft had been sent into a complete roll to the right in which the pilot continued to recover the aircraft. No official cause but I can only guess wake turbulence from the Heavy traffic sent him into an uncontrolled roll. I acknowledged, inquired if any assistance was required to which the pilot responded in the negative, and I continued to work the traffic to include breaking out a Heavy behind him to allow him to continue the Visual Approach. The aircraft continued on the approach and double confirmed that everything was okay and no assistance was required before sending him to the Tower for landing.No recommendation, but awareness for all pilots of potential wake turbulence induced events. I personally could have ensured the aircraft was at a higher altitude to possibly prevent the wake trajectory, but I was originally setting up Aircraft X for an ILS Approach to follow at the appropriate wake turbulence minimums. Only after the pilot called traffic and field in sight was he given the Visual Approach clearance to follow. If the pilot did not feel comfortable with this, I did not know or could have recommended a different method of approach.
ASRS:1793827.s: Aircraft X experienced a complete right roll and upset during a visual approach behind a Heavy, likely caused by wake turbulence. The pilot recovered without assistance, continued the approach, and landed safely after the controller adjusted spacing for a following Heavy.

ASRS:1793943.n: [This is] the same aircraft we took in to ZZZ and landed with MAIN PITCH TRIM INOP. Upon landing, the FO thought he smelled an odor. During taxi, we both started to smell a roasting burning smell. We turned off pack 1 and it dissipated. When we arrived at the ramp, I smelled another burning smell. We turned off pack 2 and it went away again. After troubleshooting with maintenance, we could not get it to reproduce. Captain recommended replacement all packs and ductwork or investigate more into why a burning smell is such a common issue.
ASRS:1793943.s: The crew of an aircraft with inoperative main pitch trim smelled a burning odor during taxi and at the ramp, which dissipated after turning off packs 1 and 2. Maintenance could not reproduce the issue, prompting the Captain to recommend replacing all packs and ductwork.

ASRS:1793948.n: Briefed low level level off at gate. On taxi out, ship phone rang in cubby hole and I couldn't reach it. Dispatch informed us that we needed to hold on the ground for a maintenance carry over item that would expire before the completion of the mission. We waited ready for takeoff for almost an hour with several updates from Dispatch that sounded like we were going back to the gate. Then suddenly told to go. Briefed again the low level level off while waiting. Took off and did not execute the maneuver as we briefed. Got ATC call to switch to departure control right before ALT CAP. Noticed the FMA was not matching the calls. I switched my eyesight to the FO's hand on MCP. Once correct, I returned to ADI and discovered altitude was approaching 2,500 feet. Corrected pitch to return to 2,000 feet. ATC then assigned us 5,000 feet. No comment was made about the altitude deviation. Cleaned up aircraft, engaged autopilot, no further incidents.Cause - Pilot flying distracted to monitoring. Pilot monitor error in MCP. Pilot proficiency played a role. This was my first flight in 2 months and second in 5 months as pilot flying.Pitched down to correct altitude. FO contacted departure and we got an immediate climb to 5,000 feet.The main thing that sticks out is pilot proficiency. Briefed low altitude level off thoroughly. While taxiing, received phone call to hold for Maintenance waiver issue that affected later flights. Held for nearly 45 minutes at end of runway. Got the go ahead and proceeded to takeoff. Normal Takeoff until 'Alt Cap' called. VNAV was pushed initially then immediately corrected to Speed Mode and set 200 knots. Scanned back to instruments and noticed and called out altitude deviation. Pilot flying corrected immediately. Called departure with no further comments from ATC and rest of flight was uneventful. After MCP operation, noticed altitude deviation. Made deviation call out and pilot flying corrected immediately. Pilot flying became distracted with MCP operation. Pilot monitoring procedural error in MCP operation. Pilot proficiency. Time compression. Aggressively corrected and contacted departure. No comment from them and received immediate climb to 5,000 feet.Pilot proficiency should be maintained/bettered through flight/simulator scheduling efficiency.
ASRS:1793948.s: The pilot flying and first officer experienced an altitude deviation during departure after a ground hold caused distraction and MCP errors. The crew corrected the pitch to 2,000 feet, received a climb to 5,000 feet from ATC, and attributed the incident to reduced pilot proficiency.

ASRS:1793950.n: Approximately 20 minutes after departure I received a call from the Flight Attendant that we had a couple passengers that weren't complying with the mask mandate and asked me to make our announcement reminding passengers of the Federal mask mandate. I made our announcement. Just prior to going through sterile flight deck period the Flight Attendant called again with passenger seat numbers X3 and YX4 and asked me to relay non mask compliance to the station. We made several attempts to contact Operations. After being unable to do so I sent an ACARS to Dispatch notifying them of mask non-compliance and asked them to have a CSR meet the aircraft. Being so close to the destination we elected to continue to the destination. After landing we tried several more times to contact Operations on taxi in and were unable to do so. Upon arriving at the gate the CSR came on board and informed me they had LEOs waiting at the counter and the TSA had been notified but she wasn't sure if they were sending a representative to speak with the passengers. She requested keeping the passengers on board for several minutes, so they could make sure everyone was prepared to receive the passengers. Given the all clear, the passengers disembarked without incident.The Flight Attendant mentioned she made multiple announcements and handed the passengers the information describing the penalties for non-compliance that are included in the packs of masks/alcohol wipes. It sounds like she made every available effort per SOP to have the passengers comply with the mask mandate. As states continue to withdraw mask mandates I foresee this becoming an increasingly widespread issue. I thought the idea of handing the passengers the information card was a very smart idea as seeing this in writing may carry more weight. Perhaps aircraft can be stocked with additional copies of these cards to hand out. Also our current guidance on the mask mandates in the flight crew memo make this policy sound like it is just per company policy. Updated guidance stating that this is a Federal mandate may make it more clear to the passengers that this is a serious federal violation. Every day we see passengers wearing masks that are not allowed on our flights and have to be given masks the meet standards, gate agents policing masks that required standard would also be helpful.
ASRS:1793950.s: The flight crew encountered two passengers violating the Federal mask mandate during the cruise and descent phases. After notifying Dispatch via ACARS, the aircraft landed, and the passengers disembarked without incident following coordination with a CSR and law enforcement.

ASRS:1793954.n: North Little Rock regional airport, has commissioned an ATIS that is on the same frequency (123.77) as the DFW arrival ATIS. This makes picking up the arrival ATIS at DFW difficult to impossible until 120-140 NM away, well into the arrival.Change ORK frequency. Swap DFW arrival and departure ATIS frequencies (you can hear departure ATIS from FAR away and that's just not necessary - swapping the frequencies would fix it). Get digital ATIS. Allow access to the WiFi so airline pilots can use the Jepp's in the air to get digital ATIS (only resolves the problem if the plane has working WiFi).
ASRS:1793954.s: A pilot reported that North Little Rock Regional's ATIS on 123.77 MHz interferes with DFW arrival ATIS reception until 120–140 NM out. The reporter suggested changing the ORK frequency, swapping DFW ATIS frequencies, implementing digital ATIS, or enabling in-flight WiFi for Jeppesen access.

ASRS:1793962.n: While descending through approximately 20,000 feet on the arrival we encountered a compressor stall with self recovery on engine number 1 (heard loud popping, aircraft experienced slight yaw moment). All engine parameters indicated normal. PM (Pilot Monitoring) briefed the Flight Attendants and made a PA to the passengers explaining what happened. Approximately 3 minutes later we had an indication of N2 overspeed (~103%). PF (Pilot Flying) reduced thrust on the engine to bring it within normal limits which was immediately followed by a ENG 1 FUEL CNTRL FAULT. FO (First Officer) continued to fly the airplane while CA (Captain) was completing the ECAM procedure. The ECAM procedure directed the ENG 1 to be shut down. PF notified ATC and requested vectors to final approach for Runway XXL. PM completed the ECAM procedure and the QRH follow up for the ENG FAIL. PM briefed the Flight Attendants on a Precautionary Landing according to the Non Routine Landing Considerations. PM conducted a PA to the passengers to explain the situation and to expect ARFF (Aircraft Rescue & Fire Fighting) to check the airplane on the outside. We were cleared for a visual approach to Runway XXL which we backed up with the ILS. PF conducted a normal approach and landing and stopped the aircraft on the runway short of Taxiway D. PM requested that the Fire Commander check the outside of the aircraft for any damage or leaks. After ARFF inspected the aircraft and reported no signs of damage or leaks we taxied to the gate. After arriving at the gate, we called Dispatch to notify them of the precautionary landing. Dispatch patched us through to Maintenance Control. We discussed the ECAM / engine indications with Maintenance to aid in the log discrepancy write up. While descending through approximately 20,000 Feet we encountered a compressor stall with Self Recovery on engine number 1. All engine parameters indicated normal. I briefed the Flight Attendants and made a PA to the passengers explaining what happened. A Captain sitting in the cabin reported a big flash on the left side of the aircraft. Approximately 3 minutes later we had an indication of N2 overspeed (~103%). Reduced thrust on the engine to bring it within normal limits which was immediately followed by an ENG 1 FUEL CNTRL FAULT. FO (First Officer) continued to fly the airplane while I was completing the ECAM procedure. The ECAM procedure directed the ENG 1 to be shut down. We requested priority handling and vectors to final approach for RWY XXL. Completed the ECAM procedure and the QRH follow up for the ENG FAIL. Briefed the Flight Attendants on a Precautionary Landing according to the Non Routine Landing Considerations. Conducted a PA to the passengers to explain the situation and to expect ARFF (Aircraft Rescue and Fire Fighting) to check the airplane on the outside. We were cleared for a visual approach to RWY XX L which we backed up with the ILS. FO conducted a normal approach and landing and stopped the aircraft on the Runway near taxiway D. Communicated to the Fire Commander to check the outside of the aircraft for any damage or leaks. After ARFF inspected the aircraft and reported no signs of damage or leaks we taxied to the Gate. After arriving at the gate, we called dispatch to notify them of the precautionary landing. Dispatch patched us through to Maintenance. We discussed the ECAM / engine indications with Maintenance to aid in the Log discrepancy write up.
ASRS:1793962.s: During descent through 20,000 feet, the crew encountered an Engine 1 compressor stall followed by an N2 overspeed and fuel control fault, triggering an ECAM shutdown. The aircraft executed a precautionary landing on Runway XXL with no damage found after ARFF inspection.

ASRS:1793963.n: While descending to FL240 we were cleared to descended via the ZZZZZ X RNAV Arrival. I selected 11,000 feet. Approaching ZZZZZ Intersection I noticed that we were in open descent. I disconnected the autopilot and leveled off at FL238 and then started a climb back to FL240. Cause- While level at FL350 ATC cleared us to FL240 with a restriction to descend below FL310. I selected open descent to meet the restriction. After being cleared to descend via the arrival I did not select the managed mode.I need to increase vigilance when flying with people coming back from leaves for both PF and PM roles.
ASRS:1793963.s: The pilot descended via the ZZZZZ X RNAV Arrival but inadvertently selected open descent instead of managed mode, causing an uncommanded descent below FL240. The pilot disconnected the autopilot to level at FL238 and climb back, attributing the error to reduced vigilance while flying with crew returning from leave.

ASRS:1793982.n: We were with ZZZ Center and I was having trouble understanding the Controller. I told him that he was coming in 3x5. The Controller proceeded to tell me that he had numerous complaints about being hard to understand and the reason was, that he was required to wear a mask while at work. I started thinking about this and realized that I was having trouble with other controllers throughout the country and never made the connection. We never had an issue but the Controller had to repeat himself several times which seemed to clog the radio.Suggestion - Have the controllers not wear face masks that might make their transmission difficult to understand.
ASRS:1793982.s: A pilot reported communication difficulties with a ZZZ Center controller who was wearing a face mask, causing the controller to repeat instructions and clog the radio. The pilot attributed the issue to the mask and suggested controllers stop wearing them to improve transmission clarity.

ASRS:1793995.n: Turning for a 7 to 8 NM final from left base to Runway XX with aircraft configured flaps 20, PF established aircraft on ILS Runway XX GS and LOC for visual approach. PM made a VFR traffic call for an 8 NM final landing Runway XX. Another jet on the ground at ZZZ made multiple calls for a radio check and the PM responded he could hear the jet loud and clear.
