PF called autopilot off, and request the visual approach for Runway XX in the FMS. The PM entered the Runway XX visual approach into the FMS. PM made a 5 NM final call on CTAF. The jet on the ground informed the PM they were taxiing on Runway XX and would clear the runway prior to aircraft landing and then engaged the PM in a conversation about their inability to contact ATC Clearance. PF called flaps 30 and flaps 45 and slowed the aircraft on speed and Glide Slope. PM read the before landing check and at the LANDING GEAR DOWN call both the PF and PM noted the lack of DOWN 3 GREEN on the display panel and then visually checked the gear handle and noted it was in the up position. This occurred at about 1,100 feet HAT and was follow by the gear horn going off. PF immediately began a go-around and made call outs PM preformed G/A TO actions and traffic calls. The aircraft descended to 900 to 1000 HAT before entering the upwind for Runway XX and performed an uneventful left traffic pattern landing on Runway XX.This was my first day back from a month of leave and my Captain had also recently returned from leave. Rust may have been a factor. Additionally, we were flying at a high altitude airport with terrain at night with no Tower. There was definitely a communication break down and I was tasked saturated and should have let the Captain know I was in the red, and I could have missed the gear call. The final distraction was the jet on the ground taxiing on Runway XX where they should not have been, and fixation on them clearing the runway and engaging in a conversation about contacting ATC to get their IFR clearance was also a factor taking my awareness outside the aircraft.In the future I need to be more aware of my saturation level and communicate this correctly to my captains and avoid engaging in extraneous ground communications with other aircraft. Also, I need to visually and verbally verify my actions and confirm call outs by myself and other pilots regardless if I am PM or PF and verbally verify ambiguous calls or situations.
ASRS:1793995.s: The Pilot Monitoring failed to lower the landing gear during a night visual approach at a non-towered high-altitude airport due to task saturation and distraction from ground traffic. The crew executed a go-around at 1,100 feet after discovering the gear handle was up, then completed an uneventful landing.

ASRS:1794011.n: I was told by my Captain we are to expect two FAMs (Federal Air Marshalls) and one LEO on our flight. When boarding commenced, one of them showed his ID and asked me if he could check in with the Captain. After doing so, I asked him if he was aware of 'the other two.' He seemed confused. I told him we were supposed to have 'two FAMs and a LEO. Are you the LEO?' He said yes. I told him we have two FAMs too, but I'm not sure yet what seats they're in. He said OK and sat in seat. As he walked away, my Captain called me into the flight deck and said LEOs aren't supposed to know about the FAMs, but the FAMs are supposed to know about the LEOs. I was dumbfounded and anxious because I thought all armed persons are supposed to know about each other, with the exception of FBI agents, which is not in our manual anywhere, but was told to me when I inquired years ago at recurrent. I asked if ever someone can be armed on our plane and not have to tell us. The trainer answered FBI only. In flight, I looked it up in my manual because I hate not being sure of a rule, and I needed to read it to verify. I found two spots referencing FAM discretion, and to me, it says LEOS ARE supposed to be informed about the FAMs. All armed persons are informed about each other. Is our manual wrong? Am I interpreting it wrong? I informed my Captain what I had found. He said the Company gate agent was the one who told him LEOs aren't supposed to know about FAMs.My thought is, what if the FAM steps in to help us and pulls his gun out and the LEO shoots him. It could totally happen, because there would obviously be a commotion, the LEO thinks he's the only one on board with a gun, it's his job to help.Later that day, I asked a different company gate agent what their policy was. I wanted to verify. She said if the LEO asks if there is anyone else armed, she will answer 'yes, but they are not in your category;' but she will not disclose the seat number(s). If he or she (LEO) does not ask, she (gate agent) does not tell.Unless I'm reading my manual wrong, I think we have a policy discrepancy. Please let me know what's correct so I may comply in the future.
ASRS:1794011.s: A flight attendant reported a policy discrepancy regarding armed law enforcement on board, where a gate agent instructed the Captain that Law Enforcement Officers should not know about Federal Air Marshals. The crew expressed concern that this lack of communication could lead to a dangerous misunderstanding if both armed officers intervene during an incident.

ASRS:1794131.n: Descending into ZZZ, I was keeping my speed below 250 knots while descending through 10,000 feet using speedbrakes (power at idle). As I was reaching my level off altitude in the descent, I retracted the speedbrakes and the aircraft speed increased to around 258 knots. Upon seeing this excess speed, I re-extended the speedbrakes and slowed the aircraft to below 250 knots. Cause - Not noticing the increasing airspeed was a rusty move on my part, I believe, due to lack of flying over the past few months. To prevent this from occurring again, I'll be more focused on the task at hand when changing configurations.
ASRS:1794131.s: The pilot descended into ZZZ below 250 knots using speedbrakes but oversped to 258 knots after retracting them near level-off altitude. The pilot attributed the speed increase to inattention caused by recent lack of flying and re-extended speedbrakes to recover.

ASRS:1794137.n: I was working a Henderson departure on the SCAMR1 SID. The crossing restriction is 6,000 and he climbed well. The air carrier was departing Runway 19 at LAS and was climbing o the NIITZ1 SID. The crossing restriction is 7,000 over top of the SCAMR1, but 3 miles was lost and no divergence before the air carrier reached the crossing restriction.Move the flight paths away from each other as not to lose lateral separation. These are new routes for Metroplex and this was the first I've seen of these 2 departures at the same time.
ASRS:1794137.s: An air traffic controller observed a potential loss of lateral separation between a Henderson departure on the SCAMR1 SID and an air carrier on the NIITZ1 SID at LAS. The controller attributed the issue to new Metroplex routes causing the flights to converge before the air carrier reached its 7,000-foot crossing restriction.

ASRS:1794146.n: On approach at night extremely bright lights, said to be golf driving range over water (by local ATC) is to the north and west of the airport. Too bright for a normal approach. This is causing a hazard to the arriving aircraft. During landing flare the lights were not a distraction. On approach into RNO [Airport], extremely bright lights presented a hazard.Maybe change the intensity of the lights, or no lights during north flow approach.
ASRS:1794146.s: A pilot reported that extremely bright lights from a golf driving range north and west of RNO Airport created a hazard during a night approach. The lights were not distracting during the landing flare, but the pilot recommended reducing intensity or turning them off for north flow approaches.

ASRS:1794158.n: We were cleared approach RNAV Z XXR. I looked at the navigation display and saw a solid unbroken magenta line from our position to the runway. LNAV and VNAV displayed in FMA's. Prior to this we were given delete speeds and at some point, I think we were assigned 210 knots. Weather was clear VMC. We were looking for traffic. At some point traffic was called to us. I did not see the discontinuity at ZZZZZ in the MCDU. Approaching ZZZZZ I felt the plane was not turning to follow the path as it should. I disengaged the autopilot and hand flew the rest of the procedure. ATC asked us if we were turning and then asked if we could land.In the 10 months preceding this incident, I have 18 hours of block time. I have 2 hours of block time in the last 90 days. I was an X type aircraft Captain but was retrained as a First Officer (FO). I have 0 hours as an FO in this aircraft prior to training. My training consisted of one 4-hour sim period and two OE legs. I believe the Captain was just back from a medical issue, had done a short training course and this was his second trip on the line. Arrival into ZZZ during daytime VFR conditions with excellent visibility. Our FMC was programmed for the arrival as well as the RNAV RNP Z to XXR with the transition at ZZZZZ intersection. Our primary error was that we did not close the FMC discontinuity between the arrival and the approach. The result was that we overflew ZZZZZ1 intersection and corrected immediately after recognizing that we were not turning at the appropriate time. In hindsight it appears that multiple distractions contributed to our failure to remove the discontinuity. The change in speed assignments as well as a request by the Controller to watch for Aircraft Y traffic on a parallel runway and the timing associated with the issuance of our approach clearance.We were able to visually identify the Aircraft Y parallel traffic and kept visual separation. Once established on the extended runway centerline we received TA/RA warnings associated with the proximity of the Aircraft Y on XXL. Also, there was never any indication that our aircraft deviated laterally of the extended runway centerline that would have compromised separation.Immediately after arrival at the gate I called approach control to discuss the late turn on the approach. (I was not asked to call.) I requested to speak with a Supervisor and we had a 5-10 minute discussion. I was told there was 'nothing on their end' in the way of a complaint. We also had an additional discussion about the traffic advisories associated with our approach given the close proximity of parallel traffic.One of the challenges of flying into ZZZ is that we typically are issued our runway assignment, approach, and transition in the latter stage of our arrival. Also, once issued, it seems to be relatively common to be reassigned to yet another runway, approach and transition. It is also common to receive speed modifications on the arrival.We were prepared for the RNAV Z to XXR and per company procedure we had the default arrival transition programmed. In hindsight I believe that if our clearance to fly the approach had come earlier in the arrival phase (when we had less distractions) that we would have been more likely to close the link between the arrival and approach and avoid our error.
ASRS:1794158.s: A First Officer and Captain flying an X-type aircraft overflew the ZZZZZ intersection during an RNAV Z approach to XXR due to an unremoved FMC discontinuity caused by multiple distractions. The crew disengaged the autopilot to manually correct the path, maintained visual separation from parallel traffic, and landed safely.

ASRS:1794180.n: Landing 24 at night. Coming in over mountains in VMC. We knew we were fine however we got a terrain alert so we cleaned the aircraft up and went around and came back around landed on 34.Cleaned up and did a go around and decided to land on 34.At night when landing on 24 you need to go out further for the approach on 24 to avoid getting a terrain alert.
ASRS:1794180.s: The crew received a terrain alert while landing runway 24 at night over mountains in VMC. They executed a go-around and subsequently landed on runway 34, noting that a longer approach is needed on runway 24 to avoid such alerts.

ASRS:1794232.n: I was made aware that our flight was flagged for a passenger location/count audit. Apparently, we sent two requests via ACARS for a manifest/performance numbers with the location/count of the second one being off from the first. I cannot recall the exact details of this flight but I believe what happened is that I was notified of passengers moving zones due to social distancing. When this happens, I request a manual location/count be completed by the flight attendants to ensure we have accurate zones for the takeoff data. I believe there was a count error that was missed by us or the cabin crew.Although every effort was made to ensure we had accurate zones for departure, we ended up with three extra passengers than what the final location/count included. We were doing our best to ensure we had accurate numbers before block-out and perhaps the final count was overlooked as we were pressured for time. I am often notified of these changes with only minutes to spare before departure, so I feel that letting the passengers move rushes us and exposes errors like this one.While I understand some peoples need to distance on an airplane, I think there should be a cutoff in time before departure for this to be allowed. This creates an unnecessary distraction for the crew, and could create potential discrepancies like this one for the location/count. I think it could easily be explained to a passenger that they are free to move at some point after departure.
ASRS:1794232.s: The flight crew reported a discrepancy where three extra passengers were onboard compared to the final location/count submitted via ACARS. The pilot attributed this error to last-minute passenger zone changes for social distancing, which rushed the manual count process before departure.

ASRS:1794252.n: I wouldn't mind to serve the passengers with our normal service any other time however with the national crisis still going on and only about 20% vaccination rates. With the new menu option, I feel that it is still too early to provide these options.At first, I noticed even with the menu placard, several people lower down their masks to order their drinks despite the numerous PA about the mask compliance. It is quite distracting and uncomfortable environment to other passengers who are sitting next to them and myself. Few people were chewing their food and talking to me without the mask.The second thing is that more people are traveling which I am happy for however the social distance is impossible already. After serving snacks they immediately remove their masks. By the time I bring my drinks to serve, I am exposed to all these passengers and passengers themselves while they are chewing and talking themselves.The third problem is that more drinks, more contacts. Almost everyone touched my hands when I served the drinks. And immediate contacts with them handing over the drinks, it makes some passengers quite uncomfortable and distracted events for the crews.The fourth problem is that WiFi is inadequate and lots of people ask how or where to find the menu, it may sound simple to do it but it's not something that generally people are familiar with our website and not many frequent fly members on board. It takes lots of crew time and distraction in fact.Lots of crew members are still not having the access of the vaccine yet. I feel that our company put our crews in great danger in our work environment. If we follow the federal guideline, I strongly believe that we are not ready for this, yet.Thank you for your consideration and help in advance.We must vaccinate the crews 100%. I believe it is the upmost important event the company needs to focus on and resume the service we normally do after. This extra menu service, is simple I understand, however it still too early to say we are safe.
ASRS:1794252.s: Cabin crew reported that serving an expanded menu during a national crisis increased exposure risks as passengers removed masks to eat and touch crew hands. The reporter concluded that inadequate vaccination rates and social distancing make the current service environment unsafe for unvaccinated staff.

ASRS:1794298.n: After landing at ZZZ on the roll out towards the taxiway exit the aircraft landing gear system failed and buckled in. Consequently the aircraft fell to the ground causing the propeller to strike the ground. Damage observed and assured by A&P was the propeller, aux tank drain sump fell off, scratches on the bottom of fuselage, side step and landing gear. Airport operations did not want us to load the plane on a flat dollie and insisted on using a crane. When the crane was used the flaps were bent. No further damage was observed.
ASRS:1794298.s: After landing at ZZZ, the aircraft's landing gear buckled during rollout, causing the propeller to strike the ground. Subsequent crane recovery operations bent the flaps, while airport operations refused the use of a flat dolly.

ASRS:1794310.n: While at 3,000 feet about 21 miles southwest of Deland (OMN) (and flying southwest enroute to LAL), I saw on my EFB a possible convergence between myself and two other aircraft. The first aircraft, a twin-engine, was at my five o'clock, slightly higher than me, flying southeast. The second aircraft, a single-engine high wing was at my ten o'clock, slightly below me, and flying southwest. I found myself in the middle of this impending convergence, so I turned right and behind the twin, knowing that the aircraft would safely pass me. In this position, I could observe the other two aircraft quickly converge. I could see they still had vertical separation during the convergence until I saw the high-wing perform a climbing left turn towards the twin's path. There was no collision, but I genuinely think neither aircraft saw each other considering the higher aircraft was a twin-engine low-wing and the lower aircraft was a high-wing. I estimate the aircraft were within 500 feet of each other.
ASRS:1794310.s: A pilot at 3,000 feet southwest of Deland observed a potential convergence between a twin-engine and a single-engine high-wing aircraft. The pilot maneuvered to avoid the situation, estimating the two aircraft came within 500 feet of each other during a climbing left turn by the high-wing, likely due to neither seeing the other.

ASRS:1794317.n: I departed Wings field while a TFR was active. Wings field has a cut-out for the TFR but I still got a discrete code and frequency from Philly ATC before departing. When I departed, there was one plane that had just done a go-around and another coming from the north to cross the field and enter the pattern. Rather than do a left turn out and add congestion to the left downwind, I decided to do a right turnout to stay away from the traffic in the downwind and provide room for the incoming traffic to enter the pattern. I announced my intentions on CTAF and the inbound plane acknowledged my intent. The runway I departed (24) headed directly at the TFR. My plan was to call Philly, turn into the TFR and get clearance through the Bravo airspace. As I climbed, the TFR was coming up very quickly. I was not at TPA (Traffic Pattern Altitude) but I was also not talking to Philly yet. I was concerned about entering the TFR without talking even though I was transmitting a discrete code. So, I made a hard turn to the right to stay out of the TFR but was anxious about calling Philly. I changed off CTAF and called Philly (but was still climbing to TPA). Just as I did, my traffic alert system started sounding an alarm. I could not hear what Philly was saying because the traffic alert system was extremely loud. I assumed it was alerting me to the traffic in the left downwind and I tried to silence it. As a result of trying to talk to Philly and trying to silence the traffic alert system, I got distracted and failed to keep my head outside the aircraft (failed to aviate above everything else). When I finally looked outside there was another plane crossing about fifty feet from me. I have asked several people, but it is still not clear to me whether I can enter the TFR while transmitting a discrete code but not talk to ATC until I reach a safe altitude clear from the traffic pattern at the airport. I would think that is the case, but I don't want to assume that. I also think more room should be given for airport cut-outs for TFRs. The TFR starts about .9 miles from the end of the runway which should be enough to get to TPA, but it still requires a pretty sharp U-turn to avoid the TFR.
ASRS:1794317.s: A pilot departing Wings Field during an active TFR became distracted by a loud traffic alert system while attempting to contact ATC, causing a loss of situational awareness. This distraction resulted in a near-miss with another aircraft crossing approximately fifty feet away, highlighting confusion over TFR entry procedures and cut-out dimensions.

ASRS:1794321.n: We encountered clear air turbulence at FL320. Turbulence at the time was moderate. We encountered a 1,000 feet climb followed by a rapid downward descent of 4,000 feet plus. I disengaged the autopilot and tried to regain control. By the time we were level, we were at FL230. In the descent we did advise ATC that we were unable to maintain altitude and had experienced severe turbulence. We did not declare any emergency and there were no injuries on board or damage to aircraft. ATC did advise us that there could be a light mountain wave and turbulence before this occurred. The turbulence was not too bad up until that point. I have never encountered that in my life. The best way I can describe it was a rogue wave of air and we hit it just right. The weather was clearing up to almost clear skies when this occurred. Lesson learned is don't judge a book by its cover.
ASRS:1794321.s: The flight crew encountered severe clear air turbulence at FL320, causing a rapid 4,000-foot descent to FL230 despite prior ATC advisories of light mountain waves. The pilot disengaged the autopilot to regain control, resulting in no injuries or aircraft damage.

ASRS:1794343.n: We were held down at 5,000 feet for traffic while essentially on a left downwind departure. After flying level at 5,000 feet for a couple of minutes we were cleared to climb to 16,000 feet. Once established in the climb and climbing out of 6,000 feet, we were climbing at a rather high rate. As we were established in climb, we received a TCAS TA on traffic at 1 o'clock, which appeared to be converging on us. No sooner than we noticed, we received a 'DESCEND, DESCEND' TCAS RA. I disconnected the autopilot and autothrottles while simultaneously idling the thrust levers and pitching down to comply with the RA. Essentially, we went from full climb thrust in a climb at 250 knots below 10,000 feet to needing to descend promptly. That's a pretty dramatic change of aircraft energy state. I saw from the corner of my eye that it appeared to be a twin turboprop. The conflict aircraft passed right over us, most certainly less than 500 feet. As we were descending in our RA maneuver, ATC warned us to stop climb immediately. We informed him we were responding to TCAS RA already. After the threat aircraft was behind us, we resumed our climb and queried ATC as to why they didn't point out the traffic to us. The Controller said he 'didn't see him and wasn't talking to him.' I found that answer to be strange, but as it turned out, the top of the Class B airspace was below us. We reported the event to Dispatch and the Captain filed an incident report as per the policy. The question I have is whether the ATC can somehow remove VFR targets outside of their airspace band that are squawking VFR and wonder if that's what happened here. The threat aircraft was well within his rights to fly VFR above Class B airspace without talking to ATC, but without TCAS and without Controller pointing out traffic, because they may be 'squelching' VFR traffic outside of Class B, this could have ended really badly especially considering several cloud layers that we encountered. I recently flew an aircraft with TCAS MELed and I'm sure glad this happened when we actually had a functioning TCAS.
ASRS:1794343.s: The crew received a TCAS RA while climbing from 6,000 feet after a hold at 5,000 feet, forcing an immediate descent to avoid a VFR twin turboprop passing less than 500 feet above. The controller stated they did not see the traffic, which the pilot suspects was due to VFR targets being filtered outside the Class B airspace.

ASRS:1794414.n: This flight was a planned departure from ZZZ to ZZZ1. Weather was overcast, rainy with relatively calm winds and temperatures decreased during preflight from around 10C to 4C prior to departure. Pushback was delayed due to ramp congestion but only delayed takeoff slightly. The Captain was operating as Pilot Flying (PF) for this flight. The First Officer was Pilot Monitoring (PM). Takeoff was uneventful. The departure was flown autopilot off. While heading toward ZZZZZ and climbing at 280 KIAS, sometime after passing FL180 and climbing to FL230 in Instrument Meteorological Conditions (IMC), Boeing 737-800 aircraft experienced extreme airspeed indicator swings on both sides of the cockpit. Indications wildly fluctuated between 300 KIAS down to 180 KIAS. The PF asked the PM if his indications were normal and the PM responded that his indications appeared erroneous as well and he had an airspeed disagree indication. The pitot heat was verified ON. The autothrottles started to chase the airspeed fluctuations and were subsequently turned off. PF maintained the climb power and pitch angle and asked the PM to get a higher altitude from ATC. ATC responded with a 'standby for higher' response. The PM attempted to select Vertical Speed and it would not engage. All vertical guidance was unavailable. The PF asked the PM for a groundspeed and the PM responded that he did not see one. There was no groundspeed on the Captain's (PF) side as well. The Standby Flight Instruments were difficult to read as they had been dimmed for the takeoff and now the sun was coming up. Simultaneously, we were approaching a turn from ZZZZZ to ZZZZZ1. PF elected to maintain wings level and continued straight ahead as to not compound the problem by turning in IMC conditions with obvious airspeed errors. Since the sun was just rising we could see the top of the weather was very close. As we approached FL230 we continued to climb and notified ATC. ATC cleared us to FL380. After reaching an altitude, probably FL240/FL250 in Visual Meteorological Conditions (VMC) the aircraft returned to nominal limits. The flight continued under VMC to ZZZ1. The aircraft flew normally after the event and landed safely. Discrepancies were noted in the Aircraft Maintenance Logbook (AML) and maintenance personnel were debriefed by the Captain. Recommend a third air data inertial reference unit (ADIRU) on the B-737 so the bad ADIRU can be removed from the equation during a failure and still have a comparator feature. Early morning departure out of ZZZ to ZZZ1. During climbout on the SID just after passing through the transition through FL180 I noticed we had lost the flight director and a yellow 'speed disagree' flag on the PFD (Primary Flight Display). I then looked at the MCP and VNAV/LNAV was off. Tried to re-engage and it wouldn't due to the PFD flag. About that time I noticed the speed had dropped from 280 KIAS to about 260 KIAS and we were off course having missed a slight turn on the SID. The Captain then said his was not right and asked me what mine said. I had said mine didn't seem correct either. Then he asked me what our ground speed was and I looked and mine was blank, not showing and wind/GS/TAS. At that time I told Center that we were having a problem with our instruments since we were off course and altitude. He came back and gave us present heading and FL230. The Captain then asked me to see if we could continue our climb since we weren't far from being on top of the weather, I asked and was told to stand by. A few seconds later Center gave us FL380. At this time I notified ATC having noticed we were getting further off our heading and the situation was getting worse. As we started to climb everything came back, air speeds matched, flag went away, was able to re engage LNAV/VNAV and flight directors. Few seconds after that we were on top in VMC. Everything came back just as quickly as we lost it. We were cleared to our next fix and resumed normal operations. We discussed our options and mutually decided that since there was clear weather for the rest of the way to ZZZ1 and everything was working that it was best to continue rather than turn back into the weather and return to ZZZ. The rest of the flight was uneventful and sent an ACARS message to let Maintenance know we would be writing the aircraft up when we landed. We landed in ZZZ1 and the Captain made the entry in the logbook when we got to the gate.
ASRS:1794414.s: During the climb of a Boeing 737-800 from ZZZ to ZZZ1, the crew experienced erratic airspeed indications and lost vertical guidance in IMC. The anomalies resolved upon reaching VMC above FL240, allowing a safe landing after maintenance was notified.

ASRS:1794415.n: On the arrival in MGGT, winds were reported out of the south at 10 kts, so MGGT was landing Runway 20. Referencing WSI (Weather Services International), there were two active areas for volcanic ash, one for Pacaya and one for Agua. Both had plumes and ash clouds from the surface to 14,000 ft, and both were moving west. While selecting what approach we were planning, we looked at the different missed approaches and decided the VOR Z Runway 20 would be best in the event of a missed approach and avoid any ash cloud. The Missed Approach procedure for the VOR Z Runway 20 is AUR, 1 DME past the VOR, a slight left turn via the 169 radial to 17 DME and then hold at 11,000 ft with no special climb rates associated with it. Then our briefing turned to the Engine-Out (EO) Procedure. We immediately noticed the EO procedure splits the gap of the volcanos Pacaya and Agua, and right through the SIGMET area.We thought about what to do in the event of an engine-out missed approach. I decided, in this situation, the EO procedure would not be appropriate due to the active SIGMETs for volcanic ash, and I decided the missed approach for the VOR Z Runway 20 would be more appropriate and safer than the EO as published. We reviewed the terrain that shows on the EO procedure, terrain charts, and considered our landing weight. Landing was normal and no missed approach was accomplished. But planning for worse case revealed challenges to our procedures of following company EO procedures as published.Our training has us brief and setup EO procedures for missed approaches as well as takeoff, and fly them as published in the event of an engine-out event. This particular procedure, on this night, sets a crew up for a terrible scenario of going missed approach or takeoff, losing an engine, and flying directly into a volcanic ash cloud with one engine while these volcanoes are active.My suggestion would be to give the aircrews more options, have the EO procedure ready but review all the missed approaches as published and note whether we can fly them as a published engine-out. In this case, I believe we could have safely executed the missed approach for the VOR Z Runway 20, and possibly an engine-out scenario on initial takeoff, but I just don't have access to the information to confirm this. Blindly following EO procedures when other factors encroach on the procedures could result in a worse outcome.
ASRS:1794415.s: The flight crew arriving at MGGT on Runway 20 identified that the published engine-out missed approach procedure would fly directly into active volcanic ash SIGMETs. They determined the standard VOR Z missed approach was safer, concluding that blindly following published engine-out procedures without considering weather hazards could lead to a catastrophic outcome.

ASRS:1794436.n: Started APU shortly after arrival to cockpit and noticed a dusting of what we thought was debris coming from the ducts. I asked the support crew to get in touch with maintenance to take a look. Me and the crew continued with our duties and at some point we noticed an odor. We felt it must be the COVID spray so we were not alarmed. Spoke with maintenance about the dusting but language was a barrier. Later alerted by the crew that smoke in the supernumerary was getting worse. In the cockpit we had not noticed. Maintenance came into the cockpit and told us to leave and shut down. We vacated immediately.
ASRS:1794436.s: The flight crew noticed debris and odor from APU ducts after arrival, initially mistaking the smell for COVID spray. Maintenance later ordered an immediate evacuation due to worsening smoke in the supernumerary area, citing a language barrier as a factor in the delayed response.

ASRS:1794473.n: While the loaders unloaded my plane in ZZZZ, a gust of wind blew over some boxes one of these was a Hazmat box that I had not been informed was put on my plane back in ZZZZ1.This loader and I have had problems with multiple times he'll not listen to what I want for Max loading so I have to watch him closely as well as tell him a lower number because if I look away he always goes between 50-100 over, and will wait to tell me the door weight until after he's finishes his paperwork so I have less time to do my paperwork when they finish. I've spoken to another pilot in base and they've had the same issues. I will have to be even more diligent when he loads my plane. I have informed the chief pilot of this issue.Recommend this company develop should a similiar paper to other freight operators that states if they are or are not loading Hazmat. That way in case the Hazmat is put in a bag or hidden behind a larger box I would be able to say this is missing.
ASRS:1794473.s: A pilot reported that a loader at ZZZZ overfilled the aircraft and concealed an undeclared Hazmat box, which was later blown over by wind during unloading. The pilot attributed the incident to the loader's history of ignoring weight limits and failing to communicate cargo details, prompting a report to the chief pilot.

ASRS:1794500.n: Aircraft X has had two tail pipe fires on March XXth and XYth reported to the pilot by the Flight Attendant, Passengers and another aircraft that was behind them. Both times the engine was ran and signed off as no faults, it would appear that there is an issue if there have been two tailpipe fires in one week. The Number 2 engine has also used twice the amount of oil as the Number 1 for the month of March. Number 2 engine is leaking a large amount of oil into the tail pipe causing a tail pipe fire two times. Investigate leak and repair.
ASRS:1794500.s: Aircraft X experienced two tailpipe fires on March XXth and XYth, reported by crew and passengers. The reporter attributes the fires to a Number 2 engine oil leak into the tailpipe, noting the engine consumed twice the oil of Number 1.

ASRS:1794507.n: We, a C172S G1000, were flying to ZZZ under VFR radar vector with RNAV Y RWYXX for practice approach. While approaching to FAF, right after Approach told us to contact Tower, we found a Piper Cherokee on our 11 o'clock less than 500 feet horizontal above us and descending and approaching to us. We could not see them until last moment because they were above our wing 'blind spot.' Approach never mentioned about this traffic and our G1000 display never displayed its ADS-B location. After I found the traffic, I took over the control from student who was under the hood and started descent in about 500-700 feet per minute. We reported to Approach after the traffic passed behind us. Approach responded that, it was showing 1,000 feet vertical separation with us so Approach did not mentioned that traffic. Also, that traffic was not talking to Approach, so Approach did not know their intention. After that, we continued the approach and landed at ZZZ.
ASRS:1794507.s: A C172S G1000 pilot and student encountered a Piper Cherokee during a VFR practice approach when the traffic appeared in a blind spot without ADS-B display or ATC advisories. The pilot descended to avoid the aircraft, which Approach claimed had 1,000 feet vertical separation but was not in contact with them.

ASRS:1794523.n: Winds were moderate, variable, and gusty, but within limits for the aircraft. In accordance with accepted technique, half the gust factor, approximately 6 knots, was added to the final approach and landing speeds. Just after touchdown on the centerline, with all three gears established on the runway, a gust was felt and corrected for. As the correction was made with what was perceived as moderate aileron and rudder input, the airplane veered sharply to the left. With the thought that over-controlling back to the right could lead to the left wingtip dipping and then digging into the runway resulting in the aircraft tumbling (worst case) or a ground loop at high energy (best case), I elected to input enough control to keep the aircraft tracking as straight ahead as possible. This resulted in departing the runway surface to the left of the runway. Once in the gravel that was lining the left side of the runway, my entire focus was on maintaining enough control not to hit obstacles or dig in gear or wingtips so as to cause tumbling. In the process of dissipating energy, I crossed two high-speed taxiways at almost a perpendicular angle and at a still relatively high-speed resulting in the aircraft becoming lighter on the struts. The struts compressed again on the other side of the taxiways resulting in enough energy depletion to safely steer back to the runway surface.Upon re-establishing safe contact with asphalt, the aircraft was taxied a short distance to parking. Upon the post-flight walk-around inspection, there was visible damage to two of three propeller blade tips (of composite material made by Hartzell) from contact with gravel likely occurring when the struts compressed after crossing the taxiways. No other visible damage to the aircraft was observed nor were fluids observed to be leaking. It is very likely the root cause of this event was the application of too much rudder for the capabilities of the aircraft in countering the cross-wind gust after landing.The PA-46 line of aircraft is known to have very sensitive nose wheel steering, especially at higher speeds, and while being aware of it and managing it were trained to extensively, it's entirely possible that too much rudder was applied as was appropriate for this aircraft type. Habit pattern transference is a likely contributing factor in that I have several thousand hours in other type aircraft, to include very recent and continued professional flying experience in the Pilatus PC-12, and all of which do not exhibit the level of sensitivity in nose wheel steering that the PA-46 does. In instinctively applying the crosswind gust correction I'm used to, it is very possible that I applied an amount that was too much for safe control of the PA-46 at the time of occurrence.I do not feel training was a contributing factor as I received very thorough Piper-authorized training and initial conditioning in the aircraft with a Piper-authorized instructor. However, overall low time in type is definitely a contributing factor. Up to the time of this event, I had logged 20 landings in the PA-46 and several of which were in gusty conditions and or crosswinds similar to what was experienced during this event. In the future, the biggest take away from the event for me for flying the PA-46 is to concentrate on keeping the nose wheel off the runway as long as possible as energy depletes so that when the nose wheel does contact the runway, it's at the lowest speed practical. During this event the nose wheel was centered upon initial contact with the runway, as was emphasized in training. Any application of nose wheel steering at higher speeds should always be done very lightly at first to ensure the aircraft remains under control.
ASRS:1794523.s: The pilot of a PA-46 veered off the runway left after applying excessive rudder to correct a gust, likely due to habit transfer from less sensitive aircraft and low type experience. The aircraft crossed taxiways in gravel, sustaining damage to two propeller blade tips before safely returning to the runway.

ASRS:1794529.n: During a normal takeoff, I announce my intentions to taxi to take off on Runway 32 since the wind was calm at the moment. Before reaching the runway's beginning, I announced I would enter the runway to take off. Before entering the runway, I announce myself one more time with a call sign and intentions for departure and direction of the turn. After turning into the runway, I notice at the other end of the runway, approximately 200 ft in the air, the landing lights of an aircraft taking off. At the moment, I see the airplane already beginning its right turn out at no time where both of the aircraft were in immediate danger or close to collusion. Still, neither of the aircraft realizes the intentions of the other aircraft or position. It is unknown if the other aircraft notice me on the opposite runway since they were on a climb and no radio call acknowledge me. As for my part, I did not hear any radio call or notice the aircraft until turning into the center of the runway and only notice due to the landing lights reflection.
ASRS:1794529.s: The pilot entered Runway 32 for takeoff without hearing radio calls from another aircraft already climbing 200 feet at the opposite end. The near-miss occurred because neither crew realized the other's intentions or position until the pilot saw the other aircraft's landing lights after turning onto the runway.

ASRS:1794544.n: Pilot on parallel Runway XXR lost his engine and made a return to my Runway XXL for [a priority] landing. I was given a lineup and wait clearance, followed by a clear for takeoff straight out on XXL. Upon establishing the aircraft on centerline I spotted the incoming aircraft and before I was able to bring it to Tower's attention they cleared us for takeoff. My student read back the clearance and initiated the takeoff. Shortly after our roll started I took the flight controls back and began a sharp right turn to exit XXL on taxiway Charlie as another aircraft had taken our place.We conducted the training flight as planned afterword.
ASRS:1794544.s: A student pilot on Runway XXL received a takeoff clearance while an aircraft with an engine failure was landing on the parallel runway. The instructor aborted the takeoff and exited via Taxiway Charlie after another aircraft replaced them in the lineup, allowing the training flight to continue as planned.

ASRS:1794546.n: While working [sector] X there were significant areas of weather that were impeding aircraft transitioning the sector. One area in particular was south of ZZZ and it was causing large deviations for aircraft inbound to ZZZ. Due to a recent Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) that drastically alters Controller's working conditions on sector, which mandates the wear of facial coverings due to COVID-19 communication began to break down with aircraft on frequency. While trying to describe the precipitation to pilots the mask created interference and the pilots could not decipher what I was trying to relay, which was weather that would affect their route. This was especially the case with a handful of aircraft inbound to ZZZ that needed information on the weather and on the other aircraft they would have to follow into their destination airport. My only option was to remove the face covering so that I could communicate directly and effectively to the aircrews trying to navigate these storms. I am simply trying to comply with the duty priority. Management at this Center is more concerned with complying with the MOU regarding face coverings than they are about safely moving aircraft about the National Aerospace System. If I were to be seen without my face covering on sector I would undoubtedly be reprimanded for the 'face mask violation.' Ironically enough, if I were to not be able to communicate with the aircrews effectively and they enter an area of severe turbulence associated with thunderstorms I would also be reprimanded by management. We have now entered a situation where controllers are going to be forced to decide what is more important, the aircraft on frequency or the arbitrary rules being enforced by management due to a 'pandemic' that is now over a year old that has proven to represent little-to-no risk to the controlling workforce. By the end of the session I had several instances where separation errors almost occurred because of deviating aircraft and having to repeat transmissions to climbing/descending aircraft...this was even after I removed the face covering.I would recommend that someone in the Air Traffic Organization stand up for the safety of the system and issue some direction for controllers that need to communicate with aircrews. It is unreasonable to expect controllers to day after day wear a face mask while on position that causes distractions and limits the ability to safely conduct air traffic control procedures. There is currently no direction as to when a Controller can remove a face mask in order to promote safety.
ASRS:1794546.s: An air traffic controller reported that a mandatory face mask impaired communication with pilots navigating severe weather, causing repeated transmissions and near separation errors. The controller removed the mask to ensure safety but fears reprimand for violating the Memorandum of Understanding, highlighting a conflict between pandemic rules and operational safety.

ASRS:1794548.n: I had a civilian jet at 6,000 feet on a vector to miss ZZZ west airspace that was hot 6,000 feet and above. He was in ZZZ central that I was showing active 8,000 and above. Turns out ZZZ central was active 060 and above.Make sure airspace is coordinated correctly and is reflected in airspace status. I walked into the aisle to split 3 sectors out to a different position but the current radar working it all/receiving the briefing from the shift leaving for the day said he needed a D-side now. I sat on the D-side and was given a verbal briefing when he had time. I did not know the previous shift changed to bottom limits of a MOA to an altitude that is usually reserved for summer dates, 8,000 feet, and is frequently displayed wrong because the default in the EDST is 080 not 060. The Radar Controller cleared aircraft into the MOA/ATCAA with normal winter base limits of 6,000 feet. I received a call from XX [Sector] asking if he can have control of a departure to climb to 7,000 feet and I questioned his request. I asked the radar is the ZZZZZ airspace normal altitudes, he said yes and I explained to the controller that the base limits should be 6,000 feet not 8,000 feet. I asked the XX [Sector] Controller if something else was coordinated from the day shift on a higher altitude limit and he said no. I only assumed it was displayed incorrectly as 080 because it happens more often than not in winter time. Come to find out, the day shift controllers did coordinate the base altitudes of 8,000 feet, that information was given to the Radar Controller I was working with as part of the briefing. I was unaware of this information at the time this event happened.During the Summer months the MOA has a section of airspace with a base of 8,000 feet to allow for arrivals and departures out of a regional airport that sees most of its traffic during the summer. In the winter time this base altitude is 6,000 feet. In the EDST (Enroute Decision Support Tool) to activate the airspace, the default is 8,000 feet.Because the default is 8,000 feet, it is a REGULAR occurrence that 080 is incorrectly displayed. Controllers open the airspace activation menu, change the Top altitude and hit enter. There should be a procedure, an additional memory aid or something else that happens if we change the base altitudes outside of the normal because it cannot be relied upon during the winter months that it is accurate. I questioned it because it happens all the time and in this situation, I was incorrect is saying the base was 6,000 feet. In the X years I have worked here, this is the first time that during the winter months I have been incorrect when saying the base should show 6,000 feet, not 8,000 feet.
ASRS:1794548.s: An Air Traffic Controller cleared a civilian jet into ZZZ airspace at 6,000 feet, unaware the day shift had coordinated a winter base limit of 8,000 feet. The error occurred because the Enroute Decision Support Tool defaults to 8,000 feet, leading to a briefing gap and incorrect altitude assumptions.

ASRS:1794557.n: This is a very large sector that when worked on its own has 6 different VHF frequencies spread apart for coverage. In between these frequencies is a fairly large gap where aircraft below about 7,000 feet may have a brief period of no communication with ATC depending on how the Controller handles the frequency change. I received a handoff from Approach Control on Aircraft X which was level at 4,000 feet. An experienced Controller's first thoughts would be that this aircraft could not only go NORDO (No Radio) but also that the Minimum IFR Altitude (MIA) gradually increases to 5,100 feet to the western part of this sector. These thoughts came to my mind, and to be proactive, I issued a climb to 5,000 or 6,000 feet (don't recall which). Immediately after checking in, I realized this aircraft wouldn't need to be at 6,000 feet for a while and by then I'd be in communication with this aircraft on another frequency.Aircraft X requested to remain at 4,000 feet for better winds and flight conditions. I saw where the aircraft was landing, which was a few miles west of my sector, and measured from there to where I'd need the aircraft to be level at 5,000 feet. I instructed the aircraft to cross 120 miles east of the destination airport level at 5,000 feet and also to eventually check in on a different frequency when I was no longer coming in on the current frequency. Approximately 10 to 15 minutes later, MSAW (Minimum Safe Altitude Warning) was going off on this flight and flashing 4200 feet. It took a second for me to realize I made a mistake and overlooked a section of the MIA chart that was 4,200 feet. When MSAW flashed, the aircraft was beyond my frequency reach and we were unable to communicate.The aircraft was also just barely clipping the corner of this particular MIA section and then it was back to at or below 4,000 feet. Instead of trying to relay through an aircraft, I allowed the aircraft to fly through this corner since it was a 200 feet. difference we were talking about and it was such a brief time period. I was confident with my knowledge that although not ideal, this aircraft wasn't in danger. The Aircraft went on to meet my previous requirements of crossing at 5,000 feet at 120 miles from destination and checked in the next frequency and no further issues arose.I frequently skip a frequency that would likely work in between the check in frequency and the frequency at the western part of the sector. It's never been an issue because we very seldom allow an aircraft to make it that far west at 4,000 feet to begin with. I was confident I had been proactive and covered my bases when indeed I had not. I used a type of crossing restriction, at least for this purpose, that I never use and one that I had never used prior and I overlooked an important section of the MIA. I need to start using this intermediate frequency even if for a short time period. Pay more attention to detail when issuing a restriction of this kind. This was completely my fault.
ASRS:1794557.s: An Air Traffic Controller issued a crossing restriction to Aircraft X at 4,000 feet, overlooking a 4,200-foot Minimum IFR Altitude section. This caused a Minimum Safe Altitude Warning while the aircraft was out of radio contact, though the controller allowed the brief 200-foot deviation to continue safely.

ASRS:1794586.n: On a 14 mile final Runway 24R LAX Airport [at] 4300 MSL I spotted a drone approach another airplane at our 10:00 position on parallel final RWY 25R off their right wing. Drone then turned and flew off of our left wing tip opposite direction at an estimated distance of 300 feet. It appeared to be a silver quad propeller drone but not totally positive.
ASRS:1794586.s: A pilot on a 14-mile final to LAX Runway 24R at 4,300 feet MSL observed a silver quad-propeller drone near an aircraft on parallel Runway 25R. The drone passed 300 feet from the pilot's left wingtip before flying away in the opposite direction.

ASRS:1794633.n: There were storms in the area, and we were given a reroute by ATC, to go south to the coast, and then follow the coast west to IAH. The FO (First Officer, Pilot Monitoring) had made a passenger announcement telling them that we were expecting storms along the route of flight, and that we were anticipating a bumpy ride. I, the CP (Captain, Pilot Flying), had advised the FA that it was going to be bumpy. In the climb out, we encountered light turbulence. Upon reaching cruising altitude of FL280, it was smooth, so we briefly let the passengers up. Upon reaching the coast, ATC advised us of multiple storms and cells along our route of flight, and had mentioned that several aircraft ahead of us had gone south of these storms, had stayed within 50 NM of the coast, and had reported nothing worse than light turbulence, and advised we do the same. After discussing with the FO, we agreed that flying south of our route, and staying within 50 NM of the coast, was our best option. At this time, I had my radar up, and the FO had his terrain map up. We advised the passengers and the FA to expect a few bumps, turned the seat belt sign back on, and to remain seated. We also decided to slow to turbulence penetration speed. We were painting multiple red and magenta cells which we were staying south of, and had a lot of green all over the radar. We were dodging and avoiding the cells to the north, while staying within the 50 NM range of the coast. We then must have hit an embedded cell that the radar did not pick up, as it was only reading green. Almost instantly, we went into severe turbulence, and lost approximately 400 feet. The aircraft did not go into any unusual or upset attitudes, and the Auto-Pilot remained on. During this turbulence, we also had a suspected lightning strike - we saw a flash of light all around us, heard a bang, and smelt the 'fireworks' smell that you usually smell associated with lightning. After being struck, we got a Stall Protection System advanced master caution message appear. It disappeared within 5 seconds of it showing. As quick as the severe turbulence hit us, it disappeared. ATC queried us regarding our loss of altitude, at which point the FO reported the severe turbulence and suspected lightning strike. ATC asked if we needed further assistance, to which we replied no. As previously mentioned, this happened very quickly. All in all, I would say it lasted no longer than 30 seconds, and closer to 20 seconds. Once we were back at FL280, we had completely exited all weather (which we had been in for a majority of the time upon reaching the coast), and were in clear blue skies. I spoke to the FA, and asked if she was OK, to which she replied she was. She then asked if it was OK for her to check on the passengers, which she did. There were no injuries, and the only thing she mentioned is that the passengers were staring at her wide eyed. ATC asked if there were any injuries onboard, we replied with none. The flight continued with no further incidents. Upon landing, both pilots thoroughly inspected the outside of the plane on the walk around, noting a black mark on the right side of the nose which may be the entry point to the suspected lightning strike, but with no damage seen. I wrote up the plane with 3 write ups - Severe turbulence, Lightning strike, and Lock out/Tag out installed.CRM was effectively utilized during this event, with the PF using the radar, and the PM using the terrain. With the information available to us at the time, with ATC advising us of going south of the cells, as opposed to north, the decision, at the time, to go south was the correct one. That being said, I think it would have been smarter to go north of the cells, but we did not have that information. Utilizing the radar was key during this event, by staying out of the red and magenta cells. However, the radar has its limitation, especially considering they are older pieces of equipment, and can not 100% accurately paint embedded cells, of which we hit. After the event, ATC began recommending to other aircraft to go north of the cells. Ultimately, I would say the crew were stuck between a rock and a hard place - staying within the 50 NM boundary of the coast, but staying as far south as possible of the mega cells to the north. Additionally, I would like to mention the extraordinary job that the company did after the incident. Upon reaching the gate, multiple members of both [safety teams] reached out to me and the crew, checking that we were OK, and that the passengers were OK. I feel our company truly encompassed themselves with the company values, of which we stand for, and has made me thoroughly proud and joyful to be a part of.
ASRS:1794633.s: The flight crew encountered severe turbulence and a suspected lightning strike while avoiding storms south of the coast at FL280, losing 400 feet due to an embedded cell not detected by radar. No injuries occurred, and the aircraft sustained only a minor nose mark, with the crew attributing the event to radar limitations regarding embedded cells.

ASRS:1794646.n: While in cruise at 35,000 feet and in excess of 90 knots of wind from the tail, the flight had been in constant light and occasionally moderate chop. I requested 37,000 feet after confirming performance capability, and hearing ATC advice that higher altitudes were better than lower and the closer we got to 40,000 feet the better the ride. We were told 'Aircraft X, I have your request' and we were handed off to three subsequent controllers each assuring us that the next would assign our climb. Both PM (Pilot Monitoring) and PF (Pilot Flying) recognized the flight path was taking us directly into a cloud bank, and the turbulence levels were becoming more of a solid moderate chop. As a result, PM (the Captain) advised the Cabin Crew to secure themselves and instructed the passengers to take their seats and securely fasten their seat belts. This event took place less than 10 minutes from entry into extreme turbulence.On the last handover, we had a converging aircraft 1,000 feet above us and traveling in the opposite direction. When ATC called the traffic for each of us, we were just entering the cloud bank into IMC conditions. Almost immediately, we encountered an increase in turbulence to solid moderate (changes in aircraft attitude and altitude occurred, but the aircraft remained in positive control). However, within seconds, we encountered severe turbulence including large abrupt changes in altitude, attitude, airspeed, as well as wind shear and updrafts. The result was initially a traffic alert. Within a few more seconds, we were in extreme turbulence and the aircraft was being tossed about violently, control was practically impossible, and the aircraft was being pushed upwards.The PM called the increase in speed and retarded the thrust levers as the aircraft was being shaken so violently that it took both hands of the PF to maintain positive control. Then a TCAS RA alerted us with a 'LEVEL OFF' command with the converging traffic icon in the PFD illuminated yellow. Almost immediately after, the icon turned red and PF pressed the FORCE TRIM INTERRUPT" button and shoved the yoke forward into the RA box to comply with the given guidance. The turbulence continued so violently that the autopilot was fully kicked offline, and the aircraft remained in a diving attitude per the TCAS guidance.During this period, and as a result of the wind shear and turbulence, the aircraft's speed fluctuated between a momentary illumination of the green PLI (Pitch Limit Indicator) and the triggering speed for a stick shaker activation. PM continued to apply speed brake and retard thrust levers to maintain the aircraft speed within limit (at no time did we encounter either a yellow or red PLI, or the stick shaker). At 30,500 feet we came out of the most violent turbulence and were able to reestablish a climb back to assigned altitude. Immediately after, the Captain contacted the cabin crew for an evaluation on any injuries or known damage. Beyond all the drinks and unsecured items being thrown around, none were reported, so we continued to the assigned destination. After landing, the post flight walk around revealed what appeared to be abnormal alignment or misalignment on the right outboard aileron."
ASRS:1794646.s: The flight crew encountered extreme turbulence and wind shear while climbing from 35,000 to 37,000 feet, triggering a TCAS RA with converging traffic. The aircraft was violently tossed, requiring manual control and speed management, but no injuries occurred; however, a post-flight inspection revealed a misaligned right outboard aileron.

ASRS:1794652.n: I was sitting in the left jump seat. Less than an hour into the flight from ZZZZ to ZZZZ1, a status message alerted the CA (Captain) and FO (First Officer) to an Oil quantity of '4' on the number four engine. Another CA, sitting center seat, was direct by the PIC CA to call dispatch and begin discussing options. During this conversation with Dispatch and Maintenance the oil quantity continued to fall. By the end of the conversation the oil quantity was '2.' As there were no secondary indications, and the procedures call for continued operation of the engine, the crew, Dispatch, and Maintenance concurred that continuing to ZZZ1 was best. Shortly thereafter, the oil quantity indication read '0' but oil pressure and oil temps remained normal. At approximately XA:50, oil pressure began to fall on the number 4 engine. Dispatch and Maintenance were again consulted. As an engine shutdown was imminent, it was agreed by all that returning to ZZZZ was the best course of action. ATC was contacted and provided return routing. The crew reviewed all checklists and reviewed the emergency section of FOM. When oil pressure dropped into the 'red' at '10' the engine was shutdown IAW the QRH. ATC was notified, and the PIC landed uneventfully at ZZZZ. Overall, I believe the aircrew effectively utilized all resources and employed effective CRM during this inflight shutdown. Takeoff and climbout were uneventful. Shortly after top of climb the secondary engine indications appeared on the lower EICAS. The #4 Engine Oil Quantity indicated around 5 quarts. I called the second Captain back to the flight deck. I had him Satcom Dispatch and Maintenance Control. I checked engine out performance and noted that an altitude change was not necessary. We discussed the issue and had Dispatch calculate 3 engine cruise to ZZZZ1. Several minutes later the Oil Pressure began to slowly drop. We updated Dispatch with the deteriorating indications. We contacted Dispatch and Maintenance control to update them as to this not being an indication error. We discussed proactively returning to ZZZZ verses waiting for an engine shutdown to steer our decisions. This time a Duty Pilot was brought into the conversation and it was agreed by all that returning to ZZZZ would be the best course of action. We asked Maintenance Control if we should consider shutting down the engine to avoid damage. Maintenance Control wanted us to wait until the QRH called for the shutdown. We turned back to ZZZZ at XA:50. At XB:24 we shut down the engine as required by the QRH due to Oil Pressure. We followed all guidance in the FCOM and FOM and notified ATC of the engine shutdown. The arrival, approach, and landing were uneventful. Ground Maintenance later told me that the O-ring was not installed when the starter was replaced causing the oil leak.I would suggest that Duty Pilots are included in all calls to Maintenance Control. They could easily be subject experts on simple MEL applications in line operations as well as help steer events such as Diversions. I feel as they are the liaison between flight operations, Dispatch, and Maintenance departments and they bind the working groups together. Without the Duty Pilots input, it feels like an uphill battle between departments where no department wants to be responsible for a decision. There is a lot of resistance from the mentioned departments until the Duty Pilot enters the conversation at which time everyone seems to concur when the Duty Pilot agrees with the crew.
ASRS:1794652.s: During a flight from ZZZZ to ZZZZ1, the crew managed a number 4 engine oil leak caused by a missing O-ring from a recent starter replacement. After consulting Dispatch and Maintenance, the crew returned to ZZZZ and shut down the engine per QRH due to low oil pressure, landing uneventfully.

ASRS:1794663.n: Turning final ZZZZ fully configured at 150 knots I armed the Localizer first than the Approach mode. First Officer inquired and received the landing clearance. I noticed that the glide slope didn't capture and that we were going above the path. I tried to descend in Vertical Speed, but it didn't come active, so it wouldn't work. Approach mode light still on. I disconnected the Autopilot, lowered the nose and started a descend using the VGSI (Visual Glideslope) path indicator and the outside PAPI (Precision Approach Path Indicator). During the descent we tried to reset the Approach/Glideslope unsuccessfully. The approach was pretty bumpy with some good downdrafts. The aircraft went below the glide slope and I started to correct back when the pull up warning came on then stopped right away. Then the glide slope warning followed. I was just under the path recovering and had 3 red lights and 1 white on the PAPI. Speed around 10 knots above Vref and decreasing toward Vref. I was very focused on the approach and continued to an uneventful normal landing.We were configured early, ready for approach, but the Glideslope not capturing and the uncertainty concerning the landing clearance created a distraction that put me behind the aircraft and I developed some tunnel vision trying to remedy the approach. I became fixated and continued when I should have discontinued the approach and gone around. After landing the First Officer said to me that she had mentioned going around, but it hadn't registered with me during the approach. I tell First Officers that there is no mission, but today I didn't follow my own advice. It's easy to become over focused without realizing it. When in doubt, go-around. The event began while beginning the ILS Approach. The company notes on the approach dictate not to arm the ILS until reaching a certain position because of the possibility of false localizer signals. The Captain was the Pilot Flying and I was the Pilot Monitoring. I remember thinking that the Pilot Flying armed the approach later than I would have since we were well beyond the designated point. My best guess on what happened is that because of the delay the localizer armed but the glideslope never captured because we were already too high. Whatever the reason for the automation not doing what we had expected, the result was that we realized that the Glideslope never captured and were trying to get the aircraft to come down.Not only were we distracted with being above the intended glide path, but we were handed over to tower late and I was busy with getting clearance to land while the Pilot Flying was flying the plane trying to get back to a stabilized approach. As the aircraft was getting back to a normal glide path (3 red, 1 white on PAPI) around the 500 foot mark I gave my stabilized approach callout and realizing we were slightly above speed and correcting, but the vertical speed exceeded what is acceptable. At this point I said 'I think we should go around'. I can't remember if it was just before or after I said this that we got a 'PULL UP' alert. The Captain elected to continue the landing. Later after discussion, I learned he may have had tunnel vision to the point where my go around call didn't register with him.My unfamiliarity with ZZZZ did not help our situational awareness as well as being distracted with getting switched over to tower (late) and attempting to get landing clearance around the same time we realized the automation did not perform as expected. As a FO/PM not being assertive enough when a go-around was needed.Abiding by company SOP to the letter. No matter what, at 500 feet if stabilized approach criteria aren't met, it's an automatic and firm 'GO AROUND'.
ASRS:1794663.s: The Captain and First Officer experienced a missed glideslope capture during an ILS approach at ZZZZ due to late arming and high altitude. Despite a "PULL UP" warning and the First Officer's go-around call, the Captain continued to a stabilized landing, later attributing the error to tunnel vision and distraction.

ASRS:1794666.n: I was PM. On initial climb passing 1,500 feet there was no power reduction as programmed on T/O page X. I reached up and manually reduced power then checked T/O page X to find it was in fact still programmed properly. Passing 3,000 feet the speed bug did not bug up for flap retraction. That is when I realized VNAV was not selected. I selected VNAV. We retracted the flaps on schedule and continued the flight to destination.I have low experience with only 40 hours on the aircraft. My Relief Pilot also was not yet consolidated and my FO just recently consolidated. I must have incorrectly responded 'checked' to the 'MCP' challenge on the before Start checklist and missed that VNAV was not selected.Fly more often. But hard to do under COVID. Be more deliberate in accomplishing checklist especially at the gate before airborne when stress and task demand is low. Departing ZZZZ at 1,500 feet power did not reduce to climb power. The Captain checked the takeoff pg X for altitudes, they were correct. At 3,000 feet the speed bug did not bug up for cleanup, that's when the Captain realized VNAV was not engaged. He engaged VNAV and I called for flap retraction on schedule.Cause - Recency in right seat. Monitoring. Refrain from staying heads down in the checklist. Confirm selected items.
ASRS:1794666.s: The Pilot Monitoring and Captain experienced a failure of automatic power reduction and speed bug engagement during initial climb due to VNAV not being selected. The crew manually corrected the settings, attributing the error to low recency and inadequate checklist verification.

ASRS:1794703.n: Once established in descent just below FL180, we received a call from the Flight Attendants that there was an odor in the vicinity of row X. This odor was described by FA 'A' as something similar to fuel and/or oil, but not a burning or acrid smell. The odor was not detectable to any other passengers or crew on the aircraft except the passengers in row X, to whom it was very noticeable, which was also confirmed by FA 'B', but only when they walked up to row X. There was no visible plume anywhere in the airplane. The pilots did not detect any irregular odor in flight.The FO was flying the airplane (PF) so they took the radios as the CA (PM) looked in the QRH checklist. The comment about a fuel smell drove the pilots to suspect a fuel leak, but after running through the fuel leak checklist, no fuel leak indications (per checklist) were confirmed (fuel imbalance normal/not increasing, both engine fuel flow rates equivalent, quantity as expected for phase of flight plan). CA then confirmed with FA 'A' that the smell was indeed still noticeable, but there was still no plume and the odor was still confined to row X.We continued descent into ZZZ1 on what looked to be a fairly expedited vector, while we requested ARFF to be on standby at time of arrival. However, after we received another vector away from an expedited intercept course, we quickly [advised ATC] to gain traffic priority, which ATC quickly accommodated, clearing other aircraft from our path. We were cleared to land and we confirmed with Tower that ARFF would be standing by. Tower indicated we would exit [Runway] XXR at Taxiway 1 for ARFF coordination.Upon exit at Taxiway 1, we were cleared to cross runway XXL, and brought the aircraft to a stop on Taxiway 1 clear of runway. We requested ARFF check/scan the exterior of the aircraft for leaks/heat/fire/abnormalities. CA made a PA to pax noting that ARFF would be approaching the aircraft as a precaution. After ARFF indicated no abnormalities, we taxied to the gate, making clear to Ops that as an extra precaution, we would not start the APU. After we had taxied into the gate and set the parking brake, we immediately shut down (left-hand-side) engine #1, confirmed good/stable AC external power connection, then shut down (right-hand-side) engine #2. Prior to departure from ZZZ, we were sprayed with both Type I 'Deice' and Type IV 'Anti-Ice' fluid, with engines running, at the X Pad.After landing, FA 'B' said passengers had complained that the odor became more noticeable after landing gear was extended on final approach. FO also said that after landing they briefly noticed an odor.We could have [advised ATC] earlier on in the event. This would have allowed us traffic priority earlier in the descent (and speeds above 250 KIAS once below 10,000), getting us on the ground sooner and reducing the overall time of pax/FA exposure to fumes.We flew the same airplane the following day, and the airplane was cleared by Maintenance with no defects found. Nothing was wrong with the airplane itself. Fumes remaining localized in a certain area of the cabin suggests internal point source emission rather than external ingestion or airplane system malfunction. However, at time of writing, we still do not know, definitively, what caused the fumes.The FAs are commended for their prompt notification and accurate description of the nature and extent of the fumes. FO is commended for flying the aircraft while coordinating with ATC and requesting ARFF, while the CA ran checklists and coordinated with the FAs, then flying the approach almost to minimums. Working together seamlessly is key in these situations, and the CA commends the crew for a job well done. Prior to departure from ZZZ, we were sprayed with both Type I and Type IV fluid, with engines running, at the South De-Ice Pad.Once established in descent just below FL180, we received a call from the FA's. I (the FO) assumed it was the FA's notification that they were seated. Instead, they communicated to the CA that there was an odor in the vicinity of row x. This odor was described by FA 'A' as something similar to fuel and/or oil, but not a burning smell. The odor was not detectable to any other passengers or crew on the aircraft except the passengers in row x, to whom it was very noticeable. The pilots did not detect any irregular odor in flight.I (the FO) was flying the airplane (PF) so I took the radios as the CA (PM) looked in the QRH checklist. Since the CA was communicating with the FA's, I trusted his lead on necessary checklists to run, as he had the first hand information on the situation in the cabin. During this time, we had entered IMC conditions, and I was flying the airplane and working the radios, receiving several heading, altitude and speed changes during this time.The comment about a fuel smell drove us to suspect a fuel leak, but after running through the fuel leak checklist, no fuel leak indications (per checklist) were confirmed (fuel imbalance normal/not increasing, both engine fuel flow rates equivalent, quantity as expected for phase of flight plan). CA then confirmed with FA 'A' that the smell was indeed still noticeable, but there was still no plume and the odor was still confined to row X.We continued descent into ZZZ1 on what looked to be a fairly expedited vector, during which I requested ARFF to be on standby at time of arrival. However, after we received another vector away from an expedited intercept course, we quickly [advised ATC] to gain traffic priority, which ATC quickly accommodated. We were cleared to land and we confirmed with Tower that ARFF would be standing by. Tower indicated we would exit XXR at Taxiway 1 for ARFF coordination.Upon landing, I cracked the Thrust Reversers (TRs), and briefly noticed a smell in the flight deck. I then decided that the use of TRs may not be the safest procedure, as it was still unclear what was causing this smell. Thus, I immediately stowed the TRs and decelerated using only the brakes (long runway, good braking action).Upon exit at Taxiway 1, we were cleared to cross runway XXL, and brought the aircraft to a stop on Taxiway 1 clear of XXL. We requested ARFF check/scan the exterior of the aircraft for leaks/heat/fire/abnormalities. CA made a PA to pax noting that ARFF would be approaching the aircraft as a precaution. After ARFF indicated no abnormalities, we taxied to the gate, making clear to Ops that as an extra precaution, we would not start the APU. After we had taxied into the gate and set the parking brake, we immediately shut down engine #1, confirmed good/stable AC external power connection, then shut down engine #2.After landing, FA 'B' said passengers had complained that the odor became more noticeable after landing gear was extended on final approach. This was my 2nd precautionary ARFF event on 2 consecutive workdays (though separated by a period of leave). Having had the time to reflect upon the first event, I felt calmer and more prepared this time. I focused on making a successful approach (almost down to minimums).One error I made was to start configuring and thus slowing down too early. Due to several heading changes and an ATC request for us to slow down while the aircraft in front of us on the approach sped up to best forward speed, I had felt momentarily disoriented regarding our distance to the ZZZ1. Luckily, my brain was about 5 miles ahead of the airplane. Once I realized my error, I paused further configuration (which was gear down flaps 3 at that time) until closer to the ZZZ1.Considerations that were made were items for fire and emergency evacuation, should a fire develop after landing. Luckily, this was not the case.To my knowledge, it is still unclear what caused the smell. If it would have been more severe (filling the entire cabin and flight deck), then the checklist for smoke/fumes would have been appropriate.Overall, I feel that this event was handled well by everyone involved.
ASRS:1794703.s: During descent below FL180, flight attendants reported a localized fuel-like odor in row X, prompting the crew to request ARFF standby and traffic priority. After landing and an ARFF inspection found no abnormalities, the aircraft was shut down at the gate with no defects identified by maintenance.

ASRS:1794733.n: I was assigned to work position Flight Attendant (FA) D on the aircraft and completely forgot my exit rows briefing duty the flight. I didn't realize my failure to brief exit row passengers the entire flight. It was during the boarding process of the second flight when I briefed those exit row passengers, that I became aware of what I overlooked on the first flight.I believe upon freshly returning to active duty, after almost an entire year being on extended leave of absence during COVID-19 schedule reductions, led to my lack of attention to flight steps in which years of routines were disrupted.
