To prevent this event from reoccurring, I need to refresh my memory and utilize my work manual in reviewing duties of each phases of flight.Realized mistake of skipped exit briefing for ZZZ-ZZZ1 flight while initiating exit briefing for the return flight ZZZ1-ZZZ.
ASRS:1794733.s: A flight attendant on flight ZZZ-ZZZ1 failed to brief exit row passengers due to disrupted routines after returning from extended leave. The omission was discovered during the boarding of the return flight, ZZZ1-ZZZ, prompting the crew member to review flight phase duties to prevent recurrence.

ASRS:1794747.n: The container loader operator checked inside cargo compartment to confirm that the Dangerous Goods (DG) shipment was secure. He found it not properly secured. Notified the cargo dept and they sent someone to secure it.
ASRS:1794747.s: A container loader operator discovered a Dangerous Goods shipment was not properly secured during a cargo compartment check. The operator notified the cargo department, which sent personnel to secure the shipment.

ASRS:1794760.n: Aircraft ground-looped on landing damaging landing gear, prop and wingtip.
ASRS:1794760.s: The aircraft ground-looped during landing, resulting in damage to the landing gear, propeller, and wingtip. The narrative does not specify the cause or the personnel involved.

ASRS:1794790.n: Inbound to ZZZ from the south. Reported on CTAF 5 nm south of airport inbound for landing on Runway XX. A flight of 3 RVs reported taxiing out for XX. Approaching the airport RVs reported their takeoff roll, just prior to entering the downwind leg RVs reported they would be departing southbound. I then reported I was 2 minutes south. At that time, I observed the RVs over the departure end turning left. At this time, I could see them on a direct course toward me, they were climbing, I was level at pattern altitude (900 feet MSL). They were basically climbing or about to climb through my altitude, my best option was to descend underneath them, as they were climbing. At that point one of the RVs, I assume the leader reported seeing me headed underneath them. After we passed, I climbed back to pastern altitude and turned downwind, the RVs continued southbound.I saw the RVs from their x-wind turn. I thought they would make a standard 45 departure from the x-wind leg prior to turning southbound but they continued south. I should have been a little more to the East so that I joined the downwind at mid-field. They should have departed on a 45 to the x-wind. Fortunately, I was watching for them and saw them in time to avoid them. Everybody being on frequency was a positive.
ASRS:1794790.s: A pilot inbound for landing at 900 feet MSL encountered three climbing RVs departing southbound on a direct course toward the aircraft. The pilot descended to avoid a collision, attributing the near miss to the RVs failing to execute a standard 45-degree departure and the pilot's late downwind entry.

ASRS:1794793.n: I had just assumed responsibility of the position about a minute prior when the pilot of Aircraft X informed me that they were 'Over HOMAI, what do you want?' The previous controller, still observing the 2-minute overlap, confirmed what she stated in the relief briefing, that Aircraft X had been assigned direct HOMAI, which ties into their flight plan routing of the LNDHY1 STAR into OGG. I responded to the pilot that he should track outbound of HOMAI on the LNDHY1 arrival, which publishes a 204 degree track. The pilots were obviously confused, but began to correct. In the process of doing so, the aircraft may have clipped the boundary of a higher 6,300 ft. MVA. Aircraft X was level at 4,000 ft. in a 3,500 ft. MVA, and would have had no problems remaining so if they were established on the STAR. In an effort to salvage the situation, I asked the pilots if they had the airport in sight for a visual approach. They replied in the affirmative. Then I asked if they had traffic to follow in sight. They replied in the affirmative and I issued the visual approach clearance. The MSAW (Minimum Safe Altitude Warning) did not activate and I did not issue a low altitude alert. The pilots did not question the 'direct HOMAI' clearance they received from the previous controller until they were about a half mile past the fix. If there was any question about their routing, they should've clarified much earlier. But the confusion is not infrequent, and I have had pilots question the routing before. The published STAR clearly shows a 204 degree track after HOMAI on both the visual layout and written description. When I state this fact to querying pilots, the confusion is resolved. But the lack of a fix after HOMAI may cause pilots to ignore the track, or (as some controllers suspect) cause the track to drop out of the FMS when an approach is pre-loaded. My recommendation is for another fix to be added on the 204 degree track after HOMAI, to resolve the confusion, and to help ensure that aircraft don't fly on a free heading toward a higher MVA.My other recommendation is to look into how the LNDHY1 STAR is being programmed into FMS displays, and whether the addition of a (yet to be assigned) approach (e.g. RNAV Z RWY 2 from HOMAI) erases or otherwise obfuscates the 204 degree track outbound of HOMAI.
ASRS:1794793.s: An air traffic controller and the pilot of Aircraft X experienced confusion over the LNDHY1 STAR routing after a direct HOMAI clearance, causing the aircraft to potentially clip a 6,300 ft MVA while at 4,000 ft. The controller issued a visual approach clearance, and the reporter attributed the incident to ambiguous STAR design and potential FMS programming issues.

ASRS:1794794.n: Aircraft X was released IFR off UDD, which off of RWY (Runway) 28 would be an immediate left turn (Southeast) to TRM, climbing to 4,000 feet. When they were released, there was no immediate traffic threat for the departure. By the time Aircraft X departed there was a target flying westbound (opposite direction) at 2,500 feet. On initial contact with Aircraft X, I told them about the traffic and asked if they could stop their climb at 2,000 feet (MVA in the area is 4,000 feet). They questioned the altitude initially, and I explained the situation to them. They agreed to stop at 2,000 feet. I issued a traffic alert, and Aircraft X eventually said they had to turn to avoid the traffic.I am recommending that there be some sort of real controlled airspace in the Palm Springs valley. The TRSA is not mandatory, and there are frequently aircraft (many high performance) that choose not to call the approach controllers and just go straight to the tower. The airspace in the months between September and May is extremely busy at times, and the controllers/pilots have no safe space in which to operate. It is called 'The Wild West' over there for a reason. Everything is shoot from the hip, because you have no idea what is about to happen next. We can not plan on anything, we can never assume anything. The most controlled airspace in the valley is the PSP Delta, which requires participation, while the approach controllers work 20x the traffic and have no 'safe space'.I ask that the airspace be reviewed and considered for a Class Bravo/Charlie airspace to avoid future NMACs or worse.
ASRS:1794794.s: An air traffic controller advised Aircraft X departing UDD Runway 28 to stop climbing at 2,000 feet due to westbound traffic at 2,500 feet, causing the pilot to turn for avoidance. The controller attributed the risk to non-mandatory TRSA participation and recommended upgrading the airspace to Class Bravo or Charlie to prevent future NMACs.

ASRS:1794806.n: Aircraft X was southbound at 030 for a visual approach to Runway XX at ZZZ. I accepted a VFR point out from ZZZ1 facility on a XXXX code just a few miles east of ZZZZZ intersection going a few miles west of ZZZZZ to turn back to ZZZ1 airspace along the coastline at 015. I did not tag up the point out because there was no traffic in that vicinity, and I was busy messing with my COVID mask. I was trying to put my mask on which I had in my pocket. I cleared Aircraft X into Runway XX for the visual approach. I switched Aircraft X to the Tower when the point out aircraft was 7NM East of Aircraft X at 015. The tower controller issued traffic to Aircraft X three times. The first traffic call Aircraft X reported seeing the aircraft on TCAS. The third traffic call Aircraft X reported the traffic insight. No traffic alert was given to Aircraft X and no TCAS RA was performed. Aircraft X continued inbound and landed without further incident. I lost track of the point out because when I took it I was working planes while trying to fix my COVID-19 mask. When I decided to just work without one, I had moved on to other traffic and forgot to tag up the point out.The fact that I was more concerned with getting in trouble for not having my mask on rather than doing a completely efficient job is the FAA's fault. The FAA is making us fear the repercussions of the mask mandate, so much its eroding the safety of the NAS...DO NOT REQUIRE MASK TO BE WORN ON POSITION IF WE ARE ALREADY SIX FEET APART, which we are based on the distance of scope to scope. Whether its distracting, [probably] muffles transmissions, the mask mandate on position is depleting the safety of the NAS. I was working LC. Runway XX was the active Runway, advertising RNAVs.Aircraft X, checked on Tower frequency on an 11 mile final at an altitude of 1,700 feet. I noticed a target moving east to west at a high rate of speed (240 knots) and was not tagged up. I called traffic to Aircraft X at his 2 o'clock 3 to 4 miles moving westbound at 1,500 feet. Aircraft X said he had it on his TCAS and he was looking for traffic. I continued to watch the westbound traffic realizing it was going to potentially become a conflict for Aircraft X and continued to call traffic to them. I advised Aircraft X to try and maintain 1,700 feet based on the fact the westbound traffic appeared to be holding 1,500 and Aircraft X was on an instrument approach. I also told Aircraft X it appeared the traffic was going to pass underneath. Aircraft X reported the traffic in sight right as my Ground Control and I realized the target was making a hard 180 degree turn back to the east while climbing up into Aircraft X's flight path and altitude. I responded back to Aircraft X to maneuver at his discretion to avoid the aircraft. The target continued eastbound. Aircraft X landed without incident. I asked Aircraft X if he would give me a call so that I may ask questions. I told him he was not in trouble, he obliged and I gave him the tower number. I then attempted to call the Supervisor from our communications counsel to ask what was going on with the target to no avail, the Supervisor did not pick up. Once on break I was able to speak with the pilot: The Pilot said it was a [description]. He caught a glimpse of it while it passed underneath then Aircraft Y did the 180 degree turn back east and passed right off the nose of his aircraft at his altitude. The pilot also mentioned that his passengers had asked about the aircraft, leading me to believe in fact Aircraft Y was extremely close and causing this to be a significant event. The pilot said he was also going to file a report.I took the information down to my Supervisor. My Supervisor called the ZZZ [TRACON] Supervisor who said he didn't know anything of the event and that he was too busy to look into at the moment. Seeing as how Aircraft Y came from ZZZ's TRACON airspace, my Supervisor gave them a call to see if they knew anything about Aircraft Y and what it was doing. ZZZ4 said they were talking to Aircraft Y and had coordinated with ZZZ with a point out, ZZZ accepted the point out on Aircraft Y. There was never any coordination from ZZZ to myself on LC in reference to Aircraft Y.Note: I did not issue a Traffic Alert because I had no clue what Aircraft Y was doing, I was focused on calling the traffic from the beginning, and with the 180 degree high speed turn I felt like giving the pilot discretion to maneuver as needed (since he had him in sight then) was the best course of action for the pilot to be able to keep his passengers alive.Note: Aircraft Y was never tagged up on the scope. They appeared to be VFR but I'm really unsure if they were.Events like this in the ZZZ [TRACON] airspace and ZZZ [Tower] environment in my opinion are a consistent problem.1. ATC 101: coordination and positive control. ZZZ1 [TRACON] coordinated with ZZZ [TRACON] as a point out. ZZZ [TRACON] accepting the point out. In all reality both facilities should be monitoring what Aircraft Y was doing. The original point out coordination was that Aircraft Y was going 6 miles west of the fix ZZZZZ. Once Aircraft Y passed 6 miles there were 2 possible controllers to notice and do something about it. ZZZ [TRACON] should have questioned ZZZ1 [TRACON] and myself reference Aircraft X, ZZZ1 [TRACON] should have reached out to Aircraft Y and ZZZ [TRACON]. Because no one did Aircraft Y was 15 miles west of ZZZZZ and crossing through the final of Runway XX at ZZZ.2. Take responsibility when you have accepted a point out by keeping an eye on the target as well as looking at your current traffic and what may be aconflict between the point out and current traffic. Do NOT lose track of your traffic and or point outs (which was the excuse of the ZZZ [TRACON] Controller). If you're busy do not accept the point out potentially causing yourself to 'lose track' of traffic.3. CARE! This job is not a game. There is not time to not care when human lives are at stake.For my side:1. I have re-played this 1000 times over in my head. I think maybe I could have called a traffic alert but what I can't see is what I would have suggested to Aircraft X. I called the traffic early and continued too, once he got it I felt like the pilot knew how to fly that plane better than me, and could see what Aircraft Y was doing better than me as well. If I had given him a suggestion based on how erratic Aircraft Y was I truly think it would have ended badly. The pilot's RA never went off, and speaking to the pilot he wasn't sure why but he said it probably had no idea what to do based on what that Aircraft Y was doing.2. Suggestion, call the pilot if able or the airport and question said pilot. Potentially file a deviation or ask what was going on.3.Stop the 'holes in the swiss cheese'. This was always my favorite CBI [Computer Based Instruction]. In order to not have the holes line up you have to be vigilant always. I try and will continue to try. Maybe I could have even been more vigilant today? Saw it coming earlier?4. Encourage pilots to file reports so this information can be turned into learning experiences.Thank you for reading some recommendations, and there are probably 100 more things that could be done. This event took a toll on myself the rest of my shift. Some things you just can't un-see, but for myself it makes me better and care even more for our pilots in the sky and their passengers.
ASRS:1794806.s: A TRACON controller lost track of an untagged VFR point-out aircraft while adjusting a mask, failing to coordinate with the Tower. The unmonitored aircraft made a sudden 180-degree turn, passing close to an inbound jet on final approach, though the pilot maintained visual separation and landed safely.

ASRS:1794827.n: We were cleared to FL 230. Passing through 17,500 feet, #1 engine rolled back to approximately 30%N1. The N1 and EGT had flashing red and yellow arcs and the lower section had a red flashing box around both engine indications. Our initial analysis was engine failure. We requested to level at FL 180, communicated to ATC our situation and requested vectors to return to ZZZ. Upon further analysis of the engine condition, the Captain (Pilot Flying) stated the engine was still running but noted the indications were not normal. We also saw the EEC in ALTN mode. Captain continued to fly and directed me into the QRH for the EEC ALT MODE checklist since the engine was running and not surging, stalling, or any indications dictating complete failure or the need to shutdown. We completed the QRH for the EEC ALT MODE according to our situation and indications. We discussed and agreed to also reference and ran the QRH [for] One Engine Inoperative Landing. I continued communications with ATC, while the Captain communicated with F/A's and made a PA to passengers. I computed [landing] data and set up the FMC. Captain flew the approach and landing, taxiing clear of the runway to a safe location. Autobrakes were used and no manual braking activated until slowed (approximately 50 knots) and prior to the exit of the runway. Based on our weight and configuration [calculations] prior to landing required the use of autobrakes and brake cooling calculations. I calculated the [landing data] for Non-Normal One engine Inop with 15 Flaps landing. Brake Cooling calculations returned a 58 minute cooling period, which we accomplished at the turnout abeam runway. Emergency Rescue Crews communicated to us no visible smoke from brakes and heat signature negative. After the 58 minute cool down, we were given clearance to taxi and proceeded to our gate. When we arrived at the gate, Maintenance was working on the #1 engine. The previous crew that had the aircraft had returned to the gate. When they started the number one engine they got the Engine Control light. Maintenance cleaned the cannon plugs did an engine run and returned the aircraft to service. Our engine start and initial climb were all normal. We were on radar vectors for our route and climbing through 17,500 feet or so when the #1 N1 Gauge flashed yellow twice. We both saw it, then the #1 engine rolled back to 31% on the N1 but the engine didn't quit. We leveled at FL 180 and requested vectors back to ZZZ. We ran the EEC ALT Mode Checklist and the Engine Failure or Shutdown Checklist from the QRH. Landed Flaps 15, autobrakes 3. We ran the brake cooling calculation prior to landing. We had a 58 minutes of break cooling.
ASRS:1794827.s: The crew experienced a #1 engine N1 rollback to 30% at 17,500 feet with EEC in ALTN mode, prompting a return to ZZZ. They completed relevant QRH checklists, landed safely with autobrakes, and maintenance resolved the issue by cleaning cannon plugs.

ASRS:1794835.n: I was in the pit when I loaded an electric scooter. I asked leads loading prior to closing out the flight if this electric scooter was scanned they had said yes. Operations checked the Departure Staging Guide (DSTG) and noticed that the scooter did not show up on the DSTG as a dangerous goods item. We realized that the wrong tag was used to tag the electric scooter.
ASRS:1794835.s: A ground handler in the pit loaded an electric scooter that was not flagged as dangerous goods on the Departure Staging Guide due to an incorrect tag. Operations discovered the error after the handler confirmed the item had been scanned prior to closing the flight.

ASRS:1794858.n: Flying a steeper than usual glide path to a runway with displaced threshold. During transition to visual I inadvertently descended below the glide slope to achieve a normal sight picture. Received a Ground Proximity Warning and Glide Slope. Too much focus outside the aircraft. We were over the touchdown zone and a normal landing was completed. Attention inside and outside the airplane during transition to landing flare. We were in the flare over the runway and received the 'Glideslope' EGPWS advisory immediately prior to touchdown. Aural Glideslope advisory while we were in the landing hover/flare. The First Officer hand flew the Visual Approach and maintained the Glideslope until we were approaching the threshold and he shifted his attention to the external environment. The Glideslope and PAPI (Precision Approach Path Indicator) for this runway may have been the cause when he transitioned to flying by outside reference and attempting to achieve a sight picture closer to our typical 3.00 degree glide path. We were over the touchdown zone and completed a very normal and uneventful landing.
ASRS:1794858.s: The First Officer hand-flew a visual approach to a runway with a displaced threshold and descended below the glide slope to achieve a normal sight picture. This triggered aural Glideslope and Ground Proximity warnings during the flare, but the crew completed a normal landing over the touchdown zone.

ASRS:1794877.n: Assigned to descend via. Inside ZZZZZ assigned 300 knots. Captain used the speed window to adjust speed. Approaching ZZZZZ1, realized he was crossing low. He attempted to correct but still crossed low by what I estimate to be 500-800 feet low. I looked and realized he did not use Speed Intervention but instead had used LVL Change. ATC did not query us about the error nor was there traffic in the area.Captain new to aircraft and seat with limited recency of experience confused speed/descent modes. FO (PM) limited recency of experience involved with approach programming and communications did not notice the error.For our part better announcement and verification of MCP changes. Better monitoring during busy descent.
ASRS:1794877.s: A new Captain and First Officer descended an aircraft via ZZZZZ, crossing ZZZZZ1 500–800 feet low due to the Captain selecting LVL Change instead of Speed Intervention. The error went unnoticed by the crew and ATC, attributed to limited recency and confusion over descent modes.

ASRS:1794879.n: I was PF from ZZZ-ZZZ1, during the climbout at 17,000 feet with the autopilot engaged we had just started to get some trace ice on the windshield wipers (probe heat and engine anti-ice on) when we got 'IAS DISAGREE' caution lights on both CA (Captain) and FO (First Officer) PFDs. No other alerts. We requested priority handling with ATC. We looked at the IAS disagree checklist in the Quick Reference Handbook which then told us to go to the 'AIRSPEED UNRELIABLE' checklist. I performed the initial Quick Reference Checklist procedures and then the CA read through the rest of the Quick Reference Handbook as I followed procedures and continued hand flying up to cruise altitude of 34,000 feet. We determined that the problem was on the FO side so once the checklists were complete and we were leveled off at cruise altitude, we swapped controls and the CA became PF since he had the accurate airspeed indication. 'IAS DISAGREE' flashed on and off frequently as the spread between CA and FO IAS +/- 10-15 kts and then it stayed on consistently for ~30 minutes during climb. Once we were at cruise and clear of icing and clouds then the 'IAS DISAGREE' indication went away and the FO IAS indicator appeared to work normally. We discussed with dispatch our possible diversion choices but all of them either involved going through a line of weather or re-encountering icing, we decided that the safest course of action was to continue on to ZZZ1 where the weather was VFR. Then as we started our VFR descent into ZZZ1, we got the 'IAS DISAGREE' indication flashing on and off again sporadically several times with no further issues associated and landed uneventfully.The logbook had showed that an inspection had been performed on pitot static system overnight in ZZZ. Icing conditions present during taxi and climb. ATC gave us everything we asked for. Captain said that crew phone to contact Dispatch was valuable. Recent MAX training definitely made our response simple and effective. We found out from the mechanics that met us at our gate that this aircraft had had multiple pitot/airspeed problems in the past. Aircraft was a MAX.I've heard now that we are the 2nd 737 (ours being a MAX, other being an NG) that has had 'Unreliable Airspeed' in the last week! Need to ground these aircraft until the source(s) of the problems are resolved.
ASRS:1794879.s: The crew of a Boeing 737 MAX experienced an 'IAS DISAGREE' caution during climb in icing conditions, likely due to a faulty First Officer pitot system. They followed unreliable airspeed checklists, swapped controls to the Captain, and landed safely after the indication cleared at cruise altitude.

ASRS:1794882.n: We were level 5,000 feet 250 knots approaching ZZZ VOR on the ZZZZZ2 Star. Approach gave a heading 280 and slow to 180 and asked if we had the field in sight. We were heading 330 and I was thinking a turn to 350 was coming so 280 heading caught me a little off guard. I (FO) was pilot flying. The sun was just above the horizon as I looked west and across the cockpit for the field. Simultaneously I was looking cross-cockpit and programing the speed and heading change into the FMC. I could make out the field so I said to the Captain (PM), 'I can see the field, you can call it in sight.' I noticed another aircraft on TCAS at our altitude on TCAS and then saw them visually less than ten miles away, also headed west toward ZZZ [Airport], I noted the paint scheme and relayed to the PM all that information and that they were probably headed to the north side of the airport. In my head I was thinking that our airplane was not slowing down as fast as I would like when the PM said 'where is that airplane, I think we need to turn.' I pushed the localizer button on the FMC but the airplane did not turn so I turned the autopilot off and manually turned to intercept final for [Runway] XXR. As I did, we received at TCAS TA then a few seconds later a TCAS RA to climb. The ADI showed a red boxed area from level flight down (I was descending) so I just leveled off until we heard 'clear of conflict.' Then Approach gave us a 180 heading, paused, and then said 'you guys can't do that;' and switched us to Tower. I was able to correct the high energy level of the airplane using gear, flaps, and speed brakes and continued the approach and landed uneventfully.Fast close to the airfield, sun in eyes, failure on my part to use automation.Something from ATC that I was going to turn towards the runway instead of downwind in the [Runway] XXR pattern or an advisory where we were in the sequence. My recency of experience led to not arming the localizer, while I did brief that at the start of the first leg I could have reemphasized it during the approach brief.
ASRS:1794882.s: The First Officer, flying a jet at 5,000 feet, manually turned to intercept final after failing to arm the localizer, triggering a TCAS RA climb. The pilot attributed the high-energy conflict to sun glare, automation errors, and recency of experience, but corrected speed and landed uneventfully.

ASRS:1794915.n: While on climb out shortly after the 10,000 foot checklist, I noticed our oil pressure was in the amber range. The Captain checked the left engine oil quantity on the MFD and it indicated 2 quarts. I started the Low Oil Pressure checklist which lead to the Precautionary Engine Shutdown checklist. We secured the engine, [advised ATC] and headed back ZZZ. I called Flight Attendant and told her what the situation was, made a PA, and we continued to land safely in ZZZ. I cannot answer this as I am not a mechanic and do not know why the engine lost oil. I feel like we took all appropriate actions in a timely manner. If this happens in the future, I would maybe try to slow down a bit and delay the flaps 22 extension to short final as we were heavy and airplane wouldn't hold altitude after we extended the gear down/flaps 22. We retracted the flaps back up to 9 to be able to hold altitude which worked well, and then re extended the flaps to 22 on short final. I think overall, we did what we were trained to do and the Captain even made a smooth landing. After landing, we taxied in and parked with no issues.
ASRS:1794915.s: During climb out, the crew secured the left engine after observing low oil pressure and quantity, then returned to ZZZ for a safe landing. The pilot noted that delaying flap extension to 22 helped maintain altitude due to the aircraft's heavy weight before re-extending flaps on short final.

ASRS:1794931.n: Arriving in gusty crosswind conditions. VMC. I was hand flying the ILS. At runway threshold, I inadvertently descended below the glide slope during transition to outside and received a glide slope warning. As we were in the flare over the runway landing was the safest option. [Identified by] GPWS warning, glide slope. Began transition to outside too early preoccupation with winds. Failed to continue cross checking indications. I heard the annunciation in the landing flare and completed a normal landing. The flight director indications guide the airplane to the touchdown zone use this information in combination with outside.
ASRS:1794931.s: The pilot hand-flew an ILS approach in gusty crosswinds and inadvertently descended below the glide slope at the threshold due to early transition to outside visual references and preoccupation with winds. A GPWS glide slope warning occurred during the flare, but the pilot completed a normal landing.

ASRS:1794991.n: Intended to land flaps 30 in windy conditions with add speed of 14 knots. Visual approach on Visual Approach Slope indicator and slightly below ILS glide slope. We received a Ground Proximity Warning alert for 'too low terrain'. Rechecked landing gear was down and landed. We realized on very short final that flaps were actually set to 25 instead of 30. We did not select flaps to 30 since we were so low. With the extra speed we had added for the gusty winds, I felt we were safer to leave them set at 25 and land. While on final approach we experienced a Ground Proximity Warning 'Too Low Terrain' aural warnings. Knowing that we were on glide slope and Precision Approach Path Indicator and the runway was in sight in VFR conditions, we decided to continue the landing. We ensured that the landing gear was down and that we were free of terrain, however, on short final the Captain noticed we were at flaps 25 instead of 30. It was decided to safely complete the landing since we were stable on speed and path. We already had built in a 14 knot wind additive for the windy conditions. The entire approach was stable including at the 500 foot 'Stable' call out point. I take responsibility for misreading the flap gauge, and will certainly give it more focus in the future. One potential factor, not an excuse, is there was the distraction of balloons going by our aircraft around the time of the landing checklist. I reported the balloons to Tampa Tower.
ASRS:1794991.s: The crew received a "Too Low Terrain" GPWS alert during a visual approach in windy conditions while intending flaps 30. They landed with flaps 25 after the Captain misread the gauge, attributing the error to a distraction from passing balloons.

ASRS:1795003.n: The taxiway centerline markings on ORD Taxiway K, K3 and A9 are worn off. The line is almost gone in a number of locations. At night using a 737 taxi light, it's very hard to see where you are going. This area is away from the large bright lights of the terminal, and is a mass of darkness with a lot of blue lights. It's even worse on a night when it is raining.
ASRS:1795003.s: A 737 pilot reported that worn centerline markings on ORD Taxiways K, K3, and A9 made navigation difficult at night, especially in rain. The lack of visible lines in the dark area, illuminated only by blue lights, obscured the taxi path.

ASRS:1795019.n: On the ZZZZZ X arrival into ZZZ, we were given a descent to FL230. As PF, I re-cruised for FL230. Prior to ZZZZZ1 we were told to descend via the arrival. I dialed in 6,000 feet for the Runway XXL approach. Initially the descent point was visible and looked normal. After flying several more minutes it became clear that we were past the descent point. It was about this time that the descent point disappeared from the ND. We started an immediate Open Descent with full speed brakes. We were unable to get relief from the altitude/airspeed requirement at ZZZZZ2 (250/110) due to radio congestion. We were given a frequency change and got relief from ZZZ Approach who gave us a descent to 6,000 feet which we accomplished. The rest of the approach and landing was uneventful. When the PF re-cruised he inadvertently typed in '320' instead of '230'. There was not an immediate erroneous depiction on the ND. Everything looked normal, however we continued past the descent point. Just as we realized there was something wrong, the ND descent point disappeared. The PF has been on reserve and has flown very little in the last two months. The next two flights went well with no problems.The two pilots were on the first leg of the trip. It was the first time they'd flow together. They were working well together and both were attempting to follow policies/procedures. This was a dumb mistake by one pilot that was not caught by the other. By re-cruising, the goal was to have the ND provide usable descent point information. I listed this as a 'Moderate' risk rating because we easily received relief from ATC. If they had not assisted us, the risk would have been higher.
ASRS:1795019.s: Two pilots on a ZZZZZ X arrival inadvertently re-cruised to FL320 instead of FL230 due to a data entry error by the PF, causing them to overshoot the descent point. They executed an immediate open descent and received ATC clearance to 6,000 feet, resulting in an uneventful landing.

ASRS:1795041.n: Advised by Dispatcher (name) that ZZZ had undeclared DG on the aircraft. Advised crew of position and contents. position XX, can [container number]. [Hazmat container] Can was loaded by ZZZ1 ramp and trucked to ZZZ. DG included 4 items.
ASRS:1795041.s: The dispatcher advised the crew that ZZZ had loaded undeclared dangerous goods in container XX at position XX. The four items were loaded by ZZZ1 ramp and trucked to ZZZ.

ASRS:1795100.n: After a local solo flight of 30 minutes and a full stop landing, I taxied back to the active runway with the intent of doing more traffic pattern work. I applied full power at the start of the takeoff and confirmed correct engine indications. Shortly after liftoff, 5 to 10 feet above the ground, I perceived what I judged was a loss in engine power and decided to perform a cautionary landing on the remaining runway. Upon landing, directional control of the aircraft was lost and contributed to a ground loop to the left of approximately 270 degrees. The aircraft departed the active runway and came to a stop in the transient parking area to the southeast side of the runway. I secured the fuel, ignition, and electrical systems and exited the aircraft. Minor damage was sustained during the ground loop to the right wheel/hubcap, and the right rear portion of the wingtip. A close inspection revealed no other damage and the propellor did not strike the ground. No immediate visual evidence of a malfunction was evident. The aircraft was secured in place and the FAA and NTSB were notified jointly via phone in the presence of the airport manager, who also took a report for airport records. A bystander notified local fire department authorities, who were dispatched, but they also observed no major damage, fluid, gas, or oil leakage that would cause a hazard to persons or property. No injuries were sustained by myself.
ASRS:1795100.s: A pilot performing a solo traffic pattern flight perceived an engine power loss shortly after liftoff and executed a cautionary landing, resulting in a ground loop that damaged the right wheel and wingtip. No mechanical malfunction was visually identified, and the pilot sustained no injuries.

ASRS:1795103.n: Private pilot, instrument student flying ZZZ direct to ZZZ1. Flew the RNAV Runway XX, circling approach to Runway XY for circling practice as well as winds were favorable to Runway XY. Before the Final approach Fix we performed our pre-landing checklist which included gear selector down. Gear selector switch came down at the Final approach fix, and showed 3 green lights indicating gear is down and locked. Student and instructor confirmed 3 green lights indicating gear down. Landing was very smooth, lightly touched down and began sliding. We were unaware that the gear was not down and locked. There was no impact or sparks. The plane remained on the runway, veered slightly to the left due to the left gear collapsing more than the right. I was with my instrument student who was flying ZZZ direct to ZZZ1. Upon completion of the descent checklist, we confirmed we would fly the RNAV XX approach and circle to land Runway XY as winds were favoring XY. Prior to the Final Approach Fix, we performed the pre-landing checklist. Upon arrival at the Final Approach Fix, the landing gear selector was set to the down position. Shortly after putting the gear down, both my student and I confirmed 3 green lights indicating the gear was down and locked. We later started our circle to Runway XY and performed the landing checklist and confirmed landing gear indicated down and locked. Shortly after flaring, the airplane touched down then we began sliding to the left of the runway. Once realizing the propeller stopped spinning and was bent, we promptly performed shutdown procedures and exited the aircraft. Upon exiting the aircraft, the right main was partially extended while the nose gear and left main appeared mostly collapsed. Neither myself nor my student experienced any injury.
ASRS:1795103.s: A private pilot and instrument student landed an aircraft on Runway XY after confirming three green gear lights during a circling approach. The nose and left main gear collapsed upon touchdown despite the indicators, causing the aircraft to slide left with no injuries.

ASRS:1795120.n: Was flying with a friend around the area. We departed and executed a 45 departure. After reaching 3 miles northwest of the airport (directly over coast) I turned southbound. I made a call on CTAF that Aircraft X was 3 miles northwest at 1,000 feet following the shore southbound. About 20 seconds after making that call I was looking out the left window and noticed an aircraft whiz from underneath and behind me and begin a turn inland. It is hard to judge the distance but he was way too close for comfort. Correcting an incident like this will only happen in 3 ways.1.Pilots use more time looking outside (I am sure he would've seen how close he was to me if he was paying attention).2.Radio usage especially in busy Class E surface like that of Astoria.3.Require the use of ADS-B in all controlled airspace. I had my ADSB on. This aircraft was not on ADSB and was not making calls. Further, he proceeded to preform touch and goes at Astoria without making a single call.
ASRS:1795120.s: A pilot flying a 45 departure near Astoria reported a near-midair collision with an uncommunicating aircraft that passed underneath and behind at 1,000 feet. The reporter attributed the incident to the other pilot's failure to scan visually, use the radio, or operate ADS-B equipment.

ASRS:1795121.n: I was pilot monitoring. We were given a clearance to maintain 250 knots until advised. Upon reaching 10,000 feet we accelerated to 290 knots (our normal profile). I advised the Captain that we were given a 250 knot clearance...we discussed and I probed the Controller and confirmed we were given a 250 knot speed restriction until 14,000 feet. We began to slow down. I believe the cause of this is the fact that we have not been flying a lot because of COVID. I had been furloughed and brought back to the line and retrained. I believe if I had been flying more often than I would have been able to catch this lapse earlier or could have reminded the Captain once we reached 10,000 feet.
ASRS:1795121.s: The pilot monitoring and captain exceeded a 250-knot clearance until 14,000 feet by accelerating to 290 knots at 10,000 feet. The pilot attributed this speed violation to a lapse in vigilance caused by reduced flight time and retraining following a furlough.

ASRS:1795155.n: Departed FNL airport to stay in the pattern during uncontrolled operations of Class Echo Airspace XA:00. Operations for Tower begin at XB:00.Reported Visibility ASOS was 1SM. Actual visibility on ground and in air was 10+ due to having a clear view of the entire mountain range, which is a given for visibility. One landing in the pattern was performed, 10+ miles visibility and clear of clouds. The Tower opened and reported that the ATIS was reporting 3/4 SM VIS, however multiple aircraft in the pattern gave a PIREP of 10+ visibility. Tower refused our PIREP, asked if we wanted to request SVFR, however if the reported visibility was under 1 SM they could not grant this. We still asked for SVFR since visibility was clear and clear of clouds. Upon asking Tower for SVFR, he said no, asked if we had visual with the runway, which of course we did, and cleared us to land number 2 behind another aircraft ahead of us in the pattern. We landed and terminated the flight. I have previously flown VFR into FNL Airport when the fires were lowering visibility. The METAR and ATIS were reporting 1/4 mile visibility making it IFR, however having full visibility in the aircraft, I called Tower before entering their airspace and asked if the reported visibility was correct. They said no, the RVR is not reliable, visibility was greater than 6SM and to proceed inbound for VFR landing.
ASRS:1795155.s: A pilot operating VFR in the pattern at FNL Airport reported 10+ mile visibility while ATIS indicated 3/4 SM. Despite the pilot's PIREP and request for SVFR, the Tower refused the request but cleared the aircraft to land behind another after confirming visual contact with the runway.

ASRS:1795166.n: Returning to 7B3 (Hampton Airfield) late at night, turned on the runway lights, and landed in-between them. However, the lights border the grass runway rather than the asphalt runway that I meant to land on. As a result, I landed on the grass runway, when I expected to land on asphalt. This was potentially dangerous, if the grass runway was blocked with snow (it was not, fortunately). The grass runway was not operational at the time (NOTAM to that effect).No adverse effect happened, but it was not ideal.It's not clear that in order to land on the asphalt, I'd have to land OUTSIDE the two sets of runway lights which border the turf runway. Adding a third row of runway lights (on the other side of the asphalt runway) would make it much clearer for a night landing.
ASRS:1795166.s: A pilot landing at night at Hampton Airfield (7B3) mistakenly landed on a closed grass runway instead of the intended asphalt runway due to confusing runway light placement. The pilot reported no adverse effects but recommended adding a third row of lights to clarify the asphalt runway boundaries.
